# BIB121 — Introduction to Hermeneutics

## Course objectives

- 1. Explain the need for hermeneutical principles to guide interpretation.
- 2. Summarize the qualifications, tools, and goals of a biblical interpreter.
- 3. Identify key issues in the history of hermeneutics.
- 4. Analyze the historical and literary contexts of a given passage of Scripture.
- 5. Analyze word meanings and relationships in a given biblical passage.
- 6. Contrast figurative and literal language, and the keys for interpreting each.
- 7. Distinguish between biblical genres, and the principles for interpreting them.
- 8. Summarize the relationship between the Old and New Covenants and God’s kingdom.
- 9. Value and identify timeless, cross-cultural principles based on a passage of Scripture.
- 10. Discuss the role of the Holy Spirit in interpreting, using, and applying Scripture.

## 1 - Introduction to Hermeneutics

### The Definition of and Need for Hermeneutics

#### 1.1.1 — Define hermeneutics.

A Big Word for a Big Task

Welcome to this study. Hermeneutics comes from the Greek word hermeneuo that means “to interpret , translate, or explain” (Gingrich 1975, 84). Hermeneuo is related to Hermes. In ancient times, the Greeks thought Hermes was a messenger of their gods. His job was to deliver and interpret divine messages.

Hermeneutics is the study of principles for interpreting the Bible. In this course, we will study two types of principles. First , we will study general principles (Chapters 3–6). These apply to the entire Bible. Second , we will study principles for specific genres (Chapters 7–12). For example, there are specific principles for poetry and specific principles for prophecy. The table of contents gives more details on these principles.

Four Reasons to Study Hermeneutics

1. To Learn Principles for Interpreting Scripture

Principles help us in many areas of life, such as driving. Because drivers have rules or principles, they drive on the correct side of the road. They do not pass on hills, because others might be coming. They go slowly in crowded areas. They park beside the road, not in traffic!

When drivers do not follow the proper principles, accidents happen. People get hurt. Imagine the problems we would have if there were no principles for drivers. We would have chaos on our roads.

Just as we need principles for drivers, we need principles to interpret Scripture. Believers must practice the proper principles for interpreting the Bible. Otherwise, accidents happen—people get hurt.

In the introduction to this chapter, we mentioned some problems that occur when people interpret Scripture in any way they desire. Today, some believers continue to interpret the Bible in ways that seem right in their own eyes. They ignore the basic principles of hermeneutics. Then, there is chaos.

• One says we can eat pork; another says we cannot.

• One says to worship on Sunday; another says we must worship on Saturday.

• One says to call the elders to pray when we are sick; another says we should never admit we are sick.

• One says believers should pray in tongues today; another says tongues ceased when the Bible was completed.

• One says Jesus is divine; another says Jesus was only human.

• One says Mary never sinned; another says all have sinned.

These examples show what happens when each person interprets the Bible in his or her own way (Gibbs 1994, 16). Chaos! Therefore, we need principles to guide us as we interpret the Bible.

2. To Develop Skills for Answering Difficult Questions

Philip asked the Ethiopian, “‘Do you understand what you are reading?’ The Ethiopian replied, ‘How can I, unless someone explains it to me?’” (Acts 8:30–31). The principles in this course will guide us in understanding what we read in the Bible. By the end of this book you should be able to answer hard questions like these:

• The Holy Spirit teaches us all things. We do not need anyone to teach us (1 John 2:27). So why do we need teachers?

• Jesus did not come to bring peace on earth, but a sword (Matthew 10:34). So why did the angels sing “and on earth peace to men on whom his favor rests” (Luke 2:14)?

• Whoever sacrifices a bull is like one who kills a man (Isaiah 66:3). So is it wrong to kill a bull?

• Is it right to use a little wine because of stomach problems (1 Timothy 5:23)?

• Are all of Abraham’s blessings ours (Galatians 3:14)?

• Paul said, “For I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out. For what I do is not the good I want to do; no, the evil I do not want to do—this I keep on doing” (Romans 7:18–19)? Are believers slaves of sin?

• Jesus said, “Do not take along any gold or silver or copper in your belts; take no bag for the journey, or extra tunic, or sandals or a staff.” (Matthew 10:9–10). Is it wrong to travel with money and a suitcase? Should we travel barefooted?

We will learn to answer these and other hard questions in this course.

3. To Correctly Handle the Word of Truth

Have you ever been misquoted? Perhaps you spoke to someone about a personal matter. Then, that person falsely “interpreted” what you said, and told it to another person. The result was that someone blamed you for something you never said.

The people of Jesus’ day used His words to accuse Him. But they did not interpret His words correctly. They accused Him of planning to destroy Herod’s temple and of rebuilding it in three days (Mark 14:58). They did not discern that Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body. So we see that it was the interpreters who erred, not Jesus. God’s Word is always true, but we must be careful to interpret it correctly. Otherwise, we may base our beliefs on the instability of human interpretation rather than the rock of God’s Word.

A rumor circulated that Thomas Harris—author of I’m Okay, You’re Okay— had killed himself. A well-known Bible teacher believed this rumor, and used it in one of his messages. He said that Harris’s death by suicide proved that Harris’s book was false. But the rumor was not true—Thomas Harris was still alive. As a result, Harris sued the Bible teacher, who had to pay a large sum of money for slander (Baron 1987, 64). This sad story illustrates a great truth. It is not enough to be sincere in what we believe—we must believe the truth.

Many people are sincere, but wrong. They are seldom in doubt, but seldom right. Many refer to Scripture, and think they are doing God’s will. But being sincere is not enough, as this passage reveals:

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only he who does the will of my Father in heaven. Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and in your name drive out demons and perform many miracles?’ Then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you. Away from me, you evildoers!’” (Matthew 7:21–23)

The people described in that passage seem to be sincere. But somewhere along the way they got off the right path. God’s Word is true, and His promises are sure. But we must use God’s Word for the purpose He intended. “So is my word that goes out from my mouth: It will not return to me empty, but will accomplish what I desire and achieve the purpose for which I sent it” (Isaiah 55:11). God did not promise to bless His Word for every purpose that we would want to use it.

Satan is bold. He even tried to get Jesus to use God’s Word for the wrong purpose. The devil reminded Jesus that God promised to send angels to protect us (Psalm 91). So the deceiver urged Jesus to jump off the temple (Matthew 4:6). Jesus, of course, withstood him, quoting Deuteronomy 6:16. God did not send the promise of Psalm 91:11–12 to allow His people to test Him. Satan did not interpret God’s Word correctly, so Jesus rebuked him.

Today, Satan continues to twist the Scriptures. He leads false teachers to interpret the Bible in ways that lead people to destruction.

• The Spirit clearly says that in later times some will abandon the faith and follow deceiving spirits and things taught by demons (1 Timothy 4:1).

• But there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the sovereign Lord who bought them—bringing swift destruction on themselves. Many will follow their shameful ways and will bring the way of truth into disrepute (2 Peter 2:1–2).

• He writes the same way in all his letters, speaking in them of these matters. His letters contain some things that are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction (2 Peter 3:16).

We do not want to twist the Scriptures or follow those who interpret them falsely. Rather, we want to correctly handle the Word of Truth (2 Timothy 2:15). We must interpret the Bible in ways that match God’s purposes. This is the reason we study hermeneutics—to use God’s Word for His purposes. Then we can be sure that we are standing on the promises—not tripping on them.

4. To Relate Biblical Times to Our Times

Consider these great gaps between Scripture and us.

1. The time gap: Almost two thousand years are between any book of the New Testament and us. We are therefore interpreting a book that was written about two millennia ago. Thus, we need principles to guide us.

2. The culture gap: The people of the Bible had different values, traditions, customs, and practices than we do. Old Testament writers wrote in Hebrew from right to left. Sometimes they worshiped in temples and synagogues, washed feet, greeted each other with a kiss, or sacrificed animals. They ate different food than ours and lived by different rules. We need principles to interpret what God said to them.

3. The language gap: The people of the Bible spoke Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek—so the Bible was written in these languages. There is always a need for principles as we translate languages.

4. The historical gap: Each book of the Bible was written at a specific time in history. Sometimes God spoke to slaves, to masters, to warriors, or prisoners. He sent His Word to Jews and to Gentiles. Principles will guide us to understand the historical settings of the first readers.

**Q:** Why do we need principles to interpret the Bible?

**A:** Believers must practice the proper principles for interpreting the Bible, if not we can be harmed by a misinterpretation. Hermeneutics teaches 1. Principles to guide us in interpreting Scripture. 2. Skills to answer difficult questions. 3. Us to stand on God’s Word, not stumble on it. 4. Us to cross over the gaps between biblical times and our times.

**Q:** In quoting a person, why is it important to give the proper meaning to his or her words? Explain.

**A:** The misquoted person could be blamed for something he or she never said.

**Q:** How did the people of Jesus’ day twist what He said about the temple?

**A:** The Jews used the words of Jesus to accuse Him. But they did not interpret His words correctly. They accused Him of planning to destroy Herod’s temple and of rebuilding it in three days (Mark 14:58). They did not discern that Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body.

### The Qualifications of a Biblical Interpreter

#### 1.2.1 — Explain six qualifications of a biblical interpreter.

In this lesson, we will examine six qualities a person needs to interpret the Bible correctly:

1. Accept the Bible as the inspired Word of God.

2. Be born again.

3. Depend on the Holy Spirit.

4. Obey what you understand.

5. Have an open mind and a teachable spirit.

6. Study to be approved by God.

Accepting the Bible as the Inspired Word of God

Definition of Inspiration

We believe that God gave the Bible to us through a process called inspiration . The word inspire means “to breathe into.” The Scriptures are inspired—God breathed Scripture into the biblical writers. “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:16).

Inspiration is the process God used to breathe His message into the original writers and carry them along by the Holy Spirit, so that they wrote what He wanted, free from error. “Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture came about by the prophet’s own interpretation. For prophecy never had its origin in the will of humans, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:20–21). Various things happened before a person wrote Scripture.

Scripture

Explanation of how the Spirit led a biblical writer

a ) Exodus 17:14

b ) Jeremiah 30:1–2

c ) Ecclesiastes 12:9–10

d ) Luke 1:1–4

e ) Revelation 1:9–11

We have looked at the basic meaning of inspiration. Still, people use the word inspiration in many ways. So let us examine six words that explain the nature and level of inspiration in the Bible.

Verbal

The Scriptures are verbally inspired in the original writings called autographs . This means that God inspired every word in the Old and New Testaments. He allowed the writers to choose the words, but He guided them to choose words He approved. In contrast to verbal inspiration, some people believe that God only inspired the thoughts, not the words of Scripture. Yet Matthew 5:18 illustrates that God watches over the smallest parts of Scripture: “I tell you the truth, until heaven and earth disappear, not the smallest letter, not the least stroke of a pen, will by any means disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished.”

Plenary

We believe in the plenary inspiration of Scriptures. The word plenary comes from a Latin word meaning “full or complete . ” We say our needs are met fully or completely when we have plenty . When we speak of plenary inspiration, we mean that the entire Bible is fully inspired. Some people falsely say that the Bible contains the Word of God, but we believe the Bible is the Word of God. Others who do not believe in verbal plenary inspiration wrongly say that only verses about salvation are inspired. Others believe there are levels of inspiration. These say verses in the genealogy of the first chapter of Matthew are less inspired than the words of Christ. For sure, the teachings of Christ affect our lives more than His family tree affects us. But those who believe in plenary inspiration believe that “All Scripture is God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16).

Revelation

Through Scripture, God reveals himself to us. Imagine how little we would know about God without the Bible. Nature, signs, wonders, and divine acts show us something about God. But people can come to many different beliefs by just looking at nature, miracles, and events. In contrast, the Bible clearly reveals God: His person, character, will, deeds, demands, and decrees. Through the Scriptures, God gives us the revelation of himself and teaches us how to relate to Him.

For in the gospel a righteousness from God is revealed, a righteousness that is by faith from first to last, just as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.” (Romans 1:17).

This is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words. (1 Corinthians 2:13).

Infallible

The Bible is infallible — it cannot fail. This means Scripture cannot be wrong about faith and morals. God’s Word cannot deceive, mislead, or disappoint us (Menzies and Horton 1993, 27).

The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul. The statutes of the Lord are trustworthy, making wise the simple. The precepts of the Lord are right, giving joy to the heart. The commands of the Lord are radiant, giving light to the eyes. The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever. The ordinances of the Lord are sure and altogether righteous. (Psalm 19:7–9)

Some have falsely taught that the biblical authors reflected the morals of their day, not God’s timeless standards. For example, some false teachers say that homosexuality was wrong in biblical times, but it is not wrong today. It is true that biblical customs change, and the Bible may use customs to illustrate the truth. But the Bible’s moral standards—its teachings about what is right and wrong—remain the same from generation to generation (Gibbs 1994, 43). Scripture is breathed by God, and God “cannot lie” (Titus 1:1–2, KJV).

Inerrant

The Bible is infallible on matters of doctrine and morals; and it is inerrant (without error) on matters of history and science.

Some people claim that the Bible contains mistakes because they do not discern its figurative language. For example, the Bible often refers to the sun rising and setting (Ecclesiastes 1:5). Although the sun does not rise, from a human point of view, we describe the dawn as sunrise. The Bible is written—not as a science book—but a revelation of God that people can understand.

Dr. Stanley Horton once heard a Harvard University professor say that the Bible contained a mistake. He said that sevenfold lamps did not exist in the days of Moses (Exodus 37:17–24). Later, those digging at Dothan found a sevenfold lamp from approximately 1400 BC. This find demonstrated that the professor, not the Bible, was in error (Menzies and Horton 1993, 27). “Every word of God is flawless; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him” (Proverbs 30:5).

Authoritative

The Bible is the highest authority on religious matters. Some wrongly place the church on the same level as the Bible. This leads to many types of errors, such as declaring that Mary had no sin. Others say human reason has the same authority or more authority than the Bible. As humans, we make many mistakes in our thinking. Our knowledge is not complete: “Now we see but a poor reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). We are thankful for our God-given human minds and how they help us, but we trust in the Word of God as the highest authority. It guides us in our beliefs, thoughts, and actions.

We believe that all Scriptures are

• Inspired by God in a verbal, plenary way;

• The revelation of God to us;

• Infallible and inerrant and;

• The authority over our faith and living.

Discerning between the Inspired Record and the Words of People

Pentecostals agree that the Bible is the inspired, infallible, inerrant Word of God. Still, an approved worker “correctly handles the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). This is true because the Bible records not only the words of God, apostles, and angels, but also the words of Satan, heretics, and demons. God has seen fit to record in the Bible human successes and failures and human revelations and lies. The biblical authors were inspired to record many things because God wanted us to know what was said. Peter vowed, “Even if all fall away on account of you, I never will” (Matthew 26:33). Is this statement inspired? Yes and no! Yes, it is a part of what the Holy Spirit inspired Matthew to write, so we could learn from Peter’s mistake. So, from a historical point of view Matthew 26:33 is inspired. It is true that Peter said it. But Peter himself was not inspired to say it! What he said was a lie based on too much self-confidence. Jesus tried to help Peter by telling him he was wrong. But Peter was blinded by his own pride. So we can say that the record of Peter’s statement in Matthew 26:33 is inspired, but the statement itself is false.

The biblical record is always inspired. But remember, especially when conversations are recorded, you must discern whether or not a speaker’s statements are inspired. We do not base any doctrine on the words of Satan or demons. Neither do we accept as truthful the statements of sinful people like Ananias and Sapphira, the rich young ruler, lying prophets, and enemies of the Cross. It is often obvious in the Bible when someone is not inspired. For example, we know that Peter was not inspired when he rebuked the Lord and told him that He would never be crucified (Matthew 16:22). “Jesus turned and said to Peter, ‘Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me; you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men’” (Matthew 16:23).

Being Born Again as a Qualification for Interpreting

Jesus declared, “I tell you the truth, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again” (John 3:3). God’s Spirit enters a person at the new birth. At that time, a person is in the Kingdom—under God’s rule. Also, God’s Spirit within a person enables spiritual understanding.

The wisest teacher on earth, without the Spirit, may be blind to spiritual truth. But children with the Spirit may understand the Bible, “At that time Jesus said, ‘I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was your good pleasure’” (Matthew 11:25–26).

Those without the Spirit may understand basic things about the Bible, such as facts, places, events, and some teachings. But no one can fully grasp the deep truths of God’s Word without the Spirit within. In the final chapter of this course, we will study more about the Spirit’s role in interpreting Scripture.

Depending on the Holy Spirit

King David recognized that he needed God to help him understand the Scriptures. He prayed, “Open my eyes that I may see wonderful things in your law” (Psalm 119:18).

Jesus taught that the Holy Spirit would lead us into truth:

“But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all truth. He will not speak on his own; he will speak only what he hears, and he will tell you what is yet to come. He will bring glory to me by taking from what is mine and making it known to you. All that belongs to the Father is mine. That is why I said the Spirit will take from what is mine and make it known to you.” (John 16:13–15)

Therefore, we must depend on the Holy Spirit as we seek to interpret the Scriptures. In contrast to this attitude, liberal theologians like Rudolph Bultmann trust in themselves. Bultmann writes, “The interpretation of biblical writings is not subject to conditions different than those that apply to all other types of literature” (Braten 1964, 154). We strongly disagree with Bultmann. There are ways in which we study the Bible as we would study other books. We will discuss this later in this lesson. But we must study the Bible like no other book because, unlike all other literature, the Bible is inspired by God. So unlike those who trust in themselves alone, we humbly confess our need for the Holy Spirit to guide us.

Scripture is the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17). We must have His help to handle the Bible correctly. So we pray as we seek to interpret, so that we do not grieve the Spirit within us (Ephesians 4:30). And we ask Him for illumination — for light and insight. In response to our prayers, humble attitude, and hard work, the Spirit helps guide us to understand and apply God’s Word.

Obeying What Is Understood

Obedience precedes mature spiritual understanding. Jesus said: “If anyone chooses to do God’s will [obeys] , he will find out [know]” (John 7:17). As we obey, God adds to our understanding. As the eye of the needle follows the point, understanding follows obedience.

We will examine two principles related to obedience and interpreting Scripture.

The Understanding of the Disobedient will Decrease

Read Romans 1:18–25. Because these people disobeyed God, they understood less and less truth.

The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men who suppress the truth by their wickedness, since what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them . . . For although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks to him, but their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened. Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools . . . Therefore God gave them over in the sinful desires of their hearts to sexual impurity for the degrading of their bodies with one another. They exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served created things rather than the Creator—who is forever praised. Amen. (Romans 1:18–19, 21–22, and 24–25)

Many members of cults today were once in Bible-believing churches. They cannot discern truth today because they refused to obey. To interpret the Bible well, we must obey what we know.

The Understanding of the Obedient will Increase

Notice that the Magi understood more and more.

After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod, Magi from the east came to Jerusalem and asked, “Where is the one who has been born king of the Jews? We saw his star in the east and have come to worship him.” When King Herod heard this he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. When he had called together all the people’s chief priests and teachers of the law, he asked them where the Christ was to be born. “In Bethlehem in Judea,” they replied, “for this is what the prophet has written.” (Matthew 2:1–5)

At first the Magi knew little. A new king had been born, but they did not know where. Yet they traveled in the starlight God gave them. Riding a camel night after night was physically exhausting, but they were faithful. They followed God’s leading to the new king. Dim starlight led to the full light of knowing Jesus. In contrast, the Scribes never recognized the Messiah. Their knowledge was becoming less and less. Hence, God takes away from those who disobey, but adds to those who obey. He subtracts from the negligent, and adds to the diligent.

David was a man who loved God’s Word. He showed his love through obedience. Therefore, a great blessing came upon him, “Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long. Your commands make me wiser than my enemies, for they are ever with me. I have more insight than all my teachers, for I meditate on your statutes. I have more understanding than the elders, for I obey your precepts. I have kept my feet from every evil path so that I might obey your word” (Psalm 119:97–101). Obedience affects what people discern: “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining ever brighter till the full light of day. But the way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know what makes them stumble” (Proverbs 4:18–19).

An Open Mind and a Teachable Spirit

No one understands less than those who do not want to learn. So it is necessary to listen with an open heart. “Then Jesus said, ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear’” (Mark 4:9). The Phillips translation says, “‘Every man who has ears should use them.’” Note that Revelation 2–3 repeats this thought seven times. Likewise, James says we should be “quick to listen”—and that means to listen with an open mind (James 1:19).

In contrast, the Pharisees did not learn much from Jesus because they did not want to learn from Him. Their minds were closed. They heard John the Baptist, but did not repent. They saw blind people healed in the temple, but did not see themselves. They saw Jesus raise Lazarus from the dead, but did not follow Christ. They had ears, but they hardly heard (Matthew 13:15).

But not all Pharisees were close-minded. Nicodemus wanted to learn new truth, so he asked Jesus questions and listened with all of his heart. Having an open mind is a key to understanding the Bible. Like Mary, let us sit at the feet of Jesus to learn (Luke 10:38–42). And like the Bereans, let us search the Scriptures to see what is true (Acts 17:11).

Studying to Be Approved by God

“Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a workman who does not need to be ashamed and who correctly handles the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). Christians should depend on the Holy Spirit to help interpret the Bible. This does not make study useless–it makes study fruitful (Radmacher, 3). God feeds the birds, but the birds work hard to get that food (Sterett 1974, 17).

The English word “Bible” comes from the Latin word biblia , meaning “book.” The Bible is a book. Interpreting the Bible requires all the skills needed to study any other book. In 1 Corinthians 10:15, Paul says, “I speak to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.” He tells his readers to use their minds. The following verses emphasize that spiritual insights require mental work.

Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked or stand in the way of sinners or sit in the seat of mockers. But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he meditates day and night. (Psalm 1:1–2)

“Do not be afraid, Daniel. Since the first day that you set your mind to gain understanding and to humble yourself before your God, your words were heard, and I have come in response to them.” (Daniel 10:12)

One man considers one day more sacred than another; another man considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. (Romans 14:5)

Reflect on what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all this. (2 Timothy 2:7)

Therefore, prepare your minds for action. (1 Peter 1:13)

In studying the Bible, there are several tools to use. We will examine these tools in the next lesson.

**Q:** Fill in the adjacent chart.

**A:** a) The Lord said to Moses to write the account of the battle on a scroll. b) The word came to Jeremiah directly from the Lord to write in a book the words that the Lord had spoken to him. c) The Teacher pondered and searched out and set in order many proverbs. He searched to find the right words; he wrote what was upright and true. d) He carefully investigated everything from the beginning and he wrote an orderly account. e) He was in the Spirit, and he heard a loud voice telling him to write what he saw.

**Q:** Did God inspire the words of Scripture or just the thoughts? Explain.

**A:** God inspired every word in the Old and New Testaments. He allowed the writers to choose the words, but He guided them to choose words He approved. In contrast to verbal inspiration, some people believe that God only inspired the thoughts, not the words of Scripture.

**Q:** What does verbal plenary inspiration mean?

**A:** Full or complete

**Q:** In what sense is Scripture a revelation?

**A:** The Bible clearly reveals God: His person, character, will, deeds, demands, and decrees. Through the Scriptures, God gives us the revelation of himself and teaches us how to relate to Him.

**Q:** Underline seven words in Psalm 19:7–9 that show the Bible is infallible.

**A:** “The law of the Lord is ­­perfect , reviving the soul. The statutes of the Lord are trustworthy , making wise the simple. The precepts of the Lord are right , giving joy to the heart. The commands of the Lord are radiant, giving light to the eyes. The fear of the Lord is pure , enduring forever . The ordinances of the Lord are sure and altogether righteous ” (Psalm 19:7–9).

**Q:** In Matthew 26:33, who was inspired: Matthew, Peter, or both? Explain.

**A:** It is a part of what the Holy Spirit inspired Matthew to write, so we could learn from Peter’s mistake. So, from a historical point of view, Matthew 26:33 is inspired. It is true that Peter said it, but Peter himself was not inspired to say it! What he said was a lie based on too much self-confidence. Jesus tried to help Peter by telling him he was wrong. But Peter was blinded by his own pride. So we can say that the record of Peter’s statement in Matthew 26:33 is inspired, but the statement itself is false.

**Q:** Can a person without the Spirit understand anything about the Bible? Explain.

**A:** Those without the Spirit may understand basic things about the Bible, such as facts, places, events, and some teachings. But no one can fully grasp the deep truths of God’s Word without the Spirit within. In the final chapter of this course, we will study more about the Spirit’s role in interpreting Scripture.

**Q:** Why did God allow some to trade the truth for a lie (Romans 1:21–25)?

**A:** Because these people disobeyed God, they understood less and less truth. “For although they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks to him, but their thinking became futile and their foolish hearts were darkened. Although they claimed to be wise, they became fools . . . Therefore God gave them over in the sinful desires.”

**Q:** Why did David have more understanding than others (Psalm 119:101)?

**A:** He was a man who loved God’s Word. He showed his love through obedience. Therefore, a great blessing came upon him.

**Q:** Contrast the understanding of the obedient and disobedient (Proverbs 4:18–19).

**A:** “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining ever brighter till the full light of day. But the way of the wicked is like deep darkness; they do not know what makes them stumble” (Proverbs 4:18–19). So, obedience affects what people discern.

### The Tools of a Biblical Interpreter

#### 1.3.1 — Summarize the value of each of these: study Bibles, translations, concordances, Bible dictionaries, and commentaries.

The most valuable tools of Bible study are those God has given to us:

• The ability to read

• A mind to think, reflect, and meditate

• The Holy Spirit to help us

So always begin by praying and seeking to understand the Bible yourself. Reading what someone else says before you study is like asking others to carry you. Learn to walk on your own. Depend on others to help you up the steepest places or over the biggest rocks. But there is no joy like discovering truths directly from the Lord as you study your Bible. Reap the blessings of your own, personal study first. Afterward, use the five types of tools we will examine in this lesson.

The Benefits of Study Bibles

In recent times, believers have been blessed by a variety of study Bibles. The authors of this book prefer the Life in the Spirit Study Bible and the Fire Bible . Keep in mind that every study Bible is written from some point of view. The Life in the Spirit Study Bible is from a Pentecostal perspective. Likewise, The NIV Study Bible often emphasizes a Calvinist viewpoint (Hebrews 3:14; 6:4–6). It is often silent on key verses that emphasize the responsibility of the believer in salvation (Hebrews 1:9; 10:14). There are several benefits of having a study Bible:

• A study Bible contains an introduction for each book of the Bible. This includes facts about the author, the first readers, the theme, the outline, the background, the purpose, a survey of the book, and special features.

• A study Bible contains full color maps, and also many black and white maps.

• A study Bible contains charts. For example, it has charts of the patriarchs, judges, kings, and prophets. It has charts on journeys, feasts, ethics, and such.

• A study Bible contains subheadings, references in the margins, and a concordance.

• The Life in the Spirit Study Bible contains over eighty articles on key topics such as the kingdom of God, the Holy Spirit, the will of God, faith and grace, parents and children, divine healing, power over demons, and end times.

• A study Bible contains explanations for all weights and measures.

• A study Bible contains comments on key verses. (Remember to read these after you have studied a verse.)

It is our prayer that every pastor and teacher will have a copy of the Life in the Spirit Study Bible . In many ways, it is like a Bible school in a book!

Translations and Paraphrases

Remember that the Old Testament was first written mostly in Hebrew and the New Testament mostly in Greek. We believe that the original writers of the Bible were inspired—carried along by the Holy Spirit. But we do not claim that translations are inspired, even though many are very good. Comparing translations helps us understand the exact thoughts of the biblical writers. Almost everyone has a favorite translation, such as the King James Version (KJV), New International Version (NIV), New American Standard Bible (NASB), and so on.

Every translation has its strengths and weaknesses:

• The King James Version is written in beautiful, older-style English. Some people find its verses easier to memorize because it is so different. But it is written on a twelfth-grade reading level and is often hard to understand.

• The New International Version is written on level eight, using more modern English. It is easier to understand, but it does not strictly translate many phrases. For example, when the Hebrew text says “Lord of hosts,” the NIV says “Lord Almighty” ( NIV Study Bible 1984, xii). When the Greek text says “a little,” the NIV says “a bite” (John 6:7). When the Greek texts says “truly, truly,” the NIV says “I tell you the truth” (John 6:26). And when the Greek text says “flesh” (Greek: sarx ), the NIV says “sinful nature.”

• In contrast, the New American Standard Bible is a very strict translation, but is a little harder to read. This translation puts subheadings at the top of the page.

• Paraphrases, such as The Living Bible , Good News for Modern Man , The New Testament in Modern English ( J. B. Phillips ), and The Message , do not translate the original authors. Still, they often make the meaning of verses clearer by trying to state the main thoughts in a modern way. Please note that The Living Translation and J. B. Phillips Translation are translations, not paraphrases.

Every believer should compare two or three versions of the Bible when studying. “Many advisers make victory sure” (Proverbs 11:14). “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (2 Corinthians 13:1). Likewise, using two or three Bible versions helps us understand God’s Word more clearly.

Concordances

A concordance is an alphabetical listing of all the words used within the Bible. The entry for each word gives the Scripture references where the word occurs. Some concordances are more complete than others. Exhaustive concordances list every appearance of every word in the Bible. Many Bibles have an abridged concordance in their back pages. A concordance is most helpful when you want to find out where a word is used in the Bible, or how many times it occurs. But remember that biblical writers use the same words in different ways. For example, Luke emphasizes that the Holy Spirit gives us power to serve—to witness to the lost and help believers. John emphasizes that the Spirit enables us to serve, but also that the Spirit convicts of sin. Paul emphasizes the Spirit’s role in service, salvation, and living a life of victory over sin and the world (Wood and McGhee 2001, 39–40). So although a concordance is helpful, recall that writers use the same words in different ways.

Large, complete concordances like Young’s Analytical Concordance to the Bible and Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance of the Bible list the times each word of the Bible occurs. Also, these tools will enable you to study the Greek and Hebrew words of the original. For example, look up the word hope in Young’s concordance. You will see that as a noun, “hope” is a translation of ten different words. And as a verb, “hope” is the translation of at least six different words. Using a concordance will help you discern the many different ways a word is used. For more advanced students, there are Greek and Hebrew lexicons that give more help in understanding word usage.

Bible Dictionaries and Encyclopedias

All people know their mother tongue—the language they speak at home. Some people know two or more languages, but none of us knows any language perfectly. Dictionaries and encyclopedias help us understand words better. These books explain different ways a word is used. They often list synonyms—words that mean the same thing, or antonyms—words that mean the opposite. For example, one dictionary lists six different meanings of faith and gives belief as a synonym (Landau 1974, 228). A common dictionary gives the meanings of words as they are used today. In contrast, a Bible dictionary helps us understand how words were used in biblical times. So for some words, it is better to use a Bible dictionary. A concordance gives some facts about word meanings and the places in the Bible where a word occurs. A Bible dictionary or encyclopedia gives an author’s research and opinions on subjects like the Trinity, the Second Coming, and such. A Bible dictionary may have several paragraphs or pages about one word. For example, if you look up the word Pharisee, the dictionary uses a complete page to summarize the Pharisee’s history, relation to other parties, and teachings.

In using a Bible dictionary, discern that, like a translation, or a study Bible, it is written from someone’s point of view. For example:

• Look up the word covenant in The New Bible Dictionary. This article by J. Murray emphasizes the Calvinist point of view—that God does everything and humans do nothing. It will state that a covenant is never an agreement between two parties or groups (Douglas 1978, 264–265).

• In contrast, look up the word covenant in Baker’s Dictionary of Theology. This article by Gleason Archer, Jr., states that a covenant is “an agreement between two parties, binding them together, and giving responsibilities to each” (Harrison 1975, 142–143). Thus, Archer emphasizes an Arminian view—that salvation is by grace, but we use our free will to accept or reject the covenant God offers us.

A Bible dictionary or encyclopedia, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, is one of the most helpful tools an interpreter can have.

Commentaries, Textbooks, and Other Believers

Commentaries

A commentary gives an author’s opinion on each verse in a biblical book. For example, a commentary on Luke will give the background of the book and then discuss the meaning of each verse in Luke’s Gospel. Commentaries vary in length and purpose. There are commentaries on just one book of the Bible, and there are sets of commentaries that cover the entire Bible. Matthew Henry produced a one-book commentary on the whole Bible. It is devotional, though Calvinistic. John Wesley’s two-book commentary: Wesley’s Notes on the New Testament is a favorite of the authors of this course. It is less devotional, and focuses more on the meaning of each verse. The New International Commentary on the New Testament is a helpful set, as is the Tyndale commentary set. For the Old Testament, Keil and Delitzcsh is technical, but thorough.

Textbooks

Textbooks, like the one you are reading, or What the Bible is All About by Henrietta Mears, have helped many understand the Scriptures. Also, the Bible student should not overlook the help of other believers, such as teachers and friends. A commentary or textbook contains only the printed words of a person. Spoken words can be just as helpful as words in a book.

Using tools

We have examined five helpful tools for interpreting Scripture. Buy these tools as your budget allows, and use them to help you understand God’s Word. Remember that tools do not replace the need for the personal study you should do first. Nothing replaces the need for prayer and depending on the Holy Spirit.

**Q:** When should a Christian use other books to help interpret the Bible?

**A:** Begin by praying and seeking to understand the Bible yourself. Depend on others to help you up the steepest places, or over the biggest rocks. But there is no joy like discovering truths directly from the Lord as you study your Bible. Reap the blessings of your own, personal study first. Afterward, use the five types of tools examined in this lesson.

**Q:** What are at least five benefits of having a good study Bible?

**A:** A study Bible contains 1. An introduction for each book of the Bible. 2. Full color maps, and also many black and white maps. 3. Charts. 4. Subheadings, references in the margins, and a concordance. 5. Over eighty articles on key topics. 6. Explanations for all weights and measures. 7. Comments on key verses.

**Q:** What are some strengths and weaknesses of the NIV?

**A:** Every translation has strengths and weaknesses. The NIV is written on level eight in modern English. It is easier to understand, but it does not strictly translate many phrases. For example, when the Hebrew text says “Lord of hosts,” the NIV says “Lord Almighty” (NIV Study Bible 1984, xii). When the Greek text says “a little,” the NIV says “a bite” (John 6:7). When the Greek texts says “truly, truly,” the NIV says “I tell you the truth” (John 6:26). And when the Greek text says “flesh” (Greek: sarx ), the NIV says “sinful nature.”

**Q:** Are all Bible dictionaries written from the same point of view? Explain.

**A:** A Bible dictionary, like a translation, or a study Bible, is written from someone’s point of view. For example: the definition for covenant in The New Bible Dictionary emphasizes the Calvinist point of view—that God does everything and humans do nothing. It will state that a covenant is never an agreement between two parties or groups. In contrast, the word covenant in Baker’s Dictionary of Theology states that a covenant is an agreement between two parties, binding them together, and giving responsibilities to each. Thus, Archer emphasizes an Armenian view—that salvation is by grace, but we use our free will to accept or reject the covenant God offers us.

**Q:** How is a commentary different from a Bible dictionary?

**A:** A commentary gives an author’s opinion on each verse in a biblical book. For example, a commentary on Luke will give the background of the book, and then discuss the meaning of each verse in Luke’s Gospel. Commentaries vary in length and purpose. There are commentaries on just one book of the Bible, and there are sets of commentaries that cover the entire Bible. Some are more devotional in nature than others and some focus more on the meaning of each verse.

### The Goals of a Biblical Interpreter

#### 1.4.1 — Explain the first goal of interpreting Scripture.

We have studied the qualifications and tools of a biblical interpreter. But it is not enough to be qualified and have the right tools. A biblical interpreter must always fulfill the two goals we will study in this lesson.

The First Goal of Interpreting Scripture

“What did the author mean?” Answering this question is the first and most important task of hermeneutics. Imagine that a rich person died and left a will. He had decreed that all of his wealth would go to one person. When the will was read, many people were present. All claimed that the will named them as the heir. But the most important thing to determine was what the writer of the will had intended. So it is with interpreting Scripture. Our task is to discover what the author meant—not to twist the Scriptures to say what we want them to mean.

Two Greek words contrast the wrong and right ways of using the Bible: eisegesis and exegesis . These two Greek words begin with eis (into) and ex (out of), and are joined to a Greek verb that means “to lead.”

• Eisegesis is reading into the Bible what you want it to say. Eisegesis starts with the thoughts of humans and ends with the words of humans.

• Exegesis is reading out of a biblical text what the author meant. Exegesis starts with the Word of God and brings out its meaning.

People often use eisegesis to support their beliefs. They already believe something and want to use the Bible to justify it. For example, one young man who wanted to excuse his sin quoted the verse, “You are not under law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14). He missed the true meaning of the verse by ignoring its context. The next verse says, “Shall we sin because we are not under the law, but under grace? By no means!” (Romans 6:15). Thus, the young man practiced eisegesis—he pushed what he believed into some words he found in the Bible (Gibbs 1994, 21).

Exegesis is finding the one, single meaning of a text—the meaning the author intended. In the next chapter, we will look at the darkness in church history that has come when Christians tried to look for more than one meaning of a verse. For now, we are emphasizing the first goal of interpreting Scripture: find the one meaning that the author intended. Discover what the text meant to the first readers. Let the text speak for itself. Allow it to say all that it has to say, and only what it has to say.

The Second Goal of Interpreting Scripture

Although a passage of Scripture has only one meaning, it may contain more than one principle and have many applications. Also, there are many ways to preach one passage.

We will examine 2 Corinthians 2:5–11 in light of relationships between the author’s one meaning, some principles, and some applications.

If anyone has caused grief, he has not so much grieved me as he has grieved all of you, to some extent—not to put it too severely. The punishment inflicted on him by the majority is sufficient for him. Now instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. I urge you, therefore, to reaffirm your love for him. The reason I wrote you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything. If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And what I have forgiven—if there was anything to forgive—I have forgiven in the sight of Christ for your sake, in order that Satan might not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes. (2 Corinthians 2:5–11)

Note that the principles are true in every culture of the world and in every generation of the church. (We will teach you how to identify these principles in Chapter 14 of this course). Unlike principles, applications may vary from place to place and time to time. Applications link principles to personal, daily living.

The meaning, principles, and application of 2 Corinthians 2:5–11

Author’s One Meaning––>

(Interpretation/Explanation)

Principles–––>

Applications

Paul wrote to the Corinthians earlier, about discipline for a sinner in the church (1 Corinthians 5:1–12). Later, Paul asked the church to restore the sinful man who had repented (2 Corinthians 2:5–11).

1. Believers who sin bring grief to the church.

2. Believers who sin may be restored through church discipline.

3. Believers who repent must be loved and restored, or Satan may capture them.

Do you know those who have brought grief to the church?

How does your church know if a person truly repents?

Do you personally forgive those who sin against you but repent?

Does your church forgive and love those who repent?

Do you know a person who was disciplined and restored?

Does your church help those who are wounded in spiritual battle?

As you can see, there is only one meaning of 2 Corinthians 2:5–11. But there are many principles related to it and many more applications. Sometimes it is hard to understand the meaning of a verse. The intent of this course is to teach you principles that will help you discover the author’s meaning.

Type

Statement

a.

A member who commits sexual sin must be removed from the church and restored only after repentance is proven.

b.

The pastor has the right to take away the salvation of any member who sins.

c.

The sinning believer in the Corinthian church had to be expelled (1 Corinthians 5:1–12).

d. Principle

A church should not allow a sinning member to fellowship with those in the church.

e.

The main purpose of church discipline is to restore a believer who goes astray.

Interpretation—an explanation of the author’s meaning

Principle—a statement (based on Scripture) that is true in all cultures and in all ages

Application—an act of relating a principle to a person or local situation

In the next chapter we will see some sad examples of what has happened in church history when believers did not look for the author’s meaning. In Chapters 14–15, we will give you practice stating principles and making applications.

**Q:** What is the most important question of hermeneutics?

**A:** “What did the author mean?”

**Q:** Explain the difference in eisegesis and exegesis .

**A:** Two Greek words contrast the wrong and right ways of using the Bible: eisegesis and exegesis (www.crosswalk.com). These two Greek words begin with eis (“into”) and ex (“out of”) and are joined to a Greek verb that means “to lead.” Eisegesis is reading into the Bible what you want it to say. Eisegesis starts with the thoughts of humans and ends with the words of humans. Exegesis is reading out of a biblical text what the author meant. Exegesis starts with the Word of God and brings out its meaning.

I urge you, therefore, to reaffirm your love for him. The reason I wrote you was to see if you would stand the test and be obedient in everything. If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him. And what I have forgiven—if there was anything to forgive—I have forgiven in the sight of Christ for your sake, in order that Satan might not outwit us. For we are not unaware of his schemes. (2 Corinthians 2:5–11)

Note that the principles are true in every culture of the world and in every generation of the church. (We will teach you how to identify these principles in Chapter 14 of this course). Unlike principles, applications may vary from place to place and time to time. Applications link principles to personal, daily living.

The meaning, principles, and application of 2 Corinthians 2:5–11

Author’s One Meaning––>

(Interpretation/Explanation)

Principles–––>

Applications

Paul wrote to the Corinthians earlier, about discipline for a sinner in the church (1 Corinthians 5:1–12). Later, Paul asked the church to restore the sinful man who had repented (2 Corinthians 2:5–11).

1. Believers who sin bring grief to the church.

2. Believers who sin may be restored through church discipline.

3. Believers who repent must be loved and restored, or Satan may capture them.

Do you know those who have brought grief to the church?

How does your church know if a person truly repents?

Do you personally forgive those who sin against you but repent?

Does your church forgive and love those who repent?

Do you know a person who was disciplined and restored?

Does your church help those who are wounded in spiritual battle?

As you can see, there is only one meaning of 2 Corinthians 2:5–11. But there are many principles related to it and many more applications. Sometimes it is hard to understand the meaning of a verse. The intent of this course is to teach you principles that will help you discover the author’s meaning.

Statement

In the next chapter we will see some sad examples of what has happened in church history when believers did not look for the author’s meaning. In Chapters 14–15, we will give you practice stating principles and making applications.

**Q:** What is the most important question of hermeneutics?

**A:** “What did the author mean?”

**Q:** Explain the difference in eisegesis and exegesis .

**A:** Two Greek words contrast the wrong and right ways of using the Bible: eisegesis and exegesis (www.crosswalk.com). These two Greek words begin with eis (“into”) and ex (“out of”) and are joined to a Greek verb that means “to lead.” Eisegesis is reading into the Bible what you want it to say. Eisegesis starts with the thoughts of humans and ends with the words of humans. Exegesis is reading out of a biblical text what the author meant. Exegesis starts with the Word of God and brings out its meaning.

## 2 - Past and Present Methods of Interpreting Scripture

### Jewish Interpreters, the Apostles, and Church Fathers (200 BC–AD 600)

#### 2.1.1 — Contrast the way the schools of Alexandria and Antioch interpreted Scripture.

Jewish Interpreters

The interpreting of Scripture has a long history. The first interpreters the Bible introduces were the Levites who helped Ezra. This introduction comes after Ezra led the second group back to Jerusalem from Babylon (457 BC). The people no longer spoke Hebrew, the language in which the Scriptures had been written. Because of the seventy years of captivity, they spoke Aramaic, the language of Babylon. Therefore, when Ezra had the Scriptures read aloud to the people, these Levites had to interpret (Nehemiah 8:7–8). It is likely that the Levites interpreted and explained the Scriptures. So this is said to be the beginning of the Targum —a translation and interpretation of the Old Testament by Jewish rabbis.

About 300 BC the Jewish nation fell under the cultural and religious influence of the Greeks. The Greek word for a Greek person is Hellene ; thus, Greek ideas are called Hellenistic ideas. In 168 BC, this Hellenistic influence changed under Antiochus IV, a Greek-Syrian ruler. He attempted to destroy the Jewish religion. This persecution forced the Jews to clarify and protect their beliefs. Thus, persecution renewed their study of Scripture and caused them to develop new methods of hermeneutics.

Persecution led to three different methods of studying Scripture. Each one was centered in a geographic area. These methods of interpretation provide us with a background to the ways that the New Testament writers used to interpret the Old Testament.

Rabbinic Judaism is a branch of Judaism led by Jewish rabbis (teachers), centered in Jerusalem and Judea. It emphasizes obeying the Scriptures, especially the Torah, the five books of Moses. The Rabbis taught the Jewish people to cling to their faith, as they faced great pressure from Greek and Roman cultures. The teachings of the Rabbis were collected into several forms.

Scriptures—>Halakah and Haggadah—>Mishnah (teachings)——>Talmuds (Commentaries on the Mishnah)

The early Jewish rabbis produced two types of teachings: the Halakah and the Haggadah . Halakah means “of a legal nature.” The Halakah dictated religious laws for every part of life, including rituals, family life, personal life, and relationships with the government and non-Jews. These Halakah rules were based on laws of the Old Testament.

Haggadah used stories and proverbs of the Old Testament to explain Scripture and edify readers. For example, the Jews told the story of the Passover (Exodus 13) as they celebrated it. Haggadah was a powerful form of Jewish interpretation.

The Mishnah (“to repeat”) contains the teachings of leading rabbis, such as Hillel and Shammai. These two rabbis lived at the same time, but often disagreed on the interpretation of Scriptures. Hillel was moderate, while Shammai was strict. Hillel drew up a list of seven rules to interpret Scripture. These rules were the basis for more rules in the second century. Other rabbis added more rules, and many of these rules are still used by modern interpreters. Barnard Ramm, a modern teacher of hermeneutics, lists six of the rules from Jewish rabbis. Take a close look at these six rules the Jews used to interpret Scripture:

1. A word must be understood in the way it is used in its sentence, and a sentence must be understood within its context.

2. Scriptures on similar topics should be compared. If necessary, a third Scripture could explain the conflict between two Scriptures.

3. A clear passage is preferred over a difficult passage on the same subject.

4. Pay close attention to spelling, grammar, and figures of speech.

5. We can determine to apply Scripture to problems in life that Scripture has not mentioned.

6. The God of Israel had spoken in the tongues of men—revealing himself to them (Ramm 1970, 46–47).

The Talmuds were another form of Jewish teachings. A Talmud was a commentary on an earlier commentary—the Mishnah. There was one Talmud in Palestine* and another one in Babylon.

The Midrash was another form of Jewish commentary on Scripture. The word Midrash means (“to search”). These teachings were an attempt to discover the deeper meanings of the Scriptures. The rabbis believed that these deeper meanings were hidden in the words of the Bible. This method ignored the context of the Scriptures and emphasized the details of the passages. Rabbis used this method as they searched for ways to apply the Scriptures to the problems of their day. The rabbis became experts in stretching the law—oral and written—to cover all possible cases people brought them.

The Alexandrian School (Hellenistic Judaism)

This Greek school of interpretation was in Egypt, where Greek influence was strong. In Egypt, Greek replaced Hebrew as the language of the Jews. Some Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, so that Grecian Jews could read them. This Greek version of the Old Testament is called the Septuagint —the seventy—because it was the work of seventy scholars.

Egypt was influenced by Plato, a Greek philosopher who lived from 427 to 347 BC. He taught that objects on earth were copies of eternal things and that ideas were more real than either the physical or spiritual. Under the influence of Platonic tradition, the school in Alexandria used the method of allegory to interpret Scripture. Philo was the main Jewish teacher who developed this allegorical method. His goal was to reconcile Greek philosophy with the teaching of the Old Testament. We will study the allegorical method later in this chapter. For now, keep in mind that the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture erroneously adds to the Word of God. It gives meanings to details that neither God nor the biblical writers intended. For example, Augustine liked to use the allegorical method. When he taught on the parable of the Good Samaritan, he said that the Samaritan’s donkey represented the flesh of Jesus (Fee and Stuart 1982, 124). This type of interpretation misses the meaning of Scripture and leads people astray.

Why did Philo use the method of allegory to interpret Scripture? He was trying to build a bridge between Judaism and the Greek world. Why? Because in Alexandria, unbelievers were attacking the Bible. They were saying that the Scriptures were immoral and untrue. For example, the unbelievers did not like the story about the drunkenness of Noah, the account of Jacob’s wives and concubines, Tamar’s seduction of Judah, and the teachings about clean and unclean animals. So Philo began to teach that these stories had hidden meanings. We can understand that Philo was trying to lead people outside the church to the truth. But by using the method of allegory to interpret Scripture—looking for hidden meanings behind plain verses—he led scores of people away from the truth for over a thousand years.

Sometimes it is helpful to build a bridge between the church and the world. This is good if people in the world repent, cross the bridge, and come into the church. But the danger is that people in the church will cross the bridge and be lost in the world. Overall, the allegorical method brought much harm to the church. Because of this fleshly method of interpreting Scripture, much of the true meaning of God’s Word was lost for many centuries. When people use the allegorical method, they substitute the imaginations of humans for the thoughts of God.

The Apostles (AD 30–95)

The apostles interpreted the Old Testament writings in four ways:

1. Fulfilled messianic prophesies

2. Typology

3. The literal method

4. Principle/application

Fulfilled Messianic Prophesies

When the apostles wrote, they quoted the Old Testament to support their teachings—especially teachings about Christ. Under the New Covenant, they looked back at the Old Testament in a new way. The apostles discerned that Jesus was the Messiah who fulfilled the prophecies of the Old Testament. Thus, knowing who Jesus was guided them to interpret the Old Testament.

Jesus himself taught the apostles that the Old Testament prophesied about Him. In the synagogue in Galilee, He quoted Isaiah 61:1–2, “‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me’” (compare Mark 1:15 and Luke 4:18–21). Thus, He taught the disciples how to interpret the Old Testament in the light of His coming to earth. Another example of this is in Luke 7:21–23. This passage records the doubts of John the Baptist. In prison, John was not sure that Jesus was the Messiah. Jesus reminded John that He, the Messiah, was healing the blind, the lame, and the deaf. Thus, Isaiah 35:5–6 was being fulfilled in Jesus. We see, then, that Jesus taught His disciples to interpret the Old Testament Christologically —in reference to Christ. They discerned that Jesus fulfilled many Old Testament prophecies about the Messiah.

Typology

The apostles saw many Old Testament events, ideas, objects, and people as types—patterns or symbols of something future. These types demonstrated that the New Testament fulfilled what the Old Testament pointed to. For example, Jeremiah wrote about the mourning that would come when Babylon conquered Israel six centuries before Christ, “This is what the Lord says: ‘A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because her children are no more’” (Jeremiah 31:15).

Rachel was the ideal mother of Israel, having given birth to Joseph and Benjamin. The Spirit led Matthew to see the loss of these children as a type (Matthew 2:17). As Israel mourned the loss of her children to Babylon, Israel also mourned the loss of her children to Herod. History repeated itself in connection with Jesus, the Messiah.

The Literal Method

In this case, the apostles interpreted a verse by its normal, plain meaning. Jesus taught the disciples how to interpret Scripture in this straightforward way. For example: “‘It is written,’” he said to them, “‘My house will be called a house of prayer,’ but you are making it a ‘den of robbers’” (Matthew 21:13).

Following the example of Jesus, the apostles often quoted Scripture, interpreting it literally. The apostle Peter uses the literal meaning of Isaiah 40:6, 8: “For, ‘All men are like grass, and all their glory is like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord stands forever.’ And this is the word that was preached to you” (1 Peter 1:24–25).

Paul engaged the literal meaning of Scripture when he used Psalm 32:1–2. “‘Blessed are they whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him’” (Romans 4:7–8).

Principle/Application

Jesus taught His disciples to summarize the truth of a story or event by stating a principle. For example, in Mark 2:23–28, the Pharisees accused the disciples of picking grain on the Sabbath. However, the priests in the temple work on the Sabbath and are not guilty. Then Jesus stated the principle based on these events: The Sabbath is made for people, not people for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

Likewise, the Spirit led the apostles to state principles based on Scripture. For example, Paul referred to Deuteronomy 25:4: “When an ox is working in the grain, do not cover its mouth to keep it from eating” (New Century Version). In 1 Corinthians 9:9–11 and 1 Timothy 5:18, the principle Paul mined from this is that ministers who labor should reap benefits from their work (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 31). In this chapter, we will guide you to recognize, value, and learn to state biblical principles.

Sometimes in the literal method, a principle is already stated in a verse, such as Genesis 15:6. But in this final method, a person must analyze a verse, story, or event and then state the principle based on it.

The Church Fathers (AD 100–600)

This period is from the death of John until the time of Pope Gregory the Great (AD 604). During this time, the canon of the New Testament was established. The New Testament was the foundation for church doctrines. This whole period was characterized by debates about the Trinity and the person of Christ. Two great streams of Christianity came from this period:

1. Greek Orthodox —greatly influenced by revised teachings of Plato and mysticism

2. Latin or Western Christianity —shaped mostly by Roman legal thinking

In the beginning of this period, interpreters studied the literal meaning of Scripture. But allegory gained influence and became the main method of interpretation for at least a thousand years. Finally, it was rejected in the Reformation , when the Church returned to basic biblical doctrines.

Apostolic Fathers—Church Leaders Just After the Apostles (AD 100–150)

Clement of Rome was the best known of the early church fathers . He said the Old Testament contained types that neither Jesus nor the Apostles mentioned. For example, Clement taught from the story of Rahab. He said that the red cord she hung outside her window showed that the blood of Christ would redeem all.

Ignatius, a bishop of Antioch, saw Christ as the center of Scripture. In his writings, he warned of a future time when believers would be martyrs. He warned against heresy and emphasized faithfulness to Christ. Ignatius often referred to both the Old and New Testaments. He avoided allegorizing and interpreted the Bible in a literal way.

Alexandria Versus Antioch (AD 150–400)

There were two centers of interpretation during these 250 years: Alexandria and Antioch. They shared the same beliefs, but differed in their methods of interpreting the Bible.

The School of Alexandria in Egypt

Clement of Alexandria had great influence on the method of interpretation there. Like Philo, he sought to build a bridge between the church and the world. Recall that Plato and Philo taught that earthly objects were types of spiritual things. Clement taught that Plato’s best ideas had also been Moses’ ideas. He tried to show the Greek world that Christianity fulfilled Greek philosophy and the Old Testament. Clement taught that Scripture had two meanings: literal and spiritual.

Origen was another scholar in Alexandria. He knew the Hebrew language well. Origen taught that the text of Scripture often hid eternal truths. Thus, he used the method of allegory to interpret the Bible. He looked for hidden keys to Christian living. Origen taught that each text had three levels of meaning: body, soul, and spirit.

Characters

(Literally: “their sin happened”)

Israel, who rebelled

Athanasius was also of the Alexandrian school. He was an important person at the Council of Nicea . There, he defended the divinity of Christ against the teaching of Arius . He did not interpret the Scripture in a literal way, but used allegory to apply the Bible.

The extreme allegorical method—seeking a hidden meaning in most every verse—caused a reaction. Some church leaders started a new school in Antioch, Syria, about AD 350–400.

The School of Antioch in Syria

This school rejected allegory as a method of interpreting Scripture. They taught the historical-grammatical method: that each verse has one meaning—based on its words and grammar. This is the method we teach in this course. The historical-grammatical method teaches us to pay attention to history and grammar. For example, if we want to interpret a verse in Corinthians, we should pay attention to the history of the Corinthians. We should know who they were and what problems Paul wrote to solve. Likewise, to interpret a verse in Corinthians, such as 1 Corinthians 13:1, we should pay attention to the grammar—the way words are used in the text, and the way the text relates to its context. It helps us to discern that 1 Corinthians 13 is about love in relation to using spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:14). Otherwise, if we do not pay attention to the history of the Corinthians and the way words are used in each verse, we cannot interpret the verse correctly.

Eusebius (pronounced U-SEE-be-us) of Caesarea was one of the leading teachers in Antioch. He lived from AD 263 to AD 340 and was a pioneer of the studies of the gospels. For example, he divided them into passages common to all four. He was much more interested in the historical details of the Scripture than the teachers in Alexandria.

Theodore of Mopsuestia was the best-known teacher in Antioch. He agreed that there were some types in the Old Testament, but not as many as the school at Alexandria claimed. For example, he did not accept the traditional view that the Song of Solomon was a type of Christ’s love for the church. Rather, he taught that this book was about a celebration of one of Solomon’s marriages. (After his death, he was condemned for Nestorianism).

John Chrysostom was another teacher in Antioch (AD 347–407). A number of his sermons still exist. These show that the school at Antioch sought the one meaning of a text. Then, preachers like Chrysostom applied the text to the lives of their people.

The school in Alexandria taught that it was good to allegorize the Bible; the school at Antioch sought the one meaning of a text. Augustine was greatly influenced by this thinking. He believed we must reason from the literal sense of Scripture. But allegory was his main method. For example, in Psalm 3:5 the psalmist writes about lying down, sleeping, and rising. Augustine taught that this referred to the death and resurrection of Christ. Sadly, allegorizing took over as the method of interpreting Scripture and continued for one thousand years.

Since allegory was so popular as the method of interpreting Scripture, it is good to summarize it.

• In a positive sense, it taught that the Bible is a spiritual book, not just a historical book. Rather, God’s Word is alive and applies to the life of each Christian.

• However, on the negative side, allegory divorced the biblical text from its history. Allegory encouraged interpretations based on the imagination of each person. This opened the door for such errors as saying that Mary was born of a virgin and the Pope was on an authoritative level with Scripture.

To avoid heresies, it is critical that pastors preach the Word (2 Timothy. 4:2), not their own imaginations.
