For now, keep in mind that the allegorical method of interpreting Scripture erroneously adds to the Word of God. It gives meanings to details that neither God nor the biblical writers intended. For example, Augustine liked to use the allegorical method. When he taught on the parable of the Good Samaritan, he said that the Samaritan’s donkey represented the flesh of Jesus (Fee and Stuart 1982, 124). This type of interpretation misses the meaning of Scripture and leads people astray.

Why did Philo use the method of allegory to interpret Scripture? He was trying to build a bridge between Judaism and the Greek world. Why? Because in Alexandria, unbelievers were attacking the Bible. They were saying that the Scriptures were immoral and untrue. For example, the unbelievers did not like the story about the drunkenness of Noah, the account of Jacob’s wives and concubines, Tamar’s seduction of Judah, and the teachings about clean and unclean animals. So Philo began to teach that these stories had hidden meanings. We can understand that Philo was trying to lead people outside the church to the truth. But by using the method of allegory to interpret Scripture—looking for hidden meanings behind plain verses—he led scores of people away from the truth for over a thousand years.

Sometimes it is helpful to build a bridge between the church and the world. This is good if people in the world repent, cross the bridge, and come into the church. But the danger is that people in the church will cross the bridge and be lost in the world. Overall, the allegorical method brought much harm to the church. Because of this fleshly method of interpreting Scripture, much of the true meaning of God’s Word was lost for many centuries. When people use the allegorical method, they substitute the imaginations of humans for the thoughts of God.

The Apostles (AD 30–95)

The apostles interpreted the Old Testament writings in four ways:

1. Fulfilled messianic prophesies

2. Typology

3. The literal method

4. Principle/application

Fulfilled Messianic Prophesies

When the apostles wrote, they quoted the Old Testament to support their teachings—especially teachings about Christ. Under the New Covenant, they looked back at the Old Testament in a new way. The apostles discerned that Jesus was the Messiah who fulfilled the prophecies of the Old Testament. Thus, knowing who Jesus was guided them to interpret the Old Testament.

Jesus himself taught the apostles that the Old Testament prophesied about Him. In the synagogue in Galilee, He quoted Isaiah 61:1–2, “‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me’” (compare Mark 1:15 and Luke 4:18–21). Thus, He taught the disciples how to interpret the Old Testament in the light of His coming to earth. Another example of this is in Luke 7:21–23. This passage records the doubts of John the Baptist. In prison, John was not sure that Jesus was the Messiah. Jesus reminded John that He, the Messiah, was healing the blind, the lame, and the deaf. Thus, Isaiah 35:5–6 was being fulfilled in Jesus. We see, then, that Jesus taught His disciples to interpret the Old Testament Christologically —in reference to Christ. They discerned that Jesus fulfilled many Old Testament prophecies about the Messiah.

Typology

The apostles saw many Old Testament events, ideas, objects, and people as types—patterns or symbols of something future. These types demonstrated that the New Testament fulfilled what the Old Testament pointed to. For example, Jeremiah wrote about the mourning that would come when Babylon conquered Israel six centuries before Christ, “This is what the Lord says: ‘A voice is heard in Ramah, mourning and great weeping, Rachel weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, because her children are no more’” (Jeremiah 31:15).

Rachel was the ideal mother of Israel, having given birth to Joseph and Benjamin. The Spirit led Matthew to see the loss of these children as a type (Matthew 2:17). As Israel mourned the loss of her children to Babylon, Israel also mourned the loss of her children to Herod. History repeated itself in connection with Jesus, the Messiah.

The Literal Method

In this case, the apostles interpreted a verse by its normal, plain meaning. Jesus taught the disciples how to interpret Scripture in this straightforward way. For example: “‘It is written,’” he said to them, “‘My house will be called a house of prayer,’ but you are making it a ‘den of robbers’” (Matthew 21:13).

Following the example of Jesus, the apostles often quoted Scripture, interpreting it literally. The apostle Peter uses the literal meaning of Isaiah 40:6, 8: “For, ‘All men are like grass, and all their glory is like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord stands forever.’ And this is the word that was preached to you” (1 Peter 1:24–25).

Paul engaged the literal meaning of Scripture when he used Psalm 32:1–2. “‘Blessed are they whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him’” (Romans 4:7–8).

Principle/Application

Jesus taught His disciples to summarize the truth of a story or event by stating a principle. For example, in Mark 2:23–28, the Pharisees accused the disciples of picking grain on the Sabbath. However, the priests in the temple work on the Sabbath and are not guilty. Then Jesus stated the principle based on these events: The Sabbath is made for people, not people for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

Likewise, the Spirit led the apostles to state principles based on Scripture. For example, Paul referred to Deuteronomy 25:4: “When an ox is working in the grain, do not cover its mouth to keep it from eating” (New Century Version). In 1 Corinthians 9:9–11 and 1 Timothy 5:18, the principle Paul mined from this is that ministers who labor should reap benefits from their work (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 31). In this chapter, we will guide you to recognize, value, and learn to state biblical principles.

Sometimes in the literal method, a principle is already stated in a verse, such as Genesis 15:6. But in this final method, a person must analyze a verse, story, or event and then state the principle based on it.

The Church Fathers (AD 100–600)

This period is from the death of John until the time of Pope Gregory the Great (AD 604). During this time, the canon of the New Testament was established. The New Testament was the foundation for church doctrines. This whole period was characterized by debates about the Trinity and the person of Christ. Two great streams of Christianity came from this period:

1. Greek Orthodox —greatly influenced by revised teachings of Plato and mysticism

2. Latin or Western Christianity —shaped mostly by Roman legal thinking

In the beginning of this period, interpreters studied the literal meaning of Scripture. But allegory gained influence and became the main method of interpretation for at least a thousand years. Finally, it was rejected in the Reformation , when the Church returned to basic biblical doctrines.

Apostolic Fathers—Church Leaders Just After the Apostles (AD 100–150)

Clement of Rome was the best known of the early church fathers . He said the Old Testament contained types that neither Jesus nor the Apostles mentioned. For example, Clement taught from the story of Rahab. He said that the red cord she hung outside her window showed that the blood of Christ would redeem all.

Ignatius, a bishop of Antioch, saw Christ as the center of Scripture. In his writings, he warned of a future time when believers would be martyrs. He warned against heresy and emphasized faithfulness to Christ. Ignatius often referred to both the Old and New Testaments. He avoided allegorizing and interpreted the Bible in a literal way.

Alexandria Versus Antioch (AD 150–400)

There were two centers of interpretation during these 250 years: Alexandria and Antioch. They shared the same beliefs, but differed in their methods of interpreting the Bible.

The School of Alexandria in Egypt

Clement of Alexandria had great influence on the method of interpretation there. Like Philo, he sought to build a bridge between the church and the world. Recall that Plato and Philo taught that earthly objects were types of spiritual things. Clement taught that Plato’s best ideas had also been Moses’ ideas. He tried to show the Greek world that Christianity fulfilled Greek philosophy and the Old Testament. Clement taught that Scripture had two meanings: literal and spiritual.

Origen was another scholar in Alexandria. He knew the Hebrew language well. Origen taught that the text of Scripture often hid eternal truths. Thus, he used the method of allegory to interpret the Bible. He looked for hidden keys to Christian living. Origen taught that each text had three levels of meaning: body, soul, and spirit.

Athanasius was also of the Alexandrian school. He was an important person at the Council of Nicea . There, he defended the divinity of Christ against the teaching of Arius . He did not interpret the Scripture in a literal way, but used allegory to apply the Bible.

The extreme allegorical method—seeking a hidden meaning in most every verse—caused a reaction. Some church leaders started a new school in Antioch, Syria, about AD 350–400.

The School of Antioch in Syria

This school rejected allegory as a method of interpreting Scripture. They taught the historical-grammatical method: that each verse has one meaning—based on its words and grammar. This is the method we teach in this course. The historical-grammatical method teaches us to pay attention to history and grammar. For example, if we want to interpret a verse in Corinthians, we should pay attention to the history of the Corinthians. We should know who they were and what problems Paul wrote to solve. Likewise, to interpret a verse in Corinthians, such as 1 Corinthians 13:1, we should pay attention to the grammar—the way words are used in the text, and the way the text relates to its context. It helps us to discern that 1 Corinthians 13 is about love in relation to using spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:14). Otherwise, if we do not pay attention to the history of the Corinthians and the way words are used in each verse, we cannot interpret the verse correctly.

Eusebius (pronounced U-SEE-be-us) of Caesarea was one of the leading teachers in Antioch. He lived from AD 263 to AD 340 and was a pioneer of the studies of the gospels. For example, he divided them into passages common to all four. He was much more interested in the historical details of the Scripture than the teachers in Alexandria.

Theodore of Mopsuestia was the best-known teacher in Antioch. He agreed that there were some types in the Old Testament, but not as many as the school at Alexandria claimed. For example, he did not accept the traditional view that the Song of Solomon was a type of Christ’s love for the church. Rather, he taught that this book was about a celebration of one of Solomon’s marriages. (After his death, he was condemned for Nestorianism).

John Chrysostom was another teacher in Antioch (AD 347–407). A number of his sermons still exist. These show that the school at Antioch sought the one meaning of a text. Then, preachers like Chrysostom applied the text to the lives of their people.

The school in Alexandria taught that it was good to allegorize the Bible; the school at Antioch sought the one meaning of a text. Augustine was greatly influenced by this thinking. He believed we must reason from the literal sense of Scripture. But allegory was his main method. For example, in Psalm 3:5 the psalmist writes about lying down, sleeping, and rising. Augustine taught that this referred to the death and resurrection of Christ. Sadly, allegorizing took over as the method of interpreting Scripture and continued for one thousand years.

Since allegory was so popular as the method of interpreting Scripture, it is good to summarize it.

• In a positive sense, it taught that the Bible is a spiritual book, not just a historical book. Rather, God’s Word is alive and applies to the life of each Christian.

• However, on the negative side, allegory divorced the biblical text from its history. Allegory encouraged interpretations based on the imagination of each person. This opened the door for such errors as saying that Mary was born of a virgin and the Pope was on an authoritative level with Scripture.

To avoid heresies, it is critical that pastors preach the Word (2 Timothy. 4:2), not their own imaginations.

**Q:** Explain the difference in the Halakah and Haggadah types of teaching.

**A:** Halakah means “of a legal nature.” This teaching had religious laws for every part of life, including rituals, family life, and personal life, along with relations to the government and non-Jews. These Halakah rules were based on laws of the Old Testament. Haggadah used stories and proverbs of the Old Testament to explain Scripture and edify readers. For example, the Jews told the story of the Passover as they celebrated it. This was a powerful form of Jewish interpretation.

**Q:** What was the Septuagint? Why did Jews need it?

**A:** This Greek school of interpretation was in Egypt—where Greek influence was strong. In Egypt, Greek replaced Hebrew as the language of the Jews. Some Jewish scholars translated the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek, so that Grecian Jews could read them. This Greek version of the Old Testament is called the Septuagint—the seventy—because it was the work of seventy scholars.

**Q:** Why did Philo teach that the stories about Noah and Jacob had hidden meaning?

**A:** He was trying to build a bridge between the church and the world. Why? Because in Alexandria, unbelievers were attacking the Bible. But by using the method of allegory to interpret Scripture—looking for hidden meanings behind plain verses—he led thousands of Christians away from the truth for over a thousand years.

**Q:** What do you think is the worst thing about the allegorical method of interpreting the Bible?

**A:** Because of this fleshly method of interpreting Scripture, much of the true meaning of God’s Word was lost for many centuries.

**Q:** Explain: The apostles interpreted the OT Christologically.

**A:** Jesus taught His disciples to interpret the Old Testament Christologically—in reference to Christ. They discerned that Jesus fulfilled many Old Testament prophecies about the Messiah.

**Q:** Name one type from Hebrews 9:21–24.

**A:** The tabernacle and everything used in its ceremonies

**Q:** The weeping in Jeremiah 31:15 is a type of what?

**A:** The loss of Israel’s children to Herod

**Q:** What principle is literally stated in Genesis 15:6 and Romans 4:3?

**A:** God takes note of our faith, and He credits our account with righteousness.

**A:** a. fulfilled prophecy b. principle c. literal d. fulfilled prophecy e. principle f. fulfilled prophecy g. typology

**Q:** Summarize the method of biblical interpretation used in Alexandria, Egypt.

**A:** Clement taught that Plato’s best ideas had been similar to Moses’ ideas. He wanted the Greek world to believe that Christianity fulfilled Greek philosophy and the Old Testament. Clement taught that Scripture had two meanings: literal and spiritual. Origen taught that the text of Scripture often hid eternal truths. Thus he used the method of allegory to interpret the Bible. He looked for hidden keys to Christian living. Athanasius was also of the Alexandrian school. He was an important person at the Council of Nicea. There, he defended the divinity of Christ against the teaching of Arius. He did not interpret the Scripture in a literal way, but used allegory to apply the Bible.

**Q:** Explain the historical-grammatical method. Give an example.

**A:** Each verse has one meaning based on its words and grammar. The historical-grammatical method pays attention to history and grammar. For example, if we want to interpret a verse in Corinthians, we should consider the history of the Corinthians. We should know who they were and what problems Paul wrote to solve. Likewise, to interpret a verse in Corinthians, such as 1 Corinthians, 13:1, we should pay attention to the grammar—the way words are used in the text, and the way the text relates to its context. It helps us to discern that 1 Corinthians 13 is about love in relation to using spiritual gifts (1 Corinthians 12:14). Otherwise, if we do not pay attention to the history of the Corinthians, and the way words are used in each verse, we cannot interpret the verse correctly.

**Q:** Contrast the methods of the schools of Alexandria and Antioch.

**A:** The school at Alexandria taught the allegorical method of interpretation; the school at Antioch sought the one true meaning of biblical text.

**Q:** Is a pastor who preaches his or her own imaginations being faithful to God? Explain.

**A:** Allegory divorced the biblical text from its history. Allegory encouraged interpretations based on the imagination of each person. This opened the door for such errors as saying that Mary was born of a virgin and that the authority of the Pope was and is scriptural.

### The Middle Ages to the Reformation (AD 600–1500)

#### 2.2.1 — Summarize three methods of interpreting Scripture used during the Middle Ages.

The Method of Defending Tradition

Tradition was the guiding standard of interpreting Scripture during the Middle Ages . Scholars interpreted the Bible in the same ways as their church leaders. They supported the views the church fathers passed down for centuries and were careful to teach just what they had received. There were collections of teachings based on the method of allegory. These were taught from place to place. The method of allegory gave birth to many meanings for one word. For example, the word sea could refer to an ocean, the human heart, or baptism. The context of the passage was not used to find the meaning of a word. This method led many people astray from the truth of God’s Word.

The church fathers had written comments on the biblical text. These comments were in the margins, or between the lines of the text, and were called glosses . The comments became a biblical commentary of the Middle Ages (medieval times). This commentary was called the Glossa Ordinaria . Many teachers honored tradition and taught the comments of those who taught before them.

The Method of Allegory

Many felt that every Bible passage had four meanings. There was a rhyme in the Middle Ages that describes the four meanings of each verse:

1. The letter shows us what God and our fathers did.

2. The allegory shows us where our faith is hid.

3. The moral meaning gives us rules of daily life.

4. The analogy shows us where we end our strife (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 38).

Gerald Bray illustrates four meanings of the city of Jerusalem:

1. Literal: a city in Palestine; the capital of Israel

2. Allegorical: the church on earth

3. Moral: the soul of the believer

4. Mystical: the heavenly city; the victorious church (Bray 1996, 147)

Maximus the Confessor (AD 580–662) was a theologian of the Byzantine Empire in Constantinople. He wrote a book that contained sixty-five answers to difficult questions about the Bible. He used the allegorical method to find the correct answers. His method became the standard for the Eastern Church.

Ambrose Autpert (died in AD 781) wrote a commentary on the book of Revelation. In Revelation 12, he said the woman clothed with the sun was Mary, not Israel. The Catholic Church used this interpretation to exalt Mary.

Bede (AD 672–735) was an English historian. He wrote a number of commentaries—especially his famous Ecclesiastical History . He used allegory only a little and gave attention to historical and literal details. His commentaries were among the most popular in the Middle Ages.

The Method of Scholasticism

Thomas Aquinas (AD 1225–1274) was a famous theologian of this period. He wrote the Summa Theologica, which summarized the past three centuries of biblical and theological studies. His work became the summary of what the Roman Catholic Church of the day believed. His work was based on a literal interpretation of Scripture, because he believed that the Bible contained all we need about faith. Aquinas was the person who brought about a change in the method of interpreting the Bible—freeing it from its long past of allegorical interpretation. The use of reason was primary in his approach. Still Thomas used allegory to explain figurative language—and accepted several meanings of passages like I am the door.

The method of Thomas Aquinas followed scholasticism — a movement based on reason. This movement went from the monastic schools to the universities of Europe. It dealt mostly with the relationship of Christian faith and reason.

The Literal Method of Interpreting Scripture

As the Medieval Era closed, there was less emphasis on the allegorical method. Many returned to interpreting Scripture literally—seeking the plain meaning of a passage.

John Wycliffe (AD 1329–1384) is an example of one who used the literal method. He led the way toward the Reformation period. He believed that the meaning of the Bible was plain, not hidden. He is famous for his book, On the Truth of Scripture, published in 1378. For Wycliffe, human knowledge could not compare to Scripture. He said that the purpose of logic was to defend the Bible.

In the Middle Ages, the authority of Scripture was never questioned. The church believed in verbal inspiration—that every word of the Bible was inspired. This did not prevent figurative interpretation.

**Q:** Summarize the method of interpreting based on tradition.

**A:** Those who used the traditional method were careful to teach just what they had received. The method of allegory gave birth to many meanings for one word. For example, the word sea could refer to an ocean, the human heart, or baptism. The context of the passage was not used to find the meaning of a word. This method led many people astray from the truth of God’s Word. The church fathers had written comments on the biblical text. These comments were in the margins, or between the lines of the text, and were called glosses. These comments became a biblical commentary of the Middle Ages (medieval times). This commentary was called the Glossa Ordinaria . Many teachers honored tradition and taught the comments of those who taught before them.

**Q:** In most cases, is the meaning of the Bible plain or hidden? Explain.

**A:** Plain, not hidden. The historical/grammatical method of interpretation teaches that each verse has one meaning, based on its words and grammar. To find the meaning we must pay attention to the historical setting in which the verse is set and the grammar used by the author.

### The Reformation to the Present (AD 1500–the present)

#### 2.3.1 — Summarize the way Luther and Calvin helped believers interpret Scripture.

The Reformation Period (A. D. 1500–1650)

This period brought a reform, change, or revolution in the interpretation of the Bible. Many things led to the Reformation—but we will study three important people: Erasmus, Martin Luther, and John Calvin.

Erasmus of Rotterdam (AD 1466–1536) was known as a Christian humanist. He prepared the way for the Reformation. In 1516, Erasmus organized a Greek translation of the New Testament. (Later, Luther used it to prepare his German translation.) Erasmus studied the Bible in a systematic way. It seemed that he would be a part of the Reformation, but he never joined it. Besides his Greek translation of the New Testament, two other works he wrote were well-known. They were his Annotations (notes) and Paraphrases on the gospels. These works studied the biblical setting of texts, paying attention to both history and grammar. Then, they applied the text to doctrine and daily living. Note that Erasmus fulfilled the two goals of hermeneutics:

1. To find the meaning of a text to the first readers

2. To apply the text to us today

In the sixteenth century, many said that Erasmus laid the egg of the Reformation, and Luther hatched it (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 40).

Martin Luther of Germany (AD 1483–1546) was the main leader of the Reformation. He emphasized salvation by faith in Jesus, rather than by works.

Luther rejected the idea that every verse could have four meanings. Instead, he emphasized that each verse had only one meaning—with many applications. Also, he declared the right of every believer to interpret the Bible. To help believers, Luther prepared a German translation of the Bible.

Luther is well-known for emphasizing sola scriptura , meaning “Scripture alone.” He rejected the tradition that the teaching of church leaders had the same authority as the Bible. Rather, he taught that the Bible is our only authority for faith and practice. He also taught the principle that the Bible itself—not church fathers—is its own best interpreter.

Luther read and understood the Bible from a point of view that focused on Jesus—a Christ-centered perspective. He rejected the allegorical method, but used types from the Old Testament that were fulfilled in the New Testament. There are fifty-five works of Luther in the English edition. More than half of these contain his exegesis or interpretation of the Bible in commentary form. The rest of his work is in the form of sermons.

Luther balanced the literal and spiritual meaning of a text. He held that believers need the Holy Spirit to illumine or reveal the spiritual meaning of a passage.

John Calvin (AD 1509–1564) is famous for his commentaries on the Bible during the Reformation period. He guided believers to interpret the Bible well. Most of his work is in the form of commentaries. He wrote commentaries on all but one of the New Testament books and thirty-one out of thirty-nine of the Old Testament books. Calvin rejected the method of allegory. He taught that believers should interpret verses within their contexts—both historical and literary. Calvin believed that the Bible was our only written authority and that we should accept it by faith. He also believed that the Holy Spirit would give believers an inner witness about the correct meaning of a passage.

To summarize, the Reformation leaders—like Luther and Calvin—rejected the allegorical method of interpreting the Bible. They did not seek hidden meanings of Scripture, like those who used allegory. Rather, they sought the plain, simple, literal meaning of Scripture. Likewise, they did not rely on the tradition of the church or the teaching of the church fathers. Rather, they depended on the Bible itself. Today, many students of the Bible still study their commentaries. Luther and Calvin remind us that some tradition is good. But we should reject tradition that conflicts with Scripture or leads us away from the plain truth of God’s Word.

The Roman Catholic Church rejected the Reformation. Catholic leaders met at the Council of Trent (AD 1545—1563). There, they affirmed the Vulgate—the Latin translation of the Scripture—although it contained many translation errors. Catholics forbade anyone to interpret Scripture in a way different from church tradition. As a result of the debates related to the Reformation, two streams of biblical interpretation flowed: Protestant and Catholic.

The Creeds (AD 1564–1650) were written statements of what the Protestant Church believed. In part, the creeds were a Protestant reaction to statements by the Roman Catholic Church and their statements at the Council of Trent. But some of the Protestant creeds go back to earlier days of the Reformation. For example, the Augsburg Confession (1530) was the statement of faith of the followers of Luther. Its author was Philip Melanchthon, a close friend of Luther. Later, in 1647, the English Parliament accepted the Westminister Confession of Faith. This united the teaching of the English Church with Puritan doctrine. These confessions of faith were founded solely on the Bible—not tradition (Elwell 1984, 104, 1168).

Post–Reformation Period (AD 1650–1800)

During this period, there were many theological views. For some, reason or rationalism was the final authority. This required people to prove anything they believed. Their theology controlled the way they interpreted the Bible, instead of letting the Bible shape their beliefs. In contrast, there was another movement called pietism (godliness). It began in Germany. Pietism made reason the servant of faith and opposed religion that was dry and only mental. It sought to revive Christianity as a way of life with Bible study, prayer, and godly living. Rationalism was only a religion of the head, but pietism was a religion of the heart.

Philip Jakob Spener (AD 1635–1705) was a German pastor and leader of Pietism. He planned group Bible studies and prayer meetings. Spener taught the need to be converted and to have a personal relationship with Christ. He guided believers to study the Bible carefully and to apply it to their hearts and lives.

John Wesley (AD 1703–1791), founder of the Methodist Church, also came into contact with pietism. He began a movement that came to be known as Methodism in England and America. Wesley sought to recover personal holiness through Bible study, prayer, and the Holy Spirit.

Jonathan Edwards emphasized that what we believe must affect the way we live. Jonathan Edwards (AD 1703–1758) was the best-known leader of pietism in America in his time. He emphasized both the theology and daily living of biblical truth.

Rationalism was the label of an intellectual movement that arose during this time. This “Age of Reason” began about 1648. It lasted from the end of the Thirty Years War to the beginning of the French Revolution in 1789. Rationalists believed that the human mind was able to discern truth without God’s help. Thus, they saw no need for God to reveal truth or illumine the human mind. This type of thinking led to great damage in the nineteenth century. It lifted the human mind above the Bible and authorities of the church. This pride and confidence in human reason brought poor biblical interpretation.

The Modern Period (AD 1800 to the present)

The Nineteenth Century

During the nineteenth century (AD 1800–1900) many scholars tried to discover how the books of the Bible were written. This led to the historical-critical method of interpretation—which denied the supernatural. This method was a child of rationalism. It taught that the Bible was not different from other books and denied that the Holy Spirit led authors to write. This human method tried to explain everything through natural laws. It rejected all miracles and supernatural events in the Bible, including the deity of Christ and His resurrection. It taught that the truths of Scripture were not timeless. Consequently, the Bible was studied for its ethical and moral teaching. The focus was no longer on theology.

From this approach came what was called source criticism . This method of study was an enemy of the Bible as the inspired, infallible Word of God. It examined the Bible like any other book. One of the foremost leaders of source criticism was the German Julius Wellhausen. He is famous for his work on the Pentateuch. One of the last German scholars of this method was Adolf von Harnack.

The historical-critical method was popular in some circles—those who exercised little or no faith. At the same time, there were studies and commentaries about the Bible. These writers dealt with themes of each Bible book. They emphasized the message for the first readers. Then, they sought to apply the truth for believers today. Thus, they fulfilled the two goals of hermeneutics. These helpful leaders respected the context of Scripture. They sought the plain, simple, literal meaning of God’s Word. Three of these well-known theologians—who believed in the inspiration of the Bible—were Charles Hodge, J. B. Lightfoot, and B. F. Westcott.

Most of the nineteenth century was a time of struggle:

• On one side were the liberals––those who exercised little or no faith—especially from Germany. These did not believe the Bible was the Word of God, and they did not believe Jesus was the Son of God.

• On the other side were the conservatives, who attended most of the major churches. These believed that the Bible is God’s Word and the authority over our faith and daily living.

The Twentieth Century

The twentieth century (AD 1900–2000) was an era of change for biblical interpreters. The First World War was a turning point in biblical interpretation. It showed that humans could do great evil. In contrast, the liberals had been emphasizing that humanity is good. They had believed that the progress in the West had buried evil. The liberals had great faith in humanity, not God. So the war was like throwing a bucket of water on the small fire of the liberal teachers.

Karl Barth (1886–1968) tried to be a bridge between liberals and conservatives. He brought the authority of Scripture back to some as the Word of God. Still, he taught that God’s Word was to be discerned by literary and source criticism. His mixed system of theology was called neo-orthodoxy.

Neo-orthodoxy was a reaction against liberals. It emphasized some of the truths of the Reformation and taught that reason must depend on faith that awaits God’s Word. This method attempts to find truth through discussions and debate.

Rudolf Bultmann (1884–1976) was another important liberal of the twentieth century. He used the method of form criticism to study the Scripture, especially the Gospels. Bultmann did not believe the Bible was the Word of God, and he did not believe in miracles. He emphasized the method of demythologizing, the removing of what he called the myths (miracles) of Scripture. This liberal taught that people should get what they could from the Bible, but not pay attention to the details. His teachings have led many people away from the truth of God’s Word.

The twentieth century also brought a time of growth for ecumenism—the uniting of many denominations. Many felt that Protestants should work together when possible. Rather than the old creeds and confessions, there was a divide between liberals and conservatives.

The Twenty-First Century

The evangelicals are a group within the Protestant churches. Evangelicals are people who believe that the Bible is God’s Word and that we must be born-again. Likewise, we believe in evangelizing—testifying about our faith in Jesus Christ. That is why some people call us Great Commission Christians; we believe in obeying the Lord’s command to share the gospel with the entire world. About eighty-five percent of all Great Commission Christians are Pentecostal or charismatic (Barrett 2000, 25). Thus, Pentecostals and charismatics are a large part of the evangelical movement.

As evangelicals, we have rejected the teachings of liberals, like Welhaussen, Harnack, and Bultmann. Likewise, we have rejected ungodly methods like the historical-critical method and source criticism. We teach the same methods of biblical interpretation of the Reformation. Over time, liberal churches have declined and many have closed. In contrast, evangelical and Pentecostal churches are healthy and growing.

An international council on biblical inerrancy produced two documents. The first one was about the inerrancy of Scripture (1978). The second was about hermeneutics (1982). The purpose of these two documents was to set limits and guidelines for evangelicals (see bibliography on inerrancy). The document on hermeneutics outlined the acceptable way to study Scripture. Most evangelicals and Pentecostals agree on these guidelines.

The Chicago Statement on Biblical Hermeneutics (Articles 19–22)

• We affirm that any preunderstanding which the interpreter brings to Scripture should be in harmony with scriptural teaching and subject to correction by Scripture.

• We deny that Scripture should be required to fit pre-understandings, inconsistent with itself, such as naturalism, evolutionism, scientism, secular humanism, and relativism.

• We affirm that since God is the author of all truth—all truths, biblical and extrabiblical, are consistent and unified, and that the Bible speaks truth when it touches on matters about nature, history, or anything else. We further affirm that in some cases extrabiblical data have value for clarifying what Scripture teaches and correcting false interpretations.

• We deny that extrabiblical views ever disprove the teaching of Scripture or hold priority over it.

• We affirm the harmony of special with general revelation, and thus believe that biblical teaching is in harmony with the facts of nature.

• We deny that any genuine scientific facts contradict the true meaning of any passage of Scripture.

• We affirm that Genesis 1–11 is factual, as is the rest of Genesis.

• We deny that the teachings of Genesis 1–11 are mythical and that scientific theories about earth, history or the origin of humanity may be used to overthrow what Scripture teaches about creation.

(International Council on Biblical Inerrancy)

Evangelical Guidelines for Interpreting Scripture

Frederick Fyvie (F.F.) Bruce (1910–1991) was a great scholar in modern times. He was the author of many commentaries. Bruce used the literal method to study the Bible. Many modern evangelical and Pentecostal interpreters follow the example of Bruce. He set a high standard for research into the Word. One of Bruce’s last works was a commentary on Colossians, Philemon, and Ephesians, produced in 1984.

Stanley M. Horton is a well-known Pentecostal scholar who uses the historical/grammatical method. His latest commentary is on the book of Acts.

Don Stamps and Wesley Adams wrote one of the most helpful, hermeneutical tools of this century: the Life in the Spirit Study Bible. Stamps wrote the study notes and articles, while J. Wesley Adams wrote the introduction to each biblical book. This Pentecostal study Bible interprets verses in a plain, simple, literal manner. Likewise, it emphasizes the original meaning of a text to its first readers and contains many applications for today. Millions of believers all over the world are using this study Bible to help interpret the Scriptures.

**Q:** Does tradition have the same authority as Scripture? Explain.

**A:** The Bible is our only authority for faith and practice and the Bible itself—not church fathers—is its own best interpreter.

**Q:** When is tradition good, and when is it bad?

**A:** We should reject tradition that conflicts with Scripture, or leads us away from the plain truth of God’s Word.

**Q:** Summarize the difference between rationalism and pietism.

**A:** The rationalists required people to prove anything they believed. Their theology controlled the way they interpreted the Bible, instead of letting the Bible shape their beliefs. In contrast, there was another movement called pietism (godliness). It began in Germany. Those who taught pietism made reason the servant of faith. Pietism opposed religion that was dry and only mental. It sought to revive Christianity as a way of life with Bible study, prayer, and godly living. Rationalism was only a religion of the head, but pietism was a religion of the heart.

**A:** Liberals––those with little or no faith—did not believe the Bible was the Word of God, and they did not believe Jesus was the Son of God. On the other side were the conservatives; most of them attended the major churches. These people believed the Bible is God’s Word and the authority over our faith and daily living.

That is why some call us Great Commission Christians—we believe in obeying the Lord’s command to share the gospel with the entire world. UNIT 2

#### 2.3.2 — Explain how rationalism and pietism affected the interpretation of Scripture.

The Reformation Period (A. D. 1500–1650)

This period brought a reform, change, or revolution in the interpretation of the Bible. Many things led to the Reformation—but we will study three important people: Erasmus, Martin Luther, and John Calvin.

Erasmus of Rotterdam (AD 1466–1536) was known as a Christian humanist. He prepared the way for the Reformation. In 1516, Erasmus organized a Greek translation of the New Testament. (Later, Luther used it to prepare his German translation.) Erasmus studied the Bible in a systematic way. It seemed that he would be a part of the Reformation, but he never joined it. Besides his Greek translation of the New Testament, two other works he wrote were well-known. They were his Annotations (notes) and Paraphrases on the gospels. These works studied the biblical setting of texts, paying attention to both history and grammar. Then, they applied the text to doctrine and daily living. Note that Erasmus fulfilled the two goals of hermeneutics:

1. To find the meaning of a text to the first readers

2. To apply the text to us today

In the sixteenth century, many said that Erasmus laid the egg of the Reformation, and Luther hatched it (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 40).

Martin Luther of Germany (AD 1483–1546) was the main leader of the Reformation. He emphasized salvation by faith in Jesus, rather than by works.

Luther rejected the idea that every verse could have four meanings. Instead, he emphasized that each verse had only one meaning—with many applications. Also, he declared the right of every believer to interpret the Bible. To help believers, Luther prepared a German translation of the Bible.

Luther is well-known for emphasizing sola scriptura , meaning “Scripture alone.” He rejected the tradition that the teaching of church leaders had the same authority as the Bible. Rather, he taught that the Bible is our only authority for faith and practice. He also taught the principle that the Bible itself—not church fathers—is its own best interpreter.

Luther read and understood the Bible from a point of view that focused on Jesus—a Christ-centered perspective. He rejected the allegorical method, but used types from the Old Testament that were fulfilled in the New Testament. There are fifty-five works of Luther in the English edition. More than half of these contain his exegesis or interpretation of the Bible in commentary form. The rest of his work is in the form of sermons.

Luther balanced the literal and spiritual meaning of a text. He held that believers need the Holy Spirit to illumine or reveal the spiritual meaning of a passage.

John Calvin (AD 1509–1564) is famous for his commentaries on the Bible during the Reformation period. He guided believers to interpret the Bible well. Most of his work is in the form of commentaries. He wrote commentaries on all but one of the New Testament books and thirty-one out of thirty-nine of the Old Testament books. Calvin rejected the method of allegory. He taught that believers should interpret verses within their contexts—both historical and literary. Calvin believed that the Bible was our only written authority and that we should accept it by faith. He also believed that the Holy Spirit would give believers an inner witness about the correct meaning of a passage.

To summarize, the Reformation leaders—like Luther and Calvin—rejected the allegorical method of interpreting the Bible. They did not seek hidden meanings of Scripture, like those who used allegory. Rather, they sought the plain, simple, literal meaning of Scripture. Likewise, they did not rely on the tradition of the church or the teaching of the church fathers. Rather, they depended on the Bible itself. Today, many students of the Bible still study their commentaries. Luther and Calvin remind us that some tradition is good. But we should reject tradition that conflicts with Scripture or leads us away from the plain truth of God’s Word.

The Roman Catholic Church rejected the Reformation. Catholic leaders met at the Council of Trent (AD 1545—1563). There, they affirmed the Vulgate—the Latin translation of the Scripture—although it contained many translation errors. Catholics forbade anyone to interpret Scripture in a way different from church tradition. As a result of the debates related to the Reformation, two streams of biblical interpretation flowed: Protestant and Catholic.

The Creeds (AD 1564–1650) were written statements of what the Protestant Church believed. In part, the creeds were a Protestant reaction to statements by the Roman Catholic Church and their statements at the Council of Trent. But some of the Protestant creeds go back to earlier days of the Reformation. For example, the Augsburg Confession (1530) was the statement of faith of the followers of Luther. Its author was Philip Melanchthon, a close friend of Luther. Later, in 1647, the English Parliament accepted the Westminister Confession of Faith. This united the teaching of the English Church with Puritan doctrine. These confessions of faith were founded solely on the Bible—not tradition (Elwell 1984, 104, 1168).

Post–Reformation Period (AD 1650–1800)

During this period, there were many theological views. For some, reason or rationalism was the final authority. This required people to prove anything they believed. Their theology controlled the way they interpreted the Bible, instead of letting the Bible shape their beliefs. In contrast, there was another movement called pietism (godliness). It began in Germany. Pietism made reason the servant of faith and opposed religion that was dry and only mental. It sought to revive Christianity as a way of life with Bible study, prayer, and godly living. Rationalism was only a religion of the head, but pietism was a religion of the heart.

Philip Jakob Spener (AD 1635–1705) was a German pastor and leader of Pietism. He planned group Bible studies and prayer meetings. Spener taught the need to be converted and to have a personal relationship with Christ. He guided believers to study the Bible carefully and to apply it to their hearts and lives.

John Wesley (AD 1703–1791), founder of the Methodist Church, also came into contact with pietism. He began a movement that came to be known as Methodism in England and America. Wesley sought to recover personal holiness through Bible study, prayer, and the Holy Spirit.

Jonathan Edwards emphasized that what we believe must affect the way we live. Jonathan Edwards (AD 1703–1758) was the best-known leader of pietism in America in his time. He emphasized both the theology and daily living of biblical truth.

Rationalism was the label of an intellectual movement that arose during this time. This “Age of Reason” began about 1648. It lasted from the end of the Thirty Years War to the beginning of the French Revolution in 1789. Rationalists believed that the human mind was able to discern truth without God’s help. Thus, they saw no need for God to reveal truth or illumine the human mind. This type of thinking led to great damage in the nineteenth century. It lifted the human mind above the Bible and authorities of the church. This pride and confidence in human reason brought poor biblical interpretation.

The Modern Period (AD 1800 to the present)

The Nineteenth Century

During the nineteenth century (AD 1800–1900) many scholars tried to discover how the books of the Bible were written. This led to the historical-critical method of interpretation—which denied the supernatural. This method was a child of rationalism. It taught that the Bible was not different from other books and denied that the Holy Spirit led authors to write. This human method tried to explain everything through natural laws. It rejected all miracles and supernatural events in the Bible, including the deity of Christ and His resurrection. It taught that the truths of Scripture were not timeless. Consequently, the Bible was studied for its ethical and moral teaching. The focus was no longer on theology.

From this approach came what was called source criticism . This method of study was an enemy of the Bible as the inspired, infallible Word of God. It examined the Bible like any other book. One of the foremost leaders of source criticism was the German Julius Wellhausen. He is famous for his work on the Pentateuch. One of the last German scholars of this method was Adolf von Harnack.

The historical-critical method was popular in some circles—those who exercised little or no faith. At the same time, there were studies and commentaries about the Bible. These writers dealt with themes of each Bible book. They emphasized the message for the first readers. Then, they sought to apply the truth for believers today. Thus, they fulfilled the two goals of hermeneutics. These helpful leaders respected the context of Scripture. They sought the plain, simple, literal meaning of God’s Word. Three of these well-known theologians—who believed in the inspiration of the Bible—were Charles Hodge, J. B. Lightfoot, and B. F. Westcott.

Most of the nineteenth century was a time of struggle:

• On one side were the liberals––those who exercised little or no faith—especially from Germany. These did not believe the Bible was the Word of God, and they did not believe Jesus was the Son of God.

• On the other side were the conservatives, who attended most of the major churches. These believed that the Bible is God’s Word and the authority over our faith and daily living.

The Twentieth Century

The twentieth century (AD 1900–2000) was an era of change for biblical interpreters. The First World War was a turning point in biblical interpretation. It showed that humans could do great evil. In contrast, the liberals had been emphasizing that humanity is good. They had believed that the progress in the West had buried evil. The liberals had great faith in humanity, not God. So the war was like throwing a bucket of water on the small fire of the liberal teachers.

Karl Barth (1886–1968) tried to be a bridge between liberals and conservatives. He brought the authority of Scripture back to some as the Word of God. Still, he taught that God’s Word was to be discerned by literary and source criticism. His mixed system of theology was called neo-orthodoxy.

Neo-orthodoxy was a reaction against liberals. It emphasized some of the truths of the Reformation and taught that reason must depend on faith that awaits God’s Word. This method attempts to find truth through discussions and debate.

Rudolf Bultmann (1884–1976) was another important liberal of the twentieth century. He used the method of form criticism to study the Scripture, especially the Gospels. Bultmann did not believe the Bible was the Word of God, and he did not believe in miracles. He emphasized the method of demythologizing, the removing of what he called the myths (miracles) of Scripture. This liberal taught that people should get what they could from the Bible, but not pay attention to the details. His teachings have led many people away from the truth of God’s Word.

The twentieth century also brought a time of growth for ecumenism—the uniting of many denominations. Many felt that Protestants should work together when possible. Rather than the old creeds and confessions, there was a divide between liberals and conservatives.

The Twenty-First Century

The evangelicals are a group within the Protestant churches. Evangelicals are people who believe that the Bible is God’s Word and that we must be born-again. Likewise, we believe in evangelizing—testifying about our faith in Jesus Christ. That is why some people call us Great Commission Christians; we believe in obeying the Lord’s command to share the gospel with the entire world. About eighty-five percent of all Great Commission Christians are Pentecostal or charismatic (Barrett 2000, 25). Thus, Pentecostals and charismatics are a large part of the evangelical movement.

Likewise, we have rejected ungodly methods like the historical-critical method and source criticism. We teach the same methods of biblical interpretation of the Reformation. Over time, liberal churches have declined and many have closed. In contrast, evangelical and Pentecostal churches are healthy and growing.

About eighty-five percent of all Great Commission Christians are Pentecostal or charismatic (Barrett 2000, 25). Thus, Pentecostals and charismatics are a large part of the evangelical movement.

As evangelicals, we have rejected the teachings of liberals, like Welhaussen, Harnack, and Bultmann. Likewise, we have rejected ungodly methods like the historical-critical method and source criticism. We teach the same methods of biblical interpretation of the Reformation. Over time, liberal churches have declined and many have closed. In contrast, evangelical and Pentecostal churches are healthy and growing.

An international council on biblical inerrancy produced two documents. The first one was about the inerrancy of Scripture (1978). The second was about hermeneutics (1982). The purpose of these two documents was to set limits and guidelines for evangelicals (see bibliography on inerrancy). The document on hermeneutics outlined the acceptable way to study Scripture. Most evangelicals and Pentecostals agree on these guidelines.

The Chicago Statement on Biblical Hermeneutics (Articles 19–22)

• We affirm that any preunderstanding which the interpreter brings to Scripture should be in harmony with scriptural teaching and subject to correction by Scripture.

• We deny that Scripture should be required to fit pre-understandings, inconsistent with itself, such as naturalism, evolutionism, scientism, secular humanism, and relativism.

• We affirm that since God is the author of all truth—all truths, biblical and extrabiblical, are consistent and unified, and that the Bible speaks truth when it touches on matters about nature, history, or anything else. We further affirm that in some cases extrabiblical data have value for clarifying what Scripture teaches and correcting false interpretations.

• We deny that extrabiblical views ever disprove the teaching of Scripture or hold priority over it.

• We affirm the harmony of special with general revelation, and thus believe that biblical teaching is in harmony with the facts of nature.

• We deny that any genuine scientific facts contradict the true meaning of any passage of Scripture.

• We affirm that Genesis 1–11 is factual, as is the rest of Genesis.

• We deny that the teachings of Genesis 1–11 are mythical and that scientific theories about earth, history or the origin of humanity may be used to overthrow what Scripture teaches about creation.

(International Council on Biblical Inerrancy)

Evangelical Guidelines for Interpreting Scripture

Frederick Fyvie (F.F.) Bruce (1910–1991) was a great scholar in modern times. He was the author of many commentaries. Bruce used the literal method to study the Bible. Many modern evangelical and Pentecostal interpreters follow the example of Bruce. He set a high standard for research into the Word. One of Bruce’s last works was a commentary on Colossians, Philemon, and Ephesians, produced in 1984.

Stanley M. Horton is a well-known Pentecostal scholar who uses the historical/grammatical method. His latest commentary is on the book of Acts.

Don Stamps and Wesley Adams wrote one of the most helpful, hermeneutical tools of this century: the Life in the Spirit Study Bible. Stamps wrote the study notes and articles, while J. Wesley Adams wrote the introduction to each biblical book. This Pentecostal study Bible interprets verses in a plain, simple, literal manner. Likewise, it emphasizes the original meaning of a text to its first readers and contains many applications for today. Millions of believers all over the world are using this study Bible to help interpret the Scriptures.

**Q:** Does tradition have the same authority as Scripture? Explain.

**A:** The Bible is our only authority for faith and practice and the Bible itself—not church fathers—is its own best interpreter.

**Q:** When is tradition good, and when is it bad?

**A:** We should reject tradition that conflicts with Scripture, or leads us away from the plain truth of God’s Word.

**Q:** Summarize the difference between rationalism and pietism.

**A:** The rationalists required people to prove anything they believed. Their theology controlled the way they interpreted the Bible, instead of letting the Bible shape their beliefs. In contrast, there was another movement called pietism (godliness). It began in Germany. Those who taught pietism made reason the servant of faith. Pietism opposed religion that was dry and only mental. It sought to revive Christianity as a way of life with Bible study, prayer, and godly living. Rationalism was only a religion of the head, but pietism was a religion of the heart.

**Q:** Contrast the beliefs of liberals and conservatives.

**A:** Liberals––those with little or no faith—did not believe the Bible was the Word of God, and they did not believe Jesus was the Son of God. On the other side were the conservatives; most of them attended the major churches. These people believed the Bible is God’s Word and the authority over our faith and daily living.

**Q:** What do evangelicals believe?

**A:** Evangelicals believe that the Bible is God’s Word, and that humans must be born-again. As evangelicals, we believe in evangelizing—testifying about our faith in Jesus Christ. That is why some call us Great Commission Christians—we believe in obeying the Lord’s command to share the gospel with the entire world. UNIT 2

## 3 - The Historical-Cultural Background

### Examining the Historical-Cultural Background

#### 3.1.1 — Explain at least three reasons for examining the historical-cultural background of a passage.

The Significance of Historical-Cultural Background

The historical-cultural background refers to the original setting of Scripture. For several reasons, we need to discover the setting in which Scripture was written.

• Times have changed. The New Testament was written about two thousand years ago. The Old Testament was written over several centuries–from about 1400 to 400 BC.

• Places have changed. Moses and most of the prophets wrote to people living in the land of Israel. Likewise, the New Testament was written to those living in Israel or Asia Minor . Today, people all over the world are reading the Bible.

• Customs have changed. The people in Bible days had customs that were different from the customs of many people today.

• Circumstances have changed. The Scriptures were first written to people who lived long ago. They spoke the same language, lived in the same place, and shared the same customs. Obviously, they had a way of life different from most readers today: no bicycles, buses, trains, cars, or airplanes. Imagine the difference in living out your life in a tent and working in the desert as compared to living in an apartment and working in a big city.

Each passage was God’s Word to others before it came to us. So, in a sense, the Bible always comes to us second-hand; we get it after others who lived in different places at different times. Therefore, if we are to understand Scripture, we must always be aware of the changes that have taken place since it was first written. To interpret the Bible well, we must learn to walk in the shoes of the first readers and the authors God inspired to write. We must learn to think from the viewpoint of people who lived thousands of years ago. Before we can apply the Bible to us today, we must first understand what it said to people of that era. This brings us to an important principle: The correct interpretation of a passage must relate well to the historical-cultural backgrounds of the passage (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 172) .

To interpret Scripture correctly, we must learn to think in two worlds: the past and the present. We will teach you to do this in two steps. First, you must find the historical background of an entire book of Scripture, such as First Corinthians. Second, you must find the historical–cultural background of a specific passage, like 1 Corinthians 11:17–34. We will examine each of these two steps to finding the historical-cultural background.

The Historical Background of a Whole Book

To find the historical background of an entire book, we must answer questions about the author and those to whom he wrote. You probably already know some of the answers. A study Bible will help you answer all of these questions, so will the material in our survey courses on the Old and New Testaments (BIB212 New Testament Survey and BIB214 Old Testament Survey ). Below are the two types of questions to answer in finding the historical background of an entire book, like First Corinthians.

1. Answer five questions about the author.

a) Who was he?

b) When did he write the book?

c) What setting was he in?

d) What relationship did he have with those to whom he wrote?

e) What was his purpose?

2. Answer three questions about those who received the biblical book.

a) Who were they?

b) What was their city or town like?

c) What was their social status? (Were they Jews? Wealthy? Slaves? Educated?)

Example: Find the historical background of the book of First Corinthians.

1. Answer five questions about the author.

a) Who was he?

Paul, the apostle

b) When did he write the book?

Paul wrote 1 Corinthians about AD 56, on his third missionary trip (Acts 19:1–41).

c) What setting was he in?

Paul was ministering in Ephesus when he wrote to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 16:5–8). He had been there about three years (Acts 20:31).

d) What relationship did Paul have with the Corinthians?

Paul was the founder of the church at Corinth (Acts 18:1–18).

e) What was his purpose?

Paul wrote for two reasons: First, to correct problems that a person from the house of Cloe had told him about (1 Corinthians 1:11). These problems included division, lawsuits, and sexual sins (1 Corinthians 1–6). Second, he wrote to answer questions the Corinthians had asked in a letter (1 Corinthians 7:1–16:9). We will take a closer look at these problems and questions in the next chapter.

2. Answer three questions about those who received the biblical book.

a) Who were they?

The believers at Corinth

b) What was their city or town like?

Corinth was a big city on the northern shore of the Mediterranean Sea. It was known for business, immorality, and idolatry.

c) What was their social status?

The Corinthians were mostly Gentiles with a few Jews (See 1 Corinthians 6:9–11; 8:10; 12:13.) They were proud and educated—loved wisdom and knowledge (1 Corinthians 1:18–2:5; 4:10, 18; 5:2, 6; 8:1–13).

Now we have a good start toward correctly interpreting any verse in First Corinthians. You should be encouraged that you need to determine the historical background of a book only one time. After that, you can review it.

The Historical–Cultural Background of a Specific Passage

We have looked at how to find the historical background of an entire book. This gives us a good foundation to interpret the verses in that book. Still, there is the need to find the historical-cultural background of specific passages. For example, you may understand the historical background of Matthew. But you may still need to study the following:

• Historical references like the names in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:1–17)

• Historical figures like the magi (Matthew 2:1–12)

• The meaning of cultural items like myrrh (Matthew 2:11)

• The historical background of the Pharisees, Sadducees, Herods, Herodians, and Zealots

• The location of places like Bethlehem, Jerusalem, Nazareth, Tyre, Sidon, Galilee, Capernaum, and others

• The religious laws about lepers and leprosy (Matthew 8:1–4)

• The social status of a centurion (Matthew 8:5–13); a tax collector (Matthew 9:9–12); and a Canaanite woman (Matthew 15:21–28)

• Religious items like phylacteries (Matthew 23:5)

As we look at the background of 1 Corinthians, we must understand specific considerations like the custom of eating food offered to idols (1 Corinthians 8) and how the Lord’s Supper was celebrated (1 Corinthians 11). To find the historical-cultural background of a specific passage, like 1 Corinthians 11:17–34, answer three questions:

1. How does the specific passage relate to the author’s purpose?

2. Are there any specific historical details to explain?

3. Are there any specific cultural details, like the following, to explain?

• Social roles, values, or customs

• Economic concerns

• Political matters

• Religious beliefs or practices

We will work through these three questions to examine the historical-cultural background of a specific passage.

Example: Finding the Historical-Cultural Background of 1 Corinthians 11:17–34

In the following directives I have no praise for you, for your meetings do more harm than good. In the first place, I hear that when you come together as a church, there are divisions among you, and to some extent I believe it. No doubt there have to be differences among you to show which of you have God’s approval. When you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat, for as you eat, each of you goes ahead without waiting for anybody else. One remains hungry, another gets drunk. Don’t you have homes to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you for this? Certainly not! For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night he was betrayed, took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “This is my body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of me.” In the same way, after supper he took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.” For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord. A man ought to examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup. For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body of the Lord eats and drinks judgment on himself. That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would not come under judgment. When we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world. So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for each other. If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that when you meet together it may not result in judgment. And when I come I will give further directions. (1 Corinthians 11:17–34)

We address the three questions and their answers.

1. How does the specific passage relate to the author’s purpose?

Paul’s purpose in 1 Corinthians was to correct problems. One of these problems was what was happening at the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:17–34).

2. Are there any specific historical details to explain?

The early church met in homes to celebrate the Lord’s Supper. Jesus started this at the Passover Feast. Review Matthew 26:17–35. Our Lord taught that the bread and juice represent His body and blood of the New Covenant. (See question 3 that follows: religious beliefs.)

3. Are there any specific cultural details to explain? These could be the following:

• Social roles, values, or customs [For instance, the poor and rich were eating together. The poor, who probably arrived late because of long hours of work, were left hungry (1 Corinthians 11:21).]

• Economic concerns

• Political matters

• Religious beliefs or practices

The early believers met often, perhaps each week, to celebrate the Lord’s Supper as part of a meal. Each person brought something to share at the meal. But the Corinthians had forgotten the meaning of the meal. Those who arrived first, perhaps the wealthy, did not wait for others (1 Corinthians 11:21, 33). They started eating and drinking at once. Their concern was for food, not to remember the death and Second Coming of Christ. Paul reminded them that the purpose of the Lord’s Supper was not to eat and drink. He said that they should wait for each other. He taught that at communion, each person should look in three directions: back to Calvary; within to examine oneself; and forward to the Lord’s return.

In this lesson, we have studied how to examine the historical–cultural background of a passage. Each time you do this, you will answer the same eleven questions.

We taught you to answer eight questions on the historical background of an entire book. You do this by answering five questions about the author and three questions about those to whom he wrote. Then you answer three questions about the specific passage you want to interpret.

We worked through an example with you. First, we examined the historical background of the entire book of First Corinthians. We answered five questions about the author and three questions about his audience. Then we looked at the historical–cultural background of a specific passage (1 Corinthians 11:17–34). We answered three questions on that specific passage.

Next, we will guide you to use what you learned in this lesson. We will proceed step by step, giving you the questions to answer. As you practice answering these same questions, your work will get easier. The Holy Spirit will help you as you pray. He will anoint your ministry as you correctly preach and teach God’s Word.

**Q:** What are the reasons for researching the historical-cultural backgrounds of Scripture?

**A:** 1 Times have changed. 2 Places have changed. 3 Customs have changed. 4 Circumstances have changed.

e) What was his purpose?

Paul wrote for two reasons: First, to correct problems that a person from the house of Cloe had told him about (1 Corinthians 1:11). These problems included division, lawsuits, and sexual sins (1 Corinthians 1–6). Second, he wrote to answer questions the Corinthians had asked in a letter (1 Corinthians 7:1–16:9). We will take a closer look at these problems and questions in the next chapter.

2. Answer three questions about those who received the biblical book.

a) Who were they?

The believers at Corinth

b) What was their city or town like?

Corinth was a big city on the northern shore of the Mediterranean Sea. It was known for business, immorality, and idolatry.

c) What was their social status?

The Corinthians were mostly Gentiles with a few Jews (See 1 Corinthians 6:9–11; 8:10; 12:13.) They were proud and educated—loved wisdom and knowledge (1 Corinthians 1:18–2:5; 4:10, 18; 5:2, 6; 8:1–13).

Now we have a good start toward correctly interpreting any verse in First Corinthians. You should be encouraged that you need to determine the historical background of a book only one time. After that, you can review it.

The Historical–Cultural Background of a Specific Passage

We have looked at how to find the historical background of an entire book. This gives us a good foundation to interpret the verses in that book. Still, there is the need to find the historical-cultural background of specific passages. For example, you may understand the historical background of Matthew. But you may still need to study the following:

• Historical references like the names in the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:1–17)

• Historical figures like the magi (Matthew 2:1–12)

• The meaning of cultural items like myrrh (Matthew 2:11)

• The historical background of the Pharisees, Sadducees, Herods, Herodians, and Zealots

• The location of places like Bethlehem, Jerusalem, Nazareth, Tyre, Sidon, Galilee, Capernaum, and others

• The religious laws about lepers and leprosy (Matthew 8:1–4)

• The social status of a centurion (Matthew 8:5–13); a tax collector (Matthew 9:9–12); and a Canaanite woman (Matthew 15:21–28)

• Religious items like phylacteries (Matthew 23:5)

As we look at the background of 1 Corinthians, we must understand specific considerations like the custom of eating food offered to idols (1 Corinthians 8) and how the Lord’s Supper was celebrated (1 Corinthians 11). To find the historical-cultural background of a specific passage, like 1 Corinthians 11:17–34, answer three questions:

1. How does the specific passage relate to the author’s purpose?

2. Are there any specific historical details to explain?

3. Are there any specific cultural details, like the following, to explain?

• Social roles, values, or customs

• Economic concerns

• Political matters

• Religious beliefs or practices

We will work through these three questions to examine the historical-cultural background of a specific passage.

Example: Finding the Historical-Cultural Background of 1 Corinthians 11:17–34

In the following directives I have no praise for you, for your meetings do more harm than good. In the first place, I hear that when you come together as a church, there are divisions among you, and to some extent I believe it. No doubt there have to be differences among you to show which of you have God’s approval. When you come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat, for as you eat, each of you goes ahead without waiting for anybody else. One remains hungry, another gets drunk. Don’t you have homes to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you for this? Certainly not! For I received from the Lord what I also passed on to you: The Lord Jesus, on the night he was betrayed, took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “This is my body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of me.” In the same way, after supper he took the cup, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this, whenever you drink it, in remembrance of me.” For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of sinning against the body and blood of the Lord. A man ought to examine himself before he eats of the bread and drinks of the cup. For anyone who eats and drinks without recognizing the body of the Lord eats and drinks judgment on himself. That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a number of you have fallen asleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would not come under judgment. When we are judged by the Lord, we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world. So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for each other. If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that when you meet together it may not result in judgment. And when I come I will give further directions. (1 Corinthians 11:17–34)

We address the three questions and their answers.

1. How does the specific passage relate to the author’s purpose?

Paul’s purpose in 1 Corinthians was to correct problems. One of these problems was what was happening at the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:17–34).

2. Are there any specific historical details to explain?

The early church met in homes to celebrate the Lord’s Supper. Jesus started this at the Passover Feast. Review Matthew 26:17–35. Our Lord taught that the bread and juice represent His body and blood of the New Covenant. (See question 3 that follows: religious beliefs.)

3. Are there any specific cultural details to explain? These could be the following:

• Social roles, values, or customs [For instance, the poor and rich were eating together. The poor, who probably arrived late because of long hours of work, were left hungry (1 Corinthians 11:21).]

• Economic concerns

• Political matters

• Religious beliefs or practices

The early believers met often, perhaps each week, to celebrate the Lord’s Supper as part of a meal. Each person brought something to share at the meal. But the Corinthians had forgotten the meaning of the meal. Those who arrived first, perhaps the wealthy, did not wait for others (1 Corinthians 11:21, 33). They started eating and drinking at once. Their concern was for food, not to remember the death and Second Coming of Christ. Paul reminded them that the purpose of the Lord’s Supper was not to eat and drink. He said that they should wait for each other. He taught that at communion, each person should look in three directions: back to Calvary; within to examine oneself; and forward to the Lord’s return.

In this lesson, we have studied how to examine the historical–cultural background of a passage. Each time you do this, you will answer the same eleven questions.

We taught you to answer eight questions on the historical background of an entire book. You do this by answering five questions about the author and three questions about those to whom he wrote. Then you answer three questions about the specific passage you want to interpret.

We worked through an example with you. First, we examined the historical background of the entire book of First Corinthians. We answered five questions about the author and three questions about his audience. Then we looked at the historical–cultural background of a specific passage (1 Corinthians 11:17–34). We answered three questions on that specific passage.

Next, we will guide you to use what you learned in this lesson. We will proceed step by step, giving you the questions to answer. As you practice answering these same questions, your work will get easier. The Holy Spirit will help you as you pray. He will anoint your ministry as you correctly preach and teach God’s Word.

**Q:** What are the reasons for researching the historical-cultural backgrounds of Scripture?

**A:** 1 Times have changed. 2 Places have changed. 3 Customs have changed. 4 Circumstances have changed.
