2. Comparison of Nouns in Different Translations

Using a different translation will help you look at a verse in a new way. Also, one translation may use a synonym, a different word having the same meaning as another word. For example, it is helpful to compare translations of Revelation 10:6.

This is Revelation 10:6 in the King James Version: “And sware by him that liveth for ever and ever, who created heaven, and the things that therein are, and the earth, and the things that therein are, and the sea, and the things which are therein, that there should be time no longer.”

In the New International Version: “And he swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created the heavens and all that is in them, the earth and all that is in it, and the sea and all that is in it, and said, ‘There will be no more delay!’”

In the New Century Version: “And he made a promise by the power of the One who lives forever and ever. He is the One who made the skies and all that is in them, the earth and all that is in it, and the sea and all that is in it. The angel promised, ‘There will be no more waiting!’”

We know that time continues after the return of Christ because Satan is bound for one thousand years (Revelation 20:2, 7).

Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. (1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV)

If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal. (1 Corinthians 13:1, NIV)

3. Finding Nouns in a Dictionary, Lexicon, or Concordance

A dictionary is a basic tool for interpreting the Bible. A Bible dictionary is like other dictionaries, but it focuses on the biblical languages of Hebrew and Greek. If you can own one, it is of great value. Bible dictionaries explain many biblical words like Pharisees, Sadducees, Sanhedrin, Babylon, magi, and such. Some examples of Bible dictionaries are The New Bible Dictionary by J. D. Douglas, Smith’s Bible Dictionary, and Baker’s Dictionary of Theology. There are many other Bible dictionaries, and all of them are helpful.

A lexicon is a unique type of dictionary. It lists words in the languages of Hebrew and Greek, so a student must be able to read a little bit in these languages to use a lexicon. A lexicon is an excellent tool to show word meanings in the Bible.

A few lexicons give the history, roots, or origin of a word (its etymology). But remember that the history of a word can be quite different from its meaning in the Bible. For instance, the root of September is seven , but September is our ninth month (Gibbs 1994, 75).

Some Bible students traced the roots of the word sin and show that it once referred to an archer who shot an arrow and missed the target. Thus, they say that sin is missing the target . But in the Bible, sin is not shooting your best at a good target and missing it a little. In Scripture, sin is more like shooting an arrow at God. As David said, “Against you, you only, have I sinned . . .” (Psalm 51:4). Sin is rebellion against God and describes Adam and Eve’s wrongdoing (Genesis 3). Likewise, we may think of sin as shooting at the wrong target ; sin is choosing to do what God says is wrong. It is lawlessness, refusing to submit to God’s rule or law over us (1 John 3:4).

While a lexicon can be a helpful tool, it is always best to use the Bible as our primary source. We should let the biblical context explain what words mean, rather than search for meaning in secondary sources outside of the Bible.

As you read the Bible, you will undoubtedly come across words you do not understand. This is somewhat like seeing a sign that says “Bridge Out” and driving on anyway. Instead of risking a mishap, look up the word you do not understand in a dictionary, a different version of the Bible, or a concordance. If you pass by words you do not know, you will surely read inaccurately. Unknown words guarantee an inadequate interpretation.

Mandrakes from Genesis 30:14

Abba from Galatians 4:6

Pharisees from Matthew 22:15

Sadducees from Matthew 22:23

Talent from Matthew 25:14–30

Money changers from John 2:14

A concordance, after a study Bible, is the most helpful tool for interpreting the Bible. In Chapter 1, we mentioned several kinds of concordances; remember that different concordances are available for the various versions of the Bible. A concordance is a type of index, an alphabetical listing of the words printed within the text of the Bible. Each word entry gives the Scripture references as well as a brief excerpt of the context in which the word occurs. Perhaps you have used a concordance to help you find a verse, when you could only remember one word in that verse. Or you may have used a concordance to study a character of the Bible, like Balaam or Mary Magdalene.

A concordance is also helpful in studying the meaning of words. Young’s Concordance , or one like it, helps you understand the background of words in Hebrew or Greek, even if you cannot read these languages. For example, look up the word life in Young’s Concordance . You will see that the Bible speaks of different kinds of life. The Greek word zoe, refers to eternal life. The concordance shows you all of the verses in the New Testament that translate this word zoe, such as Matthew 7:14; John 10:10, etc. In contrast to eternal life ( zoe ), there is earthly life ( psuche ). Young’s Concordance shows you most verses in the New Testament that translate the Greek word psuche, such as Matthew 2:20; 6:25, and so on. Your concordance has instructions for doing this kind of study: you use the number at the end of each word entry to find the corresponding number in the Hebrew and Greek dictionaries at the back of the concordance.

Students who desire to understand the Bible well should sacrifice to get a concordance. It will help you handle the Word of God correctly. Comparing zoe to psuche is like comparing an orange to a banana. Consider this proverb: A concordance helps you compare oranges to oranges, not oranges to bananas.

4. Cross-References and Parallel Passages

In Chapter 4, we studied circles of context. You practiced interpreting a verse in harmony with its local context, its book context, and its whole Bible context. Likewise, to understand the meaning of a noun, you can compare the way it is used in other verses. Begin by seeing how the same author used the word in another place. For example, suppose you are studying Acts 2:38. The NIV Study Bible does not give you any cross-references in Acts on receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit. But there are many parallel passages listed in the Life in the Spirit Study Bible.

“Peter replied, ‘Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit’” (Acts 2:38). To understand what Luke means by “the gift of the Spirit,” we must compare Luke with Luke. So we search for parallel verses that Luke wrote in Acts on the gift of the Holy Spirit.

On one occasion, while he was eating with them, he gave them this command: “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift my Father promised, which you have heard me speak about.” (Acts 1:4)

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John placed their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. (Acts 8:14–17)

While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message. The circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God. (Acts 10:44–46)

So if God gave them the same gift as he gave us, who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to think that I could oppose God? (Acts 11:17)

“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They answered, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” . . . On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. When Paul placed his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. (Acts 19:2–6)

Comparing Luke with Luke, in parallel passages, helps us understand what he means by the gift of the Spirit. For Luke, the gift of the Spirit is a spiritual experience that follows believing in Jesus. The apostles, those at Samaria, and those at Ephesus received the gift of the Spirit after water baptism. The purpose of this gift of the Spirit is not to bring new life—for the Spirit brings this to us when we believe. Rather, Luke emphasizes that the gift of the Spirit, after salvation, is to give us power to witness for Christ and serve Him (Luke 24:48–49; Acts 1:4; see also Luke 3:16).

Using a concordance is similar to using the cross-references in the margins of your Bible. But unlike a concordance, the cross-reference may guide you to parallel passages—ones that have the same meaning, but not the same words. Note that in the Gospels, you can find parallel passages by looking at the Scripture references under the headings or subdivisions, by looking in the margins, and by reading footnotes.

We have seen that nouns name a person, place, or thing. Then we studied some ways to find the meanings of nouns through context, comparing translations, and using other books. Now we will look at pronouns.

Pronouns: Words that Take the Place of Nouns

Personal Pronouns

We use pronouns in place of nouns. Pronouns make sentences shorter and more readable. For example, without pronouns, John 14:6 might read, “Jesus answered, ‘Jesus is the way and the truth and the life. No person comes to the Father except through Jesus.’” Because we use pronouns, the verse reads this way: “Jesus answered, ‘I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me’” (John 14:6).

As you can see in John 14:6, the pronoun I takes the place of Jesus , and refers back to Him. The word a pronoun replaces and refers back to is called the antecedent . ( Ante means “before,” and cedent is a form of “to go” in the Roman language, Latin. So an antecedent goes before a pronoun). There are thousands of nouns, but only a few pronouns.

“Jesus replied, ‘You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.’ ‘No,’ said Peter, ‘you shall never wash my feet.’ Jesus answered, ‘Unless I wash you, you have no part with me’” (John 13:7–8).

Place

Singular

Plural

here

this

these

there

that

those

Demonstrative (Definite/Specific) Pronouns

To study a noun, you examine its meaning. But to study a pronoun, you identify its antecedent. Sometimes, finding the antecedent of a pronoun is not easy. For example, read John 21:15, and look at the pronoun these : “When they had finished eating, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon son of John, do you truly love me more than these?’” (John 21:15). Is Jesus asking Peter,

• “Do you truly love me more than these other disciples love me?” or

• “Do you truly love me more than you love these other disciples?” or

• “Do you truly love me more than these nets, fish, and boat?”

Many teachers favor the first meaning. Peter had once claimed to love Jesus more than the other disciples loved Him (John 13:37; Matthew 26:33; Mark 14:29). Other respected teachers emphasize that the local context favors the third meaning. Peter had denied Christ three times, so Jesus asked him three times if he loved Him. Thus, in front of the other disciples, Jesus was restoring Peter. And each time, Jesus turned Peter’s attention away from the other disciples and the fishing business—toward feeding lambs and adult sheep. Even if you are not sure which meaning is correct, searching for the correct meaning will drive this verse deeper into your heart and spirit. Our example of John 21:15 emphasizes that the meaning of an entire verse can depend on one word.

“These men are not drunk, as you suppose. It’s only nine in the morning!” (Acts 2:15)

“No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16).

Matthew 16:13–20 raises a big question about the pronoun this. Is the church built upon Peter, or upon the revelation that Jesus is the Son of God?

When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” “But what about you?” he asked. “Who do you say I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for this was not revealed to you by man, but by my Father in heaven. And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it.” (Matthew 16:13–18)

Jesus blessed Peter for receiving a revelation from God. God revealed to Peter that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God (Matthew 16:17). If Christ had wanted to refer to Peter, He could have said, “You are Peter, and on you I will build my church.” Also, looking at other Scriptures, we find that the church is built upon Jesus, not Peter. When Peter himself writes about the church’s foundation, he speaks only of Jesus and says nothing about himself.

As you come to the living Stone, who was rejected by men but chosen by God and precious to him, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. For in Scripture it says:

“See, I lay a stone in Zion, a chosen and precious cornerstone, and the one who trusts in him will never be put to shame.” Now to you who believe, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the capstone,” and, “A stone that causes men to stumble and a rock that makes them fall.” (1 Peter 2:4–8)

Peter compares all believers to small stones that are a part of the church. Likewise, there is a sense in which all of the prophets and apostles—not just Peter—are stones in the foundation of the church; and Jesus is the chief cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

And remember the context of Paul’s words. He wrote to the Corinthians to eliminate division. Some were claiming to follow Paul and some Peter (1 Corinthians 1:12). Peter, Paul, and all true believers know that the church is built upon a great rock: the revelation that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.

Indefinite (Non-specific) Pronouns

Indefinite pronouns, such as all and everything , need special attention. For example, sometimes words like all mean all that the author is thinking about . For example, the word all in John 16:13 refers to all that we need to know: “But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all truth.”

“‘I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know his master’s business. Instead, I have called you friends, for everything that I learned from my Father I have made known to you’” (John 15:15).

**Q:** What is the antecedent of these —what does these refer to in John 21:15?

Peter had once claimed to love Jesus more than the other disciples loved Him (John 13:37; Matthew 26:33; Mark 14:29). On the other hand, many respected teachers emphasize that the local context favors the third meaning. Peter had denied Christ three times, so Jesus asked him three times if he loved Him. Thus, in front of the other disciples, Jesus was restoring Peter. And each time, Jesus turned Peter’s attention away from the other disciples and the fishing business—toward feeding lambs and adult sheep. Even if you are not sure which meaning is correct, searching for the correct meaning will drive this verse deeper into your heart and spirit. #### 5.1.2 — Explain four different ways to find the meaning of a noun.

Have you ever read a few sentences and then had to start over because you were not concentrating? It is possible to read without understanding. A wise reader is always asking him- or herself the question, “What does this mean?” Read again the following texts that you have already read before, and see if you understood them.

Remember, the best readers are continually asking themselves the question, “What does this mean?” David wrote: “How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm 119:103). This is a chapter about grammar — the study of words, and how they are used. But the study will be sweet because we are studying the Word of God!

Many people want to study and meditate on the Bible, but they do not know how. They can read a verse—even memorize it. But they do not know how to meditate on it or chew on it to get more sweetness from it. Use this opportunity to learn how to better understand the Word of God.

Words are like tools—they have different purposes. In this chapter, we will look at six elements of grammar that are used in the Bible: nouns , pronouns , verbs , adverbs , adjectives , and conjunctions .

A noun is the name of a person, place, or thing:

• A person such as Paul, Jesus, or the Holy Spirit

• A place such as Palestine, hell, or heaven

• A thing such as faith, the Law, or the temple

There is at least one noun in each verse of the Bible. Entries in dictionaries state whether a word is a noun, pronoun, verb, and so on.

Jesus said, “‘Listen to me, everyone, and understand’” in Mark 7:14. There is a difference. Listening does not guarantee understanding. Likewise, not all who read understand what they read. After Jesus said, “Listen and understand,” He said that all foods are clean (Mark 7:19). Peter listened, but he did not understand. Years later, when he was having a vision on Simon the Tanner’s rooftop, Peter still did not understand that all food is clean and none of it can defile us. Take time to understand what you read.

Examining Nouns

The purpose of finding nouns is to examine them. Always search for the meaning of nouns you are not sure about. There are at least four ways to find the meaning of a noun:

1. Local and Biblical Context of the Noun

Words can have many different meanings. In English, the word run has ninety different meanings. But a word has only one meaning within its verse or context. For example, the Greek word sarx, often translated “flesh,” has several meanings. (Notice that in the NIV, the translators often interpret the word sarx , instead of translating it as flesh.)

The Greek word sarx, often-translated “flesh,” has different meanings in different contexts.

2. Comparison of Nouns in Different Translations

Using a different translation will help you look at a verse in a new way. Also, one translation may use a synonym, a different word having the same meaning as another word. For example, it is helpful to compare translations of Revelation 10:6.

This is Revelation 10:6 in the King James Version: “And sware by him that liveth for ever and ever, who created heaven, and the things that therein are, and the earth, and the things that therein are, and the sea, and the things which are therein, that there should be time no longer.”

In the New International Version: “And he swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created the heavens and all that is in them, the earth and all that is in it, and the sea and all that is in it, and said, ‘There will be no more delay!’”

In the New Century Version: “And he made a promise by the power of the One who lives forever and ever. He is the One who made the skies and all that is in them, the earth and all that is in it, and the sea and all that is in it. The angel promised, ‘There will be no more waiting!’”

We know that time continues after the return of Christ because Satan is bound for one thousand years (Revelation 20:2, 7).

Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. (1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV)

If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal. (1 Corinthians 13:1, NIV)

3. Finding Nouns in a Dictionary, Lexicon, or Concordance

A dictionary is a basic tool for interpreting the Bible. A Bible dictionary is like other dictionaries, but it focuses on the biblical languages of Hebrew and Greek. If you can own one, it is of great value. Bible dictionaries explain many biblical words like Pharisees, Sadducees, Sanhedrin, Babylon, magi, and such. Some examples of Bible dictionaries are The New Bible Dictionary by J. D. Douglas, Smith’s Bible Dictionary, and Baker’s Dictionary of Theology. There are many other Bible dictionaries, and all of them are helpful.

A lexicon is a unique type of dictionary. It lists words in the languages of Hebrew and Greek, so a student must be able to read a little bit in these languages to use a lexicon. A lexicon is an excellent tool to show word meanings in the Bible.

A few lexicons give the history, roots, or origin of a word (its etymology). But remember that the history of a word can be quite different from its meaning in the Bible. For instance, the root of September is seven , but September is our ninth month (Gibbs 1994, 75).

Some Bible students traced the roots of the word sin and show that it once referred to an archer who shot an arrow and missed the target. Thus, they say that sin is missing the target . But in the Bible, sin is not shooting your best at a good target and missing it a little. In Scripture, sin is more like shooting an arrow at God. As David said, “Against you, you only, have I sinned . . .” (Psalm 51:4). Sin is rebellion against God and describes Adam and Eve’s wrongdoing (Genesis 3). Likewise, we may think of sin as shooting at the wrong target ; sin is choosing to do what God says is wrong. It is lawlessness, refusing to submit to God’s rule or law over us (1 John 3:4).

While a lexicon can be a helpful tool, it is always best to use the Bible as our primary source. We should let the biblical context explain what words mean, rather than search for meaning in secondary sources outside of the Bible.

As you read the Bible, you will undoubtedly come across words you do not understand. This is somewhat like seeing a sign that says “Bridge Out” and driving on anyway. Instead of risking a mishap, look up the word you do not understand in a dictionary, a different version of the Bible, or a concordance. If you pass by words you do not know, you will surely read inaccurately. Unknown words guarantee an inadequate interpretation.

Mandrakes from Genesis 30:14

Abba from Galatians 4:6

Pharisees from Matthew 22:15

Sadducees from Matthew 22:23

Talent from Matthew 25:14–30

Money changers from John 2:14

A concordance, after a study Bible, is the most helpful tool for interpreting the Bible. In Chapter 1, we mentioned several kinds of concordances; remember that different concordances are available for the various versions of the Bible. A concordance is a type of index, an alphabetical listing of the words printed within the text of the Bible. Each word entry gives the Scripture references as well as a brief excerpt of the context in which the word occurs. Perhaps you have used a concordance to help you find a verse, when you could only remember one word in that verse. Or you may have used a concordance to study a character of the Bible, like Balaam or Mary Magdalene.

A concordance is also helpful in studying the meaning of words. Young’s Concordance , or one like it, helps you understand the background of words in Hebrew or Greek, even if you cannot read these languages. For example, look up the word life in Young’s Concordance . You will see that the Bible speaks of different kinds of life. The Greek word zoe, refers to eternal life. The concordance shows you all of the verses in the New Testament that translate this word zoe, such as Matthew 7:14; John 10:10, etc. In contrast to eternal life ( zoe ), there is earthly life ( psuche ). Young’s Concordance shows you most verses in the New Testament that translate the Greek word psuche, such as Matthew 2:20; 6:25, and so on. Your concordance has instructions for doing this kind of study: you use the number at the end of each word entry to find the corresponding number in the Hebrew and Greek dictionaries at the back of the concordance.

Students who desire to understand the Bible well should sacrifice to get a concordance. It will help you handle the Word of God correctly. Comparing zoe to psuche is like comparing an orange to a banana. Consider this proverb: A concordance helps you compare oranges to oranges, not oranges to bananas.

4. Cross-References and Parallel Passages

In Chapter 4, we studied circles of context. You practiced interpreting a verse in harmony with its local context, its book context, and its whole Bible context. Likewise, to understand the meaning of a noun, you can compare the way it is used in other verses. Begin by seeing how the same author used the word in another place. For example, suppose you are studying Acts 2:38. The NIV Study Bible does not give you any cross-references in Acts on receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit. But there are many parallel passages listed in the Life in the Spirit Study Bible.

“Peter replied, ‘Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit’” (Acts 2:38). To understand what Luke means by “the gift of the Spirit,” we must compare Luke with Luke. So we search for parallel verses that Luke wrote in Acts on the gift of the Holy Spirit.

On one occasion, while he was eating with them, he gave them this command: “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift my Father promised, which you have heard me speak about.” (Acts 1:4)

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John placed their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. (Acts 8:14–17)

While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message. The circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God. (Acts 10:44–46)

So if God gave them the same gift as he gave us, who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to think that I could oppose God? (Acts 11:17)

“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They answered, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” . . . On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. When Paul placed his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. (Acts 19:2–6)

Comparing Luke with Luke, in parallel passages, helps us understand what he means by the gift of the Spirit. For Luke, the gift of the Spirit is a spiritual experience that follows believing in Jesus. The apostles, those at Samaria, and those at Ephesus received the gift of the Spirit after water baptism. The purpose of this gift of the Spirit is not to bring new life—for the Spirit brings this to us when we believe. Rather, Luke emphasizes that the gift of the Spirit, after salvation, is to give us power to witness for Christ and serve Him (Luke 24:48–49; Acts 1:4; see also Luke 3:16).

Using a concordance is similar to using the cross-references in the margins of your Bible. But unlike a concordance, the cross-reference may guide you to parallel passages—ones that have the same meaning, but not the same words. Note that in the Gospels, you can find parallel passages by looking at the Scripture references under the headings or subdivisions, by looking in the margins, and by reading footnotes.

We have seen that nouns name a person, place, or thing. Then we studied some ways to find the meanings of nouns through context, comparing translations, and using other books. Now we will look at pronouns.

Pronouns: Words that Take the Place of Nouns

Personal Pronouns

We use pronouns in place of nouns. Pronouns make sentences shorter and more readable. For example, without pronouns, John 14:6 might read, “Jesus answered, ‘Jesus is the way and the truth and the life. No person comes to the Father except through Jesus.’” Because we use pronouns, the verse reads this way: “Jesus answered, ‘I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me’” (John 14:6).

As you can see in John 14:6, the pronoun I takes the place of Jesus , and refers back to Him. The word a pronoun replaces and refers back to is called the antecedent . ( Ante means “before,” and cedent is a form of “to go” in the Roman language, Latin. So an antecedent goes before a pronoun). There are thousands of nouns, but only a few pronouns.

“Jesus replied, ‘You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.’ ‘No,’ said Peter, ‘you shall never wash my feet.’ Jesus answered, ‘Unless I wash you, you have no part with me’” (John 13:7–8).

Place

Singular

Plural

here

this

these

there

that

those

Demonstrative (Definite/Specific) Pronouns

To study a noun, you examine its meaning. But to study a pronoun, you identify its antecedent. Sometimes, finding the antecedent of a pronoun is not easy. For example, read John 21:15, and look at the pronoun these : “When they had finished eating, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon son of John, do you truly love me more than these?’” (John 21:15). Is Jesus asking Peter,

• “Do you truly love me more than these other disciples love me?” or

• “Do you truly love me more than you love these other disciples?” or

• “Do you truly love me more than these nets, fish, and boat?”

Many teachers favor the first meaning. Peter had once claimed to love Jesus more than the other disciples loved Him (John 13:37; Matthew 26:33; Mark 14:29). Other respected teachers emphasize that the local context favors the third meaning. Peter had denied Christ three times, so Jesus asked him three times if he loved Him. Thus, in front of the other disciples, Jesus was restoring Peter. And each time, Jesus turned Peter’s attention away from the other disciples and the fishing business—toward feeding lambs and adult sheep. Even if you are not sure which meaning is correct, searching for the correct meaning will drive this verse deeper into your heart and spirit. Our example of John 21:15 emphasizes that the meaning of an entire verse can depend on one word.

“These men are not drunk, as you suppose. It’s only nine in the morning!” (Acts 2:15)

“No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16).

Matthew 16:13–20 raises a big question about the pronoun this. Is the church built upon Peter, or upon the revelation that Jesus is the Son of God?

When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” “But what about you?” he asked. “Who do you say I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for this was not revealed to you by man, but by my Father in heaven. And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it.” (Matthew 16:13–18)

Jesus blessed Peter for receiving a revelation from God. God revealed to Peter that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God (Matthew 16:17). If Christ had wanted to refer to Peter, He could have said, “You are Peter, and on you I will build my church.” Also, looking at other Scriptures, we find that the church is built upon Jesus, not Peter. When Peter himself writes about the church’s foundation, he speaks only of Jesus and says nothing about himself.

As you come to the living Stone, who was rejected by men but chosen by God and precious to him, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. For in Scripture it says:

“See, I lay a stone in Zion, a chosen and precious cornerstone, and the one who trusts in him will never be put to shame.” Now to you who believe, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the capstone,” and, “A stone that causes men to stumble and a rock that makes them fall.” (1 Peter 2:4–8)

Peter compares all believers to small stones that are a part of the church. Likewise, there is a sense in which all of the prophets and apostles—not just Peter—are stones in the foundation of the church; and Jesus is the chief cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

And remember the context of Paul’s words. He wrote to the Corinthians to eliminate division. Some were claiming to follow Paul and some Peter (1 Corinthians 1:12). Peter, Paul, and all true believers know that the church is built upon a great rock: the revelation that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.

Indefinite (Non-specific) Pronouns

Indefinite pronouns, such as all and everything , need special attention. For example, sometimes words like all mean all that the author is thinking about . For example, the word all in John 16:13 refers to all that we need to know: “But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all truth.”

“‘I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know his master’s business. Instead, I have called you friends, for everything that I learned from my Father I have made known to you’” (John 15:15).

We are emphasizing the need to pay attention to each word in the Bible. Nouns and pronouns are some of the most important words in the Word of God.

**Q:** In Matthew 16:13–20, to what does this rock refer?

**A:** The Christ, the Son of the living God

**Q:** Upon whom did Paul say the church is built (1 Corinthians 3:11)?

**A:** Jesus Christ

**Q:** What does Jesus mean by everything in John 15:15?

**A:** The teaching of Jesus in its totality

#### 5.1.3 — Identify personal, demonstrative, and indefinite pronouns in Bible verses.

Have you ever read a few sentences and then had to start over because you were not concentrating? It is possible to read without understanding. A wise reader is always asking him- or herself the question, “What does this mean?” Read again the following texts that you have already read before, and see if you understood them.

Remember, the best readers are continually asking themselves the question, “What does this mean?” David wrote: “How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm 119:103). This is a chapter about grammar — the study of words, and how they are used. But the study will be sweet because we are studying the Word of God!

Many people want to study and meditate on the Bible, but they do not know how. They can read a verse—even memorize it. But they do not know how to meditate on it or chew on it to get more sweetness from it. Use this opportunity to learn how to better understand the Word of God.

Words are like tools—they have different purposes. In this chapter, we will look at six elements of grammar that are used in the Bible: nouns , pronouns , verbs , adverbs , adjectives , and conjunctions .

A noun is the name of a person, place, or thing:

• A person such as Paul, Jesus, or the Holy Spirit

• A place such as Palestine, hell, or heaven

• A thing such as faith, the Law, or the temple

There is at least one noun in each verse of the Bible. Entries in dictionaries state whether a word is a noun, pronoun, verb, and so on.

Jesus said, “‘Listen to me, everyone, and understand’” in Mark 7:14. There is a difference. Listening does not guarantee understanding. Likewise, not all who read understand what they read. After Jesus said, “Listen and understand,” He said that all foods are clean (Mark 7:19). Peter listened, but he did not understand. Years later, when he was having a vision on Simon the Tanner’s rooftop, Peter still did not understand that all food is clean and none of it can defile us. Take time to understand what you read.

Examining Nouns

The purpose of finding nouns is to examine them. Always search for the meaning of nouns you are not sure about. There are at least four ways to find the meaning of a noun:

1. Local and Biblical Context of the Noun

Words can have many different meanings. In English, the word run has ninety different meanings. But a word has only one meaning within its verse or context. For example, the Greek word sarx, often translated “flesh,” has several meanings. (Notice that in the NIV, the translators often interpret the word sarx , instead of translating it as flesh.)

The Greek word sarx, often-translated “flesh,” has different meanings in different contexts.

2. Comparison of Nouns in Different Translations

Using a different translation will help you look at a verse in a new way. Also, one translation may use a synonym, a different word having the same meaning as another word. For example, it is helpful to compare translations of Revelation 10:6.

This is Revelation 10:6 in the King James Version: “And sware by him that liveth for ever and ever, who created heaven, and the things that therein are, and the earth, and the things that therein are, and the sea, and the things which are therein, that there should be time no longer.”

In the New International Version: “And he swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created the heavens and all that is in them, the earth and all that is in it, and the sea and all that is in it, and said, ‘There will be no more delay!’”

In the New Century Version: “And he made a promise by the power of the One who lives forever and ever. He is the One who made the skies and all that is in them, the earth and all that is in it, and the sea and all that is in it. The angel promised, ‘There will be no more waiting!’”

We know that time continues after the return of Christ because Satan is bound for one thousand years (Revelation 20:2, 7).

Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. (1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV)

If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal. (1 Corinthians 13:1, NIV)

3. Finding Nouns in a Dictionary, Lexicon, or Concordance

A dictionary is a basic tool for interpreting the Bible. A Bible dictionary is like other dictionaries, but it focuses on the biblical languages of Hebrew and Greek. If you can own one, it is of great value. Bible dictionaries explain many biblical words like Pharisees, Sadducees, Sanhedrin, Babylon, magi, and such. Some examples of Bible dictionaries are The New Bible Dictionary by J. D. Douglas, Smith’s Bible Dictionary, and Baker’s Dictionary of Theology. There are many other Bible dictionaries, and all of them are helpful.

A lexicon is a unique type of dictionary. It lists words in the languages of Hebrew and Greek, so a student must be able to read a little bit in these languages to use a lexicon. A lexicon is an excellent tool to show word meanings in the Bible.

A few lexicons give the history, roots, or origin of a word (its etymology). But remember that the history of a word can be quite different from its meaning in the Bible. For instance, the root of September is seven , but September is our ninth month (Gibbs 1994, 75).

Some Bible students traced the roots of the word sin and show that it once referred to an archer who shot an arrow and missed the target. Thus, they say that sin is missing the target . But in the Bible, sin is not shooting your best at a good target and missing it a little. In Scripture, sin is more like shooting an arrow at God. As David said, “Against you, you only, have I sinned . . .” (Psalm 51:4). Sin is rebellion against God and describes Adam and Eve’s wrongdoing (Genesis 3). Likewise, we may think of sin as shooting at the wrong target ; sin is choosing to do what God says is wrong. It is lawlessness, refusing to submit to God’s rule or law over us (1 John 3:4).

While a lexicon can be a helpful tool, it is always best to use the Bible as our primary source. We should let the biblical context explain what words mean, rather than search for meaning in secondary sources outside of the Bible.

As you read the Bible, you will undoubtedly come across words you do not understand. This is somewhat like seeing a sign that says “Bridge Out” and driving on anyway. Instead of risking a mishap, look up the word you do not understand in a dictionary, a different version of the Bible, or a concordance. If you pass by words you do not know, you will surely read inaccurately. Unknown words guarantee an inadequate interpretation.

Mandrakes from Genesis 30:14

Abba from Galatians 4:6

Pharisees from Matthew 22:15

Sadducees from Matthew 22:23

Talent from Matthew 25:14–30

Money changers from John 2:14

A concordance, after a study Bible, is the most helpful tool for interpreting the Bible. In Chapter 1, we mentioned several kinds of concordances; remember that different concordances are available for the various versions of the Bible. A concordance is a type of index, an alphabetical listing of the words printed within the text of the Bible. Each word entry gives the Scripture references as well as a brief excerpt of the context in which the word occurs. Perhaps you have used a concordance to help you find a verse, when you could only remember one word in that verse. Or you may have used a concordance to study a character of the Bible, like Balaam or Mary Magdalene.

A concordance is also helpful in studying the meaning of words. Young’s Concordance , or one like it, helps you understand the background of words in Hebrew or Greek, even if you cannot read these languages. For example, look up the word life in Young’s Concordance . You will see that the Bible speaks of different kinds of life. The Greek word zoe, refers to eternal life. The concordance shows you all of the verses in the New Testament that translate this word zoe, such as Matthew 7:14; John 10:10, etc. In contrast to eternal life ( zoe ), there is earthly life ( psuche ). Young’s Concordance shows you most verses in the New Testament that translate the Greek word psuche, such as Matthew 2:20; 6:25, and so on. Your concordance has instructions for doing this kind of study: you use the number at the end of each word entry to find the corresponding number in the Hebrew and Greek dictionaries at the back of the concordance.

Students who desire to understand the Bible well should sacrifice to get a concordance. It will help you handle the Word of God correctly. Comparing zoe to psuche is like comparing an orange to a banana. Consider this proverb: A concordance helps you compare oranges to oranges, not oranges to bananas.

4. Cross-References and Parallel Passages

In Chapter 4, we studied circles of context. You practiced interpreting a verse in harmony with its local context, its book context, and its whole Bible context. Likewise, to understand the meaning of a noun, you can compare the way it is used in other verses. Begin by seeing how the same author used the word in another place. For example, suppose you are studying Acts 2:38. The NIV Study Bible does not give you any cross-references in Acts on receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit. But there are many parallel passages listed in the Life in the Spirit Study Bible.

“Peter replied, ‘Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit’” (Acts 2:38). To understand what Luke means by “the gift of the Spirit,” we must compare Luke with Luke. So we search for parallel verses that Luke wrote in Acts on the gift of the Holy Spirit.

On one occasion, while he was eating with them, he gave them this command: “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift my Father promised, which you have heard me speak about.” (Acts 1:4)

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John placed their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. (Acts 8:14–17)

While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message. The circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God. (Acts 10:44–46)

So if God gave them the same gift as he gave us, who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to think that I could oppose God? (Acts 11:17)

“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They answered, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” . . . On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. When Paul placed his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. (Acts 19:2–6)

Comparing Luke with Luke, in parallel passages, helps us understand what he means by the gift of the Spirit. For Luke, the gift of the Spirit is a spiritual experience that follows believing in Jesus. The apostles, those at Samaria, and those at Ephesus received the gift of the Spirit after water baptism. The purpose of this gift of the Spirit is not to bring new life—for the Spirit brings this to us when we believe. Rather, Luke emphasizes that the gift of the Spirit, after salvation, is to give us power to witness for Christ and serve Him (Luke 24:48–49; Acts 1:4; see also Luke 3:16).

Using a concordance is similar to using the cross-references in the margins of your Bible. But unlike a concordance, the cross-reference may guide you to parallel passages—ones that have the same meaning, but not the same words. Note that in the Gospels, you can find parallel passages by looking at the Scripture references under the headings or subdivisions, by looking in the margins, and by reading footnotes.

We have seen that nouns name a person, place, or thing. Then we studied some ways to find the meanings of nouns through context, comparing translations, and using other books. Now we will look at pronouns.

Pronouns: Words that Take the Place of Nouns

Personal Pronouns

We use pronouns in place of nouns. Pronouns make sentences shorter and more readable. For example, without pronouns, John 14:6 might read, “Jesus answered, ‘Jesus is the way and the truth and the life. No person comes to the Father except through Jesus.’” Because we use pronouns, the verse reads this way: “Jesus answered, ‘I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me’” (John 14:6).

As you can see in John 14:6, the pronoun I takes the place of Jesus , and refers back to Him. The word a pronoun replaces and refers back to is called the antecedent . ( Ante means “before,” and cedent is a form of “to go” in the Roman language, Latin. So an antecedent goes before a pronoun). There are thousands of nouns, but only a few pronouns.

“Jesus replied, ‘You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.’ ‘No,’ said Peter, ‘you shall never wash my feet.’ Jesus answered, ‘Unless I wash you, you have no part with me’” (John 13:7–8).

Place

Singular

Plural

here

this

these

there

that

those

Demonstrative (Definite/Specific) Pronouns

To study a noun, you examine its meaning. But to study a pronoun, you identify its antecedent. Sometimes, finding the antecedent of a pronoun is not easy. For example, read John 21:15, and look at the pronoun these : “When they had finished eating, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon son of John, do you truly love me more than these?’” (John 21:15). Is Jesus asking Peter,

• “Do you truly love me more than these other disciples love me?” or

• “Do you truly love me more than you love these other disciples?” or

• “Do you truly love me more than these nets, fish, and boat?”

Many teachers favor the first meaning. Peter had once claimed to love Jesus more than the other disciples loved Him (John 13:37; Matthew 26:33; Mark 14:29). Other respected teachers emphasize that the local context favors the third meaning. Peter had denied Christ three times, so Jesus asked him three times if he loved Him. Thus, in front of the other disciples, Jesus was restoring Peter. And each time, Jesus turned Peter’s attention away from the other disciples and the fishing business—toward feeding lambs and adult sheep. Even if you are not sure which meaning is correct, searching for the correct meaning will drive this verse deeper into your heart and spirit. Our example of John 21:15 emphasizes that the meaning of an entire verse can depend on one word.

“These men are not drunk, as you suppose. It’s only nine in the morning!” (Acts 2:15)

“No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16).

Matthew 16:13–20 raises a big question about the pronoun this. Is the church built upon Peter, or upon the revelation that Jesus is the Son of God?

When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” “But what about you?” he asked. “Who do you say I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for this was not revealed to you by man, but by my Father in heaven. And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it.” (Matthew 16:13–18)

Jesus blessed Peter for receiving a revelation from God. God revealed to Peter that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God (Matthew 16:17). If Christ had wanted to refer to Peter, He could have said, “You are Peter, and on you I will build my church.” Also, looking at other Scriptures, we find that the church is built upon Jesus, not Peter. When Peter himself writes about the church’s foundation, he speaks only of Jesus and says nothing about himself.

As you come to the living Stone, who was rejected by men but chosen by God and precious to him, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. For in Scripture it says:

“See, I lay a stone in Zion, a chosen and precious cornerstone, and the one who trusts in him will never be put to shame.” Now to you who believe, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the capstone,” and, “A stone that causes men to stumble and a rock that makes them fall.” (1 Peter 2:4–8)

Peter compares all believers to small stones that are a part of the church. Likewise, there is a sense in which all of the prophets and apostles—not just Peter—are stones in the foundation of the church; and Jesus is the chief cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

And remember the context of Paul’s words. He wrote to the Corinthians to eliminate division. Some were claiming to follow Paul and some Peter (1 Corinthians 1:12). Peter, Paul, and all true believers know that the church is built upon a great rock: the revelation that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.

Indefinite (Non-specific) Pronouns

Indefinite pronouns, such as all and everything , need special attention. For example, sometimes words like all mean all that the author is thinking about . For example, the word all in John 16:13 refers to all that we need to know: “But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all truth.”

“‘I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know his master’s business. Instead, I have called you friends, for everything that I learned from my Father I have made known to you’” (John 15:15).

2. Comparison of Nouns in Different Translations

Using a different translation will help you look at a verse in a new way. Also, one translation may use a synonym, a different word having the same meaning as another word. For example, it is helpful to compare translations of Revelation 10:6.

This is Revelation 10:6 in the King James Version: “And sware by him that liveth for ever and ever, who created heaven, and the things that therein are, and the earth, and the things that therein are, and the sea, and the things which are therein, that there should be time no longer.”

In the New International Version: “And he swore by him who lives for ever and ever, who created the heavens and all that is in them, the earth and all that is in it, and the sea and all that is in it, and said, ‘There will be no more delay!’”

In the New Century Version: “And he made a promise by the power of the One who lives forever and ever. He is the One who made the skies and all that is in them, the earth and all that is in it, and the sea and all that is in it. The angel promised, ‘There will be no more waiting!’”

We know that time continues after the return of Christ because Satan is bound for one thousand years (Revelation 20:2, 7).

Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal. (1 Corinthians 13:1, KJV)

If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am only a resounding gong or a clanging cymbal. (1 Corinthians 13:1, NIV)

3. Finding Nouns in a Dictionary, Lexicon, or Concordance

A dictionary is a basic tool for interpreting the Bible. A Bible dictionary is like other dictionaries, but it focuses on the biblical languages of Hebrew and Greek. If you can own one, it is of great value. Bible dictionaries explain many biblical words like Pharisees, Sadducees, Sanhedrin, Babylon, magi, and such. Some examples of Bible dictionaries are The New Bible Dictionary by J. D. Douglas, Smith’s Bible Dictionary, and Baker’s Dictionary of Theology. There are many other Bible dictionaries, and all of them are helpful.

A lexicon is a unique type of dictionary. It lists words in the languages of Hebrew and Greek, so a student must be able to read a little bit in these languages to use a lexicon. A lexicon is an excellent tool to show word meanings in the Bible.

A few lexicons give the history, roots, or origin of a word (its etymology). But remember that the history of a word can be quite different from its meaning in the Bible. For instance, the root of September is seven , but September is our ninth month (Gibbs 1994, 75).

Some Bible students traced the roots of the word sin and show that it once referred to an archer who shot an arrow and missed the target. Thus, they say that sin is missing the target . But in the Bible, sin is not shooting your best at a good target and missing it a little. In Scripture, sin is more like shooting an arrow at God. As David said, “Against you, you only, have I sinned . . .” (Psalm 51:4). Sin is rebellion against God and describes Adam and Eve’s wrongdoing (Genesis 3). Likewise, we may think of sin as shooting at the wrong target ; sin is choosing to do what God says is wrong. It is lawlessness, refusing to submit to God’s rule or law over us (1 John 3:4).

While a lexicon can be a helpful tool, it is always best to use the Bible as our primary source. We should let the biblical context explain what words mean, rather than search for meaning in secondary sources outside of the Bible.

As you read the Bible, you will undoubtedly come across words you do not understand. This is somewhat like seeing a sign that says “Bridge Out” and driving on anyway. Instead of risking a mishap, look up the word you do not understand in a dictionary, a different version of the Bible, or a concordance. If you pass by words you do not know, you will surely read inaccurately. Unknown words guarantee an inadequate interpretation.

Mandrakes from Genesis 30:14

Abba from Galatians 4:6

Pharisees from Matthew 22:15

Sadducees from Matthew 22:23

Talent from Matthew 25:14–30

Money changers from John 2:14

A concordance, after a study Bible, is the most helpful tool for interpreting the Bible. In Chapter 1, we mentioned several kinds of concordances; remember that different concordances are available for the various versions of the Bible. A concordance is a type of index, an alphabetical listing of the words printed within the text of the Bible. Each word entry gives the Scripture references as well as a brief excerpt of the context in which the word occurs. Perhaps you have used a concordance to help you find a verse, when you could only remember one word in that verse. Or you may have used a concordance to study a character of the Bible, like Balaam or Mary Magdalene.

A concordance is also helpful in studying the meaning of words. Young’s Concordance , or one like it, helps you understand the background of words in Hebrew or Greek, even if you cannot read these languages. For example, look up the word life in Young’s Concordance . You will see that the Bible speaks of different kinds of life. The Greek word zoe, refers to eternal life. The concordance shows you all of the verses in the New Testament that translate this word zoe, such as Matthew 7:14; John 10:10, etc. In contrast to eternal life ( zoe ), there is earthly life ( psuche ). Young’s Concordance shows you most verses in the New Testament that translate the Greek word psuche, such as Matthew 2:20; 6:25, and so on. Your concordance has instructions for doing this kind of study: you use the number at the end of each word entry to find the corresponding number in the Hebrew and Greek dictionaries at the back of the concordance.

Students who desire to understand the Bible well should sacrifice to get a concordance. It will help you handle the Word of God correctly. Comparing zoe to psuche is like comparing an orange to a banana. Consider this proverb: A concordance helps you compare oranges to oranges, not oranges to bananas.

4. Cross-References and Parallel Passages

In Chapter 4, we studied circles of context. You practiced interpreting a verse in harmony with its local context, its book context, and its whole Bible context. Likewise, to understand the meaning of a noun, you can compare the way it is used in other verses. Begin by seeing how the same author used the word in another place. For example, suppose you are studying Acts 2:38. The NIV Study Bible does not give you any cross-references in Acts on receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit. But there are many parallel passages listed in the Life in the Spirit Study Bible.

“Peter replied, ‘Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins. And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit’” (Acts 2:38). To understand what Luke means by “the gift of the Spirit,” we must compare Luke with Luke. So we search for parallel verses that Luke wrote in Acts on the gift of the Holy Spirit.

On one occasion, while he was eating with them, he gave them this command: “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift my Father promised, which you have heard me speak about.” (Acts 1:4)

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then Peter and John placed their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit. (Acts 8:14–17)

While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message. The circumcised believers who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles. For they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God. (Acts 10:44–46)

So if God gave them the same gift as he gave us, who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to think that I could oppose God? (Acts 11:17)

“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They answered, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” . . . On hearing this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. When Paul placed his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. (Acts 19:2–6)

Comparing Luke with Luke, in parallel passages, helps us understand what he means by the gift of the Spirit. For Luke, the gift of the Spirit is a spiritual experience that follows believing in Jesus. The apostles, those at Samaria, and those at Ephesus received the gift of the Spirit after water baptism. The purpose of this gift of the Spirit is not to bring new life—for the Spirit brings this to us when we believe. Rather, Luke emphasizes that the gift of the Spirit, after salvation, is to give us power to witness for Christ and serve Him (Luke 24:48–49; Acts 1:4; see also Luke 3:16).

Using a concordance is similar to using the cross-references in the margins of your Bible. But unlike a concordance, the cross-reference may guide you to parallel passages—ones that have the same meaning, but not the same words. Note that in the Gospels, you can find parallel passages by looking at the Scripture references under the headings or subdivisions, by looking in the margins, and by reading footnotes.

We have seen that nouns name a person, place, or thing. Then we studied some ways to find the meanings of nouns through context, comparing translations, and using other books. Now we will look at pronouns.

Pronouns: Words that Take the Place of Nouns

Personal Pronouns

We use pronouns in place of nouns. Pronouns make sentences shorter and more readable. For example, without pronouns, John 14:6 might read, “Jesus answered, ‘Jesus is the way and the truth and the life. No person comes to the Father except through Jesus.’” Because we use pronouns, the verse reads this way: “Jesus answered, ‘I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me’” (John 14:6).

As you can see in John 14:6, the pronoun I takes the place of Jesus , and refers back to Him. The word a pronoun replaces and refers back to is called the antecedent . ( Ante means “before,” and cedent is a form of “to go” in the Roman language, Latin. So an antecedent goes before a pronoun). There are thousands of nouns, but only a few pronouns.

“Jesus replied, ‘You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.’ ‘No,’ said Peter, ‘you shall never wash my feet.’ Jesus answered, ‘Unless I wash you, you have no part with me’” (John 13:7–8).

Place

Singular

Plural

here

those

Demonstrative (Definite/Specific) Pronouns

To study a noun, you examine its meaning. But to study a pronoun, you identify its antecedent. Sometimes, finding the antecedent of a pronoun is not easy. For example, read John 21:15, and look at the pronoun these : “When they had finished eating, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon son of John, do you truly love me more than these?’” (John 21:15). Is Jesus asking Peter,

• “Do you truly love me more than these other disciples love me?” or

• “Do you truly love me more than you love these other disciples?” or

• “Do you truly love me more than these nets, fish, and boat?”

Many teachers favor the first meaning. Peter had once claimed to love Jesus more than the other disciples loved Him (John 13:37; Matthew 26:33; Mark 14:29). Other respected teachers emphasize that the local context favors the third meaning. Peter had denied Christ three times, so Jesus asked him three times if he loved Him. Thus, in front of the other disciples, Jesus was restoring Peter. And each time, Jesus turned Peter’s attention away from the other disciples and the fishing business—toward feeding lambs and adult sheep. Even if you are not sure which meaning is correct, searching for the correct meaning will drive this verse deeper into your heart and spirit. Our example of John 21:15 emphasizes that the meaning of an entire verse can depend on one word.

“These men are not drunk, as you suppose. It’s only nine in the morning!” (Acts 2:15)

“No, this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16).

Matthew 16:13–20 raises a big question about the pronoun this. Is the church built upon Peter, or upon the revelation that Jesus is the Son of God?

When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” They replied, “Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” “But what about you?” he asked. “Who do you say I am?” Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replied, “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for this was not revealed to you by man, but by my Father in heaven. And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it.” (Matthew 16:13–18)

Jesus blessed Peter for receiving a revelation from God. God revealed to Peter that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God (Matthew 16:17). If Christ had wanted to refer to Peter, He could have said, “You are Peter, and on you I will build my church.” Also, looking at other Scriptures, we find that the church is built upon Jesus, not Peter. When Peter himself writes about the church’s foundation, he speaks only of Jesus and says nothing about himself.

As you come to the living Stone, who was rejected by men but chosen by God and precious to him, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. For in Scripture it says:

“See, I lay a stone in Zion, a chosen and precious cornerstone, and the one who trusts in him will never be put to shame.” Now to you who believe, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe, “The stone the builders rejected has become the capstone,” and, “A stone that causes men to stumble and a rock that makes them fall.” (1 Peter 2:4–8)

Peter compares all believers to small stones that are a part of the church. Likewise, there is a sense in which all of the prophets and apostles—not just Peter—are stones in the foundation of the church; and Jesus is the chief cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

And remember the context of Paul’s words. He wrote to the Corinthians to eliminate division. Some were claiming to follow Paul and some Peter (1 Corinthians 1:12). Peter, Paul, and all true believers know that the church is built upon a great rock: the revelation that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.

Indefinite (Non-specific) Pronouns

Indefinite pronouns, such as all and everything , need special attention. For example, sometimes words like all mean all that the author is thinking about . For example, the word all in John 16:13 refers to all that we need to know: “But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all truth.”

“‘I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know his master’s business. Instead, I have called you friends, for everything that I learned from my Father I have made known to you’” (John 15:15).

### Verbs, Adverbs, Adjectives, and Conjunctions

#### 5.2.1 — Define verbs and show how to examine their meaning.

Verbs: Words that Show Action, Being, or State of Being

In the early 1500s, a German monk studied the verb repent. In Greek, this word is meta-noeo. Meta means “change,” and noeo is a form of the word, mind ; so metanoeo is “to change one’s mind” (Gingrich 1965, 136). The monk was amazed. He had understood from the Catholic Church that to repent meant to do penance, to confess his sins or pay for them in some way. In contrast, to repent means to “change one’s mind toward sin, to turn away from it.” As the monk continued to study, he discovered that repentance was between him and God, not between him and a priest or his church. All of this knowledge came as he studied the meaning of the word repent. The monk Martin Luther continued to study the Scriptures. In time, he led believers back to the Bible. Today, millions of people are thankful that he studied the meaning of a verb in the Bible (Gibbs 1994, 72).

Some verbs show action. A verb shows action, and a related noun (the subject) tells who is doing or receiving the action. For example, look at the verbs italicized in these sentences: (The first three examples are active verbs, since the subject is doing the action, not receiving the action).

• Jesus took the cup.

• Cornelius saw a vision.

• God has forgiven our sins.

• Jesus was baptized . (passive verb form—something is being done to Jesus, the subject).

Some verbs show relationship, or state of being.

• Jesus is Lord.

• I am Alpha and Omega.

• We are more than conquerors.

• We were sinners, but now we are saints.

Some verbs have little meaning alone, but they help other verbs. We call these helping verbs. Such verbs are can, could, do, have, has, had, let, may, might, and must. Here are examples:

• Only God can number the stars of the heaven or the hairs on one’s head.

• The royal administrators could find no fault in Daniel.

• “These are written that you may believe” (John 20:31).

• Many things must happen before the end comes.

The passage below contains fifteen verbs.

The Pharisees heard that Jesus was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John, although in fact it was not Jesus who baptized, but his disciples. When the Lord learned of this, he left Judea and went back once more to Galilee. Now he had to go through Samaria. So he came to a town in Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there, and Jesus, tired as he was from the journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour. (John 4:1–6)

Verb Meanings

In interpreting the Bible, search for the meaning of a verb in four ways:

1. Examine the local context.

2. Compare the verse in several translations.

3. Use a dictionary or concordance.

4. Compare cross-references and parallel passages.

For example, examine the meaning of the verb hate in Luke 14:26. “‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, his wife and children, his brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be my disciple’” (Luke 14:26). At first, Luke 14:26 is hard to understand. Jesus taught us to love even our enemies (Luke 6:27). Surely He wants us to love and honor our parents. A cross-reference guides us to Matthew 10:37: “‘Anyone who loves his father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me’” (Matthew 10:37).

Comparing these two verses brings clarification. We understand that we must love Jesus more than all others, even more than our parents. Thus, to hate parents, in Luke 14:26, means to love them less. (Another helpful passage, by another author, in another testament is Genesis 29:31).

Compare translations of Matthew 5:48: “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48, NIV). “In a word, what I’m saying is, ‘Grow up.’ You’re kingdom subjects. Now live like it. Live out your God-created identity. Live generously and graciously toward others, the way God lives toward you ” (Matthew 5:48, The Message ).

Verb Tense

To understand a verb, you must understand its tense, the time to which it refers. Verbs refer to such times as past, present, and future. For example, consider 1 John 3:6: “No one who lives in him [ sins ] keeps on sinning. No one who [ sins ] continues to sin has either seen him or known him” (1 John 3:6).

In the Greek, this verb shows present action that continues. First John 3:6 does not mean that believers have never sinned. John wrote that all of us have sinned in the past (1 John 1:8, 10). Likewise, John sees that some, especially children in the faith, may sin in the future (1 John 2:1, 12–14). John encourages all that our sins are forgiven as we confess them and walk in the light (1 John 1:7, 9). So what does 1 John 3:6 mean? The NIV translators have helped us by translating the Greek word sins as “continues to sin.” So we see that John means true believers do not make sin a habit. In another place John wrote “everyone who sins is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). Likewise, John quotes Jesus as saying, “‘Stop sinning or something worse may happen to you’” (John 5:14). The meaning of sin in John 5:14 and 8:34 is the same as in 1 John 3:6. Those who follow Jesus do not practice sinning. Sin is no longer our habit, custom, or master. We turn away from the darkness and walk in the light (1 John 1:5–6).

For a thorough review of verb tenses consult an English grammar book.

Adjectives: Words That Describe Nouns and Pronouns

Adjectives are words that make the meaning of a noun or pronoun clearer. In the examples that follow, the noun is in italics and the adjective is underlined. Notice how the adjectives tell more about the noun they describe.

Chief priests

“Go and make a careful search. ” (Matthew 2:8)

Then he took the seven loaves . (Matthew 15:36)

Among the most necessary adjectives are the simple words a and the . Consider the difference in a son of God and the son of God . Any male believer may be called a son of God . But only Jesus is the son of God—this obviously carries the meaning that Jesus is unique and one of a kind. First Timothy 6:10 carries a good example of the word the .

• For the love of money is the root of all evil. (1 Timothy 6:10, KJV)

• For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. (1 Timothy 6:10, NIV)

In the Greek, the word the does not appear before root, so in this verse, the NIV is the better translation. The love of money is not the only root of evil. Satan did not fall from heaven because of the love of money. David did not commit adultery with Bathsheba because of the love of money. But the love of money is a root of many kinds of evil. Achan stole because he loved money. Ahab murdered Naboth because of the love of money (wealth). Judas stole often because he loved money (John 12:6). The love of money is a root of evil, but not the root. Adjectives help people to more accurately comprehend sentences. Pay attention to adjectives:

23 Underline the adjectives by the nouns in the adjacent three sentences. When a gentle south wind began to blow . . . (Acts 27:13)

To Philemon our dear friend and fellow worker (Philemon 1)

Your love has given me great joy. (Philemon 7) Identify four types of adverbs in the Bible.

Adverbs: Words That Describe Verbs

As adjectives describe nouns, adverbs describe verbs. Adverbs can also describe adjectives or other adverbs. Adverbs can tell how actions are done: slowly, quickly, poorly, or well. There are several kinds of adverbs.

Adverbs of manner answer the question: How?

• “What you are about to do, do quickly. ” (John 13:27)

• “I tell you, he will see that they get justice, and quickly. ” (Luke 18:8)

• “ Well done, good and faithful servant!” (Matthew 25:21)

In Genesis 41:32, the adverb is firmly : The reason the dream was given to Pharaoh in two forms is that the matter has been firmly decided by God.

Adverbs of time answer the question: When or in what order?

• Then the cherubim, with the wheels beside them, spread their wings. (Ezekiel 11:22)

• And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles. (1 Corinthians 12:28)

Adverbs of place answer the question: Where?

• “ Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather.” (Matthew 24:28)

• “Come up here , and I will show you what must take place after this.” (Revelation 4:1)

Adverbs of degree (amount) answer the question: How much?

• “But in order not to weary you further, I would request that you be kind enough to hear us briefly. ” (Acts 24: 4)

• I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting the one who called you. (Galatians 1:6)

Pay attention to adverbs because they give clues to the true meaning.

Conjunctions: Words That Connect Thoughts

The word conjunction comes from two Latin words: con (“with”), and junctio (“join”). Conjunctions are word bridges—they join one thought with another. Examples of conjunctions are therefore , so , because , but , and, and yet .

Too often, people read past these connecting words. A rule of hermeneutics is: When you see a word like therefore , see what it is there for . For example, look at Romans 12:1. “ Therefore , I urge you, brothers, in view of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God—this is your spiritual act of worship” (Romans 12:1).

In Romans 12:1, the word therefore is a bridge between what Paul has said in Romans 9–11, and what he asks in Romans 12:1. In Romans 9–11, Paul reminds us that God has shown mercy on us Gentiles. We were grafted into the family of God (Romans 11:17–21). God has been very kind to us (Romans 11:22). Therefore , Paul urges us to show that we are thankful by offering our lives to Him (Romans 12:1).

The type of bridge or connecting word affects the meaning. Note how the meaning changes when the connecting word changes:

• I follow Christ because I believe.

• I follow Christ; therefore, I believe.

Connecting Word

“‘Either in this age or in the age to come’” (Matthew 12:32).

cause and effect or reason and result
