#### 5.2.2 — Define adjectives and identify them in a given Bible verse.

Verbs: Words that Show Action, Being, or State of Being

In the early 1500s, a German monk studied the verb repent. In Greek, this word is meta-noeo. Meta means “change,” and noeo is a form of the word, mind ; so metanoeo is “to change one’s mind” (Gingrich 1965, 136). The monk was amazed. He had understood from the Catholic Church that to repent meant to do penance, to confess his sins or pay for them in some way. In contrast, to repent means to “change one’s mind toward sin, to turn away from it.” As the monk continued to study, he discovered that repentance was between him and God, not between him and a priest or his church. All of this knowledge came as he studied the meaning of the word repent. The monk Martin Luther continued to study the Scriptures. In time, he led believers back to the Bible. Today, millions of people are thankful that he studied the meaning of a verb in the Bible (Gibbs 1994, 72).

Some verbs show action. A verb shows action, and a related noun (the subject) tells who is doing or receiving the action. For example, look at the verbs italicized in these sentences: (The first three examples are active verbs, since the subject is doing the action, not receiving the action).

• Jesus took the cup.

• Cornelius saw a vision.

• God has forgiven our sins.

• Jesus was baptized . (passive verb form—something is being done to Jesus, the subject).

Some verbs show relationship, or state of being.

• Jesus is Lord.

• I am Alpha and Omega.

• We are more than conquerors.

• We were sinners, but now we are saints.

Some verbs have little meaning alone, but they help other verbs. We call these helping verbs. Such verbs are can, could, do, have, has, had, let, may, might, and must. Here are examples:

• Only God can number the stars of the heaven or the hairs on one’s head.

• The royal administrators could find no fault in Daniel.

• “These are written that you may believe” (John 20:31).

• Many things must happen before the end comes.

The passage below contains fifteen verbs.

The Pharisees heard that Jesus was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John, although in fact it was not Jesus who baptized, but his disciples. When the Lord learned of this, he left Judea and went back once more to Galilee. Now he had to go through Samaria. So he came to a town in Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there, and Jesus, tired as he was from the journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour. (John 4:1–6)

Verb Meanings

In interpreting the Bible, search for the meaning of a verb in four ways:

1. Examine the local context.

2. Compare the verse in several translations.

3. Use a dictionary or concordance.

4. Compare cross-references and parallel passages.

For example, examine the meaning of the verb hate in Luke 14:26. “‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, his wife and children, his brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be my disciple’” (Luke 14:26). At first, Luke 14:26 is hard to understand. Jesus taught us to love even our enemies (Luke 6:27). Surely He wants us to love and honor our parents. A cross-reference guides us to Matthew 10:37: “‘Anyone who loves his father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me’” (Matthew 10:37).

Comparing these two verses brings clarification. We understand that we must love Jesus more than all others, even more than our parents. Thus, to hate parents, in Luke 14:26, means to love them less. (Another helpful passage, by another author, in another testament is Genesis 29:31).

Compare translations of Matthew 5:48: “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48, NIV). “In a word, what I’m saying is, ‘Grow up.’ You’re kingdom subjects. Now live like it. Live out your God-created identity. Live generously and graciously toward others, the way God lives toward you ” (Matthew 5:48, The Message ).

Verb Tense

To understand a verb, you must understand its tense, the time to which it refers. Verbs refer to such times as past, present, and future. For example, consider 1 John 3:6: “No one who lives in him [ sins ] keeps on sinning. No one who [ sins ] continues to sin has either seen him or known him” (1 John 3:6).

In the Greek, this verb shows present action that continues. First John 3:6 does not mean that believers have never sinned. John wrote that all of us have sinned in the past (1 John 1:8, 10). Likewise, John sees that some, especially children in the faith, may sin in the future (1 John 2:1, 12–14). John encourages all that our sins are forgiven as we confess them and walk in the light (1 John 1:7, 9). So what does 1 John 3:6 mean? The NIV translators have helped us by translating the Greek word sins as “continues to sin.” So we see that John means true believers do not make sin a habit. In another place John wrote “everyone who sins is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). Likewise, John quotes Jesus as saying, “‘Stop sinning or something worse may happen to you’” (John 5:14). The meaning of sin in John 5:14 and 8:34 is the same as in 1 John 3:6. Those who follow Jesus do not practice sinning. Sin is no longer our habit, custom, or master. We turn away from the darkness and walk in the light (1 John 1:5–6).

For a thorough review of verb tenses consult an English grammar book.

Adjectives: Words That Describe Nouns and Pronouns

Adjectives are words that make the meaning of a noun or pronoun clearer. In the examples that follow, the noun is in italics and the adjective is underlined. Notice how the adjectives tell more about the noun they describe.

Chief priests

“Go and make a careful search. ” (Matthew 2:8)

Then he took the seven loaves . (Matthew 15:36)

Among the most necessary adjectives are the simple words a and the . Consider the difference in a son of God and the son of God . Any male believer may be called a son of God . But only Jesus is the son of God—this obviously carries the meaning that Jesus is unique and one of a kind. First Timothy 6:10 carries a good example of the word the .

• For the love of money is the root of all evil. (1 Timothy 6:10, KJV)

• For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. (1 Timothy 6:10, NIV)

In the Greek, the word the does not appear before root, so in this verse, the NIV is the better translation. The love of money is not the only root of evil. Satan did not fall from heaven because of the love of money. David did not commit adultery with Bathsheba because of the love of money. But the love of money is a root of many kinds of evil. Achan stole because he loved money. Ahab murdered Naboth because of the love of money (wealth). Judas stole often because he loved money (John 12:6). The love of money is a root of evil, but not the root. Adjectives help people to more accurately comprehend sentences. Pay attention to adjectives:

23 Underline the adjectives by the nouns in the adjacent three sentences. When a gentle south wind began to blow . . . (Acts 27:13)

To Philemon our dear friend and fellow worker (Philemon 1)

Your love has given me great joy. (Philemon 7) Identify four types of adverbs in the Bible.

• I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting the one who called you. (Galatians 1:6)

We were grafted into the family of God (Romans 11:17–21). God has been very kind to us (Romans 11:22). Therefore , Paul urges us to show that we are thankful by offering our lives to Him (Romans 12:1).

• I follow Christ because I believe.

• I follow Christ; therefore, I believe.

“For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor demons, neither the present nor the future, nor any powers, neither height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39).

3. To transition—change from one thought to another

Finally, then, also, and

“Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord!” (Philippians 3:1).

4. To link a condition to an action or a promise

If … (then)

Condition: “For if you live according to the sinful nature,

Promise: [then] you will die;

Condition: but if by the Spirit you put to death the misdeeds of the body,

Promise: [then] you will live” (Romans 8:13).

5. To link

cause and effect or reason and result

Therefore, so then, because,

in order that, for

Result: “‘Blessed are the poor in spirit,

Reason: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’” (Matthew 5:3).

**A:** The Pharisees heard that Jesus was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John, although in fact it was not Jesus who baptized , but his disciples. When the Lord learned of this, he left Judea and went back once more to Galilee. Now he had to go through Samaria. So he came to a town in Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there, and Jesus, tired as he was from the journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour (John 4:1–6). Please note that the word “called” does not function as a verb in the paragraph above. When the word “called” within a sentence means “named,” “chosen,” or “designated,” it is functioning as an adjective to describe a noun. In this case, the words “called Sychar” describe the noun “town.” When the word “called” is used within a sentence to tell the action of a noun or pronoun, then the word “called” functions a verb. For instance, Juan called the doctor; In my dreams, Copenhagen called me home; A lost goose called out for its flock. In those three examples, the word “called” is a verb.

#### 5.2.4 — Summarize five ways conjunctions are used and give examples of each way.

Verbs: Words that Show Action, Being, or State of Being

In the early 1500s, a German monk studied the verb repent. In Greek, this word is meta-noeo. Meta means “change,” and noeo is a form of the word, mind ; so metanoeo is “to change one’s mind” (Gingrich 1965, 136). The monk was amazed. He had understood from the Catholic Church that to repent meant to do penance, to confess his sins or pay for them in some way. In contrast, to repent means to “change one’s mind toward sin, to turn away from it.” As the monk continued to study, he discovered that repentance was between him and God, not between him and a priest or his church. All of this knowledge came as he studied the meaning of the word repent. The monk Martin Luther continued to study the Scriptures. In time, he led believers back to the Bible. Today, millions of people are thankful that he studied the meaning of a verb in the Bible (Gibbs 1994, 72).

Some verbs show action. A verb shows action, and a related noun (the subject) tells who is doing or receiving the action. For example, look at the verbs italicized in these sentences: (The first three examples are active verbs, since the subject is doing the action, not receiving the action).

• Jesus took the cup.

• Cornelius saw a vision.

• God has forgiven our sins.

• Jesus was baptized . (passive verb form—something is being done to Jesus, the subject).

Some verbs show relationship, or state of being.

• Jesus is Lord.

• I am Alpha and Omega.

• We are more than conquerors.

• We were sinners, but now we are saints.

Some verbs have little meaning alone, but they help other verbs. We call these helping verbs. Such verbs are can, could, do, have, has, had, let, may, might, and must. Here are examples:

• Only God can number the stars of the heaven or the hairs on one’s head.

• The royal administrators could find no fault in Daniel.

• “These are written that you may believe” (John 20:31).

• Many things must happen before the end comes.

The passage below contains fifteen verbs.

The Pharisees heard that Jesus was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John, although in fact it was not Jesus who baptized, but his disciples. When the Lord learned of this, he left Judea and went back once more to Galilee. Now he had to go through Samaria. So he came to a town in Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there, and Jesus, tired as he was from the journey, sat down by the well. It was about the sixth hour. (John 4:1–6)

Verb Meanings

In interpreting the Bible, search for the meaning of a verb in four ways:

1. Examine the local context.

2. Compare the verse in several translations.

3. Use a dictionary or concordance.

4. Compare cross-references and parallel passages.

For example, examine the meaning of the verb hate in Luke 14:26. “‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, his wife and children, his brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be my disciple’” (Luke 14:26). At first, Luke 14:26 is hard to understand. Jesus taught us to love even our enemies (Luke 6:27). Surely He wants us to love and honor our parents. A cross-reference guides us to Matthew 10:37: “‘Anyone who loves his father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me’” (Matthew 10:37).

Comparing these two verses brings clarification. We understand that we must love Jesus more than all others, even more than our parents. Thus, to hate parents, in Luke 14:26, means to love them less. (Another helpful passage, by another author, in another testament is Genesis 29:31).

Compare translations of Matthew 5:48: “Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48, NIV). “In a word, what I’m saying is, ‘Grow up.’ You’re kingdom subjects. Now live like it. Live out your God-created identity. Live generously and graciously toward others, the way God lives toward you ” (Matthew 5:48, The Message ).

Verb Tense

To understand a verb, you must understand its tense, the time to which it refers. Verbs refer to such times as past, present, and future. For example, consider 1 John 3:6: “No one who lives in him [ sins ] keeps on sinning. No one who [ sins ] continues to sin has either seen him or known him” (1 John 3:6).

In the Greek, this verb shows present action that continues. First John 3:6 does not mean that believers have never sinned. John wrote that all of us have sinned in the past (1 John 1:8, 10). Likewise, John sees that some, especially children in the faith, may sin in the future (1 John 2:1, 12–14). John encourages all that our sins are forgiven as we confess them and walk in the light (1 John 1:7, 9). So what does 1 John 3:6 mean? The NIV translators have helped us by translating the Greek word sins as “continues to sin.” So we see that John means true believers do not make sin a habit. In another place John wrote “everyone who sins is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). Likewise, John quotes Jesus as saying, “‘Stop sinning or something worse may happen to you’” (John 5:14). The meaning of sin in John 5:14 and 8:34 is the same as in 1 John 3:6. Those who follow Jesus do not practice sinning. Sin is no longer our habit, custom, or master. We turn away from the darkness and walk in the light (1 John 1:5–6).

For a thorough review of verb tenses consult an English grammar book.

Adjectives: Words That Describe Nouns and Pronouns

Adjectives are words that make the meaning of a noun or pronoun clearer. In the examples that follow, the noun is in italics and the adjective is underlined. Notice how the adjectives tell more about the noun they describe.

Chief priests

“Go and make a careful search. ” (Matthew 2:8)

Then he took the seven loaves . (Matthew 15:36)

Among the most necessary adjectives are the simple words a and the . Consider the difference in a son of God and the son of God . Any male believer may be called a son of God . But only Jesus is the son of God—this obviously carries the meaning that Jesus is unique and one of a kind. First Timothy 6:10 carries a good example of the word the .

• For the love of money is the root of all evil. (1 Timothy 6:10, KJV)

• For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. (1 Timothy 6:10, NIV)

In the Greek, the word the does not appear before root, so in this verse, the NIV is the better translation. The love of money is not the only root of evil. Satan did not fall from heaven because of the love of money. David did not commit adultery with Bathsheba because of the love of money. But the love of money is a root of many kinds of evil. Achan stole because he loved money. Ahab murdered Naboth because of the love of money (wealth). Judas stole often because he loved money (John 12:6). The love of money is a root of evil, but not the root. Adjectives help people to more accurately comprehend sentences. Pay attention to adjectives:

23 Underline the adjectives by the nouns in the adjacent three sentences. When a gentle south wind began to blow . . . (Acts 27:13)

To Philemon our dear friend and fellow worker (Philemon 1)

Your love has given me great joy. (Philemon 7) Identify four types of adverbs in the Bible.

Adverbs: Words That Describe Verbs

As adjectives describe nouns, adverbs describe verbs. Adverbs can also describe adjectives or other adverbs. Adverbs can tell how actions are done: slowly, quickly, poorly, or well. There are several kinds of adverbs.

Adverbs of manner answer the question: How?

• “What you are about to do, do quickly. ” (John 13:27)

• “I tell you, he will see that they get justice, and quickly. ” (Luke 18:8)

• “ Well done, good and faithful servant!” (Matthew 25:21)

In Genesis 41:32, the adverb is firmly : The reason the dream was given to Pharaoh in two forms is that the matter has been firmly decided by God.

Adverbs of time answer the question: When or in what order?

• Then the cherubim, with the wheels beside them, spread their wings. (Ezekiel 11:22)

• And in the church God has appointed first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then workers of miracles. (1 Corinthians 12:28)

Adverbs of place answer the question: Where?

• “ Wherever there is a carcass, there the vultures will gather.” (Matthew 24:28)

• “Come up here , and I will show you what must take place after this.” (Revelation 4:1)

Adverbs of degree (amount) answer the question: How much?

• “But in order not to weary you further, I would request that you be kind enough to hear us briefly. ” (Acts 24: 4)

• I am astonished that you are so quickly deserting the one who called you. (Galatians 1:6)

Pay attention to adverbs because they give clues to the true meaning.

Conjunctions: Words That Connect Thoughts

The word conjunction comes from two Latin words: con (“with”), and junctio (“join”). Conjunctions are word bridges—they join one thought with another. Examples of conjunctions are therefore , so , because , but , and, and yet .

Too often, people read past these connecting words. A rule of hermeneutics is: When you see a word like therefore , see what it is there for . For example, look at Romans 12:1. “ Therefore , I urge you, brothers, in view of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God—this is your spiritual act of worship” (Romans 12:1).

In Romans 12:1, the word therefore is a bridge between what Paul has said in Romans 9–11, and what he asks in Romans 12:1. In Romans 9–11, Paul reminds us that God has shown mercy on us Gentiles. We were grafted into the family of God (Romans 11:17–21). God has been very kind to us (Romans 11:22). Therefore , Paul urges us to show that we are thankful by offering our lives to Him (Romans 12:1).

The type of bridge or connecting word affects the meaning. Note how the meaning changes when the connecting word changes:

• I follow Christ because I believe.

• I follow Christ; therefore, I believe.

### Analyze Word Relationships

#### 5.3.1 — Analyze the relationship of words in a Bible verse.

We can improve our interpretation skills if we learn to understand sentence construction and the nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and conjunctions that build the sentences of the Bible. The relationships between the elements of grammar are critical to our understanding of Scripture’s meanings.

A sentence begins with a capital letter and ends with a period. It has a subject and verb, along with words and groups of words related to the subject and verb. Each sentence may contain several nouns and verbs. But there is one noun in a sentence that is the most important: the subject. The subject and verb give direction to the sentence as they often lead the other words in the sentence. [Note that in sentences of command, the subject is an understood you , as in “‘[You] Go and tell my brothers’” (Matthew 28:10).] We can discover the relationships between words in a sentence by asking who , how , which , what , where , why , and when of the sentence. Bear in mind, however, that not all of these questions will be answered in any given sentence.

As we consider word relationships in Scripture, let us look at John 15:14: “‘You are my friends if you do what I command.’” Practice answering the seven questions as they are applied to this Scripture. The subject is “You.”

How?

Which?

What?

Where?

Why?

When?

Notice that while the subject and verb pull the sentence along, sometimes you will ask a question that has no answer. For example, there is no logical answer to the how, which, where, and when of John 15:14. But do not be confused; continue to ask questions. Some of the questions will always prove to be helpful.

Some verses in the Bible are very long. The longer the sentence, the harder it is to relate all of the words to each other. Still, remember to ask the seven questions whenever you study a verse. Begin with who and what to find the subject and verb. Now, try a sentence that has over seventy words.

It was he who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, to prepare God’s people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up until we all reach unity in the faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God and become mature, attaining to the whole measure of the fullness of Christ. (Ephesians 4:11–13)

Note that not all sentences begin with the subject. Therefore, it is necessary to identify the subject and main verb from among the several nouns and verbs in a sentence.

Suppose you are at a large gathering, and you have to find a husband and wife whom you have never met. You know that if you find the one spouse, you may soon find the other because they are a couple. You could find one of them by asking questions of those in the room. He could be the first person you approach. But eventually you would find him and his wife.

Finding the subject and verb of a sentence could be compared to finding a husband and wife in a room full of people. You succeed through asking questions. We may divide most sentences into two parts: a) the subject and verb; b) all other words and groups of words that answer questions related to the subject and verb.

Here are two rules to use when you ask questions to find the subject and verb:

1. Only questions that begin with Who or What will help you find the subject.

2. Questions that begin with How , Which , Where , Why , or When will lead to a part of the sentence that is not the subject. (Exceptions to this rule are sentences that begin with Then . In such cases, the subject comes after Then, as in Matthew 15:1 and 16:24).

Let us practice this technique by using John 3:16. If we are looking for the subject, rule one tells us to ask only questions using Who or What . Thus, the response to the question Who loved? is the subject, God . Rule two tells us that questions beginning with How , Which , Where , Why , or When will lead us away from the subject.

You may have noticed that questions beginning with Who (or Whom ) and What might also lead to other words as in James 1:2–3. However, this does not violate rule one. It only means you might have to choose between two nouns to see which is the subject. Usually the subject will be the first noun in the sentence that answers a question beginning with Who or What .

a) Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” (Romans 5:1)

Because it answers a why question.

b) As they traveled along the road, they came to some water and the eunuch said, “Look, here is water. Why shouldn’t I be baptized?” (Acts 8:36)

c) About noon the following day as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray. (Acts 10:9)

d) After Jesus was born in Bethlehem in Judea, during the time of King Herod, Magi from the east came to Jerusalem. (Matthew 2:1)

e) When King Herod heard this he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. (Matthew 2:3)

f) When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” (Matthew 16:13)

g) Furthermore, since they did not think it worthwhile to retain the knowledge of God, he gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what ought not to be done. (Romans 1:28)

Identifying the subject is like finding a specific man in a room full of people. It helps to know if he is wearing a black or blue suit. Then, you would not look for him in a brown or gray suit. Rules one and two help us find the subject. Rule one tells us that if we are looking for the subject, we should ask only Who or What questions. The subject is normally the first noun in the sentence that answers a Who or What question. Rule two tells us that questions beginning with How , Which , Where , Why , or When will lead us away from the subject. Sometimes we ask these types of questions first when we are looking for the subject. In this way we can identify groups of words where the subject will not be found. If we know where the subject is not, we are left with fewer places to search.

**A:** How? N/A Which? N/A What? My friends Where? N/A Why? If you do my command When? N/A

**Q:** Who are the five types of people (gifts) Jesus gave?

**A:** Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers

**Q:** Why did Jesus give five types of gifts to the church?

**A:** To prepare God’s people for works of service, so that the body of Christ may be built up until we all reach unity

**Q:** How mature does Jesus want believers to become?

**A:** Attaining to the whole measure of fullness of Christ

**Q:** In John 3:16, where do the questions that begin with why or how lead you?

**A:** Why? For God so loved the world How? He gave His Son.

**A:** Yes.

## 6 - Principles about Language

### Literal and Figurative Language

#### 6.1.1 — Explain the difference between literal and figurative language, and give an example of each.

God gave us Scripture to reveal himself and His will to mankind. The purpose of the Bible is to clarify, not confuse. Scripture is not a collection of dark mysteries or riddles. It is a plain message from God to humanity. When interpreting a text, look for the plainest meaning—the one that is the most obvious, natural, and simple. Sometimes the language of Scripture is literal (exact) , but other times it is figurative (symbolic) (Stein 1998, 147).

Literal Language

Literal language is plain, direct, common speech. It is straight to the point. There are no symbols in literal language.

Consider the following, literal passage:

On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Paul spoke to the people and, because he intended to leave the next day, kept on talking until midnight. There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were meeting. Seated in a window was a young man named Eutychus, who was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on. When he was sound asleep, he fell to the ground from the third story and was picked up dead. Paul went down, threw himself on the young man and put his arms around him. “Don’t be alarmed,” he said. “He’s alive!” Then he went upstairs again and broke bread and ate. After talking until daylight, he left. The people took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted. (Acts 20:7–12)

Do not ask what “midnight” represents in the second sentence of the above passage. It does not represent anything. Rather, Luke was merely telling us what time it was. Likewise, in Acts 20:7–12, do not ask what the lamps, the three stories, the window, the deep sleep, or Eutychus represent. Again, they do not represent anything. Each word means what it says. This passage uses literal language. There are no symbols in it. It teaches that believers met together to share the Lord’s Supper. Paul talked on and on. Eutychus fell asleep and fell out the window. The fall killed him. God performed a miracle; when Paul held Eutychus, life came back to him.

A preacher once compared worldly Christians to Eutychus. He said that as Eutychus slept too close to an open window, some Christians stay too close to sin. We can agree with this. The preacher was using the passage as an illustration. This is acceptable. You may teach that Eutychus was sleepy, but do not teach that he was worldly. Just as Jesus used salt, light, sheep, and so on, to illustrate truth, preachers may use the Bible to illustrate truth. Nevertheless, if you want to preach on worldly Christians, do not take your main text from Acts 20:7–12. This text is not a passage about worldly Christians, though it could illustrate them. For a message on worldly Christians, use a text like 1 Corinthians 3:1: “Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual but as worldly—mere infants in Christ.”

Matthew 17:1 records that Peter, James, and John climbed a mountain with Jesus. This is literal language. The word mountain in this verse is not a symbol for something else. Do not try to interpret this verse figuratively. Do not try to make the mountain represent something different from the physical, rocky hill they climbed. In this verse you must understand the word mountain in a literal sense or you will misinterpret the text. In this case, the natural meaning is the literal meaning.

Figurative Language

You must interpret plain speech in a plain way, or you will not understand it. In contrast, you must discern that some verses use symbols, or you will stumble.

In Revelation 17:1, John saw a prostitute sitting on many waters. This is not literal language. Later, John tells us that the harlot is a city that rules over the earth (Revelation 17:18). The waters she sits on are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages (Revelation 17:15). The language of Revelation 17:1 is figurative, not literal. Figurative language has a hidden meaning. It uses symbols, and each symbol represents something else. In Revelation 17, the prostitute is a symbol for a big city, perhaps Rome. As a prostitute leads people away from God into sin, Rome led people away from God into sin. Likewise, in Revelation 17, water is a symbol for people. If you have ever looked at a very large crowd of thousands of people, you know that the people cover the earth like a large lake of water covers the earth.

John liked to use figurative language; he used a lot of symbols. More than other writers, John often gives us the words of Jesus that have a hidden meaning. “Jesus answered them, ‘Destroy this temple, and I will raise it again in three days.’ The Jews replied, ‘It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and you are going to raise it in three days?’ But the temple he had spoken of was his body” (John 2:19–21).

“‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. This bread is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.’ Then the Jews began to argue sharply among themselves, ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’” (John 6:51–52).

Notice that the people stumbled over the words of Jesus. He had just fed them with real loaves and fish (John 6). Then, they thought He wanted them to eat His flesh! Later, Jesus told the disciples that His words had a hidden, spirit–meaning. He said that the flesh counts for nothing; that is, eating flesh does not give spiritual life (John 6:60–63). Rather, Jesus wanted all to receive Him as the bread from heaven, the One God sent to feed our spiritual hunger.

John records that people—even the apostles—often failed to interpret the words of Jesus correctly. They did not discern that He was using symbols. “‘Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep; but I am going there to wake him up.’ His disciples replied, ‘Lord, if he sleeps, he will get better.’ Jesus had been speaking of his death, but his disciples thought he meant natural sleep. So then he told them plainly, ‘Lazarus is dead’” (John 11:11–14).

Jesus used figurative language in John 11:11. He said Lazarus was asleep. In this case, sleep was a symbol for death. But the disciples did not interpret the words of Jesus correctly. They thought that sleep would make Lazarus feel better (John 11:12). Since they did not understand figurative language, Jesus spoke to them plainly, “‘Lazarus is dead’” (John 11:14).

Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God and who it is that asks you for a drink, you would have asked him and he would have given you living water.” (John 4:10)

On the last and greatest day of the Feast, Jesus stood and said in a loud voice, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, streams of living water will flow from within him.” By this he meant the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were later to receive. Up to that time the Spirit had not been given, since Jesus had not yet been glorified. (John 7:37–39)

Jesus used living water as a symbol for the Holy Spirit. As water satisfies the thirst of our bodies, the Holy Spirit satisfies our spiritual thirst. (Compare Revelation 22:17 and Matthew 3:11.)

Discerning between Literal and Figurative Language

Scripture has only one meaning: either literal or figurative. So never interpret a verse in two different ways! If a verse uses plain language, you must interpret it that way. And if a verse has symbols, you must interpret the symbols. But how do you know whether a verse is using plain language or symbols, whether it is literal or figurative? We will consider three rules that will help you.

Rule one: When the plain, literal message of the Bible makes sense, seek no other sense (Henrichsen 1981, 49–50). In other words, always try first to interpret a verse in a plain, direct, literal way. If this first method makes sense, accept the verse as plain and direct. Do not search for symbols and hidden meanings.

In our daily language, people do not intend for what they say to have more than one meaning. If a man says that he rode a bus from the city to the village, he means just that. He does not desire for us to interpret his words to mean that he crossed over life’s trials into the Promised Land. If you can interpret a verse literally, do not try to interpret it figuratively.

Rule two: If the plain, literal message does not make sense, look for symbols or a hidden meaning. When the literal meaning of words does not make sense, look for another way to interpret the words.

For example, Jesus said that the eye is the lamp of the body (Matthew 6:22). It does not make sense to think of the eye as a literal lamp. So we realize that Jesus is using figurative language. In Matthew 6:19–24, Jesus was talking to His disciples about their relationship to wealth and masters. He told them that their hearts, their inner desires, would be where they put their treasure. Also, He told them that they could not choose two masters; they must choose either God or money. When our desires are to please God, we see clearly how to live in this world. But if our desires are to gain money, we will stumble over many things. If our eye (our inner desire) is to please God, our whole being will be filled with the light of His presence. He will guide us on the right path.

3 Explain the meaning of “cloud” in Hebrews 12:1. Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off everything that hinders and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us. (Hebrews 12:1)

4 Explain the words “eyes full of adultery” in 2 Peter 2:14. With eyes full of adultery, they never stop sinning; they seduce the unstable; they are experts in greed—an accursed brood! (2 Peter 2:14)

There has been a long debate over the Lord’s words, “This is my body” (Matthew 26:26). Was the bread His body, or did it represent His body? Luther insisted on a literal interpretation. At one discussion, he took a knife and carved these words in Latin on the table: “This is my body.” Others of us believe that the bread is a symbol for the Lord’s body. Jesus did not grab His arm and say, “This is my body.” He was using the bread as a symbol to represent His body and the contents of the cup as a symbol of His blood.

Rule 3: Look for explanations in the context. Many times, the Bible tells us whether the language is literal or uses symbols.

• Matthew wrote, “Jesus told them another parable” (Matthew 13:24). The word parable tells us at once that there is a hidden meaning in the story.

• Daniel tells us that Nebuchadnezzar had a dream to interpret (Daniel 2). So we know that there are symbols in the verses from the dream. Likewise, the animals in Daniel 7 represent kingdoms. This is easy to see from the context, which gives us explanations.

• We know that the vision Peter had in Acts 10 had a hidden meaning. Luke makes this clear in the context, and tells us what the vision meant.

• John often explained that Jesus used symbols, like the temple (John 2), living water (John 4), bread (John 6), light (John 8), sheep (John 10), sleeping (John 11), a vine (John 15), and so forth. In these cases, John makes it clear to readers that Jesus uses figurative speech, words as symbols with hidden meaning.

Twisting the plain, literal meaning of Scripture started long ago. Some people like to search for a hidden meaning in every verse of the Bible. During some dark periods in church history people have misused the plain, literal, truth of the Scriptures. One teacher, living a few centuries after the apostles, could not accept the plain meaning of God’s Old Testament commandments. God’s direction to the ancient Hebrews had been to eat only animals that had a divided hoof and chewed the cud. The confused teacher made this interpretation of that commandment: “Those who chew the cud are Christians who meditate on the Word. The divided hoof means that the righteous walk in this world, but also look for the holy world to come” (Stott 1977, 22). We can agree that “chewing the cud” can be compared to meditating on Scripture. We can also agree that a Christian is a citizen of two worlds. But we cannot agree that Moses meant this when he wrote about animals with split hooves that chew the cud (Stott 1977, 22).

It is dangerous to ignore the plain meaning of a verse and search for a hidden meaning. When we do not accept the natural, plain meaning of a text, we do not accept the Word of God. When we preach and teach a message other than the plain meaning of a text, we are not preaching God’s Word but our own imagination. Remember, God has promised that His Word will inspire faith and will not return to Him void. But He has not promised to bless each person’s wild interpretations. Interpret literal language in a direct way. Discern the symbols in figurative language. Use the three rules we gave you to interpret verses.

**Q:** In John 6:51–52, why did most people misunderstand Jesus?

**A:** Because Jesus used figurative language but the people interpreted his teaching literally

**Q:** In John 4:10 and John 7:38, “living water” is a symbol for what?

**A:** The Holy Spirit

**Q:** Explain the meaning of “cloud” in Hebrews 12:1.

**A:** The cloud refers to the collection of faithful servants of God who have died and are with God in the heavenlies. It is a figurative way of describing those who are above, yet whose example and standards surround those still alive.

**Q:** Explain the words “eyes full of adultery” in 2 Peter 2:14.

**A:** This figure of speech points to the nature of wicked humans to lust after everything they see, especially that which belongs to another and requires deceit or treachery to acquire.

#### 6.1.2 — Summarize and use three rules for discerning between literal and figurative language.

God gave us Scripture to reveal himself and His will to mankind. The purpose of the Bible is to clarify, not confuse. Scripture is not a collection of dark mysteries or riddles. It is a plain message from God to humanity. When interpreting a text, look for the plainest meaning—the one that is the most obvious, natural, and simple. Sometimes the language of Scripture is literal (exact) , but other times it is figurative (symbolic) (Stein 1998, 147).

Literal Language

Literal language is plain, direct, common speech. It is straight to the point. There are no symbols in literal language.

Consider the following, literal passage:

On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Paul spoke to the people and, because he intended to leave the next day, kept on talking until midnight. There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were meeting. Seated in a window was a young man named Eutychus, who was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul talked on and on. When he was sound asleep, he fell to the ground from the third story and was picked up dead. Paul went down, threw himself on the young man and put his arms around him. “Don’t be alarmed,” he said. “He’s alive!” Then he went upstairs again and broke bread and ate. After talking until daylight, he left. The people took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted. (Acts 20:7–12)

Do not ask what “midnight” represents in the second sentence of the above passage. It does not represent anything. Rather, Luke was merely telling us what time it was. Likewise, in Acts 20:7–12, do not ask what the lamps, the three stories, the window, the deep sleep, or Eutychus represent. Again, they do not represent anything. Each word means what it says. This passage uses literal language. There are no symbols in it. It teaches that believers met together to share the Lord’s Supper. Paul talked on and on. Eutychus fell asleep and fell out the window. The fall killed him. God performed a miracle; when Paul held Eutychus, life came back to him.

A preacher once compared worldly Christians to Eutychus. He said that as Eutychus slept too close to an open window, some Christians stay too close to sin. We can agree with this. The preacher was using the passage as an illustration. This is acceptable. You may teach that Eutychus was sleepy, but do not teach that he was worldly. Just as Jesus used salt, light, sheep, and so on, to illustrate truth, preachers may use the Bible to illustrate truth. Nevertheless, if you want to preach on worldly Christians, do not take your main text from Acts 20:7–12. This text is not a passage about worldly Christians, though it could illustrate them. For a message on worldly Christians, use a text like 1 Corinthians 3:1: “Brothers, I could not address you as spiritual but as worldly—mere infants in Christ.”

Matthew 17:1 records that Peter, James, and John climbed a mountain with Jesus. This is literal language. The word mountain in this verse is not a symbol for something else. Do not try to interpret this verse figuratively. Do not try to make the mountain represent something different from the physical, rocky hill they climbed. In this verse you must understand the word mountain in a literal sense or you will misinterpret the text. In this case, the natural meaning is the literal meaning.

Figurative Language

You must interpret plain speech in a plain way, or you will not understand it. In contrast, you must discern that some verses use symbols, or you will stumble.

In Revelation 17:1, John saw a prostitute sitting on many waters. This is not literal language. Later, John tells us that the harlot is a city that rules over the earth (Revelation 17:18). The waters she sits on are peoples, multitudes, nations, and languages (Revelation 17:15). The language of Revelation 17:1 is figurative, not literal. Figurative language has a hidden meaning. It uses symbols, and each symbol represents something else. In Revelation 17, the prostitute is a symbol for a big city, perhaps Rome. As a prostitute leads people away from God into sin, Rome led people away from God into sin. Likewise, in Revelation 17, water is a symbol for people. If you have ever looked at a very large crowd of thousands of people, you know that the people cover the earth like a large lake of water covers the earth.

John liked to use figurative language; he used a lot of symbols. More than other writers, John often gives us the words of Jesus that have a hidden meaning. “Jesus answered them, ‘Destroy this temple, and I will raise it again in three days.’ The Jews replied, ‘It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and you are going to raise it in three days?’ But the temple he had spoken of was his body” (John 2:19–21).

“‘I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. This bread is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.’ Then the Jews began to argue sharply among themselves, ‘How can this man give us his flesh to eat?’” (John 6:51–52).

Notice that the people stumbled over the words of Jesus. He had just fed them with real loaves and fish (John 6). Then, they thought He wanted them to eat His flesh! Later, Jesus told the disciples that His words had a hidden, spirit–meaning. He said that the flesh counts for nothing; that is, eating flesh does not give spiritual life (John 6:60–63). Rather, Jesus wanted all to receive Him as the bread from heaven, the One God sent to feed our spiritual hunger.

John records that people—even the apostles—often failed to interpret the words of Jesus correctly. They did not discern that He was using symbols. “‘Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep; but I am going there to wake him up.’ His disciples replied, ‘Lord, if he sleeps, he will get better.’ Jesus had been speaking of his death, but his disciples thought he meant natural sleep. So then he told them plainly, ‘Lazarus is dead’” (John 11:11–14).

Jesus used figurative language in John 11:11. He said Lazarus was asleep. In this case, sleep was a symbol for death. But the disciples did not interpret the words of Jesus correctly. They thought that sleep would make Lazarus feel better (John 11:12). Since they did not understand figurative language, Jesus spoke to them plainly, “‘Lazarus is dead’” (John 11:14).

Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God and who it is that asks you for a drink, you would have asked him and he would have given you living water.” (John 4:10)

On the last and greatest day of the Feast, Jesus stood and said in a loud voice, “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, streams of living water will flow from within him.” By this he meant the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were later to receive. Up to that time the Spirit had not been given, since Jesus had not yet been glorified. (John 7:37–39)

Jesus used living water as a symbol for the Holy Spirit. As water satisfies the thirst of our bodies, the Holy Spirit satisfies our spiritual thirst. (Compare Revelation 22:17 and Matthew 3:11.)

### Interpreting Figures of Speech: Simple Comparisons

#### 6.2.1 — Explain the difference in a simile and a metaphor, and give an example of each.

We have considered two types of language: literal and figurative. Literal language is plain and direct. It has no hidden meaning, so it is the easiest to interpret. But figurative language is harder to understand. It uses symbols and has a hidden meaning, so we must spend more time studying it. In this lesson, we will examine six kinds of comparisons that all use figurative language: (1) similes, (2) metaphors, (3) parables, (4) allegories, (5) anthropomorphism, and (6) personification.

Similes

A simile compares one thing with another thing, using either the word like or as between the two things. John used two similes to describe Jesus in Revelation 1:14: “His head and hair were white like wool, as white as snow, and his eyes were like blazing fire” (Revelation 1:14).

(A) His eyes (B) Blazing fire

Like

A simile is a comparison that says “A” is like “B”.

Amos used a simile when he prophesied that God was about to judge the Northern Kingdom: “Now then, I will crush you as a cart crushes when loaded with grain” (Amos 2:13).

The length of a simile is short; it is one sentence or less. Sometimes, a sentence may contain more than one simile: “‘I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves’” (Matthew 10:16).

As soon as Jesus was baptized, he went up out of the water. At that moment heaven was opened, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and lighting on him. (Matthew 3:16)

“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were not willing.” (Matthew 23:37)

His feet were like bronze glowing in a furnace, and his voice was like the sound of rushing waters. (Revelation 1:15)

In Matthew 11:16, Jesus asked a question. “‘To what can I compare this generation?’” Every good preacher and teacher should often ask him- or herself, “To what can I compare the truth I am sharing?” People like comparisons because they help them understand, enjoy, and remember. Jesus was the greatest teacher of all. In the Gospel of Luke, three out of every four words of Jesus are either a comparison or an illustration. Learn to teach and preach like our Master did.

Metaphors

Metaphors are like similes–both compare two things, but a metaphor does not use the word like or as in comparison. A metaphor is direct–it states that A is B. “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). Like a simile, a metaphor is usually only one sentence, or part of a sentence.

Jesus used a metaphor here: “‘You are the salt of the earth’” (Matthew 5:13). He was comparing Christians with salt. Note that the meaning would have been the same if Jesus had used a simile and said, “‘You are like the salt of the earth.’”

Anthropomorphism

This word is based on two Greek words: anthropos (man) and morphos (form). An anthropomorphism is a special type of metaphor that compares God to the form of humanity. God is invisible, at least to the eyes we have now. At times we wonder what we would see if we had spiritual vision, a vision that was granted to Elisha: “‘Don’t be afraid,’ the prophet answered. ‘Those who are with us are more than those who are with them.’ And Elisha prayed, ‘O Lord, open his eyes so he may see.’ Then the Lord opened the servant’s eyes, and he looked and saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:16–17).

God is spirit, not flesh (John 4:24). Paul tells us that God is invisible, and unable to be seen: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation” (Colossians 1:15).

“Now to the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen” (1 Timothy 1:17). But does this mean that we can never see God as we are now, or that we will never see Him for all of eternity?

Since we cannot see God, or spirits, we know little about them. It is hard for us to understand how spirits see, hear, think, and feel. Do they have any shape or form? How do angels and demons war against each other if they have no form? How can Satan be bound and kept in the Abyss? Do spirits have any type of spiritual mind, eyes, ears, feet or hands? These questions are too hard for us to answer. When the Bible speaks of God’s eyes, ears, and face, it may use this type of language so we as humans can relate to God who is spirit and not flesh like we are. But we want to be humble and admit that we know very little about spirit beings. Did God allow Moses to see a temporary form (Exodus 33:23)? Or do spirit beings have a form we will one day see? We simply do not know the answers to all of these questions yet.

We do know that God is a person. He is holy and truthful. He has feelings and emotions. He loves, has mercy, and can be grieved. We also know that we are created in the image of God. In the future, we will know more than we know now. “Dear friends, now we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet been made known. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Someday, in heaven, we will see face-to-face (1 Corinthians 13:12). Until then, we can only wonder what passages like Psalm 34:15–16 fully mean: “The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous and his ears are attentive to their cry; the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to cut off the memory of them from the earth.”

Personification

Personification compares things to a person. Two types of examples follow:

A deed, action, or idea is compared to a person. “Then, after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death” (James 1:15). Note that in this verse, desire, sin, and death are all given the human attributes of conceiving, giving birth, and growing. Furthermore, elsewhere in Scripture, our sins are said to testify against us (Jeremiah 14:7).

A thing is compared to a person. “Look! The wages you failed to pay the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord Almighty” (James 5:4). “The mountains and hills will burst into song before you, and all the trees of the field will clap their hands” (Isaiah 55:12).

“‘Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own’” (Matthew 6:34). Jesus referred to tomorrow as if it were a person. This method of teaching calls attention to the lesson and helps others learn and remember it.

#### 6.2.2 — Define anthropomorphism, and give an example.

We have considered two types of language: literal and figurative. Literal language is plain and direct. It has no hidden meaning, so it is the easiest to interpret. But figurative language is harder to understand. It uses symbols and has a hidden meaning, so we must spend more time studying it. In this lesson, we will examine six kinds of comparisons that all use figurative language: (1) similes, (2) metaphors, (3) parables, (4) allegories, (5) anthropomorphism, and (6) personification.

Similes

A simile compares one thing with another thing, using either the word like or as between the two things. John used two similes to describe Jesus in Revelation 1:14: “His head and hair were white like wool, as white as snow, and his eyes were like blazing fire” (Revelation 1:14).

(A) His eyes (B) Blazing fire

Like

A simile is a comparison that says “A” is like “B”.

Amos used a simile when he prophesied that God was about to judge the Northern Kingdom: “Now then, I will crush you as a cart crushes when loaded with grain” (Amos 2:13).

The length of a simile is short; it is one sentence or less. Sometimes, a sentence may contain more than one simile: “‘I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves’” (Matthew 10:16).

Metaphors

Metaphors are like similes–both compare two things, but a metaphor does not use the word like or as in comparison. A metaphor is direct–it states that A is B. “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light for my path” (Psalm 119:105). Like a simile, a metaphor is usually only one sentence, or part of a sentence.

Jesus used a metaphor here: “‘You are the salt of the earth’” (Matthew 5:13). He was comparing Christians with salt. Note that the meaning would have been the same if Jesus had used a simile and said, “‘You are like the salt of the earth.’”

### Interpreting Figures of Speech: Complex Comparisons

#### 6.3.1 — Compare and contrast a simile and a parable.

Parables

We will cover a lot of territory in this lesson. Within the section on parables, you will study four areas:

The relationship between a simile and a parable

The historical and literary setting of a parable: its time, purpose, and application

The meaning of a parable: its characters, points of comparison, the main lesson, and lesser lessons

One main point with possible sub points and several points of comparisons Compare and contrast a simile and a parable.

The Relationship of Similes and Parables

We have seen that a simile compares two things within a sentence and connects them with the word like or as . Likewise, a parable compares two things, putting the word like or as between them. There are two main differences between a simile and a parable: length and points of comparison. A simile is short and compares two things on one point. A parable is longer than a simile (it is usually a short story) and may compare two things in several ways. Many teachers say that a parable is a lengthened or extended simile (Thompson 1989, 1).

Comparisons using like or as

Simile: “His feet were like bronze glowing in a furnace” (Revelation 1:15).

Parable: “‘The kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins’” (Matthew 25:1).

“Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock.” (Matthew 7:24)

“To what can I compare this generation? They are like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling out to others.” (Matthew 11:16)

He told them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed.” (Matthew 13:31)

“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field.” (Matthew 13:44)

Do not stumble over the word parable that is used in two ways. In the narrow sense, it means a short, simple story with a spiritual meaning. But in a broad sense, a parable is any kind of comparison. A few places in the Bible, such as Mark 7:17, use the word parable in a broad sense.

Again Jesus called the crowd to him and said, “Listen to me, everyone, and understand this. Nothing outside a man can make him ‘unclean’ by going into him. Rather, it is what comes out of a man that makes him ‘unclean.’ After he had left the crowd and entered the house, his disciples asked him about this parable.” (Mark 7:14–17)

In this course, we refer to a parable as a short story with a spiritual lesson.

The Historical and Literary Setting of a Parable

To examine the setting of a parable, analyze three things: the time, the reason, and the application. Jesus spoke all of the parables in the New Testament. As we seek to interpret them, we can group them into three periods of time.

• Period One: The historical setting of this group of parables was early in the ministry of Jesus. These parables explain the nature of the Kingdom. It is open to all, but few accept the invitation and persevere. It begins small but grows to become great. Some discern its value, but many will be rejected from it when the King returns.

• Period Two: The historical setting of this group of parables was the last few months of Christ’s ministry. As He walked from Galilee toward Calvary, He told many parables, urging people to be saved and to persevere as faithful servants as they watched for the King’s return.

• Period Three : The historical setting of this group of parables was the week before the cross. As you interpret these parables, remember that the King is about to be crucified and ascend to heaven. Before going away, He emphasizes that He will return to reward or judge all people.

After you determine the time Christ told a parable, pay attention to the reason or occasion for the parable. Sometimes, a parable is introduced by a question, a problem, or an action. For example, suppose you are interpreting the parable of the workers in the vineyard (Matthew 20:1–16). Just before this parable, the rich young ruler walked away sad. He was not willing to give up his wealth to follow Christ. Peter spoke up and reminded Jesus that the apostles had left all to follow Him. Then Peter asked what rewards the apostles would receive for following Jesus. The Lord said they would sit on twelve thrones and receive a hundred times what they gave up. But Jesus said many who are first will be last and the last first (Matthew 19:30). Then he told the parable of Matthew 20:1–16.

Once you know the time and reason, look for an application, the summary or conclusion that comes just after the parable. For example, after each parable in Luke 15, there is an application. The Pharisees complained that Jesus welcomed sinners and ate with them. The application, the short statement of truth after each parable, emphasizes the truth of the parable. The angels and the Father rejoice when one sinner repents, so Jesus ate with them to guide them toward repentance.

To understand the parables of Luke 15, examine the timing, the reason for the parable, and the application. Applications tend to be at the end of a parable. They are often introduced by words like “I tell you . . .,” “In the same way . . . or “This is how . . .”

This pattern —emphasizing the truth after a parable—is what the scholars call rule of end stress , or emphasis (Stein 1998, 147). That is, a parable will often have a summary statement after it stresses or emphasizes the lesson of the story.

The Meaning of a Parable: Its Characters, Points of Comparison, the Main Lesson, and Lesser Lessons

To analyze a parable, identify three things: (1) the characters, (2) the points of comparison, and (3) the main lesson and any lesser lessons.

The Main Characters

About two thirds of the parables of Jesus are triadic, meaning they have three characters or three groups of characters (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 338).

• At point A, at the top of the triad or triangle is usually a master (king, father, or shepherd). (In a few cases, like the parable of the Good Samaritan, there are three groups: the wounded, the merciful, and the unmerciful—although there is no master at the top who relates to contrasting groups at the bottom of the triangle.)

• At point B is a person or group who is wise, faithful, obedient, and so forth.

• At point C is a person or group that is foolish, unfaithful, disobedient, and so forth.

The wise may be at either point B or C, but not both. Note the contrast between those at the bottom of the triangle. These are opposites, although both relate in some way to the master at the top of the triangle. About two-thirds of the parables of Jesus are triadic (having three characters).

One-third of the parables of Jesus are not triadic. These either have two opposite characters (dyadic) or have only one character (monadic).

• Examples of parables with only two characters or two groups are wise and foolish builders (Matthew 7:24–27), Pharisee and tax collector (Luke 18:9–14), the warring kings (Luke 14:31–32), and the servant and his master (Luke 17:5–10).

• Examples of parables with only one character are the mustard seed and leaven (Matthew 13:31–33), the hidden treasure and the pearl of great price (Matthew 13:44–46), and the man building a tower (Luke 14:28–30).

Identifying Points of Comparison in a Parable

We begin this section with a word-picture, a comparison of hills and mountains. People generally do not see significance in hills because they are small and common. But the beauty of mountains can have special meaning to us. We can compare the details of parables to hills. The details of a parable do not have special meaning in that they do not represent anything. However, a parable usually contains a few of what we will call mountain points that stand out above the hills of details . Some authors call these mountains points of reference , or points of comparison . In any parable, you should seek to identify these big points, because big points do represent something or someone (Fee and Stuart 1982, 127–128).

For example, in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37), there are hills of details and four mountain points. This chart shows the four mountain points and those they represent.

Mountain Point of Comparison

Whom the Mountain Point Represents

1. The thieves

Those who harm others

2. The wounded man

Those in need

3. The priest and Levite

Those who do not care about others

4. The good Samaritan

Those who love their neighbors

The parable of the Good Samaritan has a few big points of comparison that stand out like mountains. Notice that these points of comparison are the main characters in the parable. We could group the thieves, priest, and Levite into one group: those who do not care about others.

The parable of the Good Samaritan also has hills of details. We need details in a parable to explain the main points, but we should not try to give special meaning to the details. This would be like trying to make hills into mountains! Mountains have special meaning; they represent something, but hills do not. Some of the details in the parable of the Good Samaritan are Jerusalem, Jericho, the road, the donkey, the inn, the innkeeper, the two silver coins, etc.

The details of a parable complete the story, but they have no special meaning. For example, in the parable of the Good Samaritan, the two silver coins do not have a hidden meaning. The story would still teach the same lesson if there were three coins, or four. Likewise, the meaning of the parable would not change if the wounded man had been traveling from Jericho to Jerusalem, instead of Jerusalem to Jericho (Stein 1998, 140).

Trying to give special meaning to the small details of a parable will only lead us away from the truth and cause us to interpret the parable falsely. So discern between the many hills and few mountains of a parable. We will discuss this more when we come to allegories and allegorizing, a little later in this lesson.

One Main Lesson of the Parable and Any Lesser Truths

Jesus told a parable to illustrate one major truth. You should learn to state in one sentence the main lesson of a parable. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the one big truth is to be a good neighbor to those who are in need. Once you find the one big truth that a parable illustrates, do not lower your hermeneutics ability by searching for a second big truth. As a nation can have only one capital location, a parable can have only one major truth.

A parable has only one main truth, but it may contain other lesser truths. It has only one main point, but it may have several sub points. As you search for the one big truth, and any lesser truths, analyze each character. Then, state a truth related to each character (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 329). For example, the main truth of the parable of the Good Samaritan is to be a good neighbor to those who are in need. But for the purpose of preaching this parable, it is helpful to note that it teaches three lesser truths that are three attitudes people may have toward neighbors:

• The attitude of the thieves: “What is yours is mine if I can take it.”

• The attitude of the priest and Levite: “What is mine is mine, and I am going to keep it.”

• The attitude of the Good Samaritan: “What is mine is yours, and I will share it if you need it.”

Likewise, the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:1–9) teaches one main truth: The fate of the seed depends on the hearers. Still, we may identify several lesser truths that relate to this big truth, like the spokes of a bicycle relate to the one center of a wheel. Some lesser truths or principles in the parable of the sower are:

• There is power in the Word of God to change people’s lives.

• Some hear the Word of God but do not understand it for various reasons.

• Some understand the Word but give only a temporary, emotional response.

• Some receive the Word and commit to following Jesus but turn away for various reasons.

• Some receive the Word, follow Jesus, and bear fruit for the kingdom.

When you interpret, teach, or preach a parable, always relate the smaller truths to the one big truth of the parable. This will help you emphasize the unity of the passage.

Let us review what we have said about interpreting parables.

• Discern the historical and literary setting of a parable by analyzing three things: the time, the reason, and the application.

• Analyze the parable itself by doing three things: identify the characters, the points of comparison, the one main lesson, and any smaller lessons. Now we will shift from parables to allegories.

“‘I am the bread of life’” (John 6:35). A parable or an allegory makes few points of comparison. Jesus is like bread because He satisfies our hunger and gives us strength to live. It would be wrong and extreme to compare the grinding of wheat to Christ’s sufferings, the baking of bread to Christ’s time in the grave, and the bread’s softness to His compassion. So to find the main point of comparison, look at the context and do not press the allegory in other directions (Gibbs 1994, 129–130).

Jesus’ favorite method of instruction was the parable. A parable is a short, simple story that illustrates a spiritual lesson. In a parable, most of the details are just for the purpose of telling the story; they do not represent anything. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the one truth of the parable is that our neighbor is anyone in need.

On the other hand, an allegory contains several truths, and many of the details are representative. An example of an allegory is the Good Shepherd illustration in John 10. There are several truths and comparisons in this passage. The gate, the shepherd, the sheep, the stranger, the robber, the hireling, the wolf, and the sheep from another fold are all points of comparison. Each symbol represents something other than itself.

So how do we know whether to interpret a story as a parable or an allegory? If an allegory is intended, Jesus will interpret it for us in the written record. Otherwise, we should treat a story as a parable. (We will have more to say about parables and allegories in Chapter 9.)

Allegories

A metaphor compares two things but does not use like or as in the comparison . An allegory is an extended metaphor. As a simile can expand to be a parable, a metaphor may lengthen to be an allegory. A parable is an expanded simile (comparison); an allegory is an extended metaphor.

Comparisons using like or as

Comparisons without like or as

Simile: “His feet were like bronze glowing in a furnace” (Revelation 1:15).

Metaphor: “‘You are the salt of the earth’” (Matthew 5:13).

Parable: “‘The kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins’” (Matthew 25:1)

Allegory: “‘I am the vine and my Father is the gardener’” (John 15:1–8).

An allegory is a short story or teaching (Mickelsen and Mickelsen 2000, 79) that compares two things without using the words like or as and in which several points represent something.

There are two main differences between a parable and an allegory. First , a parable uses the word like or as, but an allegory does not use like or as. Second, a parable contains many details and few points of comparison. But in an allegory there are few details and many points of comparison. Many points of an allegory represent something. For example, consider the allegory in Ephesians 6:13–17.

Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand. Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness in place, and with your feet fitted with [sandals] the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace. In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. (Ephesians 6:13–17)

This is an easy allegory to interpret because Paul tells us what each of the six pieces of armor represents. Allegories in the Old Testament include Psalm 80:8–19 and Ecclesiastes 12:3–7.

Symbol

“Those looking through the windows grow dim” (Ecclesiastes 12:3).

“When men rise up at the sound of birds, but all their songs grow faint” (Ecclesiastes 12:4).

“When the almond tree blossoms” (Ecclesiastes 12:5).

Jesus used an allegory with two parts during the Last Supper (Mickelsen and Mickelsen 2000, 83). He said, “This is my body . . . This is my blood’” (Matthew 26:26–28). He compared His body and blood to bread and juice. Note that the bread and juice are symbols for the Lord’s body and blood.

In John’s Gospel, the seven I am statements are metaphors that extend into allegories as Jesus teaches about them. Each of the seven I am metaphors can be stated in one sentence. But many verses of explanation or discussion lengthen the metaphors into allegories. In John 6:35, Jesus states that He is the bread of life. This metaphor leads to teaching and discussion.

Allegorizing

An allegory is a biblical method of teaching truth, but it should not be confused with allegorizing. Those who allegorize give their own meanings to details that the biblical author did not intend to represent anything. These unwise teachers do not interpret the Bible; rather, they read into the Bible what they imagine.

Except for the book of Revelation, the parables have been misinterpreted more than all other Scripture. At times in the history of the church, parables have been allegorized. That is, most everything in the parables have been used to represent something else. Allegorizing is poor hermeneutics. In the fifth century, Augustine tried to change the parable of the Good Samaritan into an allegory. He taught the following:

• “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho,” meaning Adam

• “Jerusalem,” meaning the heavenly city of peace, from which Adam fell

• “Jericho,” meaning the moon, signifying Adam’s mortality

• “Thieves,” meaning the devil and his angels

• “Stripped him” meaning namely, of his immortality

• “Beat him,” meaning persuaded him to sin

• “Left him half-dead,” meaning as a man he lives, but he died spiritually, therefore he is half-dead

• “The priest and Levite,” meaning the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament

• “The Samaritan,” meaning a guardian; therefore Christ himself is meant

• “Bound his wounds,” meaning binding the restraint of sin

• “Oil,” meaning comfort of good hope

• “Wine,” meaning exhortation to work with a fervent spirit

• “Beast,” meaning the flesh of Christ’s incarnation

• “Inn,” meaning the church

• The morrow,” meaning after the resurrection

• “Two-pence,” meaning the promise of this life and the life to come

• “Innkeeper,” meaning Paul (Fee and Stuart 1982, 124)

Although Augustine’s interpretation of the parable is interesting, it is not what Jesus intended. Remember that Paul was not allegorizing in Galatians 4:24–31. Rather, he was using Hagar and Sarah as examples to teach a point.

Allegorizing a parable is dangerous because it does not bring out the original message that Jesus taught. When we make the parts of a parable represent whatever we imagine, we are no longer preaching or teaching the Word of God. In fact, we are taking away the original meaning and adding our own imaginations to the Word of God; this is never wise (Revelation 22:18–19). This is not being faithful to the purpose and meaning of the parable as Jesus told it. If you want God to say “Well done” for the way you preach and teach, do not allegorize. Rather, teach the true meaning of a passage—the meaning God intended.

Parable

Allegory

Compares two things, with the word like or as between

Compares two things without using like or as

Has few mountains—points of comparison

Has many points of comparison

Are numerous in the New Testament (about forty)

Are few in the New Testament (about ten)

**Q:** In a parable, how do the hills of detail differ from the mountain points?

**A:** Hills of detail are elements of the parable that are not intended to be applied or to teach us anything. The mountain points are the main teaching points, the elements of the parable that reveal special meaning.

**A:** The main truth is that loving our neighbor is the essence of the righteousness God expects. **A:** Irony is stating the opposite of what is meant in order to illustrate or emphasize a point.

#### 6.3.2 — Analyze the historical and literary setting of a parable: identify its time, purpose, and application.

Parables

We will cover a lot of territory in this lesson. Within the section on parables, you will study four areas:

The relationship between a simile and a parable

The historical and literary setting of a parable: its time, purpose, and application

The meaning of a parable: its characters, points of comparison, the main lesson, and lesser lessons

One main point with possible sub points and several points of comparisons Compare and contrast a simile and a parable.

The Relationship of Similes and Parables

We have seen that a simile compares two things within a sentence and connects them with the word like or as . Likewise, a parable compares two things, putting the word like or as between them. There are two main differences between a simile and a parable: length and points of comparison. A simile is short and compares two things on one point. A parable is longer than a simile (it is usually a short story) and may compare two things in several ways. Many teachers say that a parable is a lengthened or extended simile (Thompson 1989, 1).

Comparisons using like or as

Simile: “His feet were like bronze glowing in a furnace” (Revelation 1:15).

Parable: “‘The kingdom of heaven will be like ten virgins’” (Matthew 25:1).

Do not stumble over the word parable that is used in two ways. In the narrow sense, it means a short, simple story with a spiritual meaning. But in a broad sense, a parable is any kind of comparison. A few places in the Bible, such as Mark 7:17, use the word parable in a broad sense.

Again Jesus called the crowd to him and said, “Listen to me, everyone, and understand this. Nothing outside a man can make him ‘unclean’ by going into him. Rather, it is what comes out of a man that makes him ‘unclean.’ After he had left the crowd and entered the house, his disciples asked him about this parable.” (Mark 7:14–17)

In this course, we refer to a parable as a short story with a spiritual lesson.
