Synecdoche

This figure of speech is used in two ways. Knowing these will help you interpret Scripture correctly. First , remember that a part can represent the whole. Here are some examples.

“Give us today our daily bread.” (Matthew 6:11) Bread is a part of our needs, but represents all of them.

On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Paul spoke to the people and, because he intended to leave the next day, kept on talking until midnight (Acts 20:7). Bread represents all of the Lord’s Supper, including the juice.

“And he will send his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other” (Matthew 24:31). The four winds represent all directions.

“The high places of Isaac will be destroyed and the sanctuaries of Israel will be ruined; with my sword I will rise against the house of Jeroboam” (Amos 7:9). In Amos 7:9, Isaac represents all the nation of Israel.

“How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation” (Isaiah 52:7). In Isaiah 52:7, the feet are a part of the body that represent the whole person.

Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked or stand in the way of sinners or sit in the seat of mockers (Psalm 1:1). In Psalm 1:1, one man represents all people. What is true for one is true for all.

“In your hands he has placed mankind and the beasts of the field and the birds of the air. Wherever they live, he has made you ruler over them all. You are that head of gold. After you, another kingdom will rise, inferior to yours. Next, a third kingdom, one of bronze, will rule over the whole earth” (Daniel 2:38–39). In Daniel 2:38, the king represents the whole kingdom; Nebuchadnezzar represents all of Babylon.

“The beast who once was, and now is not, is an eighth king. He belongs to the seven and is going to his destruction” (Revelation 17:11). In Revelation 17:11, the antichrist, who is the eighth king, is called a beast. Thus, one king represents the whole beast that has seven heads and ten horns (Revelation 13:1).

Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and in this way death came to all men, because all sinned—many died by the trespass of the one man (Romans 5:12, 15). In Romans 5:12, Adam represents all humans—one person represents the whole.

Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death (Romans 6:3)?

26 Explain how the death and resurrection of Christ relate to all believers (Romans 6:3; 1 Corinthians 15:22–23). For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. But each in his own turn: Christ, the firstfruits; then, when he comes, those who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:22–23).

Second, the whole can represent a part. We often find examples of this with the words like all , always , nothing , and everywhere . “‘And afterward, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions’” (Joel 2:28).

In Joel 2:28, all refers to all tribes and kinds of people, especially those who seek after God. On the day of Pentecost, God did not pour out His Spirit on all Jews. Likewise, throughout the history of the church, God pours out His Spirit on those who seek Him.

“‘Apart from me you can do nothing’” (John 15:5). In this case, the word nothing refers to nothing good, nothing of lasting value to build the kingdom of God. Yet with Christ, we can do many things that are displeasing to God. So nothing does not refer to the whole of life, but only a part.

“Then the disciples went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked with them and confirmed his word by the signs that accompanied it” (Mark 16:20).

Types

The author of Hebrews wrote that God spoke through the prophets in various ways. Sometimes God spoke directly, using plain speech. Other times He spoke indirectly, using figurative language. The revelation of God to us is progressive. Step-by-step, it becomes more clear and complete. The Old Testament contains some shadows or types. These shadows include people, events, actions, objects, and ceremonies. Also, these shadows and types are prophesies of future realities. We will look at some verses that talk about types, shadows, copies, and patterns:

Nevertheless, death reigned from the time of Adam to the time of Moses, even over those who did not sin by breaking a command, as did Adam, who was a pattern of the one to come (Romans 5:14). As death came to all through Adam, life can come to all through Christ.

These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ. (Colossians 2:17)

For Christ did not enter a man-made sanctuary that was only a copy of the true one; he entered heaven itself, now to appear for us in God’s presence. (Hebrews 9:24)

The law is only a shadow of the good things that are coming—not the realities themselves. For this reason it can never, by the same sacrifices repeated endlessly year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship. (Hebrews 10:1)

The Old Testament contains some shadows or types that are fulfilled in the New Testament. (This chart is adapted from Gibbs’ Hermeneutics , 148).

The New Testament mentions several types in the Old Testament. To recognize and interpret a type, follow three guidelines:

1. Recognize that a type is always a prophecy. It is a shadow of something in the future. For example, the high priest of Israel was a type of Jesus, the future High Priest of all believers.

2. Remember that you are safe in calling something a type, if a writer in the New Testament called it a type. Some preachers see a type behind every Old Testament bush. They want to make every color, every metal, and every piece of furniture in the tabernacle a type of something. This is dangerous and gives preaching a bad name. We are better off to use something as an illustration, but not call it a type. For example, Stephen preached on the themes of rejection and rebellion. He said that as the Israelites rejected Joseph and Moses—heroes that God raised up—likewise the Jews rejected Jesus (Acts 7:9–53). Stephen did not say that Joseph was a type of Christ. Nor is it necessary for us to call Joseph a type. But no one will find fault with us if we note that Joseph was sold and rejected, as was Christ.

3. When the New Testament calls something a type, limit the comparison to the points the Bible gives. For example, John compares the bronze snake and Jesus in two ways (Sterrett 1974, 109). (See the following chart.) There are many ways in which the serpent on the pole and Christ are not alike. We should not mention these. Rather, we should preach the Word, the things written in the Bible. When preaching about types, we should speak when the Bible speaks and be silent when it is silent. Types emphasize one truth that is fulfilled at a higher level.

Numbers 21:4–9 (Type)

Anyone who looked at the snake did not die, but lived.

All who believe in Him will not perish, but live eternally.

The bronze serpent is a type of Christ. Figurative language uses many words as symbols–they may represent something in figures of speech like similes, metaphors, parables, allegories, metonyms, synecdoche, and types. As you interpret symbols, remember two principles we have mentioned: (1) Always use the Bible to interpret the symbols of the Bible, and (2) Recognize that biblical writers use the same symbols in different ways.

Always use the Bible to interpret the symbols of the Bible. For example, Ephesians 6:17 uses the symbol of a sword: “Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). The Bible itself, in the same passage, explains that the sword is a symbol for the Word of God. We know for sure what a symbol means if the Bible explains the symbol at once, or in the same book. For example, John uses the symbol of a harlot (Revelation 17:1 – 8). But he soon tells us that the harlot is the great city that rules over the earth (Revelation 17:18).

Recognize that biblical writers use the same symbols in different ways. Therefore, seek first to interpret a symbol in the light of context. Remember the principles we studied about circles of context. To interpret a symbol, begin in the paragraph that contains it. If necessary, continue to other parts of the same book. Then you can compare other passages by the same author. As the chart below shows, even the same authors use words in different ways. As we said earlier, let the Bible speak for itself. Seek to interpret a symbol in the way an author used it. Biblical writers use symbols in different ways. The right meaning of a symbol is the meaning the author intended.

#### 6.4.2 — State the meaning of hyperbole, and give an example.

Contrasts: Irony

Did you know that many verses in the Bible would be untrue if you interpreted them literally? When a biblical author uses irony , he means the opposite of what he says. For example, to praise John the Baptist, Jesus asked, “What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed swayed by the wind? If not, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? No, those who wear fine clothes are in kings’ palaces (Matthew 11:7–8). Notice that Jesus compared John to the opposite of what the prophet was like. John was like a post driven in the ground, not a reed swayed by the wind. And he wore a rough garment of camel’s hair, not fine clothes. Using irony, stating the opposite of what you mean, calls more attention to the truth.

Job’s friends were foolish in the way they accused Him, and Job used irony to answer them: “‘Doubtless you are the people, and wisdom will die with you!’” (Job 12:2).

Practice interpreting some verses that use irony.

21 Was Michal praising David (2 Samuel 6:20)? When David returned home to bless his household, Michal daughter of Saul came out to meet him and said, “How the king of Israel has distinguished himself today, disrobing in the sight of the slave girls of his servants as any vulgar fellow would!” (2 Samuel 6:20)

22 Did the prophet think that King Ahab would win a victory (1 Kings 22:15)? When he arrived, the king asked him, “Micaiah, shall we go to war against Ramoth Gilead, or shall I refrain?” “Attack and be victorious,” he answered, “for the Lord will give it into the king’s hand.” The king said to him, “How many times must I make you swear to tell me nothing but the truth in the name of the Lord?” Then Micaiah answered, “I saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd,” and the Lord said, ‘These people have no master. Let each one go home in peace.’” The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Didn’t I tell you that he never prophesies anything good about me, but only bad?” (1 Kings 22:15–18)

In passing, since we are studying contrasts in Scripture, note that irony is not the only type of contrast in Scripture. Another form is the opposite of a simile or metaphor. For example: “God is not (like) a man, that he should lie” (Numbers 23:19).

Many times, Jesus contrasted two things, to make a teaching clear. “Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples: ‘The teachers of the law and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. So you must obey them and do everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach’” (Matthew 23:1–3).

Overstatements: Hyperboles

A hyperbole is figure of speech that exaggerates a truth to make a point. The Greek word hyper means “beyond” or “excess . ” A hyperbole is a throwing beyond —overstating a truth on purpose. Here are some examples of hyperbole:

• “You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel” (Matthew 23:24). This was a hyperbole. Pharisees did strain gnats out of their drinking water, but who could literally swallow a camel? This is figurative language. They tithed on small seeds the size of a gnat, but neglected things that were as big as a camel–they neglected justice, mercy, and faithfulness. Using hyperbole enables a speaker to make a point clear and with a lasting result.

• I am worn out from groaning; all night long I flood my bed with weeping and drench my couch with tears (Psalm 6:6). Though Psalm 6:6 reveals that David cried a lot, we know this is also figurative, extreme language since no human can cry enough tears to flood a bed.

Whenever the Israelites planted their crops, the Midianites, Amalekites, and other eastern peoples invaded the country. They camped on the land and ruined the crops all the way to Gaza and did not spare a living thing for Israel, neither sheep nor cattle nor donkeys (Judges 6:3–4). This hyperbole in Judges 6 reveals that Israel’s enemies stole almost all of their crops and wealth. Still, we know that the enemies did not take everything, since Gideon threshed wheat and sacrificed animals.

Relations (Associations): Metonyms, Synecdoche, and Types

We are studying simple figures of speech. We looked at comparisons, overstatements, and contrasts. To complete this lesson, we will look at two types of writing that deal with relationships or association.

Metonyms

You are probably familiar with synonyms–words that mean the same thing. Likewise, you probably know that antonyms are words that have opposite meanings. Metonyms are words that can be exchanged; one word can represent another. The Greek word meta means “change.” Earlier, we mentioned that metanoia , “repentance,” is a “change of mind . ” When a metonym is used, one word changes places with another. Here are some examples:

• You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies (Psalm 23:5). This verse is not saying that God builds a new piece of furniture in front of enemies. Rather, table represents all the food that goes on a table (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard 1993, 338). A shepherd prepared a table for the sheep by removing thorns and poisonous weeds from a field.

• The woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth (Revelation 17:18). The woman represents all of the sinners and sinful ways of Babylon (Rome).

• Abraham replied, “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them” (Luke 16:29). In Luke 16:29, Moses and the Prophets are metonyms for their writings. Of course Moses and the Prophets had been dead for centuries, but their writings remained.

• For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe (1 Corinthians 1:21). In 1 Corinthians 1:21, the word foolishness represents what the world considers to be foolish.

• She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you her greetings, and so does my son Mark (1 Peter 5:13). In 1 Peter 5:13, Babylon probably represents Rome.

Synecdoche

This figure of speech is used in two ways. Knowing these will help you interpret Scripture correctly. First , remember that a part can represent the whole. Here are some examples.

“Give us today our daily bread.” (Matthew 6:11) Bread is a part of our needs, but represents all of them.

On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Paul spoke to the people and, because he intended to leave the next day, kept on talking until midnight (Acts 20:7). Bread represents all of the Lord’s Supper, including the juice.

“And he will send his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other” (Matthew 24:31). The four winds represent all directions.

“The high places of Isaac will be destroyed and the sanctuaries of Israel will be ruined; with my sword I will rise against the house of Jeroboam” (Amos 7:9). In Amos 7:9, Isaac represents all the nation of Israel.

“How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation” (Isaiah 52:7). In Isaiah 52:7, the feet are a part of the body that represent the whole person.

Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked or stand in the way of sinners or sit in the seat of mockers (Psalm 1:1). In Psalm 1:1, one man represents all people. What is true for one is true for all.

“In your hands he has placed mankind and the beasts of the field and the birds of the air. Wherever they live, he has made you ruler over them all. You are that head of gold. After you, another kingdom will rise, inferior to yours. Next, a third kingdom, one of bronze, will rule over the whole earth” (Daniel 2:38–39). In Daniel 2:38, the king represents the whole kingdom; Nebuchadnezzar represents all of Babylon.

“The beast who once was, and now is not, is an eighth king. He belongs to the seven and is going to his destruction” (Revelation 17:11). In Revelation 17:11, the antichrist, who is the eighth king, is called a beast. Thus, one king represents the whole beast that has seven heads and ten horns (Revelation 13:1).

Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and in this way death came to all men, because all sinned—many died by the trespass of the one man (Romans 5:12, 15). In Romans 5:12, Adam represents all humans—one person represents the whole.

Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death (Romans 6:3)?

26 Explain how the death and resurrection of Christ relate to all believers (Romans 6:3; 1 Corinthians 15:22–23). For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. But each in his own turn: Christ, the firstfruits; then, when he comes, those who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:22–23).

Second, the whole can represent a part. We often find examples of this with the words like all , always , nothing , and everywhere . “‘And afterward, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions’” (Joel 2:28).

In Joel 2:28, all refers to all tribes and kinds of people, especially those who seek after God. On the day of Pentecost, God did not pour out His Spirit on all Jews. Likewise, throughout the history of the church, God pours out His Spirit on those who seek Him.

“‘Apart from me you can do nothing’” (John 15:5). In this case, the word nothing refers to nothing good, nothing of lasting value to build the kingdom of God. Yet with Christ, we can do many things that are displeasing to God. So nothing does not refer to the whole of life, but only a part.

“Then the disciples went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked with them and confirmed his word by the signs that accompanied it” (Mark 16:20).

Types

The author of Hebrews wrote that God spoke through the prophets in various ways. Sometimes God spoke directly, using plain speech. Other times He spoke indirectly, using figurative language. The revelation of God to us is progressive. Step-by-step, it becomes more clear and complete. The Old Testament contains some shadows or types. These shadows include people, events, actions, objects, and ceremonies. Also, these shadows and types are prophesies of future realities. We will look at some verses that talk about types, shadows, copies, and patterns:

Nevertheless, death reigned from the time of Adam to the time of Moses, even over those who did not sin by breaking a command, as did Adam, who was a pattern of the one to come (Romans 5:14). As death came to all through Adam, life can come to all through Christ.

These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ. (Colossians 2:17)

For Christ did not enter a man-made sanctuary that was only a copy of the true one; he entered heaven itself, now to appear for us in God’s presence. (Hebrews 9:24)

The law is only a shadow of the good things that are coming—not the realities themselves. For this reason it can never, by the same sacrifices repeated endlessly year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship. (Hebrews 10:1)

The Old Testament contains some shadows or types that are fulfilled in the New Testament. (This chart is adapted from Gibbs’ Hermeneutics , 148).

The exodus Jesus leads from sin to heaven, our Promised Land (Hebrews 3:7–4:11).

“‘Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up’” (John 3:14).

The New Testament mentions several types in the Old Testament. To recognize and interpret a type, follow three guidelines:

1. Recognize that a type is always a prophecy. It is a shadow of something in the future. For example, the high priest of Israel was a type of Jesus, the future High Priest of all believers.

2. Remember that you are safe in calling something a type, if a writer in the New Testament called it a type. Some preachers see a type behind every Old Testament bush. They want to make every color, every metal, and every piece of furniture in the tabernacle a type of something. This is dangerous and gives preaching a bad name. We are better off to use something as an illustration, but not call it a type. For example, Stephen preached on the themes of rejection and rebellion. He said that as the Israelites rejected Joseph and Moses—heroes that God raised up—likewise the Jews rejected Jesus (Acts 7:9–53). Stephen did not say that Joseph was a type of Christ. Nor is it necessary for us to call Joseph a type. But no one will find fault with us if we note that Joseph was sold and rejected, as was Christ.

3. When the New Testament calls something a type, limit the comparison to the points the Bible gives. For example, John compares the bronze snake and Jesus in two ways (Sterrett 1974, 109). (See the following chart.) There are many ways in which the serpent on the pole and Christ are not alike. We should not mention these. Rather, we should preach the Word, the things written in the Bible. When preaching about types, we should speak when the Bible speaks and be silent when it is silent. Types emphasize one truth that is fulfilled at a higher level.

Numbers 21:4–9 (Type)

John 3:14–15 (Fulfillment or Anti-type)

The people complained.

Not mentioned

God sent poisonous snakes; many people died

Not mentioned

People confessed: “We have sinned.”

Not mentioned

Moses prayed for them.

Not mentioned

God commanded Moses to make a fiery serpent.

Not mentioned

Moses made a bronze snake and put it on a pole.

Jesus was lifted up on a cross.

Anyone who looked at the snake did not die, but lived.

All who believe in Him will not perish, but live eternally.

The bronze serpent is a type of Christ. Figurative language uses many words as symbols–they may represent something in figures of speech like similes, metaphors, parables, allegories, metonyms, synecdoche, and types. As you interpret symbols, remember two principles we have mentioned: (1) Always use the Bible to interpret the symbols of the Bible, and (2) Recognize that biblical writers use the same symbols in different ways.

Always use the Bible to interpret the symbols of the Bible. For example, Ephesians 6:17 uses the symbol of a sword: “Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). The Bible itself, in the same passage, explains that the sword is a symbol for the Word of God. We know for sure what a symbol means if the Bible explains the symbol at once, or in the same book. For example, John uses the symbol of a harlot (Revelation 17:1 – 8). But he soon tells us that the harlot is the great city that rules over the earth (Revelation 17:18).

Recognize that biblical writers use the same symbols in different ways. Therefore, seek first to interpret a symbol in the light of context. Remember the principles we studied about circles of context. To interpret a symbol, begin in the paragraph that contains it. If necessary, continue to other parts of the same book. Then you can compare other passages by the same author. As the chart below shows, even the same authors use words in different ways. As we said earlier, let the Bible speak for itself. Seek to interpret a symbol in the way an author used it. Biblical writers use symbols in different ways. The right meaning of a symbol is the meaning the author intended.

• The woman you saw is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth (Revelation 17:18). The woman represents all of the sinners and sinful ways of Babylon (Rome).

• Abraham replied, “They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them” (Luke 16:29). In Luke 16:29, Moses and the Prophets are metonyms for their writings. Of course Moses and the Prophets had been dead for centuries, but their writings remained.

• For since in the wisdom of God the world through its wisdom did not know him, God was pleased through the foolishness of what was preached to save those who believe (1 Corinthians 1:21). In 1 Corinthians 1:21, the word foolishness represents what the world considers to be foolish.

• She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you her greetings, and so does my son Mark (1 Peter 5:13). In 1 Peter 5:13, Babylon probably represents Rome.

Synecdoche

This figure of speech is used in two ways. Knowing these will help you interpret Scripture correctly. First , remember that a part can represent the whole. Here are some examples.

“Give us today our daily bread.” (Matthew 6:11) Bread is a part of our needs, but represents all of them.

On the first day of the week we came together to break bread. Paul spoke to the people and, because he intended to leave the next day, kept on talking until midnight (Acts 20:7). Bread represents all of the Lord’s Supper, including the juice.

“And he will send his angels with a loud trumpet call, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from one end of the heavens to the other” (Matthew 24:31). The four winds represent all directions.

“The high places of Isaac will be destroyed and the sanctuaries of Israel will be ruined; with my sword I will rise against the house of Jeroboam” (Amos 7:9). In Amos 7:9, Isaac represents all the nation of Israel.

“How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation” (Isaiah 52:7). In Isaiah 52:7, the feet are a part of the body that represent the whole person.

Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked or stand in the way of sinners or sit in the seat of mockers (Psalm 1:1). In Psalm 1:1, one man represents all people. What is true for one is true for all.

“In your hands he has placed mankind and the beasts of the field and the birds of the air. Wherever they live, he has made you ruler over them all. You are that head of gold. After you, another kingdom will rise, inferior to yours. Next, a third kingdom, one of bronze, will rule over the whole earth” (Daniel 2:38–39). In Daniel 2:38, the king represents the whole kingdom; Nebuchadnezzar represents all of Babylon.

“The beast who once was, and now is not, is an eighth king. He belongs to the seven and is going to his destruction” (Revelation 17:11). In Revelation 17:11, the antichrist, who is the eighth king, is called a beast. Thus, one king represents the whole beast that has seven heads and ten horns (Revelation 13:1).

Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and in this way death came to all men, because all sinned—many died by the trespass of the one man (Romans 5:12, 15). In Romans 5:12, Adam represents all humans—one person represents the whole.

Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death (Romans 6:3)?

26 Explain how the death and resurrection of Christ relate to all believers (Romans 6:3; 1 Corinthians 15:22–23). For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. But each in his own turn: Christ, the firstfruits; then, when he comes, those who belong to him (1 Corinthians 15:22–23).

Second, the whole can represent a part. We often find examples of this with the words like all , always , nothing , and everywhere . “‘And afterward, I will pour out my Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions’” (Joel 2:28).

In Joel 2:28, all refers to all tribes and kinds of people, especially those who seek after God. On the day of Pentecost, God did not pour out His Spirit on all Jews. Likewise, throughout the history of the church, God pours out His Spirit on those who seek Him.

“‘Apart from me you can do nothing’” (John 15:5). In this case, the word nothing refers to nothing good, nothing of lasting value to build the kingdom of God. Yet with Christ, we can do many things that are displeasing to God. So nothing does not refer to the whole of life, but only a part.

“Then the disciples went out and preached everywhere, and the Lord worked with them and confirmed his word by the signs that accompanied it” (Mark 16:20).

Types

The author of Hebrews wrote that God spoke through the prophets in various ways. Sometimes God spoke directly, using plain speech. Other times He spoke indirectly, using figurative language. The revelation of God to us is progressive. Step-by-step, it becomes more clear and complete. The Old Testament contains some shadows or types. These shadows include people, events, actions, objects, and ceremonies. Also, these shadows and types are prophesies of future realities. We will look at some verses that talk about types, shadows, copies, and patterns:

Nevertheless, death reigned from the time of Adam to the time of Moses, even over those who did not sin by breaking a command, as did Adam, who was a pattern of the one to come (Romans 5:14). As death came to all through Adam, life can come to all through Christ.

These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ. (Colossians 2:17)

For Christ did not enter a man-made sanctuary that was only a copy of the true one; he entered heaven itself, now to appear for us in God’s presence. (Hebrews 9:24)

The law is only a shadow of the good things that are coming—not the realities themselves. For this reason it can never, by the same sacrifices repeated endlessly year after year, make perfect those who draw near to worship. (Hebrews 10:1)

The Old Testament contains some shadows or types that are fulfilled in the New Testament. (This chart is adapted from Gibbs’ Hermeneutics , 148).

Adam was a pattern of the One to come (Romans 5:14).

“For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19).

The Most Holy Place in the tabernacle

“The Most Holy Place”–God’s presence in heaven (Hebrews 9:25; 10:19).

“and since we have a great priest over the house of God” (Hebrews 10:21).

The Exodus that Moses led from Egypt to the Promised Land before them

The exodus Jesus leads from sin to heaven, our Promised Land (Hebrews 3:7–4:11).

The bronze serpent lifted up on a pole brought life to those who looked at it (Numbers 21:8–9).

“‘Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up’” (John 3:14).

The New Testament mentions several types in the Old Testament. To recognize and interpret a type, follow three guidelines:

1. Recognize that a type is always a prophecy. It is a shadow of something in the future. For example, the high priest of Israel was a type of Jesus, the future High Priest of all believers.

2. Remember that you are safe in calling something a type, if a writer in the New Testament called it a type. Some preachers see a type behind every Old Testament bush. They want to make every color, every metal, and every piece of furniture in the tabernacle a type of something. This is dangerous and gives preaching a bad name. We are better off to use something as an illustration, but not call it a type. For example, Stephen preached on the themes of rejection and rebellion. He said that as the Israelites rejected Joseph and Moses—heroes that God raised up—likewise the Jews rejected Jesus (Acts 7:9–53). Stephen did not say that Joseph was a type of Christ. Nor is it necessary for us to call Joseph a type. But no one will find fault with us if we note that Joseph was sold and rejected, as was Christ.

3. When the New Testament calls something a type, limit the comparison to the points the Bible gives. For example, John compares the bronze snake and Jesus in two ways (Sterrett 1974, 109). (See the following chart.) There are many ways in which the serpent on the pole and Christ are not alike. We should not mention these. Rather, we should preach the Word, the things written in the Bible. When preaching about types, we should speak when the Bible speaks and be silent when it is silent. Types emphasize one truth that is fulfilled at a higher level.

Numbers 21:4–9 (Type)

John 3:14–15 (Fulfillment or Anti-type)

The bronze serpent is a type of Christ. Figurative language uses many words as symbols–they may represent something in figures of speech like similes, metaphors, parables, allegories, metonyms, synecdoche, and types. As you interpret symbols, remember two principles we have mentioned: (1) Always use the Bible to interpret the symbols of the Bible, and (2) Recognize that biblical writers use the same symbols in different ways.

Always use the Bible to interpret the symbols of the Bible. For example, Ephesians 6:17 uses the symbol of a sword: “Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). The Bible itself, in the same passage, explains that the sword is a symbol for the Word of God. We know for sure what a symbol means if the Bible explains the symbol at once, or in the same book. For example, John uses the symbol of a harlot (Revelation 17:1 – 8). But he soon tells us that the harlot is the great city that rules over the earth (Revelation 17:18).

Recognize that biblical writers use the same symbols in different ways. Therefore, seek first to interpret a symbol in the light of context. Remember the principles we studied about circles of context. To interpret a symbol, begin in the paragraph that contains it. If necessary, continue to other parts of the same book. Then you can compare other passages by the same author. As the chart below shows, even the same authors use words in different ways. As we said earlier, let the Bible speak for itself. Seek to interpret a symbol in the way an author used it. Biblical writers use symbols in different ways. The right meaning of a symbol is the meaning the author intended.

## 7 - Genres: Historical Narrative, Stories of History

### Separate the Enduring from the Temporary

#### 7.1.1 — Use three questions to discern between commands and actions that are normative and those that are descriptive.

The Duchess of Ferrara, daughter of Louis XII of France, once complained to John Calvin that some of David’s actions in the Bible offended her. Yet, even though his actions were wrong by biblical ethics, the Bible did not condemn him (Wood 1967, 92). The Duchess and probably all of us have wondered about some of the stories in the Bible. Beside the great examples of faith and righteousness, we find accounts of incest, lying, adultery, cruelty, deceit, suicide, and murder. Often, the Bible records these acts without condemning those who sinned. Still, as readers, we must discern that all sin is wrong. God expects readers to recognize that evil is evil.

Distinguishing Normative from Descriptive

Not everything a Bible hero or heroine does is a pattern for us today. Most of the time, the Bible records righteous acts without praising them. Likewise, it describes sins without condemning them. Sometimes a character’s actions are meant to be a pattern for all believers. We call these actions normative —good examples for all to follow. Other actions and commands simply describe what happened as a background to the story. What is merely described, but not set forth as a pattern for us today, is called “descriptive.”

For example, David committed adultery with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11). The Bible describes what David did, but his actions are not normative. They are not a pattern for us to follow. Likewise, the Gibeonites deceived Joshua (Joshua 9). The Bible describes their deceit, but their actions are not normative. God does not want us to follow their example!

Biblical writers seldom tell us which actions and commands are eternal norms or patterns for all, and which are temporary. So we may struggle to determine the difference. In the early days of America and in South Africa, European Christians killed the local people. They said they were obeying God’s order to Joshua to slay the Canaanites. These believers from Europe claimed that God’s command to kill the local people and take their land was normative.

During World War II, some ministers in Nazi Germany said that murdering the Jews was God’s will because the Jews had asked for Christ’s blood to be on the heads of their children (Matthew 27:25). That was like the pogrom’s of Tsarist Russia that would kill or evict the “Christ killers,” the Jews. Some today claim that having many wives is biblical because the patriarchs had several wives. Look at the following examples and determine if the example is normative or descriptive.

Bible

Normative or Descriptive

Genesis 6:14

God commanded Noah to build an ark.

Genesis 12:1

God told Abraham to leave his home and move to a new land.

Genesis 19:30–38

Lot’s daughters had an incestuous relationship with their father.

Genesis 29:31–30:24

Jacob had four wives.

Exodus 1:19

The midwives lied to save the newborns.

Exodus 20:4

God commands not to worship idols.

Deuteronomy 20:15–18

God told Israel to kill their enemies.

Joshua 2:4–6

Rahab lied to save the spies.

Ruth 3:9

Ruth proposed marriage to Boaz.

Esther 2:14–18

Esther married an unbeliever.

Ezekiel 4:4–8

Ezekiel preached lying on his side.

The Support of Other Scriptures

What is normative must be supported by other Scriptures. Sometimes, we must study to see if a command or action is normative, meaning a guide for all believers. For example, should a modern believer test God as Gideon did with a fleece? Is a believer allowed to marry an unbeliever as Esther did? Should a new convert divorce an unbelieving mate as Ezra commanded the Jews to do (Ezra 9:1–2; 10:10–11)? Will a Christian leader be punished as David was (1 Chronicles 21:1–30) if that leader counts the people who attend church?

Below are three important questions of biblical interpretation for clarifying what a story is teaching—or what it is not teaching.

1. Does other direct teaching in the Bible condemn the action?

2. Is the action, promise, or command confirmed and repeated in other passages of the Bible?

3. Is the action or command only part of a cultural practice of the biblical person?

Apply all three questions to a passage as you seek to interpret it. For example, it is not wise to teach that greeting each other with a holy kiss is normative. Greeting each other with a holy kiss passes the test of question 1, for the Bible does not condemn it. Such a greeting also passes the test of question 2, for several passages in the New Testament refer to it (1 Peter 5:14). However, when we apply question 3, we find that greeting with a kiss was only a cultural practice. Even today, some parts of the world greet with a kiss on the cheek, but other parts of the world greet with a handshake, or in another manner. Kissing as a greeting is not normative—the type of greeting depends on the culture. So, be sure to apply all three rules when interpreting a passage. Now, let us look closer at each of the three questions.

Action Condemned by Other Biblical Teaching

The action of a Bible hero is never normative if it contradicts the clear teaching of other Scripture. Biblical stories may describe lying, adultery, deceit, and other sins. In these cases, the biblical writer assumes that his readers know the Scriptures and commands of God. He does not feel he needs to repeat what is clear from other Scriptures.

For example, Numbers 22 does not tell us the sin in Balaam’s heart. But Peter says Balaam loved the wages of unrighteousness (2 Peter 2:15). Likewise, Jude condemns Balaam’s error (v. 11).

Action, Promise, or Command Confirmed and Repeated in Scripture

You have learned that a doctrine must not be based on a single passage. In the same way, a practice of faith cannot be based only on one historical event. For all believers to follow a practice, several places in the Bible must teach us to do it.

Some events are not a pattern for us to follow—they are unique in history. Consider the following examples:

• Joshua’s command to destroy the Canaanites was never repeated in Scripture. It was a unique command in history.

• Hosea was asked to marry an adulterous wife (Hosea 1:2). The Bible never repeats this command to a believer. Rather, Hosea’s marriage was an example of God’s relationship to unfaithful Israel.

• David numbered his people and suffered God’s wrath (1 Chronicles 21:1–30). Nowhere is there a command against numbering the people of God. In fact, Numbers and Ezra contain several examples where leaders numbered God’s people and were blessed. Perhaps David’s sin was not that he counted the people, but that he was proud and trusted the many soldiers of Israel.

The following events, of course, are normative and are patterns for believers today.

• Elijah prayed for a sick boy, and God healed him. Many passages in both the Old and New Testaments teach us to pray for the sick to be healed. (James 5:14–15)

• The Israelites lifted up their hands to God in praise and prayer (Psalm 28:2; Psalm 134:2). Likewise, Paul tells us this: “I want men everywhere to lift up holy hands in prayer, without anger or disputing.” (1 Timothy 2:8)

• The Lord’s Supper was not just a one-time event in Christ’s life. Rather, it is a normal practice found in the Early Church thirty years later. (1 Corinthians 11:23–26)

Action or Command as a Cultural Practice of the Biblical Person

Sometimes the actions of a person in the Bible reflect a cultural practice of his or her time. Even though a cultural custom may have been common in Israel’s time, it may lack meaning in modern times.

Rachel’s generation believed that a mandrake plant assured that a woman would conceive a baby (Genesis 30:31). This reflected her culture and is not a medical pattern for modern believers.

Ruth asked Boaz to show he would marry her by throwing a corner of his outer robe over her (Ruth 3:9). The way she proposed marriage and the way he responded were part of an old Jewish custom. These practices are not patterns for single women today.

Practice Using the Three Questions

We will use these three questions in relation to Gideon’s fleece, when he sought a sign to know God’s will. Is Gideon’s method a pattern for believers today? Or did he already know God’s will, but lack the courage to act on it? Two of the three rules apply to Gideon.

Question 1: Other verses in the Bible discourage us from asking God for signs. God prefers that we trust Him without signs.

The Pharisees and Sadducees came to Jesus and tested him by asking him to show them a sign from heaven. He replied, ‘When evening comes, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red,’ and in the morning, ‘Today it will be stormy, for the sky is red and overcast.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. A wicked and adulterous generation looks for a miraculous sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah.’ Jesus then left them and went away. (Matthew 16:1–4)

“‘Unless you people see miraculous signs and wonders,’ Jesus told him, ‘you will never believe’” (John 4:48). So we see that Jesus encourages us to walk by faith, not by sight and signs. Thomas believed after he saw the nail prints, but Jesus blesses those who believe without seeing signs (John 20:29).

Question 2: In the Old Testament, signs are mentioned a few times. God gave signs to Moses and to Pharaoh. Isaiah invited Ahaz to ask for a sign (Isaiah 7:10). Likewise, Hezekiah asked Isaiah for a sign that God would heal him (2 Kings 20:8). But in Gideon’s case, God had already sent an angel to talk with him. Still, Gideon asked for signs. Gideon’s action seems to have been an act of doubt, rather than faith.

Question 3: This question has little or no application to the passage about Gideon since the passage does not focus on unique, cultural practices.

God gave some signs to guide and assure His people under the Old Covenant. In contrast, under the New Covenant, it is easier for us to know God’s will. He puts His Spirit within us to guide and assure us. He has given us an entire Bible to help us know His will. Likewise, He guides us through wise counsel, circumstances, and spiritual events like dreams and visions. Under the New Covenant, God has many ways to guide believers without using signs.

**Q:** Give biblical examples of actions that are normative and actions that are descriptive.

**A:** Introduction Elijah challenges Ahab concerning the true God. 18:16–20 Problem The prophets of Baal are assembled and Elijah tries, but fails, to rally the people to loyalty to God. 18:20–21 Rising action The Baal prophets attempt to get a response from Baal. 18:22–29 Turning point Elijah rebuilds the altar in preparation for victory. 18:30–31 Problem increases Elijah increases the difficulty by pouring water on the altar. 18:32–37 Climax The fire of the Lord falls and consumes the altar. 18:38–40 Result The Baal prophets are killed and rain comes to the land. 18:41–45 Post-script Elijah was empowered to outrun Ahab’s chariot. 18:46

**Q:** If someone cited the example of the Gibeonites lying, as a defense for lying, how would you answer him or her (Joshua 9)?

**A:** Accounts in the Bible are only patterns for our lives if they illustrate clear principles of righteousness. If other Bible teaching indicates a principle that conflicts with an historical account, we must not practice what is recorded.

**Q:** How would you respond to a believer who, based on Esther’s actions, wants to marry an unbeliever?

**A:** We must look at other passages that warn against such relationships. We conclude that Esther was put in a unique situation for a special purpose of God, and it is not an example for us to follow.

**Q:** Is the way Israel conquered Canaan a pattern for believers under the New Covenant? Explain.

**A:** No. Israel had special instructions from God that fulfilled His purpose in that culture at that time in history and within the covenant relationship in effect. We live in a different historical time under different covenant conditions and within far different cultural dynamics.

**Q:** Is the Bible’s description of Hosea’s marriage a pattern for believers today? Explain.

**A:** No. Hosea was used by God as an illustration. His marriage was not normal nor is it to be duplicated.

**Q:** Give an example of an Old Testament practice that is a pattern for believers today.

**A:** Answers will vary. Generosity toward foreigners and the poor; praying for the sick; honoring promises

### Discern the Author’s Purpose: Part 1

#### 7.2.1 — Explain why interpreters must discern the author’s purpose rather than allegorize.

In many cultures people avoid saying something negative to an equal or someone above them. They will tell a story or a proverb that hints at their feelings without directly stating how they feel. The prophet Nathan used this indirect method with King David. Nathan told a story that expressed how God felt about David.

A missionary shared an example of this indirect method. He asked the principal of a national Bible school to give his opinion on the school’s new books. For years, the school had used notes that the teachers copied for the students. But now the students had textbooks written at a much higher reading level.

The principal answered with a story. He said that when he was a young man, he was invited to a fellowship meeting in a town nearby. He wanted to impress his friends by wearing shoes. He had never owned a pair of shoes, so he went to the market looking for his first pair. He found a pair he liked for a good price, but they were one size too small. The seller warned him they would hurt his feet, but he insisted on buying the shoes.

He walked over fifteen miles to the meeting and had pain with every step. On the way home, he took out his knife and cut the end off of each shoe. This allowed his toes more room. Later he threw the shoes beside the road, and walked home barefoot. With that the principal stopped talking. The missionary smiled; he understood. The new books did not fit the students.

Like the story about the shoes, stories of the Bible are often told without an explanation. The interpreter must examine the story to discern the author’s purpose or intent. After the author’s purpose is clear, it is possible to apply the truth to others. If we had the story about the shoes but did not know the missionary’s question, we would not understand the purpose of the story. Likewise, to understand the purpose of biblical stories, we must examine the context of a story, the story itself, and the way the story is told. Then, and only then, can we discern the author’s purpose in telling a story.

Discerning the Author’s Purpose

As we saw in Chapter 2, the church has at times suffered from the spiritual disease of allegorizing. Recall that those who allegorize try to find hidden meanings in every story. Even today, some lead believers astray with the allegorical method. These unbiblical interpreters believe that every Old Testament story has two meanings: the author’s meaning and a spiritual meaning based on the New Testament. But it is wrong and dangerous to change the author’s meaning.

God inspired the biblical authors to write the stories He gave them. It is wrong to take away the meaning God intended, and add another meaning. Those who replace God’s meaning with their own meanings are very proud. Imagine a person so proud that he or she adds to the meaning God Almighty intended, preaching his or her own thoughts.

Some say this error of using allegory is preaching the right message from the wrong passage, but it is worse than that. Using allegory as a way to interpret shortchanges believers; it steals from them the great truths God intended in His stories. Allegory also teaches believers to interpret, with a method that is reader-centered, focusing on the imaginations of the reader. This method has no guidelines or control of the interpretation. False teaching can result, and leaders claim these teachings are based on the Bible. Instead, we must be Bible-centered, finding the one purpose of a biblical story, the meaning God himself wants us to have.

The stories of the Bible are historical narratives, not allegories. When the Bible presents a story as history, we should not search for hidden meanings that the author never imagined. All true interpreters of the Bible begin with the same goal: to find the author’s purpose. The interpreter does not dare suggest what a story means to us today, until he or she understands what the story meant to the writer and those who first heard it.

This does not mean that every biblical story has only one interpretation. Nor does it mean that only one sermon can be preached from a biblical story. We are saying that the author’s purpose is the basis of all interpretation. A thousand sermons can be preached from one passage, but all should be based on principles drawn from the author’s purpose.

At times, a biblical writer may not have understood the full application of his message. For example, Moses wrote the story of Abraham receiving the covenant promises. Perhaps Moses did not fully understand this truth. His understanding of the promises was limited. Moses may not have realized that the Messiah would bless the nations. But Moses did understand that God would give Abraham many children. These descendants would have a land, and one of these children of Abraham would bless the nations. The Holy Spirit led writers of the New Testament to explain the promises God gave Abraham. God did not leave us to interpret His stories, using our own imaginations. Rather, He inspired New Testament writers to clarify the meaning of Old Testament stories. So, we should be humble enough to preach the plain truth, and not preach things the apostles did not write about. Yet some proud preachers today think they have more insight than the apostles of Christ.

Finding the author’s purpose or intent in biblical stories is not easy. Seldom does the biblical writer explain his story. This has caused some readers to add on their own meanings, based on the New Testament. For example, a pastor was preaching about the time that Abraham sent Eliezer to search for a wife for Isaac. The preacher said that Abraham was a symbol of the Heavenly Father, and that Eliezer was a symbol of the Holy Spirit, sent to search for the bride of Christ (Genesis 24). When Eliezer found her, he placed her on a camel and brought her to the son. Likewise, the preacher claimed that pastors, like camels, bear the church to Christ. Like the camels, these pastors may drink in the Holy Spirit. Then, they must travel for days without study or prayer because the work of the Lord is heavy. This is bad preaching and bad interpreting. The preacher was not preaching the Word of God; he was preaching his own imaginations. Those who use allegory as a method to interpret should not claim to speak for God. The main truth is the plain truth, and the plain truth is the main truth.

A person who uses allegory to interpret the Old Testament does not have the authority of God. One pastor preached about the ark coming back to Israel from the land of the Philistines. He said that this was a symbol of pastors who, like the cows, lead the church back to God. He stopped his message at the point in the story when the cows were killed and sacrificed by God’s people (1 Samuel 6:14). This pastor was not preaching the plain truth. To find the main truths of this passage, you must read 1 Samuel 5–6. Review the story. It tells about God’s judgment on the Philistines. Their god Dagon near the ark fell and broke. And God struck the Philistines nearby with deadly tumors. Then, the Philistines—not the spiritual leaders of Israel—sent the ark home. The cows do not represent anything! Some principles we might draw from the story are these:

• God will judge those who use holy things in an unholy manner.

• God finds ways of speaking to those who do not know Him.

• God finds ways of bringing His people back into fellowship with Him.

Another pastor preached on the story of the woman who filled many vessels with oil. He said that the oil was a symbol of the Holy Spirit coming in Pentecostal power. But the pastor did not continue to compare the oil to the Holy Spirit when Elisha told the woman to sell the oil (2 Kings 4:7). Of course not! Pastors should preach on the great principles that are within the story.

The best thing to do with a great need is bring it to God.

• God delights to help those who come to Him.

• To receive a miracle, we must obey God in faith.

• Those who receive a miracle should continue to honor God.

Some say that Paul gave Christians an example of allegorizing the Old Testament stories. These note that Paul compared the children of Hagar and Sarah to children of the law and promise (Galatians 4:21–31). But Paul did not ignore the purpose of Moses. Rather, he used the story of Abraham to teach a lesson. Ishmael, the child of Hagar was born in the normal manner. Ishmael was born because Abraham tried to fulfill God’s promise in a fleshly manner. But the child of Sarah was born through God’s promise. It took a miracle of the Spirit for Sarah to give birth. Like Sarah’s child, we are children of the Spirit. We are not born in the normal way, as a result of human effort. Rather, we believers are those who have a supernatural birth by the Spirit. Paul uses the story of Hagar and Sarah to emphasize a great principle: “Flesh gives birth to flesh, but the Spirit gives birth to spirit” (John 3:6).

Paul discerned the principles in the Old Testament story of Hagar and Sarah. Then, he applied those principles to believers of his day. He did not create a second meaning for the story. In the same way, modern pastors should find the principles within a biblical story. Then they should apply these principles to believers today in their own culture and time. Many of the events of the Old Testament are examples for us today (1 Corinthians 10:6). Still, we must not ignore the author’s purpose. Rather, we begin by discerning the purpose of a biblical writer, and then apply a story’s principles to believers today.

Discerning the Author’s Purpose and the Plot of a Story

To find the author’s purpose, we must analyze the plot . Plot refers to the plan of a story, including all the parts in the beginning, middle, and end of a story. The longer stories in the Bible have a line of action, like a climb up a mountain. Many stories have seven parts in the plot:

1. The introduction includes the setting and some characters of the story. More characters may be introduced later as the story develops. (For example, see Ruth 1:1–2 for the setting and introduction of Elimelech, Naomi, and their two sons.)

2. The problem or need is where the climb up the mountain begins. We see a conflict. (See Ruth 1:3–22, where Naomi’s husband and sons all die. Ruth clings to her, but they have no one to help them as they return to Bethlehem).

3. The rising action means the author gives us more information as the story grows. (See Ruth 2:1–19, as Ruth gleans in the field of Boaz.)

4. The turning point is where we turn from the problem toward the solution. (See Ruth 2:20, the exact middle of the book, where Naomi rejoices at the help of Boaz).

5. The problem gets worse when the conflict increases. The fire may become seven times hotter (This step is omitted in the book of Ruth.)

6. The climax occurs when the problem is solved. We have reached the top of the mountain. (In Ruth 4:1–12, Boaz marries Ruth).

7. The results show the characters climbing down the mountain. The main character is either informed, confirmed, or transformed. In Ruth 4:13–17, Naomi is honored as Ruth bares a son named Obed, who becomes the father of Jesse, the father of David.

Note, some stories have an eighth part— a post-script after the story—such as Ruth 4:18–22.

To interpret a story correctly, we must identify its climax, the top of the mountain. Although the climax is usually near the end of the story, it is the emotional center of the story. The climax is a strong sign of what is important to the writer. It is the point in a story where the hero responds to a test, overcomes a struggle, or makes a decision. Discerning the Author’s Purpose and the Characters of a Story

Studying the characters is another key to understanding the purpose of a biblical writer. We should learn to answer three questions about a main character.

Flat or Round Character

The literary term flat character refers to a minor character who does not substantially change or grow in the course of a narrative. In contrast, a round character is a major, complex character who grows or changes by the end of the story. Authors describe round characters in greater detail. The author extensively portrays round characters. Since Bible stories tend to use few words, when a character is described in detail, the reader should take note. We will consider three examples of round characters: Esau, Jacob, and Joseph.

From the beginning, Moses describes Esau as one who cared little about his birthright. When Esau sold it for a bowl of soup, the author gives us seven verbs that describe his attitude: swore, selling, eat, drink, got up, left, and despised (Genesis 25:33–34). “But Jacob said, ‘Swear to me first.’ So he swore an oath to him, selling his birthright to Jacob. Then Jacob gave Esau some bread and some lentil stew. He ate and drank, and then got up and left. So, Esau despised his birthright” (Genesis 25:33–34). There is little doubt concerning what the author thinks of Esau’s actions.

Jacob is shown to be a deceiver. He dresses to look like his brother, lies to his father, and plots with his mother. In contrast, Joseph, our third example of a round character, is repeatedly described in positive ways. The Bible tells that God was with Joseph. “God blessed him” (Genesis 39:3, 21; 41:52). Those in authority gave Joseph honor and responsibility. The author describes him as a blessed father. And we see him as a person filled with faith and love and the ability to forgive his brothers.

Character Changing (Dynamic) or Remaining the Same (Static)

The Bible has many stories of people who change greatly during a story. Seeing how they change helps us discern the writer’s purpose. A person may change for the better or for worse. If a main character’s choice results in a negative result, it shows that the biblical writer is opposed to the character’s decision.

Note the following changes:

• Saul’s choice to sacrifice without Samuel resulted in defeat. (1 Samuel 13:8–15). Clearly, Saul is condemned for not waiting for God’s direction. Saul changed from being small in his own eyes to being big.

• Joseph is filled with sorrow, but forgives his brothers. The result is that God blesses him and his family (Genesis 40).

• Job changed and became even better.

• David changed and repented for his sin.

• King Uzziah changed; he became proud, and God struck him with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

• Esther changed and testified about her faith.

• Nebuchadnezzar changed and became a better king.

• Jonah changed and obeyed God.

• Israel, throughout the nation’s history, refused to change and remain faithful to God.

Watch for the following three types of positive changes in a Bible hero.

1. The hero may be transformed by the changing of his or her heart (Gideon went from fear to courage).

2. The hero may be informed by receiving new revelation or promises from God (Abraham received the promise after his offering of Isaac).

3. The hero may be confirmed, crowned, or established as God’s person for a position or responsibility (David killed Goliath and was confirmed as the future leader of Israel).

Noting how the hero is changed from the beginning to the end of the story is a powerful tool to discern the author’s purpose in a story.

**Q:** Why do some people tell stories instead of speaking truth directly?

**A:** Sometimes this is a sign of respect, to hint at feelings and opinions through a story rather than state them directly. The hearer’s feelings and opinions are being respected rather than directly contradicted.

**Q:** What do you think is the most important task in interpreting a biblical story?

**A:** Answer may vary. Identifying the author’s meaning should be the most important task.

**Q:** What is the difference between being Bible-centered and reader-centered?

**A:** Bible-centered means to find the meaning that is defined by the Bible text, according to the principles of hermeneutics. Reader-centered is interpreting the Bible based on personal feelings, biases, ideas, and impressions.

**Q:** What is the first goal of all true interpreters of the Bible?

**A:** To be Bible-centered, finding the true meaning that God intends us to have

**Q:** Did Paul use allegory to interpret the story of Hagar and Sarah? Explain.

**A:** This is debated among Bible scholars. This is probably not an example of allegory in the same way that we use allegory to create a new meaning for a passage that was not there by the author’s intention.

**A:** Introduction, problem, rising action, turning point, problem increases, climax, result

#### 7.2.2 — Describe how studying the climax and characters of a story may reveal the author’s purpose.

In many cultures people avoid saying something negative to an equal or someone above them. They will tell a story or a proverb that hints at their feelings without directly stating how they feel. The prophet Nathan used this indirect method with King David. Nathan told a story that expressed how God felt about David.

A missionary shared an example of this indirect method. He asked the principal of a national Bible school to give his opinion on the school’s new books. For years, the school had used notes that the teachers copied for the students. But now the students had textbooks written at a much higher reading level.

The principal answered with a story. He said that when he was a young man, he was invited to a fellowship meeting in a town nearby. He wanted to impress his friends by wearing shoes. He had never owned a pair of shoes, so he went to the market looking for his first pair. He found a pair he liked for a good price, but they were one size too small. The seller warned him they would hurt his feet, but he insisted on buying the shoes.

He walked over fifteen miles to the meeting and had pain with every step. On the way home, he took out his knife and cut the end off of each shoe. This allowed his toes more room. Later he threw the shoes beside the road, and walked home barefoot. With that the principal stopped talking. The missionary smiled; he understood. The new books did not fit the students.

Like the story about the shoes, stories of the Bible are often told without an explanation. The interpreter must examine the story to discern the author’s purpose or intent. After the author’s purpose is clear, it is possible to apply the truth to others. If we had the story about the shoes but did not know the missionary’s question, we would not understand the purpose of the story. Likewise, to understand the purpose of biblical stories, we must examine the context of a story, the story itself, and the way the story is told. Then, and only then, can we discern the author’s purpose in telling a story.

Discerning the Author’s Purpose

As we saw in Chapter 2, the church has at times suffered from the spiritual disease of allegorizing. Recall that those who allegorize try to find hidden meanings in every story. Even today, some lead believers astray with the allegorical method. These unbiblical interpreters believe that every Old Testament story has two meanings: the author’s meaning and a spiritual meaning based on the New Testament. But it is wrong and dangerous to change the author’s meaning.

God inspired the biblical authors to write the stories He gave them. It is wrong to take away the meaning God intended, and add another meaning. Those who replace God’s meaning with their own meanings are very proud. Imagine a person so proud that he or she adds to the meaning God Almighty intended, preaching his or her own thoughts.

Some say this error of using allegory is preaching the right message from the wrong passage, but it is worse than that. Using allegory as a way to interpret shortchanges believers; it steals from them the great truths God intended in His stories. Allegory also teaches believers to interpret, with a method that is reader-centered, focusing on the imaginations of the reader. This method has no guidelines or control of the interpretation. False teaching can result, and leaders claim these teachings are based on the Bible. Instead, we must be Bible-centered, finding the one purpose of a biblical story, the meaning God himself wants us to have.

Then Jacob gave Esau some bread and some lentil stew. He ate and drank, and then got up and left. So, Esau despised his birthright” (Genesis 25:33–34). There is little doubt concerning what the author thinks of Esau’s actions.

Jacob is shown to be a deceiver. He dresses to look like his brother, lies to his father, and plots with his mother. In contrast, Joseph, our third example of a round character, is repeatedly described in positive ways. The Bible tells that God was with Joseph. “God blessed him” (Genesis 39:3, 21; 41:52). Those in authority gave Joseph honor and responsibility. The author describes him as a blessed father. And we see him as a person filled with faith and love and the ability to forgive his brothers.

Character Changing (Dynamic) or Remaining the Same (Static)

The Bible has many stories of people who change greatly during a story. Seeing how they change helps us discern the writer’s purpose. A person may change for the better or for worse. If a main character’s choice results in a negative result, it shows that the biblical writer is opposed to the character’s decision.

Note the following changes:

• Saul’s choice to sacrifice without Samuel resulted in defeat. (1 Samuel 13:8–15). Clearly, Saul is condemned for not waiting for God’s direction. Saul changed from being small in his own eyes to being big.

• Joseph is filled with sorrow, but forgives his brothers. The result is that God blesses him and his family (Genesis 40).

• Job changed and became even better.

• David changed and repented for his sin.

• King Uzziah changed; he became proud, and God struck him with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

• Esther changed and testified about her faith.

• Nebuchadnezzar changed and became a better king.

• Jonah changed and obeyed God.

• Israel, throughout the nation’s history, refused to change and remain faithful to God.

Watch for the following three types of positive changes in a Bible hero.

1. The hero may be transformed by the changing of his or her heart (Gideon went from fear to courage).

2. The hero may be informed by receiving new revelation or promises from God (Abraham received the promise after his offering of Isaac).

3. The hero may be confirmed, crowned, or established as God’s person for a position or responsibility (David killed Goliath and was confirmed as the future leader of Israel).

Noting how the hero is changed from the beginning to the end of the story is a powerful tool to discern the author’s purpose in a story.

**Q:** Why do some people tell stories instead of speaking truth directly?

**A:** Sometimes this is a sign of respect, to hint at feelings and opinions through a story rather than state them directly. The hearer’s feelings and opinions are being respected rather than directly contradicted.

**Q:** What do you think is the most important task in interpreting a biblical story?

**A:** Answer may vary. Identifying the author’s meaning should be the most important task.

**Q:** What is the difference between being Bible-centered and reader-centered?

**A:** Bible-centered means to find the meaning that is defined by the Bible text, according to the principles of hermeneutics. Reader-centered is interpreting the Bible based on personal feelings, biases, ideas, and impressions.

**Q:** What is the first goal of all true interpreters of the Bible?

**A:** To be Bible-centered, finding the true meaning that God intends us to have

**Q:** Did Paul use allegory to interpret the story of Hagar and Sarah? Explain.

**A:** This is debated among Bible scholars. This is probably not an example of allegory in the same way that we use allegory to create a new meaning for a passage that was not there by the author’s intention.

### Discern the Author’s Purpose: Part 2

#### 7.3.1 — Relate the interpreter’s view of characters and miracles to discerning an author’s purpose.

Some scholars view the stories of the Bible as fictional stories that illustrate truth but that should not be taken as literary history. This perspective will short-circuit the interpretation of the Bible. Let us look at the differences among four types of stories: fables, myths, parables, and historical narratives.

View of Characters and Miracles in a Historical Story

Fables are stories that a person creates or invents to teach a principle or moral truth. Aesop was an ancient Greek teacher who knew the power of a story. He created fables. The fable he invented about the sun and the wind has lasted over two thousand years. In the story, the sun and the wind are debating about who is stronger. When they saw a traveler walking on the road, the wind suggested a test. The one who could remove the traveler’s coat would be strongest. The wind tried first, blowing with all his force, but this caused the man to hold his coat tighter. Then the sun tried. He gently shined on the man, and soon the coat was off. After telling this fable, the teacher asked: What is the principle or moral of the story? After discussion, people discerned that the moral was “kindness has more power to change a person than force.”

Myths or legends are traditional or cultural stories that never happened. These are often about heroes or nature. People imagined them to entertain or to explain something, often in nature. For example, there is a myth in Africa that people created to explain why people vary in skin color. This myth or legend says that God created all people black. Then, he created a small pond of water for people to wash in, so they would become white. God used different animals to carry the message about the water. To the Europeans, he sent a gazelle as a messenger. This animal ran quickly, so the Europeans arrived first and washed completely. But to the Africans, God sent the chameleon—which travels even slower than a turtle. So the African arrived last. There was only enough water left to wash the palms of their hands and the soles of their feet.

Parables (and allegories) are earthly stories that a leader creates to teach a spiritual lesson. Listeners recognize that parables may not have happened, but could have happened. Parables are a method of teaching. For example, Jesus used the parable of the sower to teach a spiritual lesson. The main principle is that as the fate of the seed depends on the soil, so does the effect of the gospel depend on the type of person who hears it.

Historical narratives are true stories of history. Many people call themselves Christian theologians but have inaccurate views about inspiration. Liberal teachers confuse believers; they call the Bible inspired but claim that it does not have authority over our lives. They may say the Bible does not contain principles that are true for every generation. Those who believe in inspiration without authority tend to see the Bible stories as mythos (legends) that illustrate truth. They claim the ancients merely used fables, myths, and legends to teach deeper truths.

Review Lesson 2 of Chapter 1. We studied the qualifications of a biblical interpreter. Those who do not believe that the Bible is inspired are not able to interpret it correctly. We believe that all Scriptures are

• Inspired by God in a verbal, plenary way;

• The revelation of God to us;

• Infallible and inerrant (true and without error on matters of history, science, and doctrine); and

• The authority over our faith and living.

These liberal teachers encourage modern readers to look beyond what is called a miracle to the principle or moral it illustrates. For example, false teachers say the feeding of the four thousand was not a supernatural miracle. They claim that Jesus never multiplied the loaves and fishes. Rather, they say that first the small boy was generous; he shared his fish and bread. Then, the false teachers say all of the people followed his example and shared their fish and bread. In contrast, the Scriptures say that the people had been with Jesus three days, and had nothing to eat (Matthew 15:32). Those who do not believe Jesus multiplied the loaves and fishes interpret the event in a strange way. They say the lesson of this story is about sharing, not the power of Jesus to provide for His people.

These liberal teachers see the characters in the Bible as legends. For example, they claim that people like Adam, Eve, and Abraham never lived in history. Likewise, they do not believe in prophecy. They claim that biblical writers deceived people by writing prophecies about things that had already happened to give the Bible a sense of authority. An example of this attitude is seen in the following quote by Adele Berlin: “Above all, we must keep in mind that narrative is a form of representation. Abraham in Genesis is not a real person any more than the painting of an apple is real fruit” (Ryken and Longman 1993, 19).

These same teachers do not believe Jesus was God in the flesh. They do not believe He did signs and wonders or that He rose from the dead. They are like wolves in sheep’s clothing. They define inspiration differently. They claim, for example, that the story of Adam and Eve is true, although they deny that Adam and Eve ever lived on the earth. Paul put it plainly. He said that if Jesus is not raised from the dead, our preaching is useless, and we are false witnesses about God (1 Corinthians 15:14–15).

Inspiration without divine authority lowers the Bible to the level of Greek myths and Aesop’s fables. The Pentecostal interpreter should accept biblical stories in the same way that Christ and the apostles accepted them. When Christ spoke of Old Testament characters, He accepted them as real and their actions as history. Jesus accepted the story of Jonah and the great fish as a true story of history (Matthew 12:40). Peter accepted Noah and the saving of his family as a real event (1 Peter 3:20). Likewise, Peter refers to the biblical account of the time Balaam’s donkey spoke and considers it to be a historical fact (2 Peter 2:16). Paul says that the events and people of the Exodus were real examples for us (1 Corinthians 10:5–6). Likewise, Jesus said that heaven is a real place “‘If it were not so, I would have told you’” (John 14:2).

Believing that the historical stories of the Bible really happened is important. As we believe this, we will be able to interpret the stories correctly.

The Broader Context to Clarify the Author’s Purpose

Sometimes a small story is part of a bigger story. (Some call this a multi-plot story, one big story with many smaller plots). In such a case, we must interpret each small story as one chapter in an entire book. The life of Abraham is an example of many small stories that are part of a big story or theme: walking by faith in the promise of God. At first, some of the small stories seem to lack meaning:

• Abraham lied about Sarai.

• He allowed Lot to choose the best land.

• He took Hagar as a concubine.

But we see the purpose of these small stories in the context of the promises of God in Genesis 12:1–5. The small stories are steps in Abraham’s journey of faith.

The Lord had said to Abram, “Leave your country, your people and your father’s household and go to the land I will show you. I will make you into a great nation and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you.” So Abram left, as the Lord had told him; and Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old when he set out from Haran. He took his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, all the possessions they had accumulated and the people they had acquired in Haran, and they set out for the land of Canaan, and they arrived there. (Genesis 12:1–5)

God promised Abraham a land, a seed, and a blessing for the nations. In these small stories, we see Abraham either accepting the promise by faith or trying to fulfill God’s promise by his own efforts.
