Psalms with Three Parts: Praise and Worship

Form of a Psalm with Three Parts

1. Introduction: theme (that unites the psalm), mood, people, occasion, etc.

2. Development of theme: repetition, a list, examples, comparisons, or contrasts

3. Conclusion: promise, summary, praise, and prayer

Most of the psalms have three parts: introduction, development, and conclusion. In the introduction of a psalm, the psalmist states the theme and sets the mood. In the middle section, he develops the theme through lists, contrast, comparison, repetition, or association. This middle part of a psalm, the development, is the largest section and is usually made up of several stanzas—verses of the song (musical paragraphs). The three-part form concludes with a promise, a summary, an exhortation, or a prayer.

Hallelujah or Praise Psalms

These psalms magnify the name, majesty, goodness, greatness, and salvation of God. The praise psalms have a fixed three-part form:

1. They begin with an introduction, a call to praise. The call to praise may mention who should praise, and how to praise. For example, the psalmist may ask people to praise God with singing, with musical instruments, with dancing, with clapping, and so forth.

2. The development part lists reasons to praise God. This list may emphasize praising God for His acts and praising Him for His attributes or character.

3. The conclusion ends the praise often with a prayer or exhortation. The main task of the interpreter is to find the theme that runs through all three parts of a psalm. The theme of Psalm 139 is this: praise God for knowing and caring for us. Note the three parts of Psalm 139.

Psalm 139

Part 1: Introduction (Call to Praise)

• The Psalmist praises God—the One who examines his life (vv. 1–4).

Part 2: Development (List of God’s attributes and acts)

• God knows all about me (vv. 5–6).

• God is always with me (vv. 7–10).

• God can always find me (vv. 11–12).

• God created me for a purpose (vv. 13–16).

• God thinks about me always (vv. 17–18).

• God’s enemies are my enemies (vv. 19–22).

Part 3: Invitation (Prayer)

• The psalmist invites God to examine and guide his life (vv. 23–24).

The form of Psalm 139 has three parts: introduction, development, and invitation. Some Christians believe that emotion in worship did not exist before the birth of the church. This is far from the truth. The worship at the tabernacle and temple was full of emotion: dancing, clapping, and joyful singing with musical instruments. Fifty of the psalms’ headings are to the “chief musician” (KJV) or the “director of music” (NIV). Many of the headings also include instructions on how the psalm is to be sung (for example, to the tune of “Lilies” in Psalm 45) or accompanied (for example, with stringed instruments in Psalm 54). Glance at the headings above Psalms 40 to 80 and note those headings that address the director of music and/or provide choral or instrumental notations.

The Jews sang the praise psalms with great joy. In Psalm 33:1, the psalmist calls the people to rejoice because their praise is beautiful (fitting) to the Lord. In contrast to the lament psalms, the praise psalms focus not on the psalmist’s problems but on the Lord’s worthiness. The direction of the praise psalm is away from the psalmist toward God. Psalm 33:3 commands the worshipper to sing to God.

The music that accompanies the praise psalm is to be played skillfully but not with formal professionalism. The psalm is to be sung as a new song (Psalm 33:3). One writer suggested that new song refers not to new lyrics but rather to a fresh sense of wonder.

His exhortation to sing “a new song” (v. 3) is not merely a call for new music and new hymnals. The phrase new song means to sing to God with a renewed sense of wonder at all He has done for us. The worship of God should never degenerate into something that we just do; we should always approach God with rejoicing. With the phrase skillfully (v. 3), the psalmist exhorts us never to approach our worship with a casual attitude. We are to “play skillfully” because we are playing to the Lord, and we must offer Him only our best. But skill is not the only criterion of worship music, for the psalmist’s final exhortation in verse 3 is to play “with a shout of joy.” Since God always considers our attitudes, genuine joy in the presence of our caring Lord is required for music to be truly worshipful. (Radmacher, Allen, and House 1999, 685)

Psalms 146–150, the Hallel of hallelujah psalms , serve as the conclusion of the entire book of Psalms. These five psalms each begin with hallelujah —the Hebrew word for “praise the Lord.”

The development section in these psalms is unique. Instead of listing reasons to praise, it repeats commands to praise. Psalm 148 is a good example.

• First, Psalm 148 commands the angels to praise (Psalm 148:2).

• Next, it commands the heavenly bodies and all nature on earth to praise (Psalm 148:4–6).

• Finally, the Psalm commands all men and women to praise—from the king and the judges to the old men and children (Psalm 148:11–14).

Songs about Creation or Nature

These psalms exalt God as the Creator of the heavens and the earth. The nature psalms (Psalms 8, 19, 29, 104, 108) use creation to glorify God. These psalms show God above , rather than in nature (Psalm 29:10). Pagans wrote songs and worshipped their gods as a part of nature (Ryken 1984, 118). In contrast, Jewish nature psalms worship God as the one who created and controls nature (Psalm 19:1–5). As an artist is glorified by his or her paintings, so God is glorified by His creation.

Psalm 29 traces the path of a mighty storm. It forms in the Mediterranean Sea (29:3) and enters Lebanon with fierce winds—winds that break the huge cedar trees (29:5). As the storm comes into northern Israel, it produces loud thunder and frightening lightning (29:7–8). During the storm, God sits calmly on His throne, above the flood (29:10). In response to His power and authority, the worshipper cries, “Glory!” (29:9).

Psalms about the King and Messiah

These psalms, sometimes called royal psalms , describe experiences of King David or King Solomon. Psalms like these call on God to protect His anointed king. They ask God to give him victory against his enemies (Psalm 20). In response to God’s help, the king trusts and praises Him (Psalm 21). Psalm 45 probably records a song from the wedding of one of Israel’s kings. Psalms 89 and 132 reflect on God’s covenant with King David (2 Samuel 7:1–16).

These psalms referred to kings, like David, who lived at that time. But the New Testament authors teach us that many psalms also apply to Jesus. It is good to consider what the author understood about his times and what the Holy Spirit knew about the coming Messiah.

Some psalms do not appear to be messianic. But New Testament authors quote them in referring to Christ. In this way, the psalms were fulfilled twice, first by an earthly king and later by the King of kings. Jesus Christ is the great Son of David. God promised that this King would rule the nations. Therefore, psalms about the king of Israel find their highest fulfillment in Christ.

Psalms 2 and 110 are messianic psalms. They predict that God will set up His anointed Son as King in Zion (Psalm 2:6). This King (Jesus) will rule the whole earth. All people will submit to Him or face judgment (Psalm 2:8-12). This prophecy refers to the second coming of Christ. He will come in power to rule the earth and set up His kingdom.

Jews sang the royal psalms at special events in the life of Israel’s kings. Many of these psalms refer to God’s covenant with David. Recall that God promised David that a king in his family would rule forever (2 Samuel 7). Jesus, a son of David, was the king God promised would rule. The temporary kings of Judah and the events in their lives pointed to the ministry of the Messiah—the King of kings.

Psalms about Israel’s king pointed forward to the Messiah—the King of kings.

Psalms Praising God as King

These psalms boldly declare that God reigns. When Israel first became the people of God, they understood that God would be their king. This is why, later in their history, Gideon refused to become king (Judges 8:23). The prophet Samuel warned Israel that God was the only king they should have (1 Samuel 8:4–7; 12:12–15).

God is the great King we should respect (Psalm 47:2). He reigns over all the nations of the earth. He deserves our praise (Psalm 47:6–7). There are many reasons to worship Him. He is King over all gods (Psalms 95:3; 97:9). He will judge all nations (Psalm 96:9–13). He rules the earth with strength and justice (Psalm 99:4). He is holy and almighty. We should worship Him as our Master, Lord, and King.

Most of the psalms about God as king are in Psalms 90 to 99. Like the royal psalms, they deal with kingship and point to the kingdom of God. These psalms focus on God, the divine King, rather than on the human kings of the royal psalms. The main theme of these psalms is that the Lord will reign over all the peoples of the earth. The righteous may suffer now, for a short time, but in the end they will prosper under the divine King. When you read a psalm about God as king, watch for phrases that describe Him.

Phrases about God as King

Psalm

The Lord reigns

93, 96–97; 99

The Lord is the great king

47:2

The Lord comes to judge

98:9

The psalms about God as King have key phrases that describe His rule.

Songs of Zion and Ascent to Zion

The Jews sang psalms of ascent as they went up— ascended —to Jerusalem for the yearly feasts of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles. They sang songs of Zion when they thought about Jerusalem or arrived there.

These types of psalms have three parts. You must understand the big theme of a psalm in relation to the parts. In Psalm 133, note the following:

1 The first part—the introduction—states the theme unity .

2 In the middle part of Psalm 133, the Psalmist illustrates unity twice to develop the theme.

3 The conclusion looks forward to eternal unity with God.

Psalm 133

Introduction: Statement of the theme: unity

• How good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity! (v. 1)

Development: Two illustrations—anointing oil and dew—describe unity.

• It is like precious oil poured on the head,

running down on the beard,

running down on Aaron’s beard,

down upon the collar of his robes.

• It is as if the dew of Hermon

were falling on mount Zion. (vv. 2–3)

Conclusion: Points from the present to eternal unity

• For there the Lord gives His blessing, even life forevermore.

The songs of ascents are Psalms 120 to 134 and are noted in the Bible by their superscriptions, or heading, above each. It would be easy to visualize worshippers singing as they approached the temple.

I was glad when they said unto me,

“Let us go into the house of the Lord!” (Psalm 122:1, KJV)

Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion,

which cannot be moved, but abides forever.

As the mountains are round about Jerusalem,

so the Lord is round about his people. (Psalm 125:1–2, RSV)

Setting

Song or Psalm of Zion

Psalm

“How lovely is your dwelling place, O Lord Almighty! My soul yearns, even faints, for the courts of the Lord;my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God.”

84:1–2

“Great is the Lord, and most worthy of praise,in the city of our God, his holy mountain. It is beautiful in its loftiness, the joy of the whole earth.”

“Walk about Zion, go around her, count her towers, consider well her ramparts, view her citadels that you may tell of them to the next generation.”

Parts of Judah, and later, the entire nation became captives. In these hard times they did not stop writing about Zion. Even as captives in a foreign land, they longed to worship in the temple at Jerusalem. They prayed that God would somehow send out a light and lead them back to Mount Zion. For example, a captured Jew probably wrote Psalms 42 and 43. In the beginning, these two psalms were probably together as one psalm.

As the deer pants for streams of water,

so my soul pants for you, O God. (Psalm 42:1–2)

These things I remember

as I pour out my soul:

how I used to go with the multitude,

leading the procession to the house of God,

with shouts of joy and thanksgiving

among the festive throng. (Psalm 42:4)

Send forth your light and your truth,

let them guide me;

let them bring me to your holy mountain,

to the place where you dwell. (Psalm 43:3)

Historical Songs about God’s salvation

These psalms do not relate to a specific event in the life of a believer. Instead, they review Israel’s history. They remind the hearers of the nation’s sins. They praise God for all that He has done for His people. They also invite the people to trust God because of His past faithfulness (Leupold 1969, 561–562). Read Psalm 78:11–20.

Songs for Public Worship

These psalms were for special services or feasts. Psalms 113–118 were used each year at the Passover.

Songs of Trust and Devotion

These songs worship God and express a person’s faith in Him. A favorite psalm in this group is Psalm 91.

Psalms of Wisdom and Teaching

These psalms reflect on God’s ways and instruct us about righteousness. They are sometimes called the didactic , or teaching psalms. Wisdom psalms, like wisdom books, talk about blessing or ruin; the righteous and the fool; and the suffering of the righteous. Some of the statements in the psalms are like proverbs.

Psalm 1 is an example of a wisdom psalm that teaches. It contrasts the life of the righteous (1:1–3) and the wicked (1:4–5). The people whom God blesses do not go to evil people for advice. They do not do what sinful people do. They do not mock spiritual things. Instead, they value reading God’s Word. Because of this, God blesses what they do (1:1–3). The wicked do not act like the righteous. They will not stand up under God’s judgment (1:4–5). God cares for the righteous. But the wicked will perish without God (1:6).

Psalms with Five Parts: Laments of Sorrow, Repentance, and Judgment

Psalms of sorrow, repentance, or judgment have five parts. This next chart gives examples of statements for each of the five parts. These examples will help you identify where a certain verse fits into the plan of a psalm with five parts. The order of the five parts may vary from psalm to psalm, but most of the parts will usually be present.

Parts 1–5 of some psalms

Common Statements

1. Cry for help

• I am hurting;

• You do not care;

• You do not answer;

• The enemy is winning.

2. Description of the problem

• I am hurting

• You are not answering

• They are winning.

3. Prayer for help

• Deliver me;

• Defeat my enemies.

4. Statement of confidence

• Surely God is my help;

• You are my refuge;

• God will save me.

5. Promise to give thanks

• I will go before the great congregation;

• I will declare;

• I will offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving.

Psalms of sorrow, repentance, and judgment usually have five parts.

We will look at some examples of psalms whose form has five parts.

Laments: Prayer and Petition

A lament is a cry to God by one person or a group with strong, deep feelings. There are more than sixty lament psalms, which makes it the largest group of Psalms. Are you discouraged? Is your church going through hard times? Are you part of a small or large group that is suffering? Use the lament psalms to pray your feelings to God.

For the interpreter, the most important part of the lament psalm is the “statement of confidence.” Often, the psalmist seems covered with self-pity and doubt. He complains to God about a problem. He may even accuse God of not listening. But in the statement of confidence, he turns from doubt to faith. He confesses that even in the middle of his problem, he still has confidence that God will answer his prayer. He often promises that when God sends the answer, he will make a public sacrifice of praise in the temple and testify of God’s faithfulness. Note the five parts of Psalm 54.

Psalm 54

1. A Cry to God for Help

Save me, O God, by your name; vindicate me by your might.

Hear my prayer, O God; listen to the words of my mouth. (54:1–2)

2. A Description of the Problem

Strangers are attacking me; ruthless men seek my life— men without regard for God. Selah. (54:3)

3. A Statement of Confidence

Surely God is my help; the Lord is the one who sustains me. (54:4)

4. A Prayer for God to Act

Let evil recoil on those who slander me; in your faithfulness destroy them. (54:5)

5. A Vow to Praise God

I will sacrifice a freewill offering to you; I will praise your name, O Lord, for it is good.

For he has delivered me from all my troubles, and my eyes have looked in triumph on my foes. (54:6–7)

All lament Psalms, like Psalm 54, have five parts.

Repentance Psalms

In Psalm 51, practice finding the five parts in David’s song of repentance. We have put the five parts in the order in which they appear in Psalm 51. Learn to identify the five parts from this repentance psalm.

Parts 1—5

Psalm 51

1. Cry for mercy

51:___to 51:___

2. Description of his guilt and sin

51:___to 51:___

3. Prayer for forgiveness

51:___to 51:___

4. Vow to teach others and thank God publicly

51:___to 51:___

5. Statement of Trust

51:___to 51:___

Psalm 32 teaches repentance. David is sharing what he learned from his sin. At first, he tried to hide it. This caused him to suffer. He did not have rest day or night (32:3–4). Finally, he confessed his sin. Then God forgave him (32:4–5). He enjoyed the blessing of having his sin removed (32:1–2). David learned something from this. In this psalm, he urges people to repent as soon as they sin (32:6). They should not be stubborn like mules (32:9).

Hidden sin brings great sorrow. But repentance and confession bring joy (Psalm 32:10–11). The New Testament also teaches believers to confess sin and turn away from it. If we repent and confess our sins, God “is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Read Psalm 32 and make it your prayer. Ask the Holy Spirit to search your heart. Repent and turn from anything in your life that does not please God. Then accept his forgiveness, cleansing, and joy.

Psalms of Judgment

These psalms are sometimes called imprecatory psalms. An imprecation is a curse. In these psalms, the author prays for God to curse or judge the wicked. These psalms are not calling for personal revenge. Rather, they show a strong concern for God’s name, His justice, and His righteousness. They call on God to lift up the righteous and bring down the wicked.

Many people today are troubled by this kind of psalm. This shows that they do not realize how serious sin is. Paul handed an immoral man in Corinth over to Satan (1 Corinthians 5). The apostle wanted the man to repent and come back to God. The man could not ignore his sin and still be a member of the church. Paul also cursed anyone who preached a different gospel than the gospel of Christ (Galatians 1:6–10). David and Paul were closer to God’s view of sin than many people realize. The Bible teaches that some people will go to hell because of their sins. The Old and New Testaments teach many of the same truths. For example, believers should love God and their neighbors (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 19:19). They should not seek personal revenge (Deuteronomy 32:35; Hebrews 10:30). They should hate and run from sin because God hates it (Psalms 45:7; Romans 12:9; Hebrews 1:9; Revelation 2:6).

The Psalmist often uses hyperbole (like “knock out the teeth”) and military metaphors ( spear and javelin )—as he prays for God to punish his enemies. We should not interpret these figures of speech literally. Neither should we use these psalms as an excuse to take personal vengeance.

David wrote most of these psalms asking for God to judge his enemies. As a warrior, David uses the language of a soldier in hand-to-hand battle. The interpreter should first see these statements in context. The psalm is an honest diary of the writer’s feelings—not an example of how believers should respond to evil. In some passages, the psalmist reflects fleshly bitterness early in the psalm and then returns to faith and trust in God in the latter part of the psalm. At other times, he sees his enemies as God’s enemies and prays for justice. We should remember that the psalmist leaves vengeance to God, the righteous judge.

Psalms of Thanksgiving

(Songs of thanksgiving by one person or a group)

These psalms thank God for His saving help and deliverance of individuals and the nation. The thanksgiving psalms are the exact opposite of the lament psalms. In the lament form, the psalmist describes his problem, prays for help, and pledges to thank God when the answer comes. The thanksgiving psalm is the fulfillment of that pledge. Instead of a cry for help, it begins with a call for rejoicing. The problem and prayer are remembered, but the emphasis is on the answer God sent and the lessons learned through the problem. In the thanksgiving psalm, the Psalmist publicly tells how God answered prayer and strengthened his faith. Compare each part of the lament form on the left to the thanksgiving form as outlined below.

Lament—Cry to God Before He Helps (Psalm 54)

1. A cry to God for help (vv. 1–2) 2. A description of the problem (v. 3)

3. A statement of confidence (v. 4)

4. A prayer for God to act (v. 5)

5. A vow to praise God (vv. 6–7)

Thanksgiving to God After He Helps (Psalm 30)

1. A shout of thanksgiving (vv. 1–3)

2. A description of the past problem (vv. 6–7)

3. A report of answered prayer (vv. 8–10)

4. A lesson ( toudah ) learned (vv. 4–5)

5. A vow to continue to thank God (vv. 11–12)

Lament psalms are the opposite of thanksgiving psalms. Both forms have five parts, but contrast the parts. For example, part 1 of a lament is a cry for help, before God delivers. In contrast, part 1 of a thanksgiving psalm is a shout of thanksgiving after God helps.

You should not expect the five parts of thanksgiving psalms to always be in the same order. But you can expect to find at least four of the five parts in thanksgiving psalms.

The thanksgiving psalms are responses to lament prayers that God answered. Thus, the five parts of a thanksgiving psalm are opposite the five parts of the lament psalms. We could say that together—a lament and thanksgiving psalm—account for the before and after of psalmist’s trust in God. The lament cries out to God before there is any help. The thanksgiving psalm praises Him for His response (Osborne 1991, 183).

In the lament psalm, the psalmist almost always vows to make a public thanksgiving when God answers his cry for help. With the thanksgiving psalm a person made a sacrifice. Usually, he invited all his friends to the tabernacle or temple. If there were other worshippers in the temple, they were welcome to join. The psalmist would invite them all to thank God with him as he spoke or sung the poem. The animal sacrifice would be offered, cooked, and eaten by all who came.

The key to interpreting a thanksgiving psalm is the toudah . The toudah is a Hebrew word for the “lesson,” the principle that the thankful person gave to the crowd. It is a summary of what God taught through the problem and deliverance. For example, in Psalm 30, the psalmist had sinned, but he thanks God for forgiveness. The lesson he learned was that God judges, but He quickly forgives when we repent. His anger does not last, but His favor remains.

Sing to the Lord, you saints of his;

praise his holy name.

For his anger lasts only a moment,

but his favor lasts a lifetime,

weeping may remain for a night,

but rejoicing comes in the morning. (Psalm 30:4–5)

Psalms with Twenty-Two Parts: Acrostic Psalms

Psalm 119 is unique in the Bible. There are twenty-two letters in the Hebrew alphabet. Verses 1–8 of Psalm 119 each begin with Aleph, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The next eight verses (9–16) of this Psalm begin with Beth, the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. This pattern continues, beginning eight verses with one letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Thus the entire Psalm contains 176 verses. This makes eight verses for each of the twenty-two letters in the Hebrew alphabet.

The method of beginning each verse with a certain letter is called an alphabetical acrostic . Other psalms based on acrostics of the alphabet are 25, 34, 37, 111–112, and 145. Sometimes, an author changed the pattern a little, as in Psalm 25.

In an acrostic psalm, the lines that begin with Aleph , the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, are an introduction, and the lines that begin with last letter ( Taw ) serve as the conclusion.

**Q:** How were some psalms fulfilled twice?

**A:** Messianic psalms were fulfilled in the time they were written and later, by Jesus the Messiah.

**Q:** Name the three parts of Psalm 133.

**A:** 1. The first part—the introduction—states the theme unity. 2. In the middle part of Psalm 133, the Psalmist illustrates unity twice to develop the theme. 3. The conclusion looks forward to eternal unity with God.

**Q:** Explain how each of the three parts of Psalm 133 relates to the theme unity .

**A:** The first part introduces the theme of unity. The second part develops the theme of unity by using illustrations The conclusion points toward the benefits of unity

**Q:** What is a lament?

**A:** A lament is a cry to God by an individual or group, seeking deliverance, consolation, or some other desperately needed benefit.

**Q:** Is it right to pray for God’s judgment as David did in Psalm 59:1–5? Explain (Luke 18:6–8).

**Q:** Explain: The thanksgiving psalms are responses to lament psalms God answered.

**A:** Laments are cries of help. Thanksgiving psalms are a record of God’s response and expressions of gratitude to God for the response.

**Q:** What is the key to interpreting Psalm 30?

**A:** The toudah , or lesson the psalmist is teaching is that although God judges, He quickly forgives, and restores favor. 10 CHAPTER

#### 9.2.2 — Explain three forms (three-part, five-part, and twenty-two-part) of psalms and how these forms aid interpreting.

The Psalms were the hymns of Israel and are powerful tools to strengthen doctrine. Just as believers today sing certain songs at Christmas and Easter, the Jews sang certain psalms at certain times. The Jews sang songs of Zion and songs of ascent as they went up to worship in Jerusalem.

• At the feasts, Israel sang psalms of public worship that reminded them of the promises God gave to their fathers.

• They sang royal psalms to crown a king, celebrate his wedding, or remember the promise that a son of David would rule forever.

• They sang lament psalms to comfort the discouraged.

• They sang thanksgiving psalms to worship when a person brought an offering to the Lord.

Psalms with Three Parts: Praise and Worship

Form of a Psalm with Three Parts

1. Introduction: theme (that unites the psalm), mood, people, occasion, etc.

2. Development of theme: repetition, a list, examples, comparisons, or contrasts

3. Conclusion: promise, summary, praise, and prayer

Most of the psalms have three parts: introduction, development, and conclusion. In the introduction of a psalm, the psalmist states the theme and sets the mood. In the middle section, he develops the theme through lists, contrast, comparison, repetition, or association. This middle part of a psalm, the development, is the largest section and is usually made up of several stanzas—verses of the song (musical paragraphs). The three-part form concludes with a promise, a summary, an exhortation, or a prayer.

Hallelujah or Praise Psalms

These psalms magnify the name, majesty, goodness, greatness, and salvation of God. The praise psalms have a fixed three-part form:

1. They begin with an introduction, a call to praise. The call to praise may mention who should praise, and how to praise. For example, the psalmist may ask people to praise God with singing, with musical instruments, with dancing, with clapping, and so forth.

2. The development part lists reasons to praise God. This list may emphasize praising God for His acts and praising Him for His attributes or character.

3. The conclusion ends the praise often with a prayer or exhortation. The main task of the interpreter is to find the theme that runs through all three parts of a psalm. The theme of Psalm 139 is this: praise God for knowing and caring for us. Note the three parts of Psalm 139.

Psalm 139

Part 1: Introduction (Call to Praise)

• The Psalmist praises God—the One who examines his life (vv. 1–4).

Part 2: Development (List of God’s attributes and acts)

• God knows all about me (vv. 5–6).

• God is always with me (vv. 7–10).

• God can always find me (vv. 11–12).

• God created me for a purpose (vv. 13–16).

• God thinks about me always (vv. 17–18).

• God’s enemies are my enemies (vv. 19–22).

Part 3: Invitation (Prayer)

• The psalmist invites God to examine and guide his life (vv. 23–24).

The form of Psalm 139 has three parts: introduction, development, and invitation. Some Christians believe that emotion in worship did not exist before the birth of the church. This is far from the truth. The worship at the tabernacle and temple was full of emotion: dancing, clapping, and joyful singing with musical instruments. Fifty of the psalms’ headings are to the “chief musician” (KJV) or the “director of music” (NIV). Many of the headings also include instructions on how the psalm is to be sung (for example, to the tune of “Lilies” in Psalm 45) or accompanied (for example, with stringed instruments in Psalm 54). Glance at the headings above Psalms 40 to 80 and note those headings that address the director of music and/or provide choral or instrumental notations.

The Jews sang the praise psalms with great joy. In Psalm 33:1, the psalmist calls the people to rejoice because their praise is beautiful (fitting) to the Lord. In contrast to the lament psalms, the praise psalms focus not on the psalmist’s problems but on the Lord’s worthiness. The direction of the praise psalm is away from the psalmist toward God. Psalm 33:3 commands the worshipper to sing to God.

The music that accompanies the praise psalm is to be played skillfully but not with formal professionalism. The psalm is to be sung as a new song (Psalm 33:3). One writer suggested that new song refers not to new lyrics but rather to a fresh sense of wonder.

His exhortation to sing “a new song” (v. 3) is not merely a call for new music and new hymnals. The phrase new song means to sing to God with a renewed sense of wonder at all He has done for us. The worship of God should never degenerate into something that we just do; we should always approach God with rejoicing. With the phrase skillfully (v. 3), the psalmist exhorts us never to approach our worship with a casual attitude. We are to “play skillfully” because we are playing to the Lord, and we must offer Him only our best. But skill is not the only criterion of worship music, for the psalmist’s final exhortation in verse 3 is to play “with a shout of joy.” Since God always considers our attitudes, genuine joy in the presence of our caring Lord is required for music to be truly worshipful. (Radmacher, Allen, and House 1999, 685)

Psalms 146–150, the Hallel of hallelujah psalms , serve as the conclusion of the entire book of Psalms. These five psalms each begin with hallelujah —the Hebrew word for “praise the Lord.”

The development section in these psalms is unique. Instead of listing reasons to praise, it repeats commands to praise. Psalm 148 is a good example.

• First, Psalm 148 commands the angels to praise (Psalm 148:2).

• Next, it commands the heavenly bodies and all nature on earth to praise (Psalm 148:4–6).

• Finally, the Psalm commands all men and women to praise—from the king and the judges to the old men and children (Psalm 148:11–14).

Songs about Creation or Nature

These psalms exalt God as the Creator of the heavens and the earth. The nature psalms (Psalms 8, 19, 29, 104, 108) use creation to glorify God. These psalms show God above , rather than in nature (Psalm 29:10). Pagans wrote songs and worshipped their gods as a part of nature (Ryken 1984, 118). In contrast, Jewish nature psalms worship God as the one who created and controls nature (Psalm 19:1–5). As an artist is glorified by his or her paintings, so God is glorified by His creation.

Psalm 29 traces the path of a mighty storm. It forms in the Mediterranean Sea (29:3) and enters Lebanon with fierce winds—winds that break the huge cedar trees (29:5). As the storm comes into northern Israel, it produces loud thunder and frightening lightning (29:7–8). During the storm, God sits calmly on His throne, above the flood (29:10). In response to His power and authority, the worshipper cries, “Glory!” (29:9).

Psalms about the King and Messiah

These psalms, sometimes called royal psalms , describe experiences of King David or King Solomon. Psalms like these call on God to protect His anointed king. They ask God to give him victory against his enemies (Psalm 20). In response to God’s help, the king trusts and praises Him (Psalm 21). Psalm 45 probably records a song from the wedding of one of Israel’s kings. Psalms 89 and 132 reflect on God’s covenant with King David (2 Samuel 7:1–16).

These psalms referred to kings, like David, who lived at that time. But the New Testament authors teach us that many psalms also apply to Jesus. It is good to consider what the author understood about his times and what the Holy Spirit knew about the coming Messiah.

Some psalms do not appear to be messianic. But New Testament authors quote them in referring to Christ. In this way, the psalms were fulfilled twice, first by an earthly king and later by the King of kings. Jesus Christ is the great Son of David. God promised that this King would rule the nations. Therefore, psalms about the king of Israel find their highest fulfillment in Christ.

Psalms 2 and 110 are messianic psalms. They predict that God will set up His anointed Son as King in Zion (Psalm 2:6). This King (Jesus) will rule the whole earth. All people will submit to Him or face judgment (Psalm 2:8-12). This prophecy refers to the second coming of Christ. He will come in power to rule the earth and set up His kingdom.

Jews sang the royal psalms at special events in the life of Israel’s kings. Many of these psalms refer to God’s covenant with David. Recall that God promised David that a king in his family would rule forever (2 Samuel 7). Jesus, a son of David, was the king God promised would rule. The temporary kings of Judah and the events in their lives pointed to the ministry of the Messiah—the King of kings.

Psalms about Israel’s king pointed forward to the Messiah—the King of kings.

Psalms Praising God as King

These psalms boldly declare that God reigns. When Israel first became the people of God, they understood that God would be their king. This is why, later in their history, Gideon refused to become king (Judges 8:23). The prophet Samuel warned Israel that God was the only king they should have (1 Samuel 8:4–7; 12:12–15).

God is the great King we should respect (Psalm 47:2). He reigns over all the nations of the earth. He deserves our praise (Psalm 47:6–7). There are many reasons to worship Him. He is King over all gods (Psalms 95:3; 97:9). He will judge all nations (Psalm 96:9–13). He rules the earth with strength and justice (Psalm 99:4). He is holy and almighty. We should worship Him as our Master, Lord, and King.

Most of the psalms about God as king are in Psalms 90 to 99. Like the royal psalms, they deal with kingship and point to the kingdom of God. These psalms focus on God, the divine King, rather than on the human kings of the royal psalms. The main theme of these psalms is that the Lord will reign over all the peoples of the earth. The righteous may suffer now, for a short time, but in the end they will prosper under the divine King. When you read a psalm about God as king, watch for phrases that describe Him.

Phrases about God as King

The psalms about God as King have key phrases that describe His rule.

Songs of Zion and Ascent to Zion

The Jews sang psalms of ascent as they went up— ascended —to Jerusalem for the yearly feasts of Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles. They sang songs of Zion when they thought about Jerusalem or arrived there.

These types of psalms have three parts. You must understand the big theme of a psalm in relation to the parts. In Psalm 133, note the following:

1 The first part—the introduction—states the theme unity .

2 In the middle part of Psalm 133, the Psalmist illustrates unity twice to develop the theme.

3 The conclusion looks forward to eternal unity with God.

Psalm 133

Introduction: Statement of the theme: unity

• How good and pleasant it is when brothers live together in unity! (v. 1)

Development: Two illustrations—anointing oil and dew—describe unity.

• It is like precious oil poured on the head,

running down on the beard,

running down on Aaron’s beard,

down upon the collar of his robes.

• It is as if the dew of Hermon

were falling on mount Zion. (vv. 2–3)

Conclusion: Points from the present to eternal unity

• For there the Lord gives His blessing, even life forevermore.

The songs of ascents are Psalms 120 to 134 and are noted in the Bible by their superscriptions, or heading, above each. It would be easy to visualize worshippers singing as they approached the temple.

I was glad when they said unto me,

“Let us go into the house of the Lord!” (Psalm 122:1, KJV)

Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion,

which cannot be moved, but abides forever.

As the mountains are round about Jerusalem,

so the Lord is round about his people. (Psalm 125:1–2, RSV)

Setting

Parts of Judah, and later, the entire nation became captives. In these hard times they did not stop writing about Zion. Even as captives in a foreign land, they longed to worship in the temple at Jerusalem. They prayed that God would somehow send out a light and lead them back to Mount Zion. For example, a captured Jew probably wrote Psalms 42 and 43. In the beginning, these two psalms were probably together as one psalm.

As the deer pants for streams of water,

so my soul pants for you, O God. (Psalm 42:1–2)

These things I remember

as I pour out my soul:

how I used to go with the multitude,

leading the procession to the house of God,

with shouts of joy and thanksgiving

among the festive throng. (Psalm 42:4)

Send forth your light and your truth,

let them guide me;

let them bring me to your holy mountain,

to the place where you dwell. (Psalm 43:3)

Historical Songs about God’s salvation

These psalms do not relate to a specific event in the life of a believer. Instead, they review Israel’s history. They remind the hearers of the nation’s sins. They praise God for all that He has done for His people. They also invite the people to trust God because of His past faithfulness (Leupold 1969, 561–562). Read Psalm 78:11–20.

Songs for Public Worship

These psalms were for special services or feasts. Psalms 113–118 were used each year at the Passover.

Songs of Trust and Devotion

These songs worship God and express a person’s faith in Him. A favorite psalm in this group is Psalm 91.

Psalms of Wisdom and Teaching

These psalms reflect on God’s ways and instruct us about righteousness. They are sometimes called the didactic , or teaching psalms. Wisdom psalms, like wisdom books, talk about blessing or ruin; the righteous and the fool; and the suffering of the righteous. Some of the statements in the psalms are like proverbs.

Psalm 1 is an example of a wisdom psalm that teaches. It contrasts the life of the righteous (1:1–3) and the wicked (1:4–5). The people whom God blesses do not go to evil people for advice. They do not do what sinful people do. They do not mock spiritual things. Instead, they value reading God’s Word. Because of this, God blesses what they do (1:1–3). The wicked do not act like the righteous. They will not stand up under God’s judgment (1:4–5). God cares for the righteous. But the wicked will perish without God (1:6).

Psalms with Five Parts: Laments of Sorrow, Repentance, and Judgment

Psalms of sorrow, repentance, or judgment have five parts. This next chart gives examples of statements for each of the five parts. These examples will help you identify where a certain verse fits into the plan of a psalm with five parts. The order of the five parts may vary from psalm to psalm, but most of the parts will usually be present.

Parts 1–5 of some psalms

Common Statements

1. Cry for help

• I am hurting;

• You do not care;

• You do not answer;

• The enemy is winning.

2. Description of the problem

• I am hurting

• You are not answering

• They are winning.

3. Prayer for help

• Deliver me;

• Defeat my enemies.

4. Statement of confidence

• Surely God is my help;

• You are my refuge;

• God will save me.

5. Promise to give thanks

• I will go before the great congregation;

• I will declare;

• I will offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving.

Psalms of sorrow, repentance, and judgment usually have five parts.

We will look at some examples of psalms whose form has five parts.

Laments: Prayer and Petition

A lament is a cry to God by one person or a group with strong, deep feelings. There are more than sixty lament psalms, which makes it the largest group of Psalms. Are you discouraged? Is your church going through hard times? Are you part of a small or large group that is suffering? Use the lament psalms to pray your feelings to God.

For the interpreter, the most important part of the lament psalm is the “statement of confidence.” Often, the psalmist seems covered with self-pity and doubt. He complains to God about a problem. He may even accuse God of not listening. But in the statement of confidence, he turns from doubt to faith. He confesses that even in the middle of his problem, he still has confidence that God will answer his prayer. He often promises that when God sends the answer, he will make a public sacrifice of praise in the temple and testify of God’s faithfulness. Note the five parts of Psalm 54.

Psalm 54

1. A Cry to God for Help

Save me, O God, by your name; vindicate me by your might.

Hear my prayer, O God; listen to the words of my mouth. (54:1–2)

2. A Description of the Problem

Strangers are attacking me; ruthless men seek my life— men without regard for God. Selah. (54:3)

3. A Statement of Confidence

Surely God is my help; the Lord is the one who sustains me. (54:4)

4. A Prayer for God to Act

Let evil recoil on those who slander me; in your faithfulness destroy them. (54:5)

5. A Vow to Praise God

I will sacrifice a freewill offering to you; I will praise your name, O Lord, for it is good.

For he has delivered me from all my troubles, and my eyes have looked in triumph on my foes. (54:6–7)

All lament Psalms, like Psalm 54, have five parts.

Repentance Psalms

In Psalm 51, practice finding the five parts in David’s song of repentance. We have put the five parts in the order in which they appear in Psalm 51. Learn to identify the five parts from this repentance psalm.

Parts 1—5

Psalm 51

1. Cry for mercy

51:___to 51:___

2. Description of his guilt and sin

51:___to 51:___

3. Prayer for forgiveness

51:___to 51:___

4. Vow to teach others and thank God publicly

51:___to 51:___

5. Statement of Trust

51:___to 51:___

Psalm 32 teaches repentance. David is sharing what he learned from his sin. At first, he tried to hide it. This caused him to suffer. He did not have rest day or night (32:3–4). Finally, he confessed his sin. Then God forgave him (32:4–5). He enjoyed the blessing of having his sin removed (32:1–2). David learned something from this. In this psalm, he urges people to repent as soon as they sin (32:6). They should not be stubborn like mules (32:9).

Hidden sin brings great sorrow. But repentance and confession bring joy (Psalm 32:10–11). The New Testament also teaches believers to confess sin and turn away from it. If we repent and confess our sins, God “is faithful and just and will forgive us our sins and purify us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Read Psalm 32 and make it your prayer. Ask the Holy Spirit to search your heart. Repent and turn from anything in your life that does not please God. Then accept his forgiveness, cleansing, and joy.

Psalms of Judgment

These psalms are sometimes called imprecatory psalms. An imprecation is a curse. In these psalms, the author prays for God to curse or judge the wicked. These psalms are not calling for personal revenge. Rather, they show a strong concern for God’s name, His justice, and His righteousness. They call on God to lift up the righteous and bring down the wicked.

Many people today are troubled by this kind of psalm. This shows that they do not realize how serious sin is. Paul handed an immoral man in Corinth over to Satan (1 Corinthians 5). The apostle wanted the man to repent and come back to God. The man could not ignore his sin and still be a member of the church. Paul also cursed anyone who preached a different gospel than the gospel of Christ (Galatians 1:6–10). David and Paul were closer to God’s view of sin than many people realize. The Bible teaches that some people will go to hell because of their sins. The Old and New Testaments teach many of the same truths. For example, believers should love God and their neighbors (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 19:19). They should not seek personal revenge (Deuteronomy 32:35; Hebrews 10:30). They should hate and run from sin because God hates it (Psalms 45:7; Romans 12:9; Hebrews 1:9; Revelation 2:6).

The Psalmist often uses hyperbole (like “knock out the teeth”) and military metaphors ( spear and javelin )—as he prays for God to punish his enemies. We should not interpret these figures of speech literally. Neither should we use these psalms as an excuse to take personal vengeance.

David wrote most of these psalms asking for God to judge his enemies. As a warrior, David uses the language of a soldier in hand-to-hand battle. The interpreter should first see these statements in context. The psalm is an honest diary of the writer’s feelings—not an example of how believers should respond to evil. In some passages, the psalmist reflects fleshly bitterness early in the psalm and then returns to faith and trust in God in the latter part of the psalm. At other times, he sees his enemies as God’s enemies and prays for justice. We should remember that the psalmist leaves vengeance to God, the righteous judge.

Psalms of Thanksgiving

(Songs of thanksgiving by one person or a group)

These psalms thank God for His saving help and deliverance of individuals and the nation. The thanksgiving psalms are the exact opposite of the lament psalms. In the lament form, the psalmist describes his problem, prays for help, and pledges to thank God when the answer comes. The thanksgiving psalm is the fulfillment of that pledge. Instead of a cry for help, it begins with a call for rejoicing. The problem and prayer are remembered, but the emphasis is on the answer God sent and the lessons learned through the problem. In the thanksgiving psalm, the Psalmist publicly tells how God answered prayer and strengthened his faith. Compare each part of the lament form on the left to the thanksgiving form as outlined below.

Lament—Cry to God Before He Helps (Psalm 54)

1. A cry to God for help (vv. 1–2) 2. A description of the problem (v. 3)

3. A statement of confidence (v. 4)

4. A prayer for God to act (v. 5)

5. A vow to praise God (vv. 6–7)

Thanksgiving to God After He Helps (Psalm 30)

1. A shout of thanksgiving (vv. 1–3)

2. A description of the past problem (vv. 6–7)

3. A report of answered prayer (vv. 8–10)

4. A lesson ( toudah ) learned (vv. 4–5)

5. A vow to continue to thank God (vv. 11–12)

Lament psalms are the opposite of thanksgiving psalms. Both forms have five parts, but contrast the parts. For example, part 1 of a lament is a cry for help, before God delivers. In contrast, part 1 of a thanksgiving psalm is a shout of thanksgiving after God helps.

You should not expect the five parts of thanksgiving psalms to always be in the same order. But you can expect to find at least four of the five parts in thanksgiving psalms.

The thanksgiving psalms are responses to lament prayers that God answered. Thus, the five parts of a thanksgiving psalm are opposite the five parts of the lament psalms. We could say that together—a lament and thanksgiving psalm—account for the before and after of psalmist’s trust in God. The lament cries out to God before there is any help. The thanksgiving psalm praises Him for His response (Osborne 1991, 183).

In the lament psalm, the psalmist almost always vows to make a public thanksgiving when God answers his cry for help. With the thanksgiving psalm a person made a sacrifice. Usually, he invited all his friends to the tabernacle or temple. If there were other worshippers in the temple, they were welcome to join. The psalmist would invite them all to thank God with him as he spoke or sung the poem. The animal sacrifice would be offered, cooked, and eaten by all who came.

The key to interpreting a thanksgiving psalm is the toudah . The toudah is a Hebrew word for the “lesson,” the principle that the thankful person gave to the crowd. It is a summary of what God taught through the problem and deliverance. For example, in Psalm 30, the psalmist had sinned, but he thanks God for forgiveness. The lesson he learned was that God judges, but He quickly forgives when we repent. His anger does not last, but His favor remains.

Sing to the Lord, you saints of his;

praise his holy name.

For his anger lasts only a moment,

but his favor lasts a lifetime,

weeping may remain for a night,

but rejoicing comes in the morning. (Psalm 30:4–5)

Psalms with Twenty-Two Parts: Acrostic Psalms

Psalm 119 is unique in the Bible. There are twenty-two letters in the Hebrew alphabet. Verses 1–8 of Psalm 119 each begin with Aleph, the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The next eight verses (9–16) of this Psalm begin with Beth, the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. This pattern continues, beginning eight verses with one letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Thus the entire Psalm contains 176 verses. This makes eight verses for each of the twenty-two letters in the Hebrew alphabet.

The method of beginning each verse with a certain letter is called an alphabetical acrostic . Other psalms based on acrostics of the alphabet are 25, 34, 37, 111–112, and 145. Sometimes, an author changed the pattern a little, as in Psalm 25.

In an acrostic psalm, the lines that begin with Aleph , the first letter of the Hebrew alphabet, are an introduction, and the lines that begin with last letter ( Taw ) serve as the conclusion.

**Q:** How were some psalms fulfilled twice?

**A:** Messianic psalms were fulfilled in the time they were written and later, by Jesus the Messiah.

**Q:** Name the three parts of Psalm 133.

**A:** 1. The first part—the introduction—states the theme unity. 2. In the middle part of Psalm 133, the Psalmist illustrates unity twice to develop the theme. 3. The conclusion looks forward to eternal unity with God.

**Q:** Explain how each of the three parts of Psalm 133 relates to the theme unity .

**A:** The first part introduces the theme of unity. The second part develops the theme of unity by using illustrations The conclusion points toward the benefits of unity

**Q:** What is a lament?

**A:** A lament is a cry to God by an individual or group, seeking deliverance, consolation, or some other desperately needed benefit.

**A:** In Psalm 51, practice finding the five parts in David’s song of repentance. We have put the five parts in the order in which they appear in Psalm 51. Learn to identify the five parts from this lament psalm. Parts 1—5 Psalm 51 1. Cry for mercy 51:_1_to 51:_2_ 2. Description of his guilt and sin 51:_3_to 51:_6_ 3. Prayer for forgiveness 51:_7_to 51:12_ 4. Vow to thank God publicly 51:13_to 51:15_ 5. Confession of trust 51:16_to 51:19_

**Q:** Is it right to pray for God’s judgment as David did in Psalm 59:1–5? Explain (Luke 18:6–8).

**A:** Yes. Jesus indicated in Luke 18:6–8 that God would eventually hear the prayers for justice and will punish the wicked.

**Q:** Explain: The thanksgiving psalms are responses to lament psalms God answered.

**A:** Laments are cries of help. Thanksgiving psalms are a record of God’s response and expressions of gratitude to God for the response.

**Q:** What is the key to interpreting Psalm 30?

**A:** The toudah , or lesson the psalmist is teaching is that although God judges, He quickly forgives, and restores favor. 10 CHAPTER

## 10 - Genres: Wisdom Literature

### Proverbs: The Building Blocks of Wisdom Literature

#### 10.1.1 — State the main forms used in biblical proverbs.

Proverbs are found in many books of the Bible. They are one of the major tools that writers use in the Old and New Testaments. Here we present the four rules for interpreting proverbs.

Rule One: Interpreting a Proverb by its Form

The proverbs have common forms. Discerning the forms makes it easier to interpret the proverbs. Each of these forms is a type of parallelism. We studied these parallel lines in Chapter 9 on Psalms: biblical poetry. Recall that we interpret parallel lines together; one line helps us understand another. For example, look at Proverbs 20:19. The second line appears to guide us away from a person who talks too much. But compare this half-thought of the second line with the first line. What the proverb teaches is that we should avoid people who gossip.

Line 1: “A gossip betrays a confidence;”

Line 2: “so avoid a man who talks too much” (Proverbs 20:19).

To interpret proverbs, first compare the lines to see if one line clarifies the other. For example, read line 1 of Proverbs 17:27. This does not mean that a man with knowledge speaks little. Line 2 explains that the proverb is about times of anger . Thus, we understand that it means that a wise person bridles his or her tongue when that person is angry.

Line 1: “A man of knowledge uses words with restraint,”

Line 2: “and a man of understanding is even-tempered” (Proverbs 17:27).

Another example:

Line 1: “A man of many companions may come to ruin,”

Line 2: “but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24).

If you read only line 1, you may think that the proverb says it is unwise to have many friends. But line 2 clarifies what the proverb means. It is good to have many friends, but a wise person will invest in one or more special friends who will remain close in hard times.

We will examine five common forms of proverbs. Most of these are forms of parallelism that we studied in Chapter 9.

Same Thought in Parallel Lines (Synonymous Lines in a Proverb)

In this form, line 2 repeats the idea of line 1, using different words. This form is common in the proverbs that are teachings to a son— parent-to-child. Often in Proverbs, words like listen my son are in the first verse of the chapter. These words introduce a group of proverbs to teach a child. In such chapters, the word son is not in each proverb, but all of the proverbs in the chapter are teachings to a son .

Line 1: “My son, keep your father’s commands”

Line 2: “and do not forsake your mother’s teaching” (Proverbs 6:20).

Contrast in Parallel Lines (Antithetical Lines in a Proverb)

Jewish poets liked to write parallel thoughts that were opposite. The second line uses a contrast, to clarify the first line. Usually, if but begins the second line, there is a contrast between line 1 and line 2. Sometimes the word but does not begin the second line, yet the contrast is still clear. These types of proverbs—using contrast between lines 1 and 2—are found throughout the book of Proverbs, but they are most common in Chapters 10–15. Usually, one line describes the wise person, and the other describes the fool. Often, the results of the actions are also given.

Line 1: “A wise son brings joy to his father,”

Line 2: “but a foolish son [brings] grief to his mother” (Proverbs 10:1).

Another example of contrast would be a proverb that includes this pattern of words: “Better . . . than.” Many examples of this form are in Proverbs 16–21 and 25–28.

Line 1: “Better a poor man whose walk is blameless,”

Line 2: “than a fool whose lips are perverse” (Proverbs 19:1).

Most proverbs state a general truth and do not consider the exceptions. They state that in most cases the wise person prospers, lives a pleasant life, and so on. In contrast, the fool is poor and has a sad life. But as we will soon study, proverbs state general truths, but do not describe every situation. For example, how does a righteous believer, like John the Baptist in prison, respond as an evil man like King Herod recklessly feasts? The better-than proverbs deal with the exceptions to the general rule, as in Proverbs 19:1. (We will discuss this topic more. Read the proverbs as general principles, not promises).

Comparison in Parallel Lines

In this type of parallelism, one line is an example of the other line. The first line may be the example, and it may begin with the word like or as . You can find examples of these comparisons in many proverbs, but especially in Proverbs 25–28.

Line 1: (Example) “Remove the dross from silver, and out comes material for the silversmith;”

Line 2: (Main truth) “remove the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established through righteousness” (Proverbs 25:4–5).

Line 1: “Like one who seizes a dog by the ears”

Line 2: “is a passer-by who meddles in a quarrel not his own” (Proverbs 26:17).

Completion in Parallel Lines

The second line completes and builds on the first line. In this form, sometimes the first line states a truth, and the second line states the reason.

Proverbs 22:24–25:

Line 1: (Truth) “Do not make friends with a hot-tempered man; do not associate with one easily angered.”

Line 2: (Reason) “For you may learn his ways.”

Proverbs 22:9:

Line 1: (Truth) “A generous man will himself be blessed,”

Line 2: (Reason) “for he shares his food with the poor.”

At other times, the first line states a truth, and the second completes it in a broader way . Always remember to study two parallel lines together, as one thought.

Proverbs 16:28:

Line 1: (Truth) “A perverse man stirs up dissension,”

Line 2: (Completed truth) “and a gossip separates close friends.”

Proverbs that use parallel lines to complete a thought are common in the “Sayings of the Wise” (Proverbs 22:17–24:22).

A Group in Parallel Lines

This type of proverb appears often in the “Sayings of Agur” (Proverbs 30). This chapter lists several things in a parallel form. These proverbs often use the pattern of three plus one . Sometimes, the final line is most important to the writer.

There are three things that are too amazing for me, four that I do not understand:

• the way of an eagle in the sky,

• the way of a snake on a rock,

• the way of a ship on the high seas,

• and the way of a man with a maiden. (Proverbs 30:18–19)

“There are six things the Lord hates, seven that are detestable to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that are quick to rush into evil, a false witness who pours out lies and a man who stirs up dissension among brothers” (Proverbs 6:16–19).

Proverbs

Form

“Do not exploit the poor because they are poor, and do not crush the needy in court, for the Lord will take up their case, and will plunder those who plunder them” (Proverbs 22:22–23).

Completion: Truth followed by the reason

“Better open rebuke than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5).

“Like clouds and wind without rain is one who boasts of gifts he does not give” (Proverbs 25:14).

“There are three things that are never satisfied, four that never say, ‘Enough!’: the grave, the barren womb, land, which is never satisfied with water, and fire, which never says, ‘Enough!’” (Proverbs 30:15–16).

“A wife of noble character is her husband’s crown, but a disgraceful wife is like decay in his bones” (Proverbs 12:4).

We have examined five different forms of proverbs. Knowing these forms will help you interpret many verses in wisdom writing. Also, you will discern that some proverbs combine more than one form. For example, look at Proverbs 3:11–12.

Line 1: My son, do not despise the Lord’s discipline

Line 2: and do not resent his rebuke,

Line 3: because the Lord disciplines those he loves,

Line 4: as a father the son he delights in (Proverbs 3:11–12).

Notice that lines 1 and 2 are synonyms—line 2 states the same thought as line 1. Then, line 3 completes the thought by stating the reason for the truths of lines 1 and 2. Finally, line 4 compares the Lord to an earthly father.

Therefore, Proverbs 3:11–12 combines three forms of parallel lines: Same thought (synonyms), completion, and comparison. We have studied forms, the first key for interpreting proverbs. Now we will consider the second rule.

Rule 2: The Best Time to Apply Each Proverb

Some biblical proverbs seem to conflict with each other. The solution is often to limit the meaning of the proverb to the topic the writer intended. A proverb may be true in one case, but not for another. Study the following examples:

Proverbs 26:4—“Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself.”

Proverbs 26:5—“Answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes.”

These proverbs were placed side by side to emphasize timing. Proverbs 26:4 means “Do not stoop down to the level of a fool.” There are times to remain silent when a fool speaks. But there are other times when a wise person must speak to correct foolish words (see Proverbs 14:3).

There is a time for everything, and a season for every activity under heaven: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot, a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to tear down and a time to build, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them, a time to embrace and a time to refrain, a time to search and a time to give up, a time to keep and a time to throw away, a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak, a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace. (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)

A wise person does not laugh when people are mourning. Likewise, a wise interpreter discerns the best time to apply a verse. He or she discerns that each verse has its time and place. Do not bring a hoe to the dinner table, or a casket to a wedding. Discern the time and place to use each proverb.

Rule 3: Proverbs as General Principles, Not as Promises

Proverbs are not promises. They are truths that God gave to guide us. The writer of a proverb does not prophesy a certain result for obedience. Rather, a proverb states a general truth that applies most of the time.

Example 1—Proverbs 3:9–10:

“Honor the Lord with your wealth, with the first fruits of all your crops; then your barns will be filled to overflowing, and your vats will brim over with new wine” (Proverbs 3:9–10). This passage does not promise that everyone who tithes will prosper. Most people who tithe will prosper. But many things, such as a nation’s economy, war, famine, earthquakes, fire, thieves, accidents, and bad decisions in business, may affect prosperity. I once read a newspaper article about a man who sued his church because the pastor had promised riches, based on Proverbs 3:9–10, if he tithed. The man gave his tithe, yet he lost his job, and he wanted his money back. This man did not discern that proverbs are general principles, not promises!

Example 2—Proverbs 15:1:

“A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). A soft answer usually turns away wrath, but not always. An abusive husband may beat his wife or children, whether they speak softly or not. An angry boss may act harshly, even when an employee speaks softly. And will the soft words of a thief turn away the wrath of the law? So we see that God gives us proverbs as light for our path, but proverbs do not guarantee results.

Example 3—Proverbs 13:24:

“He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is careful to discipline him” (Proverbs 13:24). Some Christian parents have disciplined their children too harshly, thinking that Proverbs 13:24 requires constant use of the rod. There are times to apply Proverbs 13:24. But the rod is not the only way to discipline a child. God disciplines all of us without using a rod. Parents may discipline their children with words, or by taking away privileges. Other Scriptures warn fathers not to be harsh with children (Ephesians 6:4).

We have looked at three examples showing that biblical proverbs often state general principles about life. But these proverbs were never written as promises. The principle that the proverb teaches is always true, but there are exceptions. As always, the goal of the interpreter is to determine the principle that the writer meant to teach us.

Example 4—Proverbs 22:6:

“Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not turn from it.” Does this proverb teach that a parent has complete control over the salvation of a child? No! The writer never intended this. As Joshua reminded Israel, each person has a free will, and must choose whom to serve (Joshua 24:15). Proverb 22:6 states what happens most of the time. It guides parents to raise their children as the Bible teaches, stressing that the role of parents is indispensable in training a child. Statistics teach us that most people who serve God today met Him at an early age. Still, exceptions to this general principle may occur. Parents may be righteous, yet have a child who rebels (Ezekiel 18:5–13). God is the most righteous Father of all, yet many of His children have rebelled.

Majority and Minority Proverbs

It is helpful to compare two groups of proverbs: majority and minority. The Majority Proverbs are in Proverbs 10–15. These tell what happens in life most of the time. Solomon writes many of these, contrasting the wise and the foolish or the righteous and the wicked. The lives of the fools and the wicked are always negative, ending in shame and ruin. On the other hand, the lives of the wise and righteous are always positive, with honor and wealth. The proverbs of chapters 10–15 tend to reflect the majority of situations.

A few Minority Proverbs are in Proverbs 16–22. These apply once in a while, in the rare exceptions to the general rule. Many of the proverbs in this group are like those in Proverbs 10–15. In this second group, Solomon mentions a few exceptions. He admits that general rules have some exceptions. Even so, it is better to obey God than to live like a fool. Many proverbs in Proverbs 16–22 refer to exceptions, but none are clearer than the “better . . . than” proverbs. The chart below gives some examples that contrast proverbs that apply to life the majority of the time and those which refer to situations that are less common. Proverbs are principles that describe the majority of cases, but there are exceptions to most rules.

Majority—General Rule

Minority—Exception to Rule

“Lazy hands make a man poor, but diligent hands bring wealth” (Proverbs 10:4).

“Better a little with the fear of the Lord, than great wealth with turmoil” (Proverbs 15:16).

“He who finds a wife finds what is good

and receives favor from the Lord” (Proverbs 18:22).

“Better to live in a corner of the roof

than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife” (Proverbs 21:9).

“When words are many, sin is not absent,

but he who holds his tongue is wise” (Proverbs 10:19).

“Better open rebuke (feelings that can be seen) than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5).

Rule 4: Interpret in the Context of the Whole Book of Proverbs

A book like Proverbs often jumps from one thought to another. Still, even in Proverbs, the writer scattered many proverbs on the same topic. So, in the context of the whole book of Proverbs, we understand that he teaches on various topics and themes.

Group all the proverbs on a certain subject and compare them. Often, you will see a pattern of thought. Or, the meaning of a proverb may become clear in the light of another one on the same topic. A quick look at a concordance reveals nineteen proverbs that mention friend or friends . Studying all of these proverbs will give balance and clarity to your wisdom about friendship.

In Chapter 4, we emphasized interpreting a text in the light of other passages on the same topic in that same book. You should practice interpreting a proverb by studying what the book says on the topic of that proverb. Proverbs 18:21 is a verse that has confused many believers: “The tongue has the power of life and death, and those who love it will eat its fruit.”

Many miss the meaning of this verse because they do not interpret it in the light of other verses in Proverbs. They claim that we can have whatever we confess and that we can avoid negative things if we do not talk about them. These confused believers think that everything depends on what we say. They tell us that we can be sick only if we say we are sick and that we become wealthy by claiming to be rich .

We want to understand God’s Word to us, and we want to say what the Scripture says. But it is important to know the meaning of Scripture—not just the words of Scripture. Proverbs has many verses about the tongue. Looking at these verses together will give us the book’s whole message about the tongue. Several verses in Proverbs help us to understand the meaning of “life and death are in the power of the tongue.”

Proverb

Life in the tongue

Proverb

Life is in the instruction of parents.

1:10–19

The tongues of sinners lead some to death.

3:1–2

Some proverbs may seem to approve sinful practices. But a wise interpreter discerns that proverbs may describe behavior that God does not approve. Again, this emphasizes the importance of synthesizing what the entire book of Proverbs says about a topic.

Proverb

“The poor are shunned even by their neighbors, but the rich have many friends.”

If a proverb is hard to understand, interpret it in the light of other proverbs on the same topic. The verses in column “A” may appear to approve favoring the rich, bribing authorities, and gossiping about others. But other proverbs and also other passages in the Bible teach us that favoritism, bribes, and gossip are wrong. The key to interpreting a hard proverb is comparing it to other proverbs on the same topic. Remember, the Bible cannot contradict itself, so any interpretation must agree with the rest of Scripture.

We have studied four keys for interpreting proverbs. We trust that these keys will help you interpret proverbs throughout the Bible in the wisdom literature and also in many passages of the New Testament. Jesus taught with many proverbs. Likewise, there are many proverbs in the epistles. Knowing the value of proverbs and the principles to interpret them will bring insight on hundreds of biblical passages.

Moral purity in government is compared to physical purity of precious metal.

**A:** Line 1: “Like one who seizes a dog by the ears” Line 2: “is a passer-by who meddles in a quarrel not his own” (Proverbs 26:17). Line 1 gives the example.

**Q:** According to Proverbs 6:16–19, do you think the Lord hates the seventh thing more than the other six? Explain.
