#### 10.1.2 — Relate how proverbs teach a truth for one setting that may not apply to other circumstances.

Proverbs are found in many books of the Bible. They are one of the major tools that writers use in the Old and New Testaments. Here we present the four rules for interpreting proverbs.

Rule One: Interpreting a Proverb by its Form

The proverbs have common forms. Discerning the forms makes it easier to interpret the proverbs. Each of these forms is a type of parallelism. We studied these parallel lines in Chapter 9 on Psalms: biblical poetry. Recall that we interpret parallel lines together; one line helps us understand another. For example, look at Proverbs 20:19. The second line appears to guide us away from a person who talks too much. But compare this half-thought of the second line with the first line. What the proverb teaches is that we should avoid people who gossip.

Line 1: “A gossip betrays a confidence;”

Line 2: “so avoid a man who talks too much” (Proverbs 20:19).

To interpret proverbs, first compare the lines to see if one line clarifies the other. For example, read line 1 of Proverbs 17:27. This does not mean that a man with knowledge speaks little. Line 2 explains that the proverb is about times of anger . Thus, we understand that it means that a wise person bridles his or her tongue when that person is angry.

Line 1: “A man of knowledge uses words with restraint,”

Line 2: “and a man of understanding is even-tempered” (Proverbs 17:27).

Another example:

Line 1: “A man of many companions may come to ruin,”

Line 2: “but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24).

If you read only line 1, you may think that the proverb says it is unwise to have many friends. But line 2 clarifies what the proverb means. It is good to have many friends, but a wise person will invest in one or more special friends who will remain close in hard times.

We will examine five common forms of proverbs. Most of these are forms of parallelism that we studied in Chapter 9.

Same Thought in Parallel Lines (Synonymous Lines in a Proverb)

In this form, line 2 repeats the idea of line 1, using different words. This form is common in the proverbs that are teachings to a son— parent-to-child. Often in Proverbs, words like listen my son are in the first verse of the chapter. These words introduce a group of proverbs to teach a child. In such chapters, the word son is not in each proverb, but all of the proverbs in the chapter are teachings to a son .

Line 1: “My son, keep your father’s commands”

Line 2: “and do not forsake your mother’s teaching” (Proverbs 6:20).

Contrast in Parallel Lines (Antithetical Lines in a Proverb)

Jewish poets liked to write parallel thoughts that were opposite. The second line uses a contrast, to clarify the first line. Usually, if but begins the second line, there is a contrast between line 1 and line 2. Sometimes the word but does not begin the second line, yet the contrast is still clear. These types of proverbs—using contrast between lines 1 and 2—are found throughout the book of Proverbs, but they are most common in Chapters 10–15. Usually, one line describes the wise person, and the other describes the fool. Often, the results of the actions are also given.

Line 1: “A wise son brings joy to his father,”

Line 2: “but a foolish son [brings] grief to his mother” (Proverbs 10:1).

Another example of contrast would be a proverb that includes this pattern of words: “Better . . . than.” Many examples of this form are in Proverbs 16–21 and 25–28.

Line 1: “Better a poor man whose walk is blameless,”

Line 2: “than a fool whose lips are perverse” (Proverbs 19:1).

Most proverbs state a general truth and do not consider the exceptions. They state that in most cases the wise person prospers, lives a pleasant life, and so on. In contrast, the fool is poor and has a sad life. But as we will soon study, proverbs state general truths, but do not describe every situation. For example, how does a righteous believer, like John the Baptist in prison, respond as an evil man like King Herod recklessly feasts? The better-than proverbs deal with the exceptions to the general rule, as in Proverbs 19:1. (We will discuss this topic more. Read the proverbs as general principles, not promises).

Comparison in Parallel Lines

In this type of parallelism, one line is an example of the other line. The first line may be the example, and it may begin with the word like or as . You can find examples of these comparisons in many proverbs, but especially in Proverbs 25–28.

Line 1: (Example) “Remove the dross from silver, and out comes material for the silversmith;”

Line 2: (Main truth) “remove the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established through righteousness” (Proverbs 25:4–5).

Line 1: “Like one who seizes a dog by the ears”

Line 2: “is a passer-by who meddles in a quarrel not his own” (Proverbs 26:17).

Completion in Parallel Lines

The second line completes and builds on the first line. In this form, sometimes the first line states a truth, and the second line states the reason.

Proverbs 22:24–25:

Line 1: (Truth) “Do not make friends with a hot-tempered man; do not associate with one easily angered.”

Line 2: (Reason) “For you may learn his ways.”

Proverbs 22:9:

Line 1: (Truth) “A generous man will himself be blessed,”

Line 2: (Reason) “for he shares his food with the poor.”

At other times, the first line states a truth, and the second completes it in a broader way . Always remember to study two parallel lines together, as one thought.

Proverbs 16:28:

Line 1: (Truth) “A perverse man stirs up dissension,”

Line 2: (Completed truth) “and a gossip separates close friends.”

Proverbs that use parallel lines to complete a thought are common in the “Sayings of the Wise” (Proverbs 22:17–24:22).

A Group in Parallel Lines

This type of proverb appears often in the “Sayings of Agur” (Proverbs 30). This chapter lists several things in a parallel form. These proverbs often use the pattern of three plus one . Sometimes, the final line is most important to the writer.

There are three things that are too amazing for me, four that I do not understand:

• the way of an eagle in the sky,

• the way of a snake on a rock,

• the way of a ship on the high seas,

• and the way of a man with a maiden. (Proverbs 30:18–19)

“There are six things the Lord hates, seven that are detestable to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that are quick to rush into evil, a false witness who pours out lies and a man who stirs up dissension among brothers” (Proverbs 6:16–19).

Proverbs

Form

“Do not exploit the poor because they are poor, and do not crush the needy in court, for the Lord will take up their case, and will plunder those who plunder them” (Proverbs 22:22–23).

Completion: Truth followed by the reason

“Better open rebuke than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5).

“Like clouds and wind without rain is one who boasts of gifts he does not give” (Proverbs 25:14).

“There are three things that are never satisfied, four that never say, ‘Enough!’: the grave, the barren womb, land, which is never satisfied with water, and fire, which never says, ‘Enough!’” (Proverbs 30:15–16).

“A wife of noble character is her husband’s crown, but a disgraceful wife is like decay in his bones” (Proverbs 12:4).

We have examined five different forms of proverbs. Knowing these forms will help you interpret many verses in wisdom writing. Also, you will discern that some proverbs combine more than one form. For example, look at Proverbs 3:11–12.

Line 1: My son, do not despise the Lord’s discipline

Line 2: and do not resent his rebuke,

Line 3: because the Lord disciplines those he loves,

Line 4: as a father the son he delights in (Proverbs 3:11–12).

Notice that lines 1 and 2 are synonyms—line 2 states the same thought as line 1. Then, line 3 completes the thought by stating the reason for the truths of lines 1 and 2. Finally, line 4 compares the Lord to an earthly father.

Therefore, Proverbs 3:11–12 combines three forms of parallel lines: Same thought (synonyms), completion, and comparison. We have studied forms, the first key for interpreting proverbs. Now we will consider the second rule.

Rule 2: The Best Time to Apply Each Proverb

Some biblical proverbs seem to conflict with each other. The solution is often to limit the meaning of the proverb to the topic the writer intended. A proverb may be true in one case, but not for another. Study the following examples:

Proverbs 26:4—“Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself.”

Proverbs 26:5—“Answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes.”

These proverbs were placed side by side to emphasize timing. Proverbs 26:4 means “Do not stoop down to the level of a fool.” There are times to remain silent when a fool speaks. But there are other times when a wise person must speak to correct foolish words (see Proverbs 14:3).

There is a time for everything, and a season for every activity under heaven: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot, a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to tear down and a time to build, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them, a time to embrace and a time to refrain, a time to search and a time to give up, a time to keep and a time to throw away, a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak, a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace. (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)

A wise person does not laugh when people are mourning. Likewise, a wise interpreter discerns the best time to apply a verse. He or she discerns that each verse has its time and place. Do not bring a hoe to the dinner table, or a casket to a wedding. Discern the time and place to use each proverb.

Rule 3: Proverbs as General Principles, Not as Promises

Proverbs are not promises. They are truths that God gave to guide us. The writer of a proverb does not prophesy a certain result for obedience. Rather, a proverb states a general truth that applies most of the time.

Example 1—Proverbs 3:9–10:

“Honor the Lord with your wealth, with the first fruits of all your crops; then your barns will be filled to overflowing, and your vats will brim over with new wine” (Proverbs 3:9–10). This passage does not promise that everyone who tithes will prosper. Most people who tithe will prosper. But many things, such as a nation’s economy, war, famine, earthquakes, fire, thieves, accidents, and bad decisions in business, may affect prosperity. I once read a newspaper article about a man who sued his church because the pastor had promised riches, based on Proverbs 3:9–10, if he tithed. The man gave his tithe, yet he lost his job, and he wanted his money back. This man did not discern that proverbs are general principles, not promises!

Example 2—Proverbs 15:1:

“A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). A soft answer usually turns away wrath, but not always. An abusive husband may beat his wife or children, whether they speak softly or not. An angry boss may act harshly, even when an employee speaks softly. And will the soft words of a thief turn away the wrath of the law? So we see that God gives us proverbs as light for our path, but proverbs do not guarantee results.

Example 3—Proverbs 13:24:

“He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is careful to discipline him” (Proverbs 13:24). Some Christian parents have disciplined their children too harshly, thinking that Proverbs 13:24 requires constant use of the rod. There are times to apply Proverbs 13:24. But the rod is not the only way to discipline a child. God disciplines all of us without using a rod. Parents may discipline their children with words, or by taking away privileges. Other Scriptures warn fathers not to be harsh with children (Ephesians 6:4).

We have looked at three examples showing that biblical proverbs often state general principles about life. But these proverbs were never written as promises. The principle that the proverb teaches is always true, but there are exceptions. As always, the goal of the interpreter is to determine the principle that the writer meant to teach us.

Example 4—Proverbs 22:6:

“Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not turn from it.” Does this proverb teach that a parent has complete control over the salvation of a child? No! The writer never intended this. As Joshua reminded Israel, each person has a free will, and must choose whom to serve (Joshua 24:15). Proverb 22:6 states what happens most of the time. It guides parents to raise their children as the Bible teaches, stressing that the role of parents is indispensable in training a child. Statistics teach us that most people who serve God today met Him at an early age. Still, exceptions to this general principle may occur. Parents may be righteous, yet have a child who rebels (Ezekiel 18:5–13). God is the most righteous Father of all, yet many of His children have rebelled.

Majority and Minority Proverbs

It is helpful to compare two groups of proverbs: majority and minority. The Majority Proverbs are in Proverbs 10–15. These tell what happens in life most of the time. Solomon writes many of these, contrasting the wise and the foolish or the righteous and the wicked. The lives of the fools and the wicked are always negative, ending in shame and ruin. On the other hand, the lives of the wise and righteous are always positive, with honor and wealth. The proverbs of chapters 10–15 tend to reflect the majority of situations.

A few Minority Proverbs are in Proverbs 16–22. These apply once in a while, in the rare exceptions to the general rule. Many of the proverbs in this group are like those in Proverbs 10–15. In this second group, Solomon mentions a few exceptions. He admits that general rules have some exceptions. Even so, it is better to obey God than to live like a fool. Many proverbs in Proverbs 16–22 refer to exceptions, but none are clearer than the “better . . . than” proverbs. The chart below gives some examples that contrast proverbs that apply to life the majority of the time and those which refer to situations that are less common. Proverbs are principles that describe the majority of cases, but there are exceptions to most rules.

Majority—General Rule

Minority—Exception to Rule

“Lazy hands make a man poor, but diligent hands bring wealth” (Proverbs 10:4).

“Better a little with the fear of the Lord, than great wealth with turmoil” (Proverbs 15:16).

“He who finds a wife finds what is good

and receives favor from the Lord” (Proverbs 18:22).

“Better to live in a corner of the roof

than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife” (Proverbs 21:9).

“When words are many, sin is not absent,

but he who holds his tongue is wise” (Proverbs 10:19).

“Better open rebuke (feelings that can be seen) than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5).

Rule 4: Interpret in the Context of the Whole Book of Proverbs

A book like Proverbs often jumps from one thought to another. Still, even in Proverbs, the writer scattered many proverbs on the same topic. So, in the context of the whole book of Proverbs, we understand that he teaches on various topics and themes.

Group all the proverbs on a certain subject and compare them. Often, you will see a pattern of thought. Or, the meaning of a proverb may become clear in the light of another one on the same topic. A quick look at a concordance reveals nineteen proverbs that mention friend or friends . Studying all of these proverbs will give balance and clarity to your wisdom about friendship.

In Chapter 4, we emphasized interpreting a text in the light of other passages on the same topic in that same book. You should practice interpreting a proverb by studying what the book says on the topic of that proverb. Proverbs 18:21 is a verse that has confused many believers: “The tongue has the power of life and death, and those who love it will eat its fruit.”

Many miss the meaning of this verse because they do not interpret it in the light of other verses in Proverbs. They claim that we can have whatever we confess and that we can avoid negative things if we do not talk about them. These confused believers think that everything depends on what we say. They tell us that we can be sick only if we say we are sick and that we become wealthy by claiming to be rich .

We want to understand God’s Word to us, and we want to say what the Scripture says. But it is important to know the meaning of Scripture—not just the words of Scripture. Proverbs has many verses about the tongue. Looking at these verses together will give us the book’s whole message about the tongue. Several verses in Proverbs help us to understand the meaning of “life and death are in the power of the tongue.”

If a proverb is hard to understand, interpret it in the light of other proverbs on the same topic. The verses in column “A” may appear to approve favoring the rich, bribing authorities, and gossiping about others. But other proverbs and also other passages in the Bible teach us that favoritism, bribes, and gossip are wrong. The key to interpreting a hard proverb is comparing it to other proverbs on the same topic. Remember, the Bible cannot contradict itself, so any interpretation must agree with the rest of Scripture.

We have studied four keys for interpreting proverbs. We trust that these keys will help you interpret proverbs throughout the Bible in the wisdom literature and also in many passages of the New Testament. Jesus taught with many proverbs. Likewise, there are many proverbs in the epistles. Knowing the value of proverbs and the principles to interpret them will bring insight on hundreds of biblical passages.

Line 2: (Completed truth) “and a gossip separates close friends.”

Proverbs that use parallel lines to complete a thought are common in the “Sayings of the Wise” (Proverbs 22:17–24:22).

A Group in Parallel Lines

This type of proverb appears often in the “Sayings of Agur” (Proverbs 30). This chapter lists several things in a parallel form. These proverbs often use the pattern of three plus one . Sometimes, the final line is most important to the writer.

There are three things that are too amazing for me, four that I do not understand:

• the way of an eagle in the sky,

• the way of a snake on a rock,

• the way of a ship on the high seas,

• and the way of a man with a maiden. (Proverbs 30:18–19)

“There are six things the Lord hates, seven that are detestable to him: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart that devises wicked schemes, feet that are quick to rush into evil, a false witness who pours out lies and a man who stirs up dissension among brothers” (Proverbs 6:16–19).

Proverbs

Form

“Do not exploit the poor because they are poor, and do not crush the needy in court, for the Lord will take up their case, and will plunder those who plunder them” (Proverbs 22:22–23).

Completion: Truth followed by the reason

“Better open rebuke than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5).

“Like clouds and wind without rain is one who boasts of gifts he does not give” (Proverbs 25:14).

“There are three things that are never satisfied, four that never say, ‘Enough!’: the grave, the barren womb, land, which is never satisfied with water, and fire, which never says, ‘Enough!’” (Proverbs 30:15–16).

“A wife of noble character is her husband’s crown, but a disgraceful wife is like decay in his bones” (Proverbs 12:4).

We have examined five different forms of proverbs. Knowing these forms will help you interpret many verses in wisdom writing. Also, you will discern that some proverbs combine more than one form. For example, look at Proverbs 3:11–12.

Line 1: My son, do not despise the Lord’s discipline

Line 2: and do not resent his rebuke,

Line 3: because the Lord disciplines those he loves,

Line 4: as a father the son he delights in (Proverbs 3:11–12).

Notice that lines 1 and 2 are synonyms—line 2 states the same thought as line 1. Then, line 3 completes the thought by stating the reason for the truths of lines 1 and 2. Finally, line 4 compares the Lord to an earthly father.

Therefore, Proverbs 3:11–12 combines three forms of parallel lines: Same thought (synonyms), completion, and comparison. We have studied forms, the first key for interpreting proverbs. Now we will consider the second rule.

Rule 2: The Best Time to Apply Each Proverb

Some biblical proverbs seem to conflict with each other. The solution is often to limit the meaning of the proverb to the topic the writer intended. A proverb may be true in one case, but not for another. Study the following examples:

Proverbs 26:4—“Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself.”

Proverbs 26:5—“Answer a fool according to his folly, or he will be wise in his own eyes.”

These proverbs were placed side by side to emphasize timing. Proverbs 26:4 means “Do not stoop down to the level of a fool.” There are times to remain silent when a fool speaks. But there are other times when a wise person must speak to correct foolish words (see Proverbs 14:3).

There is a time for everything, and a season for every activity under heaven: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot, a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to tear down and a time to build, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance, a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them, a time to embrace and a time to refrain, a time to search and a time to give up, a time to keep and a time to throw away, a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak, a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace. (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)

A wise person does not laugh when people are mourning. Likewise, a wise interpreter discerns the best time to apply a verse. He or she discerns that each verse has its time and place. Do not bring a hoe to the dinner table, or a casket to a wedding. Discern the time and place to use each proverb.

Rule 3: Proverbs as General Principles, Not as Promises

Proverbs are not promises. They are truths that God gave to guide us. The writer of a proverb does not prophesy a certain result for obedience. Rather, a proverb states a general truth that applies most of the time.

Example 1—Proverbs 3:9–10:

“Honor the Lord with your wealth, with the first fruits of all your crops; then your barns will be filled to overflowing, and your vats will brim over with new wine” (Proverbs 3:9–10). This passage does not promise that everyone who tithes will prosper. Most people who tithe will prosper. But many things, such as a nation’s economy, war, famine, earthquakes, fire, thieves, accidents, and bad decisions in business, may affect prosperity. I once read a newspaper article about a man who sued his church because the pastor had promised riches, based on Proverbs 3:9–10, if he tithed. The man gave his tithe, yet he lost his job, and he wanted his money back. This man did not discern that proverbs are general principles, not promises!

Example 2—Proverbs 15:1:

“A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). A soft answer usually turns away wrath, but not always. An abusive husband may beat his wife or children, whether they speak softly or not. An angry boss may act harshly, even when an employee speaks softly. And will the soft words of a thief turn away the wrath of the law? So we see that God gives us proverbs as light for our path, but proverbs do not guarantee results.

Example 3—Proverbs 13:24:

“He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is careful to discipline him” (Proverbs 13:24). Some Christian parents have disciplined their children too harshly, thinking that Proverbs 13:24 requires constant use of the rod. There are times to apply Proverbs 13:24. But the rod is not the only way to discipline a child. God disciplines all of us without using a rod. Parents may discipline their children with words, or by taking away privileges. Other Scriptures warn fathers not to be harsh with children (Ephesians 6:4).

We have looked at three examples showing that biblical proverbs often state general principles about life. But these proverbs were never written as promises. The principle that the proverb teaches is always true, but there are exceptions. As always, the goal of the interpreter is to determine the principle that the writer meant to teach us.

Example 4—Proverbs 22:6:

“Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not turn from it.” Does this proverb teach that a parent has complete control over the salvation of a child? No! The writer never intended this. As Joshua reminded Israel, each person has a free will, and must choose whom to serve (Joshua 24:15). Proverb 22:6 states what happens most of the time. It guides parents to raise their children as the Bible teaches, stressing that the role of parents is indispensable in training a child. Statistics teach us that most people who serve God today met Him at an early age. Still, exceptions to this general principle may occur. Parents may be righteous, yet have a child who rebels (Ezekiel 18:5–13). God is the most righteous Father of all, yet many of His children have rebelled.

Majority and Minority Proverbs

It is helpful to compare two groups of proverbs: majority and minority. The Majority Proverbs are in Proverbs 10–15. These tell what happens in life most of the time. Solomon writes many of these, contrasting the wise and the foolish or the righteous and the wicked. The lives of the fools and the wicked are always negative, ending in shame and ruin. On the other hand, the lives of the wise and righteous are always positive, with honor and wealth. The proverbs of chapters 10–15 tend to reflect the majority of situations.

A few Minority Proverbs are in Proverbs 16–22. These apply once in a while, in the rare exceptions to the general rule. Many of the proverbs in this group are like those in Proverbs 10–15. In this second group, Solomon mentions a few exceptions. He admits that general rules have some exceptions. Even so, it is better to obey God than to live like a fool. Many proverbs in Proverbs 16–22 refer to exceptions, but none are clearer than the “better . . . than” proverbs. The chart below gives some examples that contrast proverbs that apply to life the majority of the time and those which refer to situations that are less common. Proverbs are principles that describe the majority of cases, but there are exceptions to most rules.

Majority—General Rule

Minority—Exception to Rule

“Lazy hands make a man poor, but diligent hands bring wealth” (Proverbs 10:4).

“Better a little with the fear of the Lord, than great wealth with turmoil” (Proverbs 15:16).

“He who finds a wife finds what is good

and receives favor from the Lord” (Proverbs 18:22).

“Better to live in a corner of the roof

than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife” (Proverbs 21:9).

“When words are many, sin is not absent,

but he who holds his tongue is wise” (Proverbs 10:19).

“Better open rebuke (feelings that can be seen) than hidden love” (Proverbs 27:5).

Rule 4: Interpret in the Context of the Whole Book of Proverbs

A book like Proverbs often jumps from one thought to another. Still, even in Proverbs, the writer scattered many proverbs on the same topic. So, in the context of the whole book of Proverbs, we understand that he teaches on various topics and themes.

Group all the proverbs on a certain subject and compare them. Often, you will see a pattern of thought. Or, the meaning of a proverb may become clear in the light of another one on the same topic. A quick look at a concordance reveals nineteen proverbs that mention friend or friends . Studying all of these proverbs will give balance and clarity to your wisdom about friendship.

In Chapter 4, we emphasized interpreting a text in the light of other passages on the same topic in that same book. You should practice interpreting a proverb by studying what the book says on the topic of that proverb. Proverbs 18:21 is a verse that has confused many believers: “The tongue has the power of life and death, and those who love it will eat its fruit.”

Many miss the meaning of this verse because they do not interpret it in the light of other verses in Proverbs. They claim that we can have whatever we confess and that we can avoid negative things if we do not talk about them. These confused believers think that everything depends on what we say. They tell us that we can be sick only if we say we are sick and that we become wealthy by claiming to be rich .

We want to understand God’s Word to us, and we want to say what the Scripture says. But it is important to know the meaning of Scripture—not just the words of Scripture. Proverbs has many verses about the tongue. Looking at these verses together will give us the book’s whole message about the tongue. Several verses in Proverbs help us to understand the meaning of “life and death are in the power of the tongue.”

If a proverb is hard to understand, interpret it in the light of other proverbs on the same topic. The verses in column “A” may appear to approve favoring the rich, bribing authorities, and gossiping about others. But other proverbs and also other passages in the Bible teach us that favoritism, bribes, and gossip are wrong. The key to interpreting a hard proverb is comparing it to other proverbs on the same topic. Remember, the Bible cannot contradict itself, so any interpretation must agree with the rest of Scripture.

We have studied four keys for interpreting proverbs. We trust that these keys will help you interpret proverbs throughout the Bible in the wisdom literature and also in many passages of the New Testament. Jesus taught with many proverbs. Likewise, there are many proverbs in the epistles. Knowing the value of proverbs and the principles to interpret them will bring insight on hundreds of biblical passages.

**Q:** In the parallel lines of Proverbs 25:4–5 what is the comparison?

**A:** Line 1: (Example) “Remove the dross from silver, and out comes material for the silversmith;” Line 2: (Main truth) “remove the wicked from the king’s presence, and his throne will be established through righteousness” (Proverbs 25:4–5). Moral purity in government is compared to physical purity of precious metal.

**Q:** In the parallel lines of Proverbs 26:17, which line gives the example?

**A:** Line 1: “Like one who seizes a dog by the ears” Line 2: “is a passer-by who meddles in a quarrel not his own” (Proverbs 26:17). Line 1 gives the example.

**Q:** According to Proverbs 6:16–19, do you think the Lord hates the seventh thing more than the other six? Explain.

**A:** No. It is a poetic way of listing and bringing attention to the list.

### Job, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Solomon

#### 10.2.1 — Explain how knowing the structure of the book helps one interpret its parts, as in Job.

We have already studied the most popular wisdom book, Proverbs. The other three books that are identified as wisdom literature are Job, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Solomon.

1. Job tells the story of a man who loses his wealth, family, and position but still serves God to the end of his life.

2. Ecclesiastes reads like a personal testimony of a man who gains everything on earth, but does not serve God most of his life.

3. Song of Solomon records the comments of a young couple as they reflect on their meeting, courtship, and marriage. Their memories become the lyrics that Israelites sang at weddings for generations.

Each of these three wisdom books has some challenges for the interpreter.

Job: The Story of a Man Who Would Not Give Up on God

The story of Job is like a drama with several acts or parts. You can almost see it happening. The beginning takes place in heaven. God presents Job as a model of righteousness and agrees for Satan to test him (Job 1–2). As a result, Job loses his family, wealth, and health. Next we see Job surrounded by three so-called friends . In three cycles, they take turns accusing Job, and Job defends himself after each one speaks. When these older friends fail to humble Job, a youth named Elihu proudly begins to speak. Then God is no longer silent; He speaks from heaven. In the end, Job is restored and makes a sacrifice for his self-righteous friends. As we discuss interpreting Job, it is helpful to look at the outline of the book.

To interpret Job, take note of the pattern of speaking between Job and his friends (Job 4–27). Two parts of the book of Job confuse most interpreters. We will consider these parts one by one.

The Prologue (Job 1–2)

Many readers struggle to interpret these first two chapters of Job. Here are some common questions believers ask:

• Can Satan enter heaven?

• Does God get in a contest with Satan about the lives of believers?

We must remember one of the basic rules of interpretation: Do not base a doctrine or teaching on one event or one verse. We cannot say from this one passage that Satan can enter heaven often. Job 1–2 tells about one time that God talked with Satan. So we cannot use this one event, told in a poetic manner, to conclude that God and Satan talk from time to time. All we can say from this event is that God and Satan once talked about a righteous man named Job. We know that Satan is an accuser, and that he is the accuser of believers. “Then I heard a loud voice in heaven say: ‘Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ. For the accuser of our brothers, who accuses them before our God day and night, has been hurled down’” (Revelation 12:10).

Revelation 12:10 implies that Satan accuses believers day and night before God. Still, we know that all of us are before God. Our Father in heaven sees everything. So we are not sure how close Satan comes to God when he accuses us. God is omnipresent; He can be in all places at the same time. But Satan, like other angels and humans, can only be one place at a time. Since Satan is busy on earth, perhaps he accuses believers on earth. Also, Revelation 12:10 says nothing about God responding when Satan accuses us. So we must admit that we know little about talks between Satan and God. And we must be silent when the Scriptures are silent.

The Statements of Job’s Friends

Readers may ask these common questions, especially about Job 4–27:

• Did Job’s friends speak the truth?

• What value do the words of Job’s friends have for us today?

We need to keep in mind that Job’s friends use proverbs to condemn Job. Proverbs, as you have learned, are principles that apply most of the time; they do not include the exceptions. Job’s friends did not realize that it is possible to be righteous, but suffer loss, sickness, and poverty. So Job’s three friends made many errors. God himself rebuked Job’s three friends for their folly.

After the Lord had said these things to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite, ‘I am angry with you and your two friends because you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has. So now take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job and sacrifice a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly. You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.’ So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite did what the Lord told them; and the Lord accepted Job’s prayer. (Job 42:7–9)

So if the accusations of Job’s friends are foolish, why are they in the Bible? The Bible records the wisdom and the foolishness of people. It records foolish acts, such as the sins of Adam and Eve, Cain, Noah, Gideon, Samson, and the idolatry of the Israelites. And Scripture records foolish statements such as Satan’s words, “A man will give all he has for his own life” (Job 2:4). There is much that we can learn from the mistakes of others, so God has included these in the Bible.

The words of Job’s friends are an important part of the story. They are like steps leading up to the place God reveals himself (Job 38:1–42:6). The words of Job’s friends give us the complete picture of Job’s trial. They prepare the reader for God’s response from heaven. Job’s wife and friends speak what many people think. In response to their foolish ideas, God reveals himself in His own words.

Today, the book of Job has great value for the righteous person who suffers. The story of Job does not simply teach—it encourages. For generations, believers who suffer have found comfort in this book. The questions of Job’s friends are the same questions that many believers have. Likewise, the words of Job strengthen believers to remain faithful during pain and sorrow. God’s response at the end of the book of Job brings hope to us. It gives a broader purpose to our suffering. So to interpret the book of Job, do not dig for gold in every verse. Recognize the folly of Job’s friends, and see the big message of the book. God is faithful. He knows our trials, and He is worthy of our trust at all times.

Ecclesiastes: The Story of a Man Who Lived Most of His Life Rebelling against God

I remember attending a meeting when I was a young man. The speaker was once a member of a gang. He gave his testimony about the grace of God. First, he told of his great sins and how that way of life robbed him of happiness, hope, and purpose. Second, he told how he was converted and his attitude changed. Third, he warned us not to waste our lives as he had done but to serve God from that moment on.

Likewise, Ecclesiastes is the testimony of a great man who rebelled against God. He travelled on a godless road, looking for happiness and meaning in life. As an old man, he counseled all to begin serving God during youth and to honor Him throughout life, knowing that God is our judge.

If you had walked into the service when the ex-gang member was giving his testimony, you would have heard him describing a robbery. Without the context of the entire message, this would seem strange for a church service. In the same way, the book of Ecclesiastes has some thoughts from Solomon’s rebellious, worldly years, and other thoughts from his last days. How can we tell the difference between the two types of verses? We will reflect on two types of signs that will help us interpret.

Sign 1

Words like meaningless , under the sun , vanity , and chasing the wind point toward a worldly point of view. Verses that include these words describe life when Solomon was living in rebellion.

The theme of Ecclesiastes is stated twice: “‘Meaningless! Meaningless!’ says the Teacher. ‘Utterly meaningless! Everything is meaningless’” (Ecclesiastes 1:2; 12:8). Solomon learned that life without God is empty, useless, and meaningless. He was the most foolish wise man who ever lived (Ecclesiastes 4:13)! The word meaningless occurs thirty-five times in Ecclesiastes.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, the phrase in Ecclesiastes 1:2 is “Vanity of vanities” (See NASB or the NRSV). This form of writing emphasizes the greatest contrast. For example, the “holy of holies” is the holiest place in the temple . The “Song of Songs” is the greatest song . The “King of kings” is the greatest king . And the “vanity of vanities” is the most meaningless , empty thing of all—living without God (Arnold and Beyer 1999, 327) .

Likewise, consider the phrase under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:3). This phrase occurs twenty-nine times in Ecclesiastes. Under the sun is a contrast to above the sun. In Ecclesiastes, those living under the sun are those who focus only on this world. Life for them is meaningless. Those who want to find meaning in life must look to God, above the sun. Life under the sun — life without God—is a waste of time, an empty, futile, meaningless life. A person can have too much to live with , yet too little to live for .

The phrase chasing after the wind occur nine times in the book (Ecclesiastes 1:14, 17; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6, 16; 6:9) . Seeking things first and God last is like chasing after the wind. In his years of rebellion, Solomon was chasing the wind. It is as Augustine said, “The heart is restless until it finds its rest in God.”

Read the three passages that follow. Notice the signs that point toward a worldly point of view. These verses illustrate what life was like for Solomon when he lived in rebellion.

• So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. All of it is meaningless, a chasing after the wind. I hated all the things I had toiled for under the sun, because I must leave them to the one who comes after me. (Ecclesiastes 2:17–18)

• I also thought, “As for men, God tests them so that they may see that they are like the animals. Man’s fate is like that of the animals; the same fate awaits them both: As one dies, so dies the other. All have the same breath; man has no advantage over the animal. Everything is meaningless. All go to the same place; all come from dust, and to dust all return. Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and if the spirit of the animal goes down into the earth?” (Ecclesiastes 3:18–21)

• I have seen another evil under the sun, and it weighs heavily on men: God gives a man wealth, possessions and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires, but God does not enable him to enjoy them, and a stranger enjoys them instead. This is meaningless, a grievous evil. (Ecclesiastes 6:1–2)

Sign 2

Words like God , Creator , and eternity usually point toward a godly point of view. Such words show that Solomon was writing as an old man, counseling us to honor God.

• He has also set eternity in the hearts of men; yet they cannot fathom what God had done from beginning to end. I know that there is nothing better for men than to be happy and do good while they live. That everyone may eat and drink, and find satisfaction in all his toil—this is the gift of God. I know that everything God does will endure forever; nothing can be added to it and nothing taken from it. God does it so that men will revere him. (Ecclesiastes 3:11–14)

• Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of trouble come and the years approach when you will say, “I find no pleasure in them. (Ecclesiastes 12:1)

Song of Solomon: The Story of Love that Would Not Give Up

The first words of this Hebrew poem identify it as Solomon’s best song, his “song of songs.” It may be Solomon’s most beautiful poetry, but it is also the most controversial for interpreters. The first step for the interpreter is to understand the story behind the poem. Many scholars suggest that it reflects a love triangle between King Solomon, a beautiful Shulammite shepherdess, and the shepherd boy who loves her.

It is suggested that Solomon met an extremely attractive rural girl when he was visiting his vineyards. He took her to Jerusalem to prepare her for marriage. The women in the court assured this Shulammite girl that she was greatly privileged. However, she was already promised to a shepherd boy who came to seek her. He was unable to get in to see her, and she ran out of the palace in pursuit of him. Solomon ultimately conceded that his wealth could not compete with true love. “Many waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot wash it away. If one were to give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly scorned” (Song of Solomon 8:7).

This poem, often sung at weddings in ancient Israel, glorifies romantic love between a husband and wife. The poem contains several direct statements about the beauty of physical intimacy between a married couple.

The theme of married loved did not seem significant enough to many ancient scholars. Both Jews and Christians have attempted to give this poem an allegorical meaning full of the most profound theology. One verse that has often been twisted to fit the theological interests of the interpreters is Song of Solomon 1:13: “My lover is to me a sachet of myrrh resting between my breasts.” Ancient Jews allegorized this verse to mean that the bag of myrrh symbolized the mercy seat between the two cherubim. Early Christians also saw the verse as an allegory with the sachet of myrrh representing Christ resting between the Old and New Testaments. Creative Christian scholars have also wrestled with the meaning of Song of Solomon 7:2, which reads, “Your navel is a rounded goblet that never lacks blended wine.” The navel and wine, early Christians reasoned, referred to the cup of wine used in communion (Ryken and Longman 1993, 282–283).

The historical debate centers on whether this poem is to be read as a love poem or as an allegory. Most evangelical scholars feel that the author’s original purpose was to celebrate married love. This does not mean the poem does not teach theology. It teaches a theology of marriage. The poem certainly may at times illustrate the love between Christ and the church, but we should not look for hidden allegories. Almost certainly the original writer was not writing an allegory.

I am impressed that the New Testament never once refers to this book. If it were a great prophetic storehouse of revelation about Christ and the church, we would expect Christ or an apostle to cite it. It is also difficult to see deep spiritual applications in the explicit references to the married couple consummating their love.

The more direct value of this poem for preaching is to see it as a commentary on Genesis 2:24: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.”

The poem does not have a chronological order. It contains the thoughts of the couple on their wedding day as each reflects on their first meeting and courtship and anticipates the consummation of their love. I offer one word of caution. The entire poem is in the context of the couple’s wedding day and anticipation of the consummation of their marriage. The challenge of these books is not only their literary style but also the fact that the author’s larger purpose must be understood before any verse in the book can be interpreted. The interpreter must see the whole before he or she interprets the parts. It is also dangerous to take the verses too literally.

Finally, the nature of figures of speech and proverbs must be always on the mind of the interpreter. These methods add concreteness and sparkle to the text, but they create great confusion if they are not properly interpreted.

#### 10.2.2 — Relate how terms like vanity and under the sun affect the interpreting of Ecclesiastes.

We have already studied the most popular wisdom book, Proverbs. The other three books that are identified as wisdom literature are Job, Ecclesiastes, and Song of Solomon.

1. Job tells the story of a man who loses his wealth, family, and position but still serves God to the end of his life.

2. Ecclesiastes reads like a personal testimony of a man who gains everything on earth, but does not serve God most of his life.

3. Song of Solomon records the comments of a young couple as they reflect on their meeting, courtship, and marriage. Their memories become the lyrics that Israelites sang at weddings for generations.

Each of these three wisdom books has some challenges for the interpreter.

Job: The Story of a Man Who Would Not Give Up on God

The story of Job is like a drama with several acts or parts. You can almost see it happening. The beginning takes place in heaven. God presents Job as a model of righteousness and agrees for Satan to test him (Job 1–2). As a result, Job loses his family, wealth, and health. Next we see Job surrounded by three so-called friends . In three cycles, they take turns accusing Job, and Job defends himself after each one speaks. When these older friends fail to humble Job, a youth named Elihu proudly begins to speak. Then God is no longer silent; He speaks from heaven. In the end, Job is restored and makes a sacrifice for his self-righteous friends. As we discuss interpreting Job, it is helpful to look at the outline of the book.

To interpret Job, take note of the pattern of speaking between Job and his friends (Job 4–27). Two parts of the book of Job confuse most interpreters. We will consider these parts one by one.

The Prologue (Job 1–2)

Many readers struggle to interpret these first two chapters of Job. Here are some common questions believers ask:

• Can Satan enter heaven?

• Does God get in a contest with Satan about the lives of believers?

We must remember one of the basic rules of interpretation: Do not base a doctrine or teaching on one event or one verse. We cannot say from this one passage that Satan can enter heaven often. Job 1–2 tells about one time that God talked with Satan. So we cannot use this one event, told in a poetic manner, to conclude that God and Satan talk from time to time. All we can say from this event is that God and Satan once talked about a righteous man named Job. We know that Satan is an accuser, and that he is the accuser of believers. “Then I heard a loud voice in heaven say: ‘Now have come the salvation and the power and the kingdom of our God, and the authority of his Christ. For the accuser of our brothers, who accuses them before our God day and night, has been hurled down’” (Revelation 12:10).

Revelation 12:10 implies that Satan accuses believers day and night before God. Still, we know that all of us are before God. Our Father in heaven sees everything. So we are not sure how close Satan comes to God when he accuses us. God is omnipresent; He can be in all places at the same time. But Satan, like other angels and humans, can only be one place at a time. Since Satan is busy on earth, perhaps he accuses believers on earth. Also, Revelation 12:10 says nothing about God responding when Satan accuses us. So we must admit that we know little about talks between Satan and God. And we must be silent when the Scriptures are silent.

The Statements of Job’s Friends

Readers may ask these common questions, especially about Job 4–27:

• Did Job’s friends speak the truth?

• What value do the words of Job’s friends have for us today?

We need to keep in mind that Job’s friends use proverbs to condemn Job. Proverbs, as you have learned, are principles that apply most of the time; they do not include the exceptions. Job’s friends did not realize that it is possible to be righteous, but suffer loss, sickness, and poverty. So Job’s three friends made many errors. God himself rebuked Job’s three friends for their folly.

After the Lord had said these things to Job, he said to Eliphaz the Temanite, ‘I am angry with you and your two friends because you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has. So now take seven bulls and seven rams and go to my servant Job and sacrifice a burnt offering for yourselves. My servant Job will pray for you, and I will accept his prayer and not deal with you according to your folly. You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.’ So Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite did what the Lord told them; and the Lord accepted Job’s prayer. (Job 42:7–9)

So if the accusations of Job’s friends are foolish, why are they in the Bible? The Bible records the wisdom and the foolishness of people. It records foolish acts, such as the sins of Adam and Eve, Cain, Noah, Gideon, Samson, and the idolatry of the Israelites. And Scripture records foolish statements such as Satan’s words, “A man will give all he has for his own life” (Job 2:4). There is much that we can learn from the mistakes of others, so God has included these in the Bible.

The words of Job’s friends are an important part of the story. They are like steps leading up to the place God reveals himself (Job 38:1–42:6). The words of Job’s friends give us the complete picture of Job’s trial. They prepare the reader for God’s response from heaven. Job’s wife and friends speak what many people think. In response to their foolish ideas, God reveals himself in His own words.

Today, the book of Job has great value for the righteous person who suffers. The story of Job does not simply teach—it encourages. For generations, believers who suffer have found comfort in this book. The questions of Job’s friends are the same questions that many believers have. Likewise, the words of Job strengthen believers to remain faithful during pain and sorrow. God’s response at the end of the book of Job brings hope to us. It gives a broader purpose to our suffering. So to interpret the book of Job, do not dig for gold in every verse. Recognize the folly of Job’s friends, and see the big message of the book. God is faithful. He knows our trials, and He is worthy of our trust at all times.

Ecclesiastes: The Story of a Man Who Lived Most of His Life Rebelling against God

I remember attending a meeting when I was a young man. The speaker was once a member of a gang. He gave his testimony about the grace of God. First, he told of his great sins and how that way of life robbed him of happiness, hope, and purpose. Second, he told how he was converted and his attitude changed. Third, he warned us not to waste our lives as he had done but to serve God from that moment on.

Likewise, Ecclesiastes is the testimony of a great man who rebelled against God. He travelled on a godless road, looking for happiness and meaning in life. As an old man, he counseled all to begin serving God during youth and to honor Him throughout life, knowing that God is our judge.

If you had walked into the service when the ex-gang member was giving his testimony, you would have heard him describing a robbery. Without the context of the entire message, this would seem strange for a church service. In the same way, the book of Ecclesiastes has some thoughts from Solomon’s rebellious, worldly years, and other thoughts from his last days. How can we tell the difference between the two types of verses? We will reflect on two types of signs that will help us interpret.

Sign 1

Words like meaningless , under the sun , vanity , and chasing the wind point toward a worldly point of view. Verses that include these words describe life when Solomon was living in rebellion.

The theme of Ecclesiastes is stated twice: “‘Meaningless! Meaningless!’ says the Teacher. ‘Utterly meaningless! Everything is meaningless’” (Ecclesiastes 1:2; 12:8). Solomon learned that life without God is empty, useless, and meaningless. He was the most foolish wise man who ever lived (Ecclesiastes 4:13)! The word meaningless occurs thirty-five times in Ecclesiastes.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, the phrase in Ecclesiastes 1:2 is “Vanity of vanities” (See NASB or the NRSV). This form of writing emphasizes the greatest contrast. For example, the “holy of holies” is the holiest place in the temple . The “Song of Songs” is the greatest song . The “King of kings” is the greatest king . And the “vanity of vanities” is the most meaningless , empty thing of all—living without God (Arnold and Beyer 1999, 327) .

Likewise, consider the phrase under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:3). This phrase occurs twenty-nine times in Ecclesiastes. Under the sun is a contrast to above the sun. In Ecclesiastes, those living under the sun are those who focus only on this world. Life for them is meaningless. Those who want to find meaning in life must look to God, above the sun. Life under the sun — life without God—is a waste of time, an empty, futile, meaningless life. A person can have too much to live with , yet too little to live for .

The phrase chasing after the wind occur nine times in the book (Ecclesiastes 1:14, 17; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6, 16; 6:9) . Seeking things first and God last is like chasing after the wind. In his years of rebellion, Solomon was chasing the wind. It is as Augustine said, “The heart is restless until it finds its rest in God.”

Read the three passages that follow. Notice the signs that point toward a worldly point of view. These verses illustrate what life was like for Solomon when he lived in rebellion.

• So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. All of it is meaningless, a chasing after the wind. I hated all the things I had toiled for under the sun, because I must leave them to the one who comes after me. (Ecclesiastes 2:17–18)

• I also thought, “As for men, God tests them so that they may see that they are like the animals. Man’s fate is like that of the animals; the same fate awaits them both: As one dies, so dies the other. All have the same breath; man has no advantage over the animal. Everything is meaningless. All go to the same place; all come from dust, and to dust all return. Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and if the spirit of the animal goes down into the earth?” (Ecclesiastes 3:18–21)

• I have seen another evil under the sun, and it weighs heavily on men: God gives a man wealth, possessions and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires, but God does not enable him to enjoy them, and a stranger enjoys them instead. This is meaningless, a grievous evil. (Ecclesiastes 6:1–2)

Sign 2

Words like God , Creator , and eternity usually point toward a godly point of view. Such words show that Solomon was writing as an old man, counseling us to honor God.

• He has also set eternity in the hearts of men; yet they cannot fathom what God had done from beginning to end. I know that there is nothing better for men than to be happy and do good while they live. That everyone may eat and drink, and find satisfaction in all his toil—this is the gift of God. I know that everything God does will endure forever; nothing can be added to it and nothing taken from it. God does it so that men will revere him. (Ecclesiastes 3:11–14)

• Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of trouble come and the years approach when you will say, “I find no pleasure in them. (Ecclesiastes 12:1)

Song of Solomon: The Story of Love that Would Not Give Up

The first words of this Hebrew poem identify it as Solomon’s best song, his “song of songs.” It may be Solomon’s most beautiful poetry, but it is also the most controversial for interpreters. The first step for the interpreter is to understand the story behind the poem. Many scholars suggest that it reflects a love triangle between King Solomon, a beautiful Shulammite shepherdess, and the shepherd boy who loves her.

It is suggested that Solomon met an extremely attractive rural girl when he was visiting his vineyards. He took her to Jerusalem to prepare her for marriage. The women in the court assured this Shulammite girl that she was greatly privileged. However, she was already promised to a shepherd boy who came to seek her. He was unable to get in to see her, and she ran out of the palace in pursuit of him. Solomon ultimately conceded that his wealth could not compete with true love. “Many waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot wash it away. If one were to give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly scorned” (Song of Solomon 8:7).

This poem, often sung at weddings in ancient Israel, glorifies romantic love between a husband and wife. The poem contains several direct statements about the beauty of physical intimacy between a married couple.

The theme of married loved did not seem significant enough to many ancient scholars. Both Jews and Christians have attempted to give this poem an allegorical meaning full of the most profound theology. One verse that has often been twisted to fit the theological interests of the interpreters is Song of Solomon 1:13: “My lover is to me a sachet of myrrh resting between my breasts.” Ancient Jews allegorized this verse to mean that the bag of myrrh symbolized the mercy seat between the two cherubim. Early Christians also saw the verse as an allegory with the sachet of myrrh representing Christ resting between the Old and New Testaments. Creative Christian scholars have also wrestled with the meaning of Song of Solomon 7:2, which reads, “Your navel is a rounded goblet that never lacks blended wine.” The navel and wine, early Christians reasoned, referred to the cup of wine used in communion (Ryken and Longman 1993, 282–283).

The historical debate centers on whether this poem is to be read as a love poem or as an allegory. Most evangelical scholars feel that the author’s original purpose was to celebrate married love. This does not mean the poem does not teach theology. It teaches a theology of marriage. The poem certainly may at times illustrate the love between Christ and the church, but we should not look for hidden allegories. Almost certainly the original writer was not writing an allegory.

I am impressed that the New Testament never once refers to this book. If it were a great prophetic storehouse of revelation about Christ and the church, we would expect Christ or an apostle to cite it. It is also difficult to see deep spiritual applications in the explicit references to the married couple consummating their love.

The more direct value of this poem for preaching is to see it as a commentary on Genesis 2:24: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.”

The poem does not have a chronological order. It contains the thoughts of the couple on their wedding day as each reflects on their first meeting and courtship and anticipates the consummation of their love. I offer one word of caution. The entire poem is in the context of the couple’s wedding day and anticipation of the consummation of their marriage. If the interpreter does not understand this, the poem will appear to condone premarital sex. It does not. It does, however, affirm the beauty of romantic love within marriage.

The wisdom books are among the most difficult to interpret. They are not deeply theological, but they do show us how to live out our theology in all circumstances of life. The challenge of these books is not only their literary style but also the fact that the author’s larger purpose must be understood before any verse in the book can be interpreted. The interpreter must see the whole before he or she interprets the parts. It is also dangerous to take the verses too literally.

Finally, the nature of figures of speech and proverbs must be always on the mind of the interpreter. These methods add concreteness and sparkle to the text, but they create great confusion if they are not properly interpreted.

Solomon ultimately conceded that his wealth could not compete with true love. “Many waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot wash it away. If one were to give all the wealth of his house for love, it would be utterly scorned” (Song of Solomon 8:7).

This poem, often sung at weddings in ancient Israel, glorifies romantic love between a husband and wife. The poem contains several direct statements about the beauty of physical intimacy between a married couple.

The theme of married loved did not seem significant enough to many ancient scholars. Both Jews and Christians have attempted to give this poem an allegorical meaning full of the most profound theology. One verse that has often been twisted to fit the theological interests of the interpreters is Song of Solomon 1:13: “My lover is to me a sachet of myrrh resting between my breasts.” Ancient Jews allegorized this verse to mean that the bag of myrrh symbolized the mercy seat between the two cherubim. Early Christians also saw the verse as an allegory with the sachet of myrrh representing Christ resting between the Old and New Testaments. Creative Christian scholars have also wrestled with the meaning of Song of Solomon 7:2, which reads, “Your navel is a rounded goblet that never lacks blended wine.” The navel and wine, early Christians reasoned, referred to the cup of wine used in communion (Ryken and Longman 1993, 282–283).

The historical debate centers on whether this poem is to be read as a love poem or as an allegory. Most evangelical scholars feel that the author’s original purpose was to celebrate married love. This does not mean the poem does not teach theology. It teaches a theology of marriage. The poem certainly may at times illustrate the love between Christ and the church, but we should not look for hidden allegories. Almost certainly the original writer was not writing an allegory.

I am impressed that the New Testament never once refers to this book. If it were a great prophetic storehouse of revelation about Christ and the church, we would expect Christ or an apostle to cite it. It is also difficult to see deep spiritual applications in the explicit references to the married couple consummating their love.

The more direct value of this poem for preaching is to see it as a commentary on Genesis 2:24: “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh.”

The poem does not have a chronological order. It contains the thoughts of the couple on their wedding day as each reflects on their first meeting and courtship and anticipates the consummation of their love. I offer one word of caution. The entire poem is in the context of the couple’s wedding day and anticipation of the consummation of their marriage. If the interpreter does not understand this, the poem will appear to condone premarital sex. It does not. It does, however, affirm the beauty of romantic love within marriage.

The wisdom books are among the most difficult to interpret. They are not deeply theological, but they do show us how to live out our theology in all circumstances of life. The challenge of these books is not only their literary style but also the fact that the author’s larger purpose must be understood before any verse in the book can be interpreted. The interpreter must see the whole before he or she interprets the parts. It is also dangerous to take the verses too literally.

Finally, the nature of figures of speech and proverbs must be always on the mind of the interpreter. These methods add concreteness and sparkle to the text, but they create great confusion if they are not properly interpreted.

**Q:** Name the four wisdom books.

**A:** Job, Ecclesiastes, Proverbs, Song of Solomon,

**Q:** In Ecclesiastes 2:17–18, which words are signs of a worldly point of view from a rebel?

**A:** “under the sun,” “meaningless,” and “chasing after the wind”

**Q:** Explain the attitude of Ecclesiastes 6:1–2.

**A:** Answers may vary but could include reference to the frustration of the wealthy that pleasure and possessions do not satisfy to the degree they expected. 11 CHAPTER

## 11 - Genres: Prophecy and Apocalyptic Literature

### The Old Testament Prophets

#### 11.1.1 — Categorize the Old Testament Prophets into major historical periods, and describe each period.

What are they going to do with the list of names? This was undoubtedly the pressing question on the minds of all the Jewish elders. They had been working on the temple without authorization when the Persian governor suddenly appeared with his soldiers. Each worker’s name was carefully noted before that worker was allowed to leave the premises. Now that list was on its way to King Darius for his official response (Ezra 5:1–4).

We can imagine the Jews asking, “What do we do while we wait for the king’s response?” Certainly, it would be at least a year before King Darius could raise an army and return to slaughter them. Should they use the time to build a fortress? Should they train an army? In this dark moment of indecision, Zechariah came forward with a fresh word from God. God showed him a vision of the lampstand in the temple, and an angel explained its meaning: “‘This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: ‘Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says the Lord Almighty. What are you, O mighty mountain? Before Zerubbabel you will become level ground. Then he will bring out the capstone to shouts of ‘God bless it! God bless it!’” (Zechariah 4:6–7).

Zerubbabel and the people understood the angel’s message. They determined to keep working on the temple until the king issued a response (Ezra 5:5). Remarkably, when the message came back months later, the report was not only favorable, but the king ordered that the project be subsidized from the royal treasury. Because the elders were faithful to continue working and did not stop to prepare for war, the new temple was rebuilt exactly seventy years after Solomon’s Temple was destroyed. God’s divine timetable was remarkably accurate!

The Prophets as Preachers

Zechariah’s sermon is easier to understand when the passage is read against the backdrop of history (Ezra 5–6). The writings of the prophets can be compared to sermons written in highly poetic verse. These messages are called oracles , and they were given directly by God. Each chapter of prophetic literature is comprised of one or more oracles from the prophet’s ministry. Often, the oracles do not seem to be in any particular order. The poetic style gives them a concreteness that is memorable but also slows the reader to a thoughtful pace.

The historical context is always vital for the interpreter. For example, over seventy years before Zerubbabel’s crisis with the rebuilding of the temple, Jeremiah warned: “Do not trust in deceptive words and say, ‘This is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord!’” (Jeremiah 7:4). The phrase temple of the Lord by itself sounds theologically sound, but it reflects a superstitious error in this instance. The false prophets of Jeremiah’s day preached that the people were safe as long as Solomon’s Temple stood. “God,” they claimed, “would never allow His temple to be destroyed.” Jeremiah disagreed. Without national repentance, he warned, the temple would not save them. In a short time, his prophecy came true. The people were taken as slaves to Babylon and the temple was left in ruins.

Every sincere interpreter should regularly use a Bible dictionary, study Bible book introductions, and Bible handbooks to identify the historical background of a prophetic book. Another powerful tool is to study the parallel passages in the historical books. The following chart gives an overview of four crises that form the backdrop for the majority of the prophetic books. Only three of these prophetic books—Obadiah, Joel, and Jonah—were not prophesied during one of these four times of crisis.

In the introduction to this chapter, we marveled that 27 percent of the Old Testament was prophetic literature. In reality, less than 5 percent of Old Testament prophecy “specifically describes the New Covenant [church] age. Less than 1 percent concerns events yet to come” (Fee and Stuart 1993, 166). Because most of the prophets predicted the immediate future of Israel and Judah; there are vast areas of the prophetic books that cannot be understood without knowledge of their historical context. Each fulfillment builds our faith in the message of the prophets and gives us an example of how to interpret those promises yet to be fulfilled.

The Prophets as Protectors of the Covenant

The prophets are regularly degraded to merely political reformers. Liberation theology, a radical political philosophy, finds its support in the Old Testament prophets. Although the prophets often spoke of social injustice, the fundamental theme of their preaching is far more profound. They called the people to remember their covenant with God. Deuteronomy 4:25–31 summarizes that covenant relationship and reflects the essence of the prophets’ messages.

1. If God’s people reject Him and turn to idols and sin (v. 25)

“After you have had children and grandchildren and have lived in the land a long time—if you then become corrupt and make any kind of idol, doing evil in the eyes of the Lord your God and provoking him to anger . . .”

2. God will punish them by taking them out of the land (vv. 26–28)

“The Lord will scatter you among the peoples, and only a few of you will survive among the nations to which the Lord will drive you.”

3. If God’s people repent (vv. 29–30)

“But if from there you seek the Lord your God, you will find him if you look for him with all your heart and with all your soul. When you are in distress and all these things have happened to you, then in later days you will return to the Lord your God and obey him.”

4. God will remember His covenant and fulfill His promises to their forefathers (v. 31)

“For the Lord your God is a merciful God; he will not abandon or destroy you or forget the covenant with your forefathers, which he confirmed to them by oath.”

This passage reflects two types of promises within God’s covenant with His people. To Abraham and the patriarchs, He made three unconditional promises: a land, a seed, and a blessing (Genesis 22:17–18; 26:3–5; 28:14–15). In Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28–30, He established a conditional covenant. Israel’s obedience or disobedience would not change God’s overall plan, but it would determine the nation’s own blessings within God’s plan. If the people obeyed God, they would be blessed. If they turned from Him, they would be cursed and put out of the land. A list of blessings and curses followed. In the end, Moses predicted that even if they failed, God would remember His promises to their forefathers and restore the land to them.

It is no surprise that Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28–30 are cited hundreds of times in the Prophets. These passages are a key that opens up an understanding of many Scriptures in the prophetic books. When the prophets warned of sin, they stressed the curses and the danger of being thrown out of the land. When the northern tribes were scattered (722 BC) and Judah narrowly missed judgment, Isaiah’s message turned from warnings to promises (Isaiah 40–66). By God’s inspiration, Isaiah predicted the captivity of Judah, giving the people a prophetic warning one hundred years in advance. Interestingly, after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, the message of all the prophets changed from warnings to encouragement.

The generation who had endured the Babylonian captivity and returned to the land of Israel needed hope. They needed to know that God would still keep His promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In the chart below are the titles suggested by Fee and Stuart (1993, 168) for the blessings and curses of the conditional covenant. Read these passages and note how they divide into the three great themes of the Prophetic Books.

Blessings in the land for covenant faithfulness

(Leviticus 26:1–13; Deuteronomy 28:1–14)

Curses and removal from the land for disobedience

(Leviticus 26:14–39; Deuteronomy 28:15–29:29)

Restoration of God’s promises for repentance (Leviticus 26:40–46; Deuteronomy 30:1–10)

Life, health, prosperity, agricultural abundance, respect, safety

Death, disease, drought, dearth, danger, destruction, defeat, deportation, destruction, disgrace

After repentance, the covenant promises made to the forefathers are restated.

To these discouraged Jews, the Prophets enlarged greatly on the promises to their fathers. The promise of land became a promise of a millennial reign; the promise of a seed became a suffering servant who will ultimately rule the nations. The promise of a blessing to the nations became a promise of the church age when God would write His covenant on the peoples’ hearts (Jeremiah 31:33) and the nations would come to worship (Zechariah 2).

The Prophets as Predictors

When the resurrected Christ walked with the two on the road to Emmaus, He explained those things written about Him in the Scriptures. Specifically, He explained what Moses and the prophets had predicted. This does not mean that Christ is the only theme in the books of Moses and the prophets. After all, Christ had only one afternoon for this Bible lesson. It does mean that the prophets clearly reveal Christ and the plans of God that center around Him. There are approximately 127 messianic predictions in the Old Testament. Listed below are a few examples. (For a more complete list, see Kaiser 1995, 237–242).

His agony
