Like the two disciples on the road to Emmaus, most of us will, without some help, find it difficult to understand how many of the prophecies are fulfilled. Fortunately, we now have much of what Christ explained to these two recorded in the New Testament. We are not restricted to one afternoon of explanation. We can take time to meditate on the prophecies and their fulfillment. Like the two who met Christ that Sunday afternoon, this teaching can increase our hope, clarify our faith, and guide our interpretation.

The Prophet’s Intention and the New Testament Fulfillment

The first step for any interpreter is to determine what the original author meant for the audience to understand. This thought is fundamental to biblical interpretation; thus, we would expect to see it demonstrated by the writers of the New Testament.

Most New Testament fulfillments are based on direct prophecies . In these prophecies, the prophet has a clear idea of what is predicted, and the fulfillment is easy to understand. Micah’s prediction that Jesus would be born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2) is an example of a direct prophecy. Another example of this type of prophecy is Isaiah’s prophecy of a coming Messiah who would be called Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14) and would reign “from that time on and forever” (Isaiah 9:6–7).

Typological prophecy is prophecy in which a prophet reveals a truth that will one day be applied at a much higher level in the New Testament. As a shadow reveals a person’s form, these shadows do not seem significant until they are associated with the person creating the shadow. The Old Testament writer may not have been aware of the higher-level application in the New Testament, but he would recognize the parallel truth. The imagery of the high priest on the Day of Atonement is an example of typological prophecy. The truths seen in this shadow are that we need an Intercessor to reach God and a death that is necessary to atone for our sin. In Hebrews, we see this applied as a foreshadowing of Christ’s work. Christ enters the throne room of God as the high priest entered the Holy of Holies. His own blood and His intercession assure our acceptance (Hebrews 9:23–28).

Principle/application is the third type of prophecy quoted in the New Testament. These are not shadows of future truth so much as they are patterns of truth that have parallels in the Old and New Testaments. As with the typological prophecies, the New Testament writer draws applications from the principles in the prophet’s writings and applies them to Christ. In these cases, the prophet may not have been referring to a specific fulfillment in the New Testament. His original intention, however, is not lost; again, it is applied at a higher level.

A perplexing example of this type of fulfillment is found in Matthew 2:15. Matthew cites “out of Egypt I have called my son” (Hosea 11:1) as a prophecy referring to Christ. To see this as a prophecy fulfilled in Christ seems strange. In the original context “my son” referred to the nation of Israel—not the Messiah. The issue is clarified when we notice the parallels between Israel and Christ. Both Israel and Christ had a special relationship with God. Both were part of His redemptive plan for the world. Both had a crisis and were removed temporarily to Egypt for their protection. In a sense what happened to God’s son (Israel) is a type of what would happen to the Son of God (Jesus). These form a pattern of how God would fulfill His plans and protect His Son in the future. The principle has not changed; it is just applied at a much higher level.

Another difficult example is found in Matthew 2:23. Matthew claims that Jesus’ living in Nazareth fulfilled the prophecy that “he will be called a Nazarene.” The only passage this could refer to is Isaiah 11:1: “A shoot ( nezer ) will come up from the stump of Jesse.” This verse refers to the Messiah as “the shoot.” Undoubtedly, on the mind of the prophet was that Jesus would be a branch springing from the cut down root of David. Ironically, some descendants in David’s line returned from captivity and settled in Galilee. Believing that the Messiah would come from their lineage, they named their town Nazareth after the Hebrew word for branch ( nezer ). The prophet Isaiah did not have this scenario in mind, but the idea that the Messiah would come from the line of David was the common thread from Isaiah to Matthew.

The Prophet’s Perspective and the Final Fulfillment

Most of the prophecies in the Old Testament Prophets were fulfilled at a specific time. There are three types, however, that do not have one specific time to point to as the date of the fulfillment: (1) telescope fulfillment, ( 2) double fulfillment, (3) and developmental fulfillment.

Telescope fulfillment is that type of prophecy that is fulfilled in stages divided by long intervals of time. The prophet’s perspective is that of one looking at a distant mountain range. From that perspective, the mountains seem close together—almost like the mountains are connected. As you near the mountain range, you find deep valleys and great distances between them. So it is with these prophecies. The prophet often views the first and second comings of Christ as one event, but the fulfillment is in stages.

When Joel 2:28–32 is quoted on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21), the fulfillment on that day included only the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Many of the other events mentioned in Joel’s prophecy (for example, the sun turning to darkness and the moon turning to blood) did not come to pass on that day. These events anticipate the “Day of the Lord” yet to come.

Some have compared telescope fulfillment to looking through the sights of a gun. The first sight is near, but both seem to blend together as the gunman peers down the barrel. So it is with the prophet’s perspective on the future. Christ’s first and second comings are often viewed as one event.

Double fulfillment refers to prophecies where the fulfillment of a short-range prediction validates the longer-range prediction. Actually, it is better called an analogous fulfillment. The intention of the prophet is on the long-range prediction; the first event is more a harbinger of what is to come. The most common examples are prophecies that refer to what God would do through David’s son (2 Samuel 7:12–14). This may find partial fulfillment in Solomon and others but ultimately aims at Christ—the Son of David. In Deuteronomy 18:15–18, Moses mentions God’s raising up “a prophet like me.” The short-range prediction referred to Joshua, but the long-range application is to Christ (John 1:21; 6:14; Acts 3:22).

Developmental fulfillment refers to a fulfillment that comes progressively. This kind of prophecy is not fulfilled in one or two events but through a series of events. The promise that the “seed of a woman” would crush “the serpent’s head” and “bruise his heel” is an example of this type of prophecy. This prophecy is partially fulfilled with every victory of Christ over Satan. Its ultimate fulfillment will occur with Christ’s second coming.

The generation who had endured the Babylonian captivity and returned to the land of Israel needed hope. They needed to know that God would still keep His promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In the chart below are the titles suggested by Fee and Stuart (1993, 168) for the blessings and curses of the conditional covenant. Read these passages and note how they divide into the three great themes of the Prophetic Books.

Blessings in the land for covenant faithfulness

(Leviticus 26:1–13; Deuteronomy 28:1–14)

Curses and removal from the land for disobedience

(Leviticus 26:14–39; Deuteronomy 28:15–29:29)

Life, health, prosperity, agricultural abundance, respect, safety

Death, disease, drought, dearth, danger, destruction, defeat, deportation, destruction, disgrace

To these discouraged Jews, the Prophets enlarged greatly on the promises to their fathers. The promise of land became a promise of a millennial reign; the promise of a seed became a suffering servant who will ultimately rule the nations. The promise of a blessing to the nations became a promise of the church age when God would write His covenant on the peoples’ hearts (Jeremiah 31:33) and the nations would come to worship (Zechariah 2).

The Prophets as Predictors

When the resurrected Christ walked with the two on the road to Emmaus, He explained those things written about Him in the Scriptures. Specifically, He explained what Moses and the prophets had predicted. This does not mean that Christ is the only theme in the books of Moses and the prophets. After all, Christ had only one afternoon for this Bible lesson. It does mean that the prophets clearly reveal Christ and the plans of God that center around Him. There are approximately 127 messianic predictions in the Old Testament. Listed below are a few examples. (For a more complete list, see Kaiser 1995, 237–242).

Messianic prophecy

Old Testament prediction

New Testament fulfillment

His virgin birth

Matthew 1:23

His triumphal entry

Matthew 21:9

His agony

Like the two disciples on the road to Emmaus, most of us will, without some help, find it difficult to understand how many of the prophecies are fulfilled. Fortunately, we now have much of what Christ explained to these two recorded in the New Testament. We are not restricted to one afternoon of explanation. We can take time to meditate on the prophecies and their fulfillment. Like the two who met Christ that Sunday afternoon, this teaching can increase our hope, clarify our faith, and guide our interpretation.

The Prophet’s Intention and the New Testament Fulfillment

The first step for any interpreter is to determine what the original author meant for the audience to understand. This thought is fundamental to biblical interpretation; thus, we would expect to see it demonstrated by the writers of the New Testament.

Most New Testament fulfillments are based on direct prophecies . In these prophecies, the prophet has a clear idea of what is predicted, and the fulfillment is easy to understand. Micah’s prediction that Jesus would be born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:2) is an example of a direct prophecy. Another example of this type of prophecy is Isaiah’s prophecy of a coming Messiah who would be called Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14) and would reign “from that time on and forever” (Isaiah 9:6–7).

Typological prophecy is prophecy in which a prophet reveals a truth that will one day be applied at a much higher level in the New Testament. As a shadow reveals a person’s form, these shadows do not seem significant until they are associated with the person creating the shadow. The Old Testament writer may not have been aware of the higher-level application in the New Testament, but he would recognize the parallel truth. The imagery of the high priest on the Day of Atonement is an example of typological prophecy. The truths seen in this shadow are that we need an Intercessor to reach God and a death that is necessary to atone for our sin. In Hebrews, we see this applied as a foreshadowing of Christ’s work. Christ enters the throne room of God as the high priest entered the Holy of Holies. His own blood and His intercession assure our acceptance (Hebrews 9:23–28).

Principle/application is the third type of prophecy quoted in the New Testament. These are not shadows of future truth so much as they are patterns of truth that have parallels in the Old and New Testaments. As with the typological prophecies, the New Testament writer draws applications from the principles in the prophet’s writings and applies them to Christ. In these cases, the prophet may not have been referring to a specific fulfillment in the New Testament. His original intention, however, is not lost; again, it is applied at a higher level.

A perplexing example of this type of fulfillment is found in Matthew 2:15. Matthew cites “out of Egypt I have called my son” (Hosea 11:1) as a prophecy referring to Christ. To see this as a prophecy fulfilled in Christ seems strange. In the original context “my son” referred to the nation of Israel—not the Messiah. The issue is clarified when we notice the parallels between Israel and Christ. Both Israel and Christ had a special relationship with God. Both were part of His redemptive plan for the world. Both had a crisis and were removed temporarily to Egypt for their protection. In a sense what happened to God’s son (Israel) is a type of what would happen to the Son of God (Jesus). These form a pattern of how God would fulfill His plans and protect His Son in the future. The principle has not changed; it is just applied at a much higher level.

Another difficult example is found in Matthew 2:23. Matthew claims that Jesus’ living in Nazareth fulfilled the prophecy that “he will be called a Nazarene.” The only passage this could refer to is Isaiah 11:1: “A shoot ( nezer ) will come up from the stump of Jesse.” This verse refers to the Messiah as “the shoot.” Undoubtedly, on the mind of the prophet was that Jesus would be a branch springing from the cut down root of David. Ironically, some descendants in David’s line returned from captivity and settled in Galilee. Believing that the Messiah would come from their lineage, they named their town Nazareth after the Hebrew word for branch ( nezer ). The prophet Isaiah did not have this scenario in mind, but the idea that the Messiah would come from the line of David was the common thread from Isaiah to Matthew.

The Prophet’s Perspective and the Final Fulfillment

Most of the prophecies in the Old Testament Prophets were fulfilled at a specific time. There are three types, however, that do not have one specific time to point to as the date of the fulfillment: (1) telescope fulfillment, ( 2) double fulfillment, (3) and developmental fulfillment.

Telescope fulfillment is that type of prophecy that is fulfilled in stages divided by long intervals of time. The prophet’s perspective is that of one looking at a distant mountain range. From that perspective, the mountains seem close together—almost like the mountains are connected. As you near the mountain range, you find deep valleys and great distances between them. So it is with these prophecies. The prophet often views the first and second comings of Christ as one event, but the fulfillment is in stages.

When Joel 2:28–32 is quoted on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21), the fulfillment on that day included only the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Many of the other events mentioned in Joel’s prophecy (for example, the sun turning to darkness and the moon turning to blood) did not come to pass on that day. These events anticipate the “Day of the Lord” yet to come.

Some have compared telescope fulfillment to looking through the sights of a gun. The first sight is near, but both seem to blend together as the gunman peers down the barrel. So it is with the prophet’s perspective on the future. Christ’s first and second comings are often viewed as one event.

Double fulfillment refers to prophecies where the fulfillment of a short-range prediction validates the longer-range prediction. Actually, it is better called an analogous fulfillment. The intention of the prophet is on the long-range prediction; the first event is more a harbinger of what is to come. The most common examples are prophecies that refer to what God would do through David’s son (2 Samuel 7:12–14). This may find partial fulfillment in Solomon and others but ultimately aims at Christ—the Son of David. In Deuteronomy 18:15–18, Moses mentions God’s raising up “a prophet like me.” The short-range prediction referred to Joshua, but the long-range application is to Christ (John 1:21; 6:14; Acts 3:22).

Developmental fulfillment refers to a fulfillment that comes progressively. This kind of prophecy is not fulfilled in one or two events but through a series of events. The promise that the “seed of a woman” would crush “the serpent’s head” and “bruise his heel” is an example of this type of prophecy. This prophecy is partially fulfilled with every victory of Christ over Satan. Its ultimate fulfillment will occur with Christ’s second coming.

**Q:** How did the Jews respond after hearing about Zechariah’s vision? What, in turn, did King Darius do for the Jews?

**A:** Zerubbabel and the people understood the angel’s message. They determined to keep working on the temple until the king issued a response (Ezra 5:5). The king ordered that the project be subsidized from the royal treasury.

**A:** Every sincere interpreter should regularly use a Bible dictionary, study Bible book introductions, and Bible handbooks to identify the historical background of a prophetic book. Another powerful tool is to study the parallel passages in the historical books.

**Q:** Most of the prophets predicted what concerning Israel?

**A:** Most of the prophets predicted the immediate future of Israel and Judah; there are vast areas of the prophetic books that cannot be understood without knowledge of their historical context.

**Q:** What were God’s three unconditional promises to Abraham and the patriarchs?

**A:** A land, a seed, and a blessing

**Q:** In the synagogue, Christ read Isaiah 61:1–2 and claimed the prophecy had been fulfilled. When Christ quotes Isaiah 61 in this prophecy in Luke 4:18–21, He stops after the words, “proclaim the favorable year of the Lord,” without adding the next phase, “and the day of vengeance of our God.” What does this tell you about the type of prophecy this represents?

**A:** It is a telescopic fulfillment.

#### 11.1.3 — Explain how a type can have only one meaning, although it can be applied at two levels.

What are they going to do with the list of names? This was undoubtedly the pressing question on the minds of all the Jewish elders. They had been working on the temple without authorization when the Persian governor suddenly appeared with his soldiers. Each worker’s name was carefully noted before that worker was allowed to leave the premises. Now that list was on its way to King Darius for his official response (Ezra 5:1–4).

We can imagine the Jews asking, “What do we do while we wait for the king’s response?” Certainly, it would be at least a year before King Darius could raise an army and return to slaughter them. Should they use the time to build a fortress? Should they train an army? In this dark moment of indecision, Zechariah came forward with a fresh word from God. God showed him a vision of the lampstand in the temple, and an angel explained its meaning: “‘This is the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: ‘Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says the Lord Almighty. What are you, O mighty mountain? Before Zerubbabel you will become level ground. Then he will bring out the capstone to shouts of ‘God bless it! God bless it!’” (Zechariah 4:6–7).

Zerubbabel and the people understood the angel’s message. They determined to keep working on the temple until the king issued a response (Ezra 5:5). Remarkably, when the message came back months later, the report was not only favorable, but the king ordered that the project be subsidized from the royal treasury. Because the elders were faithful to continue working and did not stop to prepare for war, the new temple was rebuilt exactly seventy years after Solomon’s Temple was destroyed. God’s divine timetable was remarkably accurate!

The Prophets as Preachers

Zechariah’s sermon is easier to understand when the passage is read against the backdrop of history (Ezra 5–6). The writings of the prophets can be compared to sermons written in highly poetic verse. These messages are called oracles , and they were given directly by God. Each chapter of prophetic literature is comprised of one or more oracles from the prophet’s ministry. Often, the oracles do not seem to be in any particular order. The poetic style gives them a concreteness that is memorable but also slows the reader to a thoughtful pace.

The historical context is always vital for the interpreter. For example, over seventy years before Zerubbabel’s crisis with the rebuilding of the temple, Jeremiah warned: “Do not trust in deceptive words and say, ‘This is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord!’” (Jeremiah 7:4). The phrase temple of the Lord by itself sounds theologically sound, but it reflects a superstitious error in this instance. The false prophets of Jeremiah’s day preached that the people were safe as long as Solomon’s Temple stood. “God,” they claimed, “would never allow His temple to be destroyed.” Jeremiah disagreed. Without national repentance, he warned, the temple would not save them. In a short time, his prophecy came true. The people were taken as slaves to Babylon and the temple was left in ruins.

Every sincere interpreter should regularly use a Bible dictionary, study Bible book introductions, and Bible handbooks to identify the historical background of a prophetic book. Another powerful tool is to study the parallel passages in the historical books. The following chart gives an overview of four crises that form the backdrop for the majority of the prophetic books. Only three of these prophetic books—Obadiah, Joel, and Jonah—were not prophesied during one of these four times of crisis.

In the introduction to this chapter, we marveled that 27 percent of the Old Testament was prophetic literature. In reality, less than 5 percent of Old Testament prophecy “specifically describes the New Covenant [church] age. Less than 1 percent concerns events yet to come” (Fee and Stuart 1993, 166). Because most of the prophets predicted the immediate future of Israel and Judah; there are vast areas of the prophetic books that cannot be understood without knowledge of their historical context. Each fulfillment builds our faith in the message of the prophets and gives us an example of how to interpret those promises yet to be fulfilled.

The Prophets as Protectors of the Covenant

The prophets are regularly degraded to merely political reformers. Liberation theology, a radical political philosophy, finds its support in the Old Testament prophets. Although the prophets often spoke of social injustice, the fundamental theme of their preaching is far more profound. They called the people to remember their covenant with God. Deuteronomy 4:25–31 summarizes that covenant relationship and reflects the essence of the prophets’ messages.

1. If God’s people reject Him and turn to idols and sin (v. 25)

“After you have had children and grandchildren and have lived in the land a long time—if you then become corrupt and make any kind of idol, doing evil in the eyes of the Lord your God and provoking him to anger . . .”

2. God will punish them by taking them out of the land (vv. 26–28)

“The Lord will scatter you among the peoples, and only a few of you will survive among the nations to which the Lord will drive you.”

3. If God’s people repent (vv. 29–30)

“But if from there you seek the Lord your God, you will find him if you look for him with all your heart and with all your soul. When you are in distress and all these things have happened to you, then in later days you will return to the Lord your God and obey him.”

4. God will remember His covenant and fulfill His promises to their forefathers (v. 31)

“For the Lord your God is a merciful God; he will not abandon or destroy you or forget the covenant with your forefathers, which he confirmed to them by oath.”

This passage reflects two types of promises within God’s covenant with His people. To Abraham and the patriarchs, He made three unconditional promises: a land, a seed, and a blessing (Genesis 22:17–18; 26:3–5; 28:14–15). In Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28–30, He established a conditional covenant. Israel’s obedience or disobedience would not change God’s overall plan, but it would determine the nation’s own blessings within God’s plan. If the people obeyed God, they would be blessed. If they turned from Him, they would be cursed and put out of the land. A list of blessings and curses followed. In the end, Moses predicted that even if they failed, God would remember His promises to their forefathers and restore the land to them.

It is no surprise that Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28–30 are cited hundreds of times in the Prophets. These passages are a key that opens up an understanding of many Scriptures in the prophetic books. When the prophets warned of sin, they stressed the curses and the danger of being thrown out of the land. When the northern tribes were scattered (722 BC) and Judah narrowly missed judgment, Isaiah’s message turned from warnings to promises (Isaiah 40–66). By God’s inspiration, Isaiah predicted the captivity of Judah, giving the people a prophetic warning one hundred years in advance. Interestingly, after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, the message of all the prophets changed from warnings to encouragement.

The generation who had endured the Babylonian captivity and returned to the land of Israel needed hope. They needed to know that God would still keep His promises made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. **Q:** In the synagogue, Christ read Isaiah 61:1–2 and claimed the prophecy had been fulfilled. When Christ quotes Isaiah 61 in this prophecy in Luke 4:18–21, He stops after the words, “proclaim the favorable year of the Lord,” without adding the next phase, “and the day of vengeance of our God.” What does this tell you about the type of prophecy this represents?

**A:** It is a telescopic fulfillment.

### The Apocalyptic Literature

#### 11.2.1 — Explain how apocalyptic literature is different from other types of prophecy.

Ezekiel was given a vision of the God of the universe enthroned above an immense, dark, storm cloud. Around him were four living beings. Each had four faces: a man, an ox, a lion, and an eagle. Each had four wings and could move at incredible speed; when moving, they sounded like the roar of rushing waters. The throne sat on wheels that shone like crystal and were ringed with eyes. Within each wheel was another intersecting wheel. The person on the throne looked like a man but glowed brightly. Above his head was a great expanse, sparkling like ice, and a rainbow.

Ezekiel’s message to the slaves in Babylon was that God’s presence was not restricted to Jerusalem. His throne-chariot had wheels! Like the mobile platforms that ancient monarchs used to travel the countryside, His people were—even in Babylonian captivity—above the storm or crisis.

This passage is an early example of a type of literature that would reach its apex in the book of Revelation. This type of literature draws its name from the word apocalipsis in Greek, which means “to unveil.” In this case, the future until the consummation of history is unveiled in symbolic visions and dreams. Biblical apocalyptic literature is primarily found in the following passages:

Isaiah 24–27

Daniel 7–12

Ezekiel 1; 8–10

Zechariah 9–14

Matthew 24

Revelation

Characteristics of Apocalyptic Literature

Symbols of the Future Delivered in Dreams or Visions

In apocalyptic literature, you can expect the prophecy to be conveyed through a vision or a dream. In the revelation, the prophet is bombarded with images as if he were looking into a kaleidoscope. Where the modern reader would like to have more direct words of explanation, a revelation tends to have numerous symbols.

Walter Kaiser pointed out that images tend to stay with us longer than words (1989, 44). Undoubtedly, this accounts for part of the fascination with apocalyptic literature in our culture. The images of Ezekiel’s dry bones, Daniel’s beasts, and Revelation’s plagues have permeated our art, cinema, and popular literature. Most people do not understand what the images symbolize, but they are fascinated by them just the same.

The message in biblical apocalyptic literature is usually delivered as symbols in a dream or as a vision. You can almost imagine yourself in a dream as you read these apocalyptic descriptions. Many of the visuals are otherworldly and far removed from the normal. They are more like an impressionistic painting depicting the future than a photograph of things to come.

Conflict on a Cosmic Level with a Hope of Final Victory

The prophets who recorded apocalyptic prophecy lived during times of extreme crisis. Isaiah’s generation faced the threat of Assyria; Ezekiel and Daniel were slaves in Babylon, Zechariah faced imminent danger from Persia, and John wrote to Christians enduring persecution from Rome. We can imagine that these believers wondered why God did not intervene. Why did evil always seem to triumph and God seem to remain silent?

In these times of crisis, God pulls back the curtain to the cosmic world and puts the entire crisis in context. The prophet and his generation are part of the battle that is taking place in the cosmic world as well as on earth. God’s people seem to be traveling through a dark tunnel, and the enemy is winning. But there is a purpose to their suffering. At the end of the darkness, the prophet sees a bright light of hope. He sees Christ coming to take back control of the earth and restoring a kingdom of peace. This conflict is obvious in John’s Revelation. Notice these references to the conflict that is carried out simultaneously in heaven and on earth:

Dragon (Revelation 12:7–17)

Beast (Revelation 13:1–10)

Kings (Revelation 19:12–21)

Satan’s host (Revelation 20:7–9)

Time Orientation, the Day of the Lord, and the Consummation of History

The New Testament writers regarded the entire era from the incarnation of Christ to the end of the age as the latter times. In the apocalyptic writings, the prophets focus on the final events in that period: the Day of the Lord and the reign of Christ. The Day of the Lord is a time of great distress in the world when God comes to punish wickedness. It is followed by His millennial reign when the earth will be restored to a second Eden.

The messages of the apocalyptic prophecies are often pessimistic, but they always end with hope. Their purpose is to show the reader that God is in charge and He will win. The prophet does not deny the suffering but looks beyond it to the consummation of history. Negative images dominate the early parts of the Revelation. There is cosmic collapse and moral degeneration. In the Revelation, John sees the seemingly all-powerful Antichrist, and the Great Tribulation. The latter part of the book changes dramatically. Christ is the victor. We see the blessings of the millennial reign, a new heaven, a new earth, and a New Jerusalem. There is feasting, and Christ dwells among His people. Ironically, history goes from tree to tree. The first Adam launched the world into a long period of curses and lost dominion at the tree of good and evil. The second Adam regained that dominion and lifted the curse. In the middle of His kingdom is a new tree: the tree of life.

Principles for Interpreting the Symbols in Apocalyptic Literature

Imagine a man who was born in a country other than the United States trying to understand the meaning of political cartoons in a U.S. newspaper. He might question the significance of a small donkey kicking a huge elephant high in the air. He might wonder why a politician is pictured with extremely large ears.

Those in the U.S. culture understand that the animals are symbols of political parties and that the kicking represents one political party’s attack on another party. The physical features of the candidates are exaggerated in order to ridicule them. How foolish to think that these actions and characteristics are to be understood literally. At the same time, these images do represent a real political party, action, or person.

One scholar stated that symbols form an ideograph , in which ideas are represented in graphic images. Another compared symbols to the images in modern impressionistic paintings. Some of Picasso’s paintings symbolically present the agony of the Spanish civil war. To a person who does not know the history of modern Spain, the paintings appear to be a disjointed group of strange images. To a Spaniard who endured the civil war of the 1930s, each picture has intense meaning. They remind the person of the horror and sadness of that crisis. So it is with apocalyptic literature; we should not interpret the images literally, but we should take them seriously.

To determine the realities of symbols, we start by assuming that the symbols had a clear meaning to the original audience. Let us consider four steps for determining this meaning.

1. Look for a meaning in the context: Sometimes the immediate context explains the symbol. In Daniel’s visions, the symbols were often explained by divine revelation in the immediate context. The reader soon learns that the statue and beasts symbolize the great empires that would control Judah: Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome. The final empire depicted is Christ’s kingdom. In Revelation, the candlesticks are identified with churches (Revelation 1:20) and the smoke coming from the altar of incense with the prayers of the saints. The dragon within Revelation is identified as Satan (20:2).

Sometimes a direct explanation is not given, but the details within the context help establish the identity. Consider how the “woman in travail” in Revelation 12 is identified. Taken literally, this woman would appear to be Mary because she literally gave birth to Christ. Some have leaped on this literal interpretation and presented Mary in paintings and illustrations as being “clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head” (Revelation 12:1).

However, other aspects of this mystery woman described in Revelation 12 cannot relate to Mary. When would Mary have spent 1,260 days in the desert (Revelation 12:6)? When did she have two wings to flee from Satan (Revelation 12:14)? When did Satan try to destroy her (Revelation 12:15)? Who are the “rest of her offspring” that will make war with Satan (Revelation 12:17)?

A more reasonable explanation of the woman in Revelation 12 is as a symbol of Israel. The sun, moon, and twelve stars are symbols of Israel’s patriarchs seen in Joseph’s dreams (Genesis 37:9). The attack and time of protection in the desert (Revelation 12:6) parallel events previously mentioned during the Great Tribulation. The offspring are the spiritual heirs of Israel’s promises.

2. Look for a meaning in the history/culture of the writer: Sometimes the writers of apocalyptic literature used symbols that had meaning within the cultural/historical context of the original readers. The letters to the seven churches in Revelation 2–3 contain several classic examples of symbolic language that is clarified by a study of local history and customs.

“The white stone” (Revelation 2:17)

The white stone probably reflected the custom of using black and white stones to register the verdict of a jury. The black was for condemnation; the white was for acquittal.

“The eating of food sacrificed to idols” (Revelation 2:20)

All members of trade guilds were expected to worship the god of that guild. On regular occasions, the members of the guild would offer a sacrifice to its god and eat the meat at a licentious party. If a member did not attend this party, the absence endangered the member professionally and socially.

“The thief in the night” (Revelation 3:3)

One of the famous sculptures in Sardis was a crouching lion symbolizing watchfulness. Despite Sardis’s symbolic lion and great defenses, the enemy found a way in and at night crept as thieves into the city. The citadel was surprised and taken. Christians, likewise, are warned to be on the alert.

“The engraved pillar” (Revelation 3:12)

One way for a man to be honored in the ancient city of Philadelphia was to have a pillar built in the temple with his name engraved on it. To this day, some columns of the original city are still standing.

“The lukewarm water” (Revelation 3:15–16)

Because the water supply for Laodicea was warmed by thermal activity, it had a nauseating taste to those who were not used to it. It is likely that this water became a symbol of the lukewarm believers who remained neutral, while Christ wanted them to declare their loyalties.

3. Look for a meaning in previous apocalyptic literature: As a general rule, if a symbol is identified in the Old Testament apocalyptic literature in a certain way, we can expect that meaning will be parallel to the meaning in the New Testament apocalyptic passages. The following are a few examples of these parallels:

• Rainbow Ezekiel 1:28 parallels Revelation 4:3

• Living creatures Ezekiel 1:5–14 parallels Revelation 4:7–9

• Son of Man Daniel 3:25; 7:13 parallels Revelation 1:13

• Beasts Daniel 7:1–7 parallels Revelation 13:1–18

• Morning star Daniel 12:3 parallels Revelation 2:28

• Four horsemen Zechariah 1:8–11 parallels Revelation 6:1–8

• The great angel Zechariah 1:11 parallels Revelation 10

The Old Testament apocalyptic literature reflected times of crisis for the Jews. Daniel and Ezekiel reflect Babylon’s destruction of Judah and its temple under Persian oppression. Each prophesied beyond the crisis to a time when God would intervene in human history and destroy the enemies of God’s people. The Son of David would reign, Jerusalem would be restored, and the people would be brought back to the land to worship God.

The themes in Revelation show a fulfillment of these prophecies. As in the Old Testament literature, a war still rages between Babylon and Jerusalem. The new Babylon is destroyed and the New Jerusalem comes down from heaven. Christ rules from His temple and His people return to worship Him. We are reminded that Revelation was written during a time of crisis when Rome was persecuting the church. Again, God encourages His people by reminding them of His promises and giving them a glimpse of His final victory.

4. Look for a parallel in the great events of the salvation story: One scholar estimated that there are 350 allusions to the Old Testament in the book of Revelation (Ryken and Longman 1993, 465). An allusion is not a quotation of a passage but rather a reference to a general idea, event, or teaching. Walter Kaiser observed, “It sounds strange, but it is true; prophecy is best understood by going back into the past in order to perceive what God is going to do in the future” (1989, 51).

In apocalyptic literature, the final chapter of salvation history is stressed. This literature contains many allusions to events in earlier texts. Below are some of the major events from salvation history that are pictured symbolically in the Revelation of John (see full list in Kaiser 1989, 51–60). It is as if there is a divine pattern to history that is repeating itself in this final chapter.

• Creation—The final chapter of salvation history reveals the creation of a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1).

• Paradise lost and the serpent—The final chapter shows paradise restored and the dragon defeated. The tree of life in the Garden of Eden is replaced with the tree of life in the new paradise (Revelation 2:7; 12:9; 22:1, 2).

• The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah—The wicked are again judged and the fire and brimstone imagery is found in the lake of fire and the smoke of their torment (Revelation 11:18; 19:20).

• The plagues of Egypt and the Exodus—God again comes to judge those who persecute His people. The plagues of Egypt become symbols of this final judgment. Note the parallels between the plagues and the events associated with the seven trumpet blasts (Revelation 8–9) and the seven bowls of wrath (Revelation 16).

• The Babylonian captivity—The bondage and deliverance from ancient Babylon is a symbolic picture that predicts the judgment on a modern oppressor (Revelation 18).

One man bragged that he could find the fulfillment of biblical prophecy all over the pages of his newspaper. I appreciate his zeal, but his approach trivializes biblical prophecy. If we consider the example of prophecies already fulfilled in Scripture, there seems to be a definite pattern for interpreting long-range prophecies. They do not emphasize trivial events but show movement into the grand plan of salvation history. Ultimately, we should not begin with the present but go back to God’s promises in the Bible. The meanings of prophecies are more likely found in the pages of the Bible than the pages of the newspaper.

When we look at apocalyptic literature, we should not think of the Revelation as a literal picture of the future. The view of the future is not a photograph but an ideograph. The images are not meant to form an actual picture of the future but only to represent the future in symbols. Like the symbol on a bottle that shows a skull and crossbones, they should not be taken as literal but rather as symbols of something that is real. To understand the meaning of these symbols, we must look back to their use in past Scripture before we can interpret what they depict about the future.

**Q:** What does apocalipsis mean, and where do we find most of the biblical apocalyptic literature?

**A:** The word apocalipsis in Greek, (from which we get the English word, “apocalypse”), means “to unveil.” In this case, the future until the consummation of history is unveiled in symbolic visions and dreams. Biblical apocalyptic literature is primarily found in the following passages: Isaiah 24–27; Daniel 7–12; Ezekiel 1; 8–10; Zechariah 9–14; Matthew 24; and Revelation

**Q:** The prophets who wrote apocalyptic literature lived under what circumstances? What significance did this hold?

**A:** The prophets who recorded apocalyptic prophecy lived during times of extreme crisis. Isaiah’s generation faced the threat of Assyria; Ezekiel and Daniel were slaves in Babylon, Zechariah faced imminent danger from Persia, and John wrote to Christians enduring persecution from Rome. The prophet and his generation are part of the battle that is taking place in the cosmic world as well as on earth. God’s people seem to be traveling through a dark tunnel and the enemy is winning. But there is a purpose to their suffering. At the end of the darkness, the prophet sees a bright light of hope.

**Q:** When using the four-step method for interpreting symbols, what assumption do we begin with?

**A:** We start by assuming that the symbols had a clear meaning to the original audience.

**Q:** How does God encourage us through apocalyptic literature?

**A:** God encourages His people by reminding them of His promises and giving them a glimpse of His final victory. 12 CHAPTER
