**A:** God encourages His people by reminding them of His promises and giving them a glimpse of His final victory. 12 CHAPTER

#### 11.2.3

Ezekiel was given a vision of the God of the universe enthroned above an immense, dark, storm cloud. Around him were four living beings. Each had four faces: a man, an ox, a lion, and an eagle. Each had four wings and could move at incredible speed; when moving, they sounded like the roar of rushing waters. The throne sat on wheels that shone like crystal and were ringed with eyes. Within each wheel was another intersecting wheel. The person on the throne looked like a man but glowed brightly. Above his head was a great expanse, sparkling like ice, and a rainbow.

Ezekiel’s message to the slaves in Babylon was that God’s presence was not restricted to Jerusalem. His throne-chariot had wheels! Like the mobile platforms that ancient monarchs used to travel the countryside, His people were—even in Babylonian captivity—above the storm or crisis.

This passage is an early example of a type of literature that would reach its apex in the book of Revelation. This type of literature draws its name from the word apocalipsis in Greek, which means “to unveil.” In this case, the future until the consummation of history is unveiled in symbolic visions and dreams. Biblical apocalyptic literature is primarily found in the following passages:

Isaiah 24–27

Daniel 7–12

Ezekiel 1; 8–10

Zechariah 9–14

Matthew 24

Revelation

Characteristics of Apocalyptic Literature

Symbols of the Future Delivered in Dreams or Visions

In apocalyptic literature, you can expect the prophecy to be conveyed through a vision or a dream. In the revelation, the prophet is bombarded with images as if he were looking into a kaleidoscope. Where the modern reader would like to have more direct words of explanation, a revelation tends to have numerous symbols.

Walter Kaiser pointed out that images tend to stay with us longer than words (1989, 44). Undoubtedly, this accounts for part of the fascination with apocalyptic literature in our culture. The images of Ezekiel’s dry bones, Daniel’s beasts, and Revelation’s plagues have permeated our art, cinema, and popular literature. Most people do not understand what the images symbolize, but they are fascinated by them just the same.

The message in biblical apocalyptic literature is usually delivered as symbols in a dream or as a vision. You can almost imagine yourself in a dream as you read these apocalyptic descriptions. Many of the visuals are otherworldly and far removed from the normal. They are more like an impressionistic painting depicting the future than a photograph of things to come.

Conflict on a Cosmic Level with a Hope of Final Victory

The prophets who recorded apocalyptic prophecy lived during times of extreme crisis. Isaiah’s generation faced the threat of Assyria; Ezekiel and Daniel were slaves in Babylon, Zechariah faced imminent danger from Persia, and John wrote to Christians enduring persecution from Rome. We can imagine that these believers wondered why God did not intervene. Why did evil always seem to triumph and God seem to remain silent?

In these times of crisis, God pulls back the curtain to the cosmic world and puts the entire crisis in context. The prophet and his generation are part of the battle that is taking place in the cosmic world as well as on earth. God’s people seem to be traveling through a dark tunnel, and the enemy is winning. But there is a purpose to their suffering. At the end of the darkness, the prophet sees a bright light of hope. He sees Christ coming to take back control of the earth and restoring a kingdom of peace. This conflict is obvious in John’s Revelation. Notice these references to the conflict that is carried out simultaneously in heaven and on earth:

Dragon (Revelation 12:7–17)

Beast (Revelation 13:1–10)

Kings (Revelation 19:12–21)

Satan’s host (Revelation 20:7–9)

Time Orientation, the Day of the Lord, and the Consummation of History

The New Testament writers regarded the entire era from the incarnation of Christ to the end of the age as the latter times. In the apocalyptic writings, the prophets focus on the final events in that period: the Day of the Lord and the reign of Christ. The Day of the Lord is a time of great distress in the world when God comes to punish wickedness. It is followed by His millennial reign when the earth will be restored to a second Eden.

The messages of the apocalyptic prophecies are often pessimistic, but they always end with hope. Their purpose is to show the reader that God is in charge and He will win. The prophet does not deny the suffering but looks beyond it to the consummation of history. Negative images dominate the early parts of the Revelation. There is cosmic collapse and moral degeneration. In the Revelation, John sees the seemingly all-powerful Antichrist, and the Great Tribulation. The latter part of the book changes dramatically. Christ is the victor. We see the blessings of the millennial reign, a new heaven, a new earth, and a New Jerusalem. There is feasting, and Christ dwells among His people. Ironically, history goes from tree to tree. The first Adam launched the world into a long period of curses and lost dominion at the tree of good and evil. The second Adam regained that dominion and lifted the curse. In the middle of His kingdom is a new tree: the tree of life.

Principles for Interpreting the Symbols in Apocalyptic Literature

Imagine a man who was born in a country other than the United States trying to understand the meaning of political cartoons in a U.S. newspaper. He might question the significance of a small donkey kicking a huge elephant high in the air. He might wonder why a politician is pictured with extremely large ears.

Those in the U.S. culture understand that the animals are symbols of political parties and that the kicking represents one political party’s attack on another party. The physical features of the candidates are exaggerated in order to ridicule them. How foolish to think that these actions and characteristics are to be understood literally. At the same time, these images do represent a real political party, action, or person.

One scholar stated that symbols form an ideograph , in which ideas are represented in graphic images. Another compared symbols to the images in modern impressionistic paintings. Some of Picasso’s paintings symbolically present the agony of the Spanish civil war. To a person who does not know the history of modern Spain, the paintings appear to be a disjointed group of strange images. To a Spaniard who endured the civil war of the 1930s, each picture has intense meaning. They remind the person of the horror and sadness of that crisis. So it is with apocalyptic literature; we should not interpret the images literally, but we should take them seriously.

To determine the realities of symbols, we start by assuming that the symbols had a clear meaning to the original audience. Let us consider four steps for determining this meaning.

1. Look for a meaning in the context: Sometimes the immediate context explains the symbol. In Daniel’s visions, the symbols were often explained by divine revelation in the immediate context. The reader soon learns that the statue and beasts symbolize the great empires that would control Judah: Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome. The final empire depicted is Christ’s kingdom. In Revelation, the candlesticks are identified with churches (Revelation 1:20) and the smoke coming from the altar of incense with the prayers of the saints. The dragon within Revelation is identified as Satan (20:2).

Sometimes a direct explanation is not given, but the details within the context help establish the identity. Consider how the “woman in travail” in Revelation 12 is identified. Taken literally, this woman would appear to be Mary because she literally gave birth to Christ. Some have leaped on this literal interpretation and presented Mary in paintings and illustrations as being “clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head” (Revelation 12:1).

However, other aspects of this mystery woman described in Revelation 12 cannot relate to Mary. When would Mary have spent 1,260 days in the desert (Revelation 12:6)? When did she have two wings to flee from Satan (Revelation 12:14)? When did Satan try to destroy her (Revelation 12:15)? Who are the “rest of her offspring” that will make war with Satan (Revelation 12:17)?

A more reasonable explanation of the woman in Revelation 12 is as a symbol of Israel. The sun, moon, and twelve stars are symbols of Israel’s patriarchs seen in Joseph’s dreams (Genesis 37:9). The attack and time of protection in the desert (Revelation 12:6) parallel events previously mentioned during the Great Tribulation. The offspring are the spiritual heirs of Israel’s promises.

2. Look for a meaning in the history/culture of the writer: Sometimes the writers of apocalyptic literature used symbols that had meaning within the cultural/historical context of the original readers. The letters to the seven churches in Revelation 2–3 contain several classic examples of symbolic language that is clarified by a study of local history and customs.

“The white stone” (Revelation 2:17)

The white stone probably reflected the custom of using black and white stones to register the verdict of a jury. The black was for condemnation; the white was for acquittal.

“The eating of food sacrificed to idols” (Revelation 2:20)

All members of trade guilds were expected to worship the god of that guild. On regular occasions, the members of the guild would offer a sacrifice to its god and eat the meat at a licentious party. If a member did not attend this party, the absence endangered the member professionally and socially.

“The thief in the night” (Revelation 3:3)

One of the famous sculptures in Sardis was a crouching lion symbolizing watchfulness. Despite Sardis’s symbolic lion and great defenses, the enemy found a way in and at night crept as thieves into the city. The citadel was surprised and taken. Christians, likewise, are warned to be on the alert.

“The engraved pillar” (Revelation 3:12)

One way for a man to be honored in the ancient city of Philadelphia was to have a pillar built in the temple with his name engraved on it. To this day, some columns of the original city are still standing.

“The lukewarm water” (Revelation 3:15–16)

Because the water supply for Laodicea was warmed by thermal activity, it had a nauseating taste to those who were not used to it. It is likely that this water became a symbol of the lukewarm believers who remained neutral, while Christ wanted them to declare their loyalties.

3. Look for a meaning in previous apocalyptic literature: As a general rule, if a symbol is identified in the Old Testament apocalyptic literature in a certain way, we can expect that meaning will be parallel to the meaning in the New Testament apocalyptic passages. The following are a few examples of these parallels:

• Rainbow Ezekiel 1:28 parallels Revelation 4:3

• Living creatures Ezekiel 1:5–14 parallels Revelation 4:7–9

• Son of Man Daniel 3:25; 7:13 parallels Revelation 1:13

• Beasts Daniel 7:1–7 parallels Revelation 13:1–18

• Morning star Daniel 12:3 parallels Revelation 2:28

• Four horsemen Zechariah 1:8–11 parallels Revelation 6:1–8

• The great angel Zechariah 1:11 parallels Revelation 10

The Old Testament apocalyptic literature reflected times of crisis for the Jews. Daniel and Ezekiel reflect Babylon’s destruction of Judah and its temple under Persian oppression. Each prophesied beyond the crisis to a time when God would intervene in human history and destroy the enemies of God’s people. The Son of David would reign, Jerusalem would be restored, and the people would be brought back to the land to worship God.

The themes in Revelation show a fulfillment of these prophecies. As in the Old Testament literature, a war still rages between Babylon and Jerusalem. The new Babylon is destroyed and the New Jerusalem comes down from heaven. Christ rules from His temple and His people return to worship Him. We are reminded that Revelation was written during a time of crisis when Rome was persecuting the church. Again, God encourages His people by reminding them of His promises and giving them a glimpse of His final victory.

4. Look for a parallel in the great events of the salvation story: One scholar estimated that there are 350 allusions to the Old Testament in the book of Revelation (Ryken and Longman 1993, 465). An allusion is not a quotation of a passage but rather a reference to a general idea, event, or teaching. Walter Kaiser observed, “It sounds strange, but it is true; prophecy is best understood by going back into the past in order to perceive what God is going to do in the future” (1989, 51).

In apocalyptic literature, the final chapter of salvation history is stressed. This literature contains many allusions to events in earlier texts. Below are some of the major events from salvation history that are pictured symbolically in the Revelation of John (see full list in Kaiser 1989, 51–60). It is as if there is a divine pattern to history that is repeating itself in this final chapter.

• Creation—The final chapter of salvation history reveals the creation of a new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1).

• Paradise lost and the serpent—The final chapter shows paradise restored and the dragon defeated. The tree of life in the Garden of Eden is replaced with the tree of life in the new paradise (Revelation 2:7; 12:9; 22:1, 2).

• The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah—The wicked are again judged and the fire and brimstone imagery is found in the lake of fire and the smoke of their torment (Revelation 11:18; 19:20).

• The plagues of Egypt and the Exodus—God again comes to judge those who persecute His people. The plagues of Egypt become symbols of this final judgment. Note the parallels between the plagues and the events associated with the seven trumpet blasts (Revelation 8–9) and the seven bowls of wrath (Revelation 16).

• The Babylonian captivity—The bondage and deliverance from ancient Babylon is a symbolic picture that predicts the judgment on a modern oppressor (Revelation 18).

One man bragged that he could find the fulfillment of biblical prophecy all over the pages of his newspaper. I appreciate his zeal, but his approach trivializes biblical prophecy. If we consider the example of prophecies already fulfilled in Scripture, there seems to be a definite pattern for interpreting long-range prophecies. They do not emphasize trivial events but show movement into the grand plan of salvation history. Ultimately, we should not begin with the present but go back to God’s promises in the Bible. The meanings of prophecies are more likely found in the pages of the Bible than the pages of the newspaper.

When we look at apocalyptic literature, we should not think of the Revelation as a literal picture of the future. The view of the future is not a photograph but an ideograph. The images are not meant to form an actual picture of the future but only to represent the future in symbols. Like the symbol on a bottle that shows a skull and crossbones, they should not be taken as literal but rather as symbols of something that is real. To understand the meaning of these symbols, we must look back to their use in past Scripture before we can interpret what they depict about the future.

## 12 - Genres: Gospels, Acts, and the Epistles

### Gospels: Portraits of Christ

#### 12.1.1 — Define what is meant by a Gospel pericope and defend the statement that all the pericopes center on Christ and His kingdom.

As a boy, I saw prints of Warner Sallman’s Head of Christ on sanctuary walls in dozens of churches. Over a half million copies of this remarkable work have been sold since Sallman painted it in 1940. The reason for its success is that it is not simply a picture of what Christ might have looked like. Rather, it is an interpretation of what the artist felt Christ is like. Through this image, the personality and character of Christ are revealed.

In a similar way, the Gospels can be compared to four artists’ interpretations of Christ. Each Gospel artist/author includes only what is important for his purpose (John 20:30). One writer leaves out details that another includes. Some repeat and stress incidents that the others barely mention. The writers choose the activities and sayings of Christ carefully to project a certain point of view. The exact order of events is less important than their presentation of Christ. The four literary portraits complement rather than contradict each other. In the end, we see four distinct perspectives of Christ from the four distinct gospels.

Interpreting Individual Verses in the Context of the Entire Pericope and Its Purpose

The Gospels are similar to theological biographies. They are epics that tell a grand story through a series of smaller episodes called pericopes . Pericopes can be loosely compared to what the articles in a newspaper are to the overall issue of a daily paper. They are small, self-contained units that go together to form a Gospel.

The pericopes do not always follow a chronological order. Often, the writer groups pericopes topically or thematically to achieve a desired effect on the reader. In these cases, it is difficult to find an obvious connection between the stories. The Gospels are more like a mosaic of events in Christ’s life and quotations from His teachings. The episodes are carefully selected and sequenced to present the author’s perspective on Christ. When we stand back from the mosaic, we see how the individual pericopes contribute to the larger picture.

Each of these pericopes should be read as a unit, just as you would read an article in a newspaper as one complete unit. Imagine how confusing it would be to read a newspaper if you picked out lines from various articles and ignored the context of the articles in which they were found. So a verse of the Gospels by itself can give a distorted meaning without seeing it within the context of the entire pericope.

In contrast to newspapers, most versions of the Bible do not have bold headings indicating the beginning of each new story or pericope (although some versions do have imposed headings at the beginning of major breaks). Instead, we look for introductory phrases that introduce a new pericope. Typically, the pericope opens with a change of location, audience, or time. Notice how the following pericopes in Mark 2 are introduced.

Mark 2:1–12: “A few days later, when Jesus again entered Capernaum . . . so many gathered” (vv. 1–2).

Mark 2:13–17: “Once again . . . beside the lake. A large crowd came to him . . . As he walked along” (vv. 13–14).

Mark 2:18–22: “Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. Some people came and asked” (v. 18)

Mark 2:23–27: “One Sabbath . . . grainfields . . . Pharisees said” (vv. 23–24)

The variety in the types of pericopes can be confusing. In the chart below, the major types of story pericopes are listed. With each type, I have suggested their specific purpose and listed some examples. For a more complete description, I recommend Leland Ryken’s Words of Delight (1987, 278–282). Note that some of these categories overlap—that is, we could include some stories in more than one type of pericope. For example, the woman at the well encountered Jesus face-to-face, recognized who He was, and witnessed about Him (John 4:1–26).

Type of Pericope

Purpose of the Pericope

Examples of the Pericope

Annunciation/

nativity stories

These stories prove the uniqueness of Christ’s birth and relate it to prophecy.

Birth of John (Luke 1:5–25)

Birth of Christ (Luke 2:1–7)

Visit of Magi (Matthew 2:1–12)

Calling stories

Someone is called to follow Christ or respond to a specific command.

Calling first disciples (John 1:35–51)

Calling of Levi (Mark 2:13–17)

Miracle stories

These stories recount miracles of healing the sick, controlling nature, casting out demons, or resurrecting the dead. The miracles announce the coming of the King and His kingdom with power.

Calms storm (Matthew 8:23–27)

Casts out demons (Matthew 8:28–34)

Raises girl (Matthew 9:18–26)

Recognition and

witness stories

In recognition stories, someone discovers who Christ is. In witness stories, someone testifies about what He has done. Both present Christ as the Messiah.

Peter’s confession (Matthew 16:13–20)

Witness of the man healed of a legion of demons (Mark 5:1–20)

The centurion (Matthew 27:45–54)

Encounter stories

Jesus has face-to-face dialog with an individual. In the end, the person accepts or rejects the claims of Christ.

Nicodemus (John 3:2–21)

Samaritan woman (John 4:7–26)

Man at the pool (John 5:5–15)

Conflict stories

Jesus is confronted by an opposing person or group. These stories tend to be apologetic in nature. They show how Christ answers His critics and the accusations of His enemies.

Sabbath controversy (Luke 6:1–11)

Hand washing (Matthew 15:1–20)

Accusation (Matthew 12:22–37)

Pronouncement stories

These stories may overlap other types but are distinctive because they end with a memorial pronouncement of Christ that is linked to the story.

Paralytic healed (Mark 2:1–12)

Levi called (Mark 2:13–17)

Fasting question (Mark 2:18–22)

Sermons/teaching

Watch for Christ’s sermons to explain something about entering, serving, or proclaiming His kingdom.

Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7)

Commission (Matthew 9:35–10:42)

Last things (Matthew 23–25)

Parables

These stories illustrate a truth about Christ and His kingdom. Like the pronouncement stories, a parable (or group of parables) will end with Christ’s own application.

The soils (Matthew 13:1–23)

The wedding (Matthew 22:1–14)

The talents (Matthew 25:14–30)

Passion stories

These stories are related to the death and resurrection of Christ. They all occurred in the last week of Christ’s ministry.

Last Supper (John 13:1–30)

Crucifixion (John 19:16–27)

Resurrection (John 20:1–8)

Individual Pericopes and Theme of the King and His Kingdom

The chart on the previous page lists the specific purposes of each type of pericope. As a group, pericopes all have one common purpose—to proclaim the coming of the Messiah and His kingdom. The kingdom of God (heaven) is the governing theme of the Gospels. The word “kingdom(s)” appears 128 times in the four Gospels alone (Ludwigson 1973, 70). Like the pieces of a mosaic, each pericope contributes to present the King of Glory coming to inaugurate His kingdom on earth.

This theme is easily seen in the miracle pericopes. Their primary purpose is to confirm that Christ was the Messiah. They announced the kingdom of heaven breaking into the domain of Satan. When Christ healed a demon-possessed man, the crowd’s reaction was, “Could this be the son of David?” (Matthew 12:23). Christ himself explained, “If I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the Kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28).

Some have labeled the miracles of the Gospel pericopes as myths. These scholars claim the miraculous signs were merely a primitive way of communication. They allege that the signs reveal a spiritual truth even though what is recorded is not historically true. This theory undermines the purpose of the signs. In reality, the miracles are meant to illustrate the power of the Kingdom breaking into history through Jesus’ ministry. If the miracles do not record historical fact, they are useless as proof of the power of the Kingdom.

The Gospels refer to the kingdom of God as both at hand and yet to come . This is not a contradiction. Scholars use the phrase inaugurated theology to explain this concept. Christ inaugurated His kingdom during His first coming, but we await His second coming when He will fully claim His kingdom. At present, the Kingdom refers to a spiritual reign rather than an earthly realm. It refers more to personal transformation than to political reform.

This idea that Christ’s kingdom is both now yet future is illustrated by a common now/then pattern in Christ’s teachings. The first line of the pattern describes the now response and often begins with words like whosoever or if anyone . This line describes how a person or group relates to Christ or His message in the present. The second line changes the time orientation. This line describes how Christ will respond in kind in His future kingdom. Sometimes, the second line of the parallelism repeats a key verb from the first line.

Present: “‘If anyone will not welcome you or listen to your words, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that home or town.

Future: “I tell you the truth, it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town’” (Matthew 10:14–15).

Present: “‘Whoever acknowledges me before men,

Future: I will also acknowledge him before my Father in heaven’” (Matthew 10:32).

Present: “‘But whoever disowns me before men,

Future: I will disown him before my Father in heaven’” (Matthew 10:33).

Present: “‘If anyone is ashamed of me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation,

Future: the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his Father’s glory with the holy angels’” (Mark 8:38).

The Gospel writers also use the twin terms this age and the age to come (Mark 10:30) as a framework in which to view “God’s dramatic conclusion to the series of events that are already in motion” (Kaiser 1989, 118). Kaiser further explains the use of these terms and illustrates them with the following graph that has been adapted from his work, Back to the Future: Hints for Interpreting Bible Prophecy.

This present age began with creation and will extend in full force up to the second coming of Christ, and then beyond that in a limited fashion for the duration of the millennium, concluding there at the end of history and at the great white throne judgment of Christ. The age to come, on the other hand, began in a limited form when our Lord cast out demons by the power of God. Then it was that the kingdom of God had come (Matthew 12:28) and we began to taste the powers of the age to come (Hebrews 6:5); indeed, we are now in the last days. (Hebrews 1:2) (Kaiser 1989, 118)

The Age to Come

_ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ __________________________

This Age Millennium Eternity

____________________________________ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _

Creation 1st Coming/ 2nd Coming Great Judgment Resurrection of Christ of Christ Throne

In summary, Kaiser’s chart shows that there is an overlapping period at the end of this age and the beginning of the age to come. This period is called the last days . During these days of transition, Satan is still the prince of this world (John 14:30; 16:11) and all of creation suffers (Romans 8:20). The good news is that Christ has come in power to take back His kingdom. Now He reigns only in the hearts of believers, but one day He will overthrow Satan and wrestle control from him. This concept is foundational to understanding scores of passages in the Gospels.

Reading the Gospels both Vertically and Horizontally

Visitors to European cathedrals often find the faces of a lion, an ox, a man, and an eagle carved into the stone entrances. These four faces reflect the visions of Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1:10) and John (Revelation 4:7). Somewhere in church history, a tradition started that these images symbolized Christ as depicted in each of the four Gospels: Matthew—the promised king (lion), Mark—the suffering servant (ox), Luke—the perfect man (man), and John—the divine One (eagle). Personally, I doubt this interpretation, but it does illustrate how Christians have recognized that each Gospel has a unique point of view.

Each Gospel is more than the sum of its parts. The stories and teachings are carefully selected, crafted, and sequenced to present a unique theme. For this reason, Mark’s message makes an invaluable contribution even though only two pages of his Gospel contain content that is not repeated in the other Gospels (Fee and Stuart 1993, 115).

Because the Gospels have parallel yet unique messages, scholars recommend that they be read both vertically and horizontally. To read them vertically is to read each Gospel from beginning to end as one literary unit. The interpreter notes how each segment fits into the overall theme of the individual Gospel. To read the Gospels horizontally is to read to compare the parallel accounts for their unique differences.

Read the Gospels Vertically

At first glance, the Gospel pericopes appear random and episodic. However, on closer examination, we see that they do have literary unity. We will examine this unity in two of the Gospels. First, literary unity is evident in the Gospel of Matthew, which is divided into five sections. Each section contains a historical narrative, then a major sermon, and a concluding statement beginning with “when Jesus had finished” (Bridge 2004, 48).

Literary Pattern in the Gospel of Matthew

Chapters 1–4

Narrative

Chapters 5–7

Sermon #1 (Principles of His kingdom)

“When Jesus had finished these words . . . ” (Matthew 7:28)

Chapters 8–9

Narrative

Chapter 10

Sermon #2 (Advice to His disciples before they proclaim His kingdom)

“After Jesus had finished instructing his . . . disciples” (Matthew 11:1)

Chapters 11–12

Narrative

Chapter 13

Sermon #3 (Parables of the Kingdom)

“When Jesus had finished these parables . . . ” (Matthew 13:53)

Chapters 14–17

Narrative

Chapter 18

Sermon #4 (Greatness in the Kingdom)

“When Jesus had finished saying these things . . . ” (Matthew 19:1)

Chapters 19–22

Narrative

Chapters 23–25

Sermon #5 (Woes and prophesies of the future kingdom)

“When Jesus had finished saying all these things . . .” (Matthew 26:1)

Chapters 26–28

Narrative

Mark basically has a chronological approach, but his selection of events and emphasis on details shows that the Gospel is organized so as to bring the reader to a certain conclusion. We see that Mark presents Christ as equally interested in the salvation of the Jews and the Gentiles. Note how he records events on each side of the Sea of Galilee. Primarily Jews inhabited the west side of the sea, while the east side was the Gentile area called Decapolis. Steven Bridge (2004) observed that Mark first shows Jesus’ ministry to the Jews and then shows Jesus crossing the lake for a similar ministry to the Gentiles. He crosses back to the Jewish side, performs more healings, and ends with the feeding of the five thousand. The twelve baskets left over seem symbolic of the Hebrew nation. Again Christ crosses the sea to the Gentile side where He heals many and feeds four thousand. The seven baskets left over appear to be symbolic of completeness. On the final crossing to the Jewish side, the disciples worry because they have only one loaf of bread. Christ chastises them and reminds them of what He did with a few loaves in feeding the five thousand and the four thousand. Perhaps Mark’s Gospel implies that Jesus is the Bread of Life for all peoples.

Western Side (Jews)

Sea of Galilee (four crossings)

Eastern Side (Gentiles)

1. Exorcism of unclean spirits (1:21–27)

2. News spread throughout Galilee (1:28)

First crossing going east, accompanied by a storm (4:35–41)

Second crossing going west (5:21)

Exorcism of unclean spirits (5:1–17)

News spread throughout Decapolis (5:18–20)

1. Jesus immediately met with requests for healing (5:21–24)

2. Jesus cures a variety of individuals (5:25–43)

3. Jesus feeds a crowd of thousands (6:34–44)

4. Twelve baskets left (6:43)

Third crossing going east, accompanied by a storm (6:45–53)

Fourth crossing going west. The lack of bread is discussed (8:13–21)

1. Jesus immediately met with requests for healing (6:53–56)

2. Jesus cures a variety of individuals (7:24–37)

3. Jesus feeds a crowd of thousands (8:1–9)

4. Seven baskets left (8:8)

As you read through Luke’s Gospel notice how he pictures Christ as the anointed prophet and the compassionate Savior. The word spirit is mentioned seventeen times in Luke and prayer is a constant theme. When Luke includes a story the other gospels leave out, it tends to emphasize Christ reaching out in compassion to save the humble, the outcasts, and the rejected.

John presents Christ as God. The gospel even starts with his preexistence (John 1:1–4). Seven great signs (miracles) are carefully selected to prove Christ’s divinity. Another hint to His divinity is the allusions to the title God used for himself on Mount Sinai, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). Jesus used the phrase I am to describe himself eight times (John 4:26; 6:20; 8:24; 28, 58; 13:19; 18:5, 6, 8).

When we speak of reading a Gospel vertically, we must start with the confidence that it is one, unified, whole Gospel and the work of one inspired author. This is called the principle of literary unity . In contrast to this view, some see the Gospels as mere copies of some lost original source. Through time, they claim, various groups of Christians added layers of information to this original. The end result is that each Gospel is like an onion with several layers of additions from numerous writers. The interpreter, it is suggested, should not view the Gospel as one unified message, written by one writer, but rather as a manuscript that went through a gradual metamorphosis to evolve into its present state.

Certainly, some of the Gospel writers may have cited oral tradition and written sources. Luke freely admits that his information was handed down from eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4). However, the details he chose to include, the themes he stressed, and the sequence he used resulted in a unified and unique message. Had he changed or added false information, we can assume the eyewitnesses would have challenged his Gospel.

It is true that there are many word-for-word quotations in Luke and Matthew that are not found in Mark. To some, this suggests an unknown source that both Luke and Matthew quoted. However, there are some reasonable explanations for this exact duplication. The word-for-word quotes unique to Matthew and Luke are primarily quotations of Christ. The early church would have used these quotes in worship in the three decades between the Resurrection and the writing of the Gospels. In Jewish society, it was common to memorize long passages of Scripture. It is not surprising that the Christians would, with the help of the disciples, preserve Christ’s words verbatim and use these in their worship.

Read the Gospels Horizontally

The first three Gospels are called the Synoptic Gospels because they have so many parallel stories and sayings. Reading to compare parallel accounts is referred to as horizontal reading . The primary goal in comparing the accounts is not to harmonize them into one account. That would negate their uniqueness. Rather, our goal is to look for distinctives that highlight the special perspective of each writer. It is also helpful to have additional information to clarify a teaching or account. Jesus was a traveling teacher and certainly repeated the same message in different places in somewhat different words. Sometimes, one Gospel writer paraphrased Christ’s words or translated them into the Greek in a slightly different way. In other instances, added details from a parallel passage clarify the pericope.

You might be puzzled by Christ’s command that His disciples travel without a purse, bag, or extra sandals (Matthew 10: 9–10). Even more difficult to understand is His command that they only preach to Jews (Matthew 10:5–6). Is this a pattern for missionaries today? Why should the evangelist be so severely limited? The answer is found by looking at a parallel concept in Luke 22: 35–36: “Then Jesus asked them, ‘When I sent you without purse, bag or sandals, did you lack anything?’ ‘Nothing,’ they answered. He said to them, ‘But now if you have a purse, take it, and also a bag; and if you don’t have a sword, sell your cloak and buy one.’”

Why was there such a radical change of policy? In the first instance (Matthew 10:5–6; Luke 9:3), Christ was sending the disciples on a short missions trip. Its purpose was to offer Christ’s kingdom to Israel. For this reason, they were not to witness to other ethnic groups. Because the trip was short, Christ used it as a training lesson on living by faith. For this reason, they were not to bring extra provisions but to allow the believers to help them. Immediately after the Resurrection, the situation changed. Soon the disciples would travel to the far ends of the world to proclaim the risen Savior. This time they would be prepared, even with a sword for protection. We note, however, that when the disciples produced two swords, Christ rebuked them. He was not promoting insurrection, just prudence.

**Q:** What are pericopes and how do they help us interpret the Bible?

**A:** The Gospels are similar to theological biographies. They are epics that tell a grand story through a series of smaller episodes called pericopes. Pericopes can be loosely compared to what the articles in a newspaper are to the overall issue of a daily paper. They are small, self-contained units that go together to form a Gospel. The episodes are carefully selected and sequenced to present the author’s perspective on Christ. When we stand back from the mosaic, we see how the individual pericopes contribute to the larger picture.

**Q:** What is the difference between the terms this age and the age to come ?

**A:** The Gospel writers also use the twin terms this age and the age to come (Mark 10:30) as a framework in which to view “God’s dramatic conclusion to the series of events that are already in motion” (Kaiser 1989, 118). Kaiser further explained the use of these terms: “This present age began with creation and will extend in full force up to the second coming of Christ, and then beyond that in a limited fashion for the duration of the millennium, concluding there at the end of history and at the great white throne judgment of Christ. The age to come, on the other hand, began in a limited form when our Lord cast out demons by the power of God. Then it was that the kingdom of God had come (Matthew 12:28) and we began to taste the powers of the age to come (Hebrews 6:5); indeed, we are now in the last days (Hebrews 1:2)” (118).

**Q:** What does it mean to read the Gospels vertically and horizontally?

**A:** To read them vertically is to read each Gospel from beginning to end as one literary unit. The interpreter notes how each segment fits into the overall theme of the individual Gospel. To read the Gospels horizontally is to read to compare the parallel accounts for their unique differences.

**Q:** Why did Mark structure his gospel in the way that he did?

**A:** Mark basically has a chronological approach, but his selection of events and emphasis on details shows that the Gospel is organized so as to bring the reader to a certain conclusion.

**Q:** What is the principle of literary unity?

**A:** When we speak of reading a Gospel vertically, we must start with the confidence that it is one, unified, whole Gospel and the work of one inspired author. This is called the principle of literary unity.

**Q:** What should be our goal in reading the Gospels horizontally?

**A:** The primary goal in comparing the accounts is not to harmonize them into one account. That would negate their uniqueness. Rather, our goal is to look for distinctives that highlight the special perspective of each writer. It is also helpful to have additional information to clarify a teaching or account.

**Q:** What was the purpose of the first short missions trip?

**A:** Its purpose was to offer Christ’s kingdom to Israel. For this reason, they were not to witness to other ethnic groups. Because the trip was short, Christ used it as a training lesson on living by faith.

#### 12.1.2 — Explain what is meant by reading the Gospels both horizontally and vertically.

As a boy, I saw prints of Warner Sallman’s Head of Christ on sanctuary walls in dozens of churches. Over a half million copies of this remarkable work have been sold since Sallman painted it in 1940. The reason for its success is that it is not simply a picture of what Christ might have looked like. Rather, it is an interpretation of what the artist felt Christ is like. Through this image, the personality and character of Christ are revealed.

In a similar way, the Gospels can be compared to four artists’ interpretations of Christ. Each Gospel artist/author includes only what is important for his purpose (John 20:30). One writer leaves out details that another includes. Some repeat and stress incidents that the others barely mention. The writers choose the activities and sayings of Christ carefully to project a certain point of view. The exact order of events is less important than their presentation of Christ. The four literary portraits complement rather than contradict each other. In the end, we see four distinct perspectives of Christ from the four distinct gospels.

Interpreting Individual Verses in the Context of the Entire Pericope and Its Purpose

The Gospels are similar to theological biographies. They are epics that tell a grand story through a series of smaller episodes called pericopes . Pericopes can be loosely compared to what the articles in a newspaper are to the overall issue of a daily paper. They are small, self-contained units that go together to form a Gospel.

The pericopes do not always follow a chronological order. Often, the writer groups pericopes topically or thematically to achieve a desired effect on the reader. In these cases, it is difficult to find an obvious connection between the stories. The Gospels are more like a mosaic of events in Christ’s life and quotations from His teachings. The episodes are carefully selected and sequenced to present the author’s perspective on Christ. When we stand back from the mosaic, we see how the individual pericopes contribute to the larger picture.

Each of these pericopes should be read as a unit, just as you would read an article in a newspaper as one complete unit. Imagine how confusing it would be to read a newspaper if you picked out lines from various articles and ignored the context of the articles in which they were found. So a verse of the Gospels by itself can give a distorted meaning without seeing it within the context of the entire pericope.

In contrast to newspapers, most versions of the Bible do not have bold headings indicating the beginning of each new story or pericope (although some versions do have imposed headings at the beginning of major breaks). Instead, we look for introductory phrases that introduce a new pericope. Typically, the pericope opens with a change of location, audience, or time. Notice how the following pericopes in Mark 2 are introduced.

Mark 2:1–12: “A few days later, when Jesus again entered Capernaum . . . so many gathered” (vv. 1–2).

Mark 2:13–17: “Once again . . . beside the lake. A large crowd came to him . . . As he walked along” (vv. 13–14).

Mark 2:18–22: “Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were fasting. Some people came and asked” (v. 18)

Mark 2:23–27: “One Sabbath . . . grainfields . . . Pharisees said” (vv. 23–24)

The variety in the types of pericopes can be confusing. In the chart below, the major types of story pericopes are listed. With each type, I have suggested their specific purpose and listed some examples. For a more complete description, I recommend Leland Ryken’s Words of Delight (1987, 278–282). Note that some of these categories overlap—that is, we could include some stories in more than one type of pericope. For example, the woman at the well encountered Jesus face-to-face, recognized who He was, and witnessed about Him (John 4:1–26).

Type of Pericope

Purpose of the Pericope

Examples of the Pericope

Annunciation/

nativity stories

These stories prove the uniqueness of Christ’s birth and relate it to prophecy.

Birth of John (Luke 1:5–25)

Birth of Christ (Luke 2:1–7)

Visit of Magi (Matthew 2:1–12)

Calling stories

Someone is called to follow Christ or respond to a specific command.

Calling first disciples (John 1:35–51)

Calling of Levi (Mark 2:13–17)

Miracle stories

These stories recount miracles of healing the sick, controlling nature, casting out demons, or resurrecting the dead. The miracles announce the coming of the King and His kingdom with power.

Calms storm (Matthew 8:23–27)

Casts out demons (Matthew 8:28–34)

Raises girl (Matthew 9:18–26)

Recognition and

witness stories

In recognition stories, someone discovers who Christ is. In witness stories, someone testifies about what He has done. Both present Christ as the Messiah.

Peter’s confession (Matthew 16:13–20)

Witness of the man healed of a legion of demons (Mark 5:1–20)

The centurion (Matthew 27:45–54)

Encounter stories

Jesus has face-to-face dialog with an individual. In the end, the person accepts or rejects the claims of Christ.

Nicodemus (John 3:2–21)

Samaritan woman (John 4:7–26)

Man at the pool (John 5:5–15)

Conflict stories

Jesus is confronted by an opposing person or group. These stories tend to be apologetic in nature. They show how Christ answers His critics and the accusations of His enemies.

Sabbath controversy (Luke 6:1–11)

Hand washing (Matthew 15:1–20)

Accusation (Matthew 12:22–37)

Pronouncement stories

These stories may overlap other types but are distinctive because they end with a memorial pronouncement of Christ that is linked to the story.

Paralytic healed (Mark 2:1–12)

Levi called (Mark 2:13–17)

Fasting question (Mark 2:18–22)

Sermons/teaching

Watch for Christ’s sermons to explain something about entering, serving, or proclaiming His kingdom.

Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7)

Commission (Matthew 9:35–10:42)

Last things (Matthew 23–25)

Parables

These stories illustrate a truth about Christ and His kingdom. Like the pronouncement stories, a parable (or group of parables) will end with Christ’s own application.

The soils (Matthew 13:1–23)

The wedding (Matthew 22:1–14)

The talents (Matthew 25:14–30)

Passion stories

These stories are related to the death and resurrection of Christ. They all occurred in the last week of Christ’s ministry.

Last Supper (John 13:1–30)

Crucifixion (John 19:16–27)

Resurrection (John 20:1–8)

Individual Pericopes and Theme of the King and His Kingdom

The chart on the previous page lists the specific purposes of each type of pericope. As a group, pericopes all have one common purpose—to proclaim the coming of the Messiah and His kingdom. The kingdom of God (heaven) is the governing theme of the Gospels. The word “kingdom(s)” appears 128 times in the four Gospels alone (Ludwigson 1973, 70). Like the pieces of a mosaic, each pericope contributes to present the King of Glory coming to inaugurate His kingdom on earth.

This theme is easily seen in the miracle pericopes. Their primary purpose is to confirm that Christ was the Messiah. They announced the kingdom of heaven breaking into the domain of Satan. When Christ healed a demon-possessed man, the crowd’s reaction was, “Could this be the son of David?” (Matthew 12:23). Christ himself explained, “If I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the Kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28).

Some have labeled the miracles of the Gospel pericopes as myths. These scholars claim the miraculous signs were merely a primitive way of communication. They allege that the signs reveal a spiritual truth even though what is recorded is not historically true. This theory undermines the purpose of the signs. In reality, the miracles are meant to illustrate the power of the Kingdom breaking into history through Jesus’ ministry. If the miracles do not record historical fact, they are useless as proof of the power of the Kingdom.

The Gospels refer to the kingdom of God as both at hand and yet to come . This is not a contradiction. Scholars use the phrase inaugurated theology to explain this concept. Christ inaugurated His kingdom during His first coming, but we await His second coming when He will fully claim His kingdom. At present, the Kingdom refers to a spiritual reign rather than an earthly realm. It refers more to personal transformation than to political reform.

This idea that Christ’s kingdom is both now yet future is illustrated by a common now/then pattern in Christ’s teachings. The first line of the pattern describes the now response and often begins with words like whosoever or if anyone . This line describes how a person or group relates to Christ or His message in the present. The second line changes the time orientation. This line describes how Christ will respond in kind in His future kingdom. Sometimes, the second line of the parallelism repeats a key verb from the first line.

Present: “‘If anyone will not welcome you or listen to your words, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that home or town.

Future: “I tell you the truth, it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town’” (Matthew 10:14–15).

Present: “‘Whoever acknowledges me before men,

Future: I will also acknowledge him before my Father in heaven’” (Matthew 10:32).

Present: “‘But whoever disowns me before men,

Future: I will disown him before my Father in heaven’” (Matthew 10:33).

Present: “‘If anyone is ashamed of me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation,

Future: the Son of Man will be ashamed of him when he comes in his Father’s glory with the holy angels’” (Mark 8:38).

The Gospel writers also use the twin terms this age and the age to come (Mark 10:30) as a framework in which to view “God’s dramatic conclusion to the series of events that are already in motion” (Kaiser 1989, 118). Kaiser further explains the use of these terms and illustrates them with the following graph that has been adapted from his work, Back to the Future: Hints for Interpreting Bible Prophecy.

This present age began with creation and will extend in full force up to the second coming of Christ, and then beyond that in a limited fashion for the duration of the millennium, concluding there at the end of history and at the great white throne judgment of Christ. The age to come, on the other hand, began in a limited form when our Lord cast out demons by the power of God. Then it was that the kingdom of God had come (Matthew 12:28) and we began to taste the powers of the age to come (Hebrews 6:5); indeed, we are now in the last days. (Hebrews 1:2) (Kaiser 1989, 118)

The Age to Come

_ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ __________________________

This Age Millennium Eternity

____________________________________ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _

Creation 1st Coming/ 2nd Coming Great Judgment Resurrection of Christ of Christ Throne

In summary, Kaiser’s chart shows that there is an overlapping period at the end of this age and the beginning of the age to come. This period is called the last days . During these days of transition, Satan is still the prince of this world (John 14:30; 16:11) and all of creation suffers (Romans 8:20). The good news is that Christ has come in power to take back His kingdom. Now He reigns only in the hearts of believers, but one day He will overthrow Satan and wrestle control from him. This concept is foundational to understanding scores of passages in the Gospels.

Reading the Gospels both Vertically and Horizontally

Visitors to European cathedrals often find the faces of a lion, an ox, a man, and an eagle carved into the stone entrances. These four faces reflect the visions of Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1:10) and John (Revelation 4:7). Somewhere in church history, a tradition started that these images symbolized Christ as depicted in each of the four Gospels: Matthew—the promised king (lion), Mark—the suffering servant (ox), Luke—the perfect man (man), and John—the divine One (eagle). Personally, I doubt this interpretation, but it does illustrate how Christians have recognized that each Gospel has a unique point of view.

Each Gospel is more than the sum of its parts. The stories and teachings are carefully selected, crafted, and sequenced to present a unique theme. For this reason, Mark’s message makes an invaluable contribution even though only two pages of his Gospel contain content that is not repeated in the other Gospels (Fee and Stuart 1993, 115).

Because the Gospels have parallel yet unique messages, scholars recommend that they be read both vertically and horizontally. To read them vertically is to read each Gospel from beginning to end as one literary unit. The interpreter notes how each segment fits into the overall theme of the individual Gospel. To read the Gospels horizontally is to read to compare the parallel accounts for their unique differences.

Read the Gospels Vertically

At first glance, the Gospel pericopes appear random and episodic. However, on closer examination, we see that they do have literary unity. We will examine this unity in two of the Gospels. First, literary unity is evident in the Gospel of Matthew, which is divided into five sections. Each section contains a historical narrative, then a major sermon, and a concluding statement beginning with “when Jesus had finished” (Bridge 2004, 48).

Literary Pattern in the Gospel of Matthew

Chapters 1–4

Narrative

Chapters 5–7

Sermon #1 (Principles of His kingdom)

“When Jesus had finished these words . . . ” (Matthew 7:28)

Chapters 8–9

Narrative

Chapter 10

Sermon #2 (Advice to His disciples before they proclaim His kingdom)

“After Jesus had finished instructing his . . . disciples” (Matthew 11:1)

Chapters 11–12

Narrative

Chapter 13

Sermon #3 (Parables of the Kingdom)

“When Jesus had finished these parables . . . ” (Matthew 13:53)

Chapters 14–17

Narrative

Chapter 18

Sermon #4 (Greatness in the Kingdom)

“When Jesus had finished saying these things . . . ” (Matthew 19:1)

Chapters 19–22

Narrative

Chapters 23–25

Sermon #5 (Woes and prophesies of the future kingdom)

“When Jesus had finished saying all these things . . .” (Matthew 26:1)

Chapters 26–28

Narrative

Mark basically has a chronological approach, but his selection of events and emphasis on details shows that the Gospel is organized so as to bring the reader to a certain conclusion. We see that Mark presents Christ as equally interested in the salvation of the Jews and the Gentiles. Note how he records events on each side of the Sea of Galilee. Primarily Jews inhabited the west side of the sea, while the east side was the Gentile area called Decapolis. Steven Bridge (2004) observed that Mark first shows Jesus’ ministry to the Jews and then shows Jesus crossing the lake for a similar ministry to the Gentiles. He crosses back to the Jewish side, performs more healings, and ends with the feeding of the five thousand. The twelve baskets left over seem symbolic of the Hebrew nation. Again Christ crosses the sea to the Gentile side where He heals many and feeds four thousand. The seven baskets left over appear to be symbolic of completeness. On the final crossing to the Jewish side, the disciples worry because they have only one loaf of bread. Christ chastises them and reminds them of what He did with a few loaves in feeding the five thousand and the four thousand. Perhaps Mark’s Gospel implies that Jesus is the Bread of Life for all peoples.

Sea of Galilee (four crossings)

Eastern Side (Gentiles)

2. News spread throughout Galilee (1:28)

First crossing going east, accompanied by a storm (4:35–41)

Second crossing going west (5:21)

Exorcism of unclean spirits (5:1–17)

2. Jesus cures a variety of individuals (5:25–43)

3. Jesus feeds a crowd of thousands (6:34–44)

4. Twelve baskets left (6:43)

Third crossing going east, accompanied by a storm (6:45–53)

Fourth crossing going west. The lack of bread is discussed (8:13–21)

1. Jesus immediately met with requests for healing (6:53–56)

2. Jesus cures a variety of individuals (7:24–37)

3. Jesus feeds a crowd of thousands (8:1–9)

4. Seven baskets left (8:8)

As you read through Luke’s Gospel notice how he pictures Christ as the anointed prophet and the compassionate Savior. The word spirit is mentioned seventeen times in Luke and prayer is a constant theme. When Luke includes a story the other gospels leave out, it tends to emphasize Christ reaching out in compassion to save the humble, the outcasts, and the rejected.

John presents Christ as God. The gospel even starts with his preexistence (John 1:1–4). Seven great signs (miracles) are carefully selected to prove Christ’s divinity. Another hint to His divinity is the allusions to the title God used for himself on Mount Sinai, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). Jesus used the phrase I am to describe himself eight times (John 4:26; 6:20; 8:24; 28, 58; 13:19; 18:5, 6, 8).

### Gospels: Teaching Methods of Christ

#### 12.2.1 — Justify how hyperbole can be an effective literary tool yet not teach error.

Why does Christ’s method of teaching stand out? Why have so many of His statements become part of our everyday vocabulary? One key reason why Christ’s teachings have such appeal and are so hard to forget is because He seldom said anything in an ordinary way. Some estimate that at least 90 percent of Christ’s words use poetic method or figures of speech (Klein, Bloomberg, Hubbard 1993, 344). Christ used concrete images to illustrate abstract truths. He summarized complex truths in concise sayings, and He used overstatement and hyperbole to shock His audience. All these methods add interest, but they also add a level of complexity to interpretation.

Christ’s Concrete Imagery

Many of the figures of speech Christ used have become a part of our culture and everyday conversation. They are striking and memorable because they give a mental picture to explain an abstract truth. Notice the imagery, now common in everyday usage, in these statements from just one of Christ’s sermons (Matthew 5–7, KJV).

The salt of the earth (5:13)

A city on a hill (5:14)

Don’t let your right hand know what your left hand is doing (6:3)

Our daily bread (6:11)

The lilies of the field (6:28)

Pearls before swine (7:6)

Wolves in sheep’s clothing (7:15)

When we read Christ’s words, we should expect to see figures of speech. Interpreting them literally can create great confusion. When Christ ate the Passover with His disciples, He said, “‘Take, eat. This is my body . . . this is my blood’” (Matthew 26:26–28). To this day, millions do not see this as a figure of speech but argue that the bread and wine of communion turn into the actual blood and body of Christ.

Christ’s Sayings

Christ’s teaching is a masterful example of reducing great and complex truths to a saying that is short and easy to remember. These sayings are similar to proverbs and follow all of the rules associated with proverbs. What is different about them is that they are cited to respond to a specific situation, while proverbs are more general. Sometimes, removed from their immediate context, these sayings may create confusion. How do you explain the apparent contradiction in the following statements of Christ?

“For whoever is not against us is for us.” (Mark 9:40)

“He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me, scatters.” (Luke 11:23)

Both verses are correct for the situations in which they were spoken. In Mark 9, the context refers to a sincere believer whom the disciples forbade to minister. The statement teaches that all believers have the right to minister—not just a few chosen disciples. The verse does not teach salvation of the non-committed. Those to whom this message was directed were already believers.

The second verse refers to a much different context. The religious leaders are accusing Jesus of being an ally of Beelzebub. The people must make a decision to side either with the leaders or with Christ. In this case, to refuse to make a decision was to make a decision against Christ. These proverbs demonstrate that the meaning of a proverb should be restricted to the scope the author intended.

A classic example of how the saying must be considered in its context is the statement “Judge not that you be not judged.” Many use this saying to condemn anyone who stands up against immoral practices. However, this was not its use in the original context. Christ was rebuking the hypocritical Pharisees for their practice of condemning men for the slightest infraction of their customs. Since Christ himself judged them (Matthew 15:1–20), it is clear that this was not meant as a universal restriction on judging sin. Likewise Matthew 18:15–20 guides believers to judge sin.

In general, Christ’s sayings, like proverbs, are so generalized that they do not include incidental exceptions. Consider these two proverbs of Christ: “Only in his hometown and in his own house is a prophet without honor” (Matthew 13:57) and “For all who draw the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). Can you think of any exceptions to these proverbs? Certainly, some prophets are honored in their hometowns and not all soldiers die violent deaths. These sayings do not deny that exceptions may exist; they simply do not consider them. The power of the proverbs, however, would be lost if they always began with a qualifying phrase such as “It is generally true that . . .”

Scholars have observed that Gospel pericopes often have a similar format. They tend to end with a climatic reaction to Christ or an official pronouncement by Christ. The purpose of the entire pericope is found in this conclusion. This pattern is so common that it is called the law of end stress . Stated briefly, this law says that the key to understanding a story or parable can often be found at the end of the story.

A saying of Jesus at the end of the story is often introduced with a formula statement such as I tell you ; verily , verily I say to you ; or in the same way . This pronouncement summarizes a truth in a few short words and explains the purpose for the story (Mark 2:11; 8:12). The historical event or parable serves as an illustration of the truth Christ wants to teach. Below are a few examples of the law of end stress:

The parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14)

“‘‘I tell you that this man, rather than the other, went home justified before God. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted’” (Luke 18:14).

The calling of Levi (Mark 2:13–17)

“On hearing this, Jesus said to them, ‘It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners’” (Mark 2:17).

Christ’s Use of Exaggerated Language

One of the most powerful methods that Christ used to arrest attention was overstatement or hyperbole. This was not done to tell a lie or stretch the truth. Christ used this literary method to capture interest. Most of the time, His use of hyperbole is obvious, but when there is doubt, use the following general rule: If responding to Christ’s statement literally causes conflict with other Bible teaching, is physically impossible, or would not achieve the desired result that Christ wanted, we can assume that the saying is a figure of speech. Consider these examples:

The Statement

The Problem

The Meaning

“‘Remove the log in your eye’” (Matthew 7:5).

This is a physical impossibility.

The sin you hide may be more serious than the sin you expose.

“‘When you pray, go into your room’” (Matthew 6:6).

Christ did not limit His own prayer to a room, and restricting our praying to a certain location was not what Christ intended.

Do not pray just to show off your spiritually. Pray just as intensely in private as you do in public.

“‘Pluck out your eye’” (Matthew 5:29).

Mutilation of the body would not have the result Christ wanted.

No sin is worth it if it keeps you out of heaven.

“‘Leave your gift at altar’” (Matthew 5:23–24).

A person who had traveled weeks to worship at the temple would not be hurt by taking time to pray before he went home to make amends.

Do not delay to make things right with one who is in conflict with you.

The Statement

The Problem

The Meaning

“‘Tread on serpents’” (Luke 10:19)

Walking on snakes to test God’s protection would not achieve the objectives Christ wanted.

You can take courage in the fact that God is more powerful than your enemy and will protect you.

“Hate father and mother” (Luke 14:26)

Christ condemned those who do not honor their parents (Mark 7:9–13) and honored His earthly parent (John 19:26–27).

Do not allow your relationship with your parents to keep you from serving Christ.

Rich man…camel through the eye of a needle (Mark 10:24–25)

Rich people who converted to Christ: Zacchaeus (Luke 19:9), several rich women (Luke 8:3), and Joseph of Arimathea (John 19:38)

For a rich person to convert is very rare. This is an idiom for something requiring great difficulty.

**Q:** How do figures of speech help us in our Bible study?

**A:** They are striking and memorable because they give a mental picture to explain an abstract truth.

**Q:** What is the difference between Christ’s sayings and proverbs?

**A:** His sayings are similar to proverbs and follow all of the rules associated with proverbs. What is different about them is that they are cited to respond to a specific situation, while proverbs are more general.

**Q:** What is the law of end stress?

**A:** Stated briefly, this law says that the key to understanding a story or parable can often be found at the end of the story.

#### 12.2.2 — Apply the rules for interpreting sayings in Christ’s teaching and for using the law of end stress.

Why does Christ’s method of teaching stand out? Why have so many of His statements become part of our everyday vocabulary? One key reason why Christ’s teachings have such appeal and are so hard to forget is because He seldom said anything in an ordinary way. Some estimate that at least 90 percent of Christ’s words use poetic method or figures of speech (Klein, Bloomberg, Hubbard 1993, 344). Christ used concrete images to illustrate abstract truths. He summarized complex truths in concise sayings, and He used overstatement and hyperbole to shock His audience. All these methods add interest, but they also add a level of complexity to interpretation.

Christ’s Concrete Imagery

Many of the figures of speech Christ used have become a part of our culture and everyday conversation. They are striking and memorable because they give a mental picture to explain an abstract truth. Notice the imagery, now common in everyday usage, in these statements from just one of Christ’s sermons (Matthew 5–7, KJV).

The salt of the earth (5:13)

A city on a hill (5:14)

Don’t let your right hand know what your left hand is doing (6:3)

Our daily bread (6:11)

The lilies of the field (6:28)

Pearls before swine (7:6)

Wolves in sheep’s clothing (7:15)

When we read Christ’s words, we should expect to see figures of speech. Interpreting them literally can create great confusion. When Christ ate the Passover with His disciples, He said, “‘Take, eat. This is my body . . . this is my blood’” (Matthew 26:26–28). To this day, millions do not see this as a figure of speech but argue that the bread and wine of communion turn into the actual blood and body of Christ.
