### Acts: An Interpretive History

#### 12.3.1 — Explain how to distinguish between normative and descriptive historical actions.

The book of Acts reads like an adventure story. It is one of the most interesting literary works ever written. Leland Ryken’s description captures the essence of this exciting report. “The book of Acts gives us twenty-eight chapters packed with trials, riots, persecutions, escapes, martyrdoms, voyages, shipwrecks, and rescues. And all of this action takes place in the major cities of the ancient world: Jerusalem, Antioch, Philippi, Corinth, Antioch, Ephesus, and Rome. There is an equal variety in the settings: temples, prisons, courts, deserts, ships, seas, barracks, and theaters” (1992, 422).

The book of Acts is far more than a historical record. It is an interpretive history . Luke presents theology through history. He has carefully selected those events and speeches that lead to certain conclusions. He saw Acts as a sequel to his Gospel. In his Gospel, Luke presents an interpretive biography of what Christ began to do and teach (Acts 1:1–2). In Acts, an interpretive history, Luke shows how the apostles and the church continued what Christ began.

Determining the Difference Between Normative and Descriptive

All the events and actions recorded in the book of Acts are useful for instructing modern believers (2 Timothy 3:16). This does not imply, however, that whatever was done by a first-century Christian is automatically a pattern for us today. Some actions recorded in the Bible are meant to be normative. Others are descriptive.

You will remember from Chapter 7 that an action that is meant to be a pattern for all believers of all time is called normative . An action that only describes what happened or illustrates the faith of biblical characters is called descriptive . We have studied these terms in relation to Old Testament stories. Now we will see how they apply to the events in the book of Acts. “How can we tell if an action is meant to be normative or descriptive?”

Acts

Possible meaning

Normative

Descriptive

1:26

Select leaders by casting lots.

X

2:1–4

Be baptized in the Spirit/speak in tongues.

4:32–35

Sell all you own and give the proceeds to the church.

5:15

Use a shadow of the preacher to heal the sick.

6:1–7

Select deacons to assist in ministry.

8:36–38

Be saved and baptized the same day.

15:20

Avoid eating certain types of meat.

20:7

Take communion every Sunday.

21:26

Continue Old Testament purification rites.

Did you struggle to determine which practices are normative and which are descriptive? Why should the baptism in the Spirit in Acts 2:1–4 be normative and the practice of Christian shared ownership in Acts 4:32–35 be descriptive? Is it normative to use a cloth as a medium for divine healing? What about using the shadow of a preacher in a healing service? The answer to these questions should not be based on our opinion but on God’s Word. Let us consider three rules for distinguishing between what is normative and what is descriptive.

Must Not Be Based on a Single Event Alone

Certainly, we should not base a doctrine on a single passage of Scripture. Why then would we have a different standard for determining if an action is a temporary illustration or a permanent pattern? Just because we have one example of a shadow associated with healing (Acts 5:15) does not imply a biblical pattern. We should not use this passage to restrict healing services to daylight hours on clear, sunny days. The issue of casting lots to find a church leader is only mentioned once in the New Testament. However, the practice of praying before selecting a leader is repeated (Acts 1:24; 13:2). I would not advise using dice to choose a pastor, but I would recommend prayer.

It would be foolish to teach that Christians should maintain the sacrificial system based on the example of Paul in Acts 21:26. In the same way, I doubt that Luke intended to start a rash of book burnings when he reported that the Ephesians had burned fifty thousand drachma worth of scrolls (Acts 19:19–20).

Undoubtedly, a single event can have great doctrinal value (that is, the Resurrection; the Ascension). However, for an event to be used to establish doctrine, there must be other Scripture that explains its significance. If something merely happened once without commentary, it is not normative.

You may be wondering about the value are these descriptive passages if they are not normative. They serve as illustrations of how truth was applied in the lives of biblical characters. We must look for the principle they illustrate. The following table provides some suggestions:

Descriptive event

The principle drawn from the illustration

Casting lots to find leaders (Acts 1:26)

We must seek the direction of God in the selection of leaders.

Peter’s shadow and the healing service (Acts 5:15)

It is the power of God, not a method, that brings healing.

Burning books that teach witchcraft (Acts 19:19)

The believer should not keep anything that would tempt him or her to return to a life of sin.

Joining in purification rites in the temple (Acts 21:24)

To lead people into the future, a leader must relate to their past and present.

Confirmed by Consistent Witness of Scripture

As we have already noted, a single example in the Bible does not make a normative practice. In the same way, simply finding another reference to the same practice does not make it doctrine. The practice must be presented consistently and uniformly in Scripture to call it normative.

Is water baptism necessary to being filled with the Spirit? Water baptism precedes Spirit baptism for the Samaritans (Acts 8:16) and the Ephesians (Acts 19:5), but Cornelius and his family are baptized in the Spirit before they are baptized in water (Acts 10:46–47). Thus, there is no pattern to show that one must be baptized in water before being filled with the Spirit. A common pattern in the New Testament is to repent, accept Christ, be baptized in water, and receive the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38). Still, Acts 10:46–47 shows that it is possible to be filled with the Spirit before being baptized in water.

The interpreter should first look for direct statements to determine if a practice is normative. However, a pattern of activity can also serve as the basis for doctrine. For example, Acts gives three examples showing that believers spoke in tongues when they were baptized in the Holy Spirit. We see a pattern in three of the four incidents where a group receives the gift of the Spirit (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6). The one possible exception is found in Acts 8:15–19. This passage does not directly mention that the Samaritans spoke in tongues upon receiving the Holy Spirit, but it does strongly suggest it. Luke records that a dramatic sign accompanied the receiving of the Holy Spirit. Something visible or audible must have occurred when these believers were baptized. Why else would Simon the sorcerer offer money for the power to duplicate it (Acts 8:18–19)? Luke wrote history with a purpose. Acts covers thirty years of church history, but Luke recorded only a few things. So the examples he chose have great weight. His examples on being filled with the Spirit guide us to expect believers to speak in tongues when they receive the gift of the Spirit. At the same time, the fire and wind of Acts 2:1–4 is never repeated, so we can assume that those signs were descriptive in nature.

The New Testament relates two other situations where the evidence of tongues is implied. We are told that Paul received the gift of Holy Spirit (Acts 9:17). Later, Paul told the Corinthians, “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you” (1 Corinthians 14:18). This was not a gift restricted to apostles. Again, Paul wrote to the Corinthian believers, “I would like everyone of you to speak in tongues” (1 Corinthians 14:5).

What about the process for selecting deacons for church leadership? Can we use Acts 6:1–7 as a normative pattern? Yes, the idea of appointing deacons to assist in the ministry is confirmed in 1 Timothy 3:8–12 and Philippians 1:1. What is not confirmed is the method of selecting deacons. In Acts 6, the leaders set the standard for candidates and the congregation voted. In other instances, God gave a prophecy to call leaders (Acts 1–2), or a leader selected other leaders (Acts 6:5). Obviously, there is no clear testimony in Scripture for the process of selecting deacons.

Must Reflect the Intention of the Original Writer

The litmus test for determining if a practice is normative is to ascertain the original writer’s purpose. The modern student must always ask, “Do I have reason to believe that the author intended to present this practice as normative?”

Did Luke intend for the experiences of being filled with the Spirit and speaking in tongues to be normative for the church? Certainly there is strong evidence that Spirit anointing for prophetic ministry is a major theme of Luke in both his Gospel and in Acts. We also see a strong literary pattern in Acts that puts the baptism in the Holy Spirit in a central position in the Acts narrative.

1. The parallels between Luke and Acts indicate a pattern of Spirit empowerment for prophetic ministry: speaking through the anointing. Roger Stronstad (1984), in The Charismatic Theology of St. Luke , makes a strong argument for a continuity of themes between the Gospel of Luke and Acts. One of the consistent themes in both of Luke’s volumes is the anointing of the Spirit with special power to speak and serve. Nearly every time a person receives the Spirit or is filled with the Spirit, the result is some sort of prophetic ministry: speaking through the anointing (11).

The work of the Holy Spirit in Christ’s ministry shows Him as the promised prophet that was to be the new Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15,18; Acts 3:22; 7:37). Like Moses, Christ is empowered for service (Luke 4:14, 18). Just as Moses passed that anointing on to the seventy elders, so Christ, the new Moses, passes the Spirit anointing to His disciples (Numbers 11:10–30; Acts 1:5). This time, it is not limited to a few men. As Joel predicted, this gift would be available to all classes of believers (Joel 2:28–29; Acts 2:17–18).

Luke also consistently uses the phrases baptized with the Spirit (three times) and filled with the Spirit (nine times). He uses the first phrase to refer to an initial experience of commissioning for service. He uses the phrase filled with the Spirit to describe the continuous enablement for service. Luke never uses these phrases to refer to regeneration or salvation.

2. The pattern of Acts shows that Pentecostal power is emphasized in five of the six stages of church growth. Acts is carefully divided into the six waves of the expansion of the church. Each wave ends with a concluding comment that summarizes the spiritual and numerical growth of the church. The centrality of the charismatic anointing is seen in all but the final wave of growth. Clearly, the charismatic empowerment with the evidence of tongues is a major theme in Acts.

In Acts 2:1–4, the Jewish disciples in Palestine receive the gift of the Spirit. Peter preaches and explains that this is the promised outpouring of the Spirit that was for all believers. It was no longer limited to a select group of elect prophets. Now, all believers—regardless of their gender, race, or social standing—could be filled with the Spirit (2:17–18). That day, three thousand responded to Peter’s sermon.

We notice that the Spirit baptism of the Samaritans was delayed until the witnesses from Jerusalem could observe the event (Acts 8:14–17). How amazing that the early Jewish Christians could accept the Samaritans as brothers! Were they convinced because they witnessed a repeat of the speaking in tongues as on the Day of Pentecost?

The believers in Jerusalem criticized Peter’s experience in Cornelius’s home (Acts 10:34–48) until Peter explained how their experiences were parallel to what happened at Pentecost (Acts 11:16–18). In the same way, Paul’s first missionary trip was criticized until the testimony of the Holy Spirit was given coming on “them, just as he did to us” (Acts 15:6–9). During Paul’s third missionary trip, another Pentecostal experience occurs (Acts 19:1–6). I believe Luke used this event to authenticate the work of God among the Gentiles in Europe and Asia.

Wave of growth in geography, numbers, and unity

The role of the baptism in the Spirit

Concluding statement concerning growth in numbers and faith

1. Jerusalem. The church begins with explosive growth in Jerusalem and struggles to include the Greek-speaking Jews (Acts 1:1–6:7).

Event : Christ promises the baptism in the Spirit (1:5) and the gift is given on the Day of Pentecost (2:1–41). Sermon : In Peter’s sermon, he claims that this fulfills the promise that in the last days the Spirit would be poured out on “all flesh” (2:17–18, 28, 39).

“So the word of the Lord spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem increased rapidly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith” (Acts 6:7).

2. Samaria. The church reaches out to the Samaritans, an African Eunuch, and an ex-persecutor of the church (Acts 6:8–9:31).

Event: Philip, a Greek-speaking deacon, evangelizes the Samaritans. Peter and John are present to witness the Samaritans receiving the Holy Spirit. This helps the Samaritans to be accepted as brothers (Acts 8:14–17).

“Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria enjoyed a time of peace. It was strengthened; and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it grew in numbers, living in the fear of the Lord” (Acts 9:31).

3. Caesarea. The church extends to the Gentile part of Palestine up to Antioch (Acts 9:32–12:24).

Event: The household of Cornelius receives the Holy Spirit and speaks in tongues (Acts 10:44–48). Sermon: Peter explains that the miracle continues to fulfill Christ’s promise of Spirit baptism and shows that God accepts the Gentiles (Acts 11:16–18).

“But the word of the Lord continued to increase and spread” (Acts 12:24).

4. Galatia. Paul goes on his first missionary trip. The church includes Gentiles on an equal standing as Jewish Christians—even without the keeping of Jewish customs (Acts 13:1–16:5).

Sermon: The church councils hear the report of Paul and Barnabas concerning the Gentiles. Because they had a similar Pentecostal experience, they are accepted without circumcision (Acts 15:8–19).

“So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers” (Acts 16:5).

(continued)

Wave of growth in geography, numbers, and unity

The role of the baptism in the Spirit

Concluding statement concerning growth in numbers and faith

5. Ephesus. Paul plants churches in Eastern Europe and Asia Minor (Acts 16:6–19:20).

Event: Another Pentecost takes place in Ephesus (Acts 19:1–20).

“In this way the word of the Lord spread widely and grew in power” (Acts 19:20).

6. Rome. Paul meets with kings and the Word of God reaches Rome (Acts 19:21–28).

Events: No Pentecost is reported in these chapters, but the result of previous fillings is noted, since Paul healed many.

“Boldly and without hindrance he preached the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 28:31).

X 2:1–4 Be baptized in the Spirit/speak in tongues. X 4:32–35 Sell all you own and give the proceeds to the church. X 5:15 Use a shadow of the preacher to heal the sick. X 6:1–7 Select deacons to assist in ministry. X 8:36–38 Be saved and baptized the same day. X 15:20 Avoid eating certain types of meat. X 20:7 Take communion every Sunday. X 21:26 Continue Old Testament purification rites. X

**Q:** Acts 20:7 says the church broke bread on the first day of the week. Does this mean we must have communion once a week?

**A:** No. As we have already noted, a single example in the Bible does not make a normative practice. In the same way, simply finding another reference to the same practice does not make it doctrine. The practice must be presented consistently and uniformly in Scripture to call it normative.

**Q:** The Ethiopian eunuch was baptized the same hour he was saved. Is this normative for modern churches?

**A:** No.

**Q:** Would it be right to use the example of the thief on the cross to prove that water baptism is not normative for believers today?

**A:** No.

**Q:** What is a major theme in Acts regarding church growth?

**A:** Pentecostal power

#### 12.3.2 — Use rules of interpretation to determine if an activity should be considered normative.

The book of Acts reads like an adventure story. It is one of the most interesting literary works ever written. Leland Ryken’s description captures the essence of this exciting report. “The book of Acts gives us twenty-eight chapters packed with trials, riots, persecutions, escapes, martyrdoms, voyages, shipwrecks, and rescues. And all of this action takes place in the major cities of the ancient world: Jerusalem, Antioch, Philippi, Corinth, Antioch, Ephesus, and Rome. There is an equal variety in the settings: temples, prisons, courts, deserts, ships, seas, barracks, and theaters” (1992, 422).

The book of Acts is far more than a historical record. It is an interpretive history . Luke presents theology through history. He has carefully selected those events and speeches that lead to certain conclusions. He saw Acts as a sequel to his Gospel. In his Gospel, Luke presents an interpretive biography of what Christ began to do and teach (Acts 1:1–2). In Acts, an interpretive history, Luke shows how the apostles and the church continued what Christ began.

Determining the Difference Between Normative and Descriptive

All the events and actions recorded in the book of Acts are useful for instructing modern believers (2 Timothy 3:16). This does not imply, however, that whatever was done by a first-century Christian is automatically a pattern for us today. Some actions recorded in the Bible are meant to be normative. Others are descriptive.

You will remember from Chapter 7 that an action that is meant to be a pattern for all believers of all time is called normative . An action that only describes what happened or illustrates the faith of biblical characters is called descriptive . We have studied these terms in relation to Old Testament stories. Now we will see how they apply to the events in the book of Acts. “How can we tell if an action is meant to be normative or descriptive?”

Acts

Possible meaning

Normative

Descriptive

1:26

Select leaders by casting lots.

X

2:1–4

Be baptized in the Spirit/speak in tongues.

4:32–35

Sell all you own and give the proceeds to the church.

5:15

Use a shadow of the preacher to heal the sick.

6:1–7

Select deacons to assist in ministry.

8:36–38

Be saved and baptized the same day.

15:20

Avoid eating certain types of meat.

20:7

Take communion every Sunday.

21:26

Continue Old Testament purification rites.

Did you struggle to determine which practices are normative and which are descriptive? Why should the baptism in the Spirit in Acts 2:1–4 be normative and the practice of Christian shared ownership in Acts 4:32–35 be descriptive? Is it normative to use a cloth as a medium for divine healing? What about using the shadow of a preacher in a healing service? The answer to these questions should not be based on our opinion but on God’s Word. Let us consider three rules for distinguishing between what is normative and what is descriptive.

Must Not Be Based on a Single Event Alone

Certainly, we should not base a doctrine on a single passage of Scripture. Why then would we have a different standard for determining if an action is a temporary illustration or a permanent pattern? Just because we have one example of a shadow associated with healing (Acts 5:15) does not imply a biblical pattern. We should not use this passage to restrict healing services to daylight hours on clear, sunny days. The issue of casting lots to find a church leader is only mentioned once in the New Testament. However, the practice of praying before selecting a leader is repeated (Acts 1:24; 13:2). I would not advise using dice to choose a pastor, but I would recommend prayer.

It would be foolish to teach that Christians should maintain the sacrificial system based on the example of Paul in Acts 21:26. In the same way, I doubt that Luke intended to start a rash of book burnings when he reported that the Ephesians had burned fifty thousand drachma worth of scrolls (Acts 19:19–20).

Undoubtedly, a single event can have great doctrinal value (that is, the Resurrection; the Ascension). However, for an event to be used to establish doctrine, there must be other Scripture that explains its significance. If something merely happened once without commentary, it is not normative.

You may be wondering about the value are these descriptive passages if they are not normative. They serve as illustrations of how truth was applied in the lives of biblical characters. We must look for the principle they illustrate. The following table provides some suggestions:

Descriptive event

The principle drawn from the illustration

Casting lots to find leaders (Acts 1:26)

We must seek the direction of God in the selection of leaders.

Peter’s shadow and the healing service (Acts 5:15)

It is the power of God, not a method, that brings healing.

Burning books that teach witchcraft (Acts 19:19)

The believer should not keep anything that would tempt him or her to return to a life of sin.

Joining in purification rites in the temple (Acts 21:24)

To lead people into the future, a leader must relate to their past and present.

Confirmed by Consistent Witness of Scripture

As we have already noted, a single example in the Bible does not make a normative practice. In the same way, simply finding another reference to the same practice does not make it doctrine. The practice must be presented consistently and uniformly in Scripture to call it normative.

Is water baptism necessary to being filled with the Spirit? Water baptism precedes Spirit baptism for the Samaritans (Acts 8:16) and the Ephesians (Acts 19:5), but Cornelius and his family are baptized in the Spirit before they are baptized in water (Acts 10:46–47). Thus, there is no pattern to show that one must be baptized in water before being filled with the Spirit. A common pattern in the New Testament is to repent, accept Christ, be baptized in water, and receive the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38). Still, Acts 10:46–47 shows that it is possible to be filled with the Spirit before being baptized in water.

The interpreter should first look for direct statements to determine if a practice is normative. However, a pattern of activity can also serve as the basis for doctrine. For example, Acts gives three examples showing that believers spoke in tongues when they were baptized in the Holy Spirit. We see a pattern in three of the four incidents where a group receives the gift of the Spirit (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6). The one possible exception is found in Acts 8:15–19. This passage does not directly mention that the Samaritans spoke in tongues upon receiving the Holy Spirit, but it does strongly suggest it. Luke records that a dramatic sign accompanied the receiving of the Holy Spirit. Something visible or audible must have occurred when these believers were baptized. Why else would Simon the sorcerer offer money for the power to duplicate it (Acts 8:18–19)? Luke wrote history with a purpose. Acts covers thirty years of church history, but Luke recorded only a few things. So the examples he chose have great weight. His examples on being filled with the Spirit guide us to expect believers to speak in tongues when they receive the gift of the Spirit. At the same time, the fire and wind of Acts 2:1–4 is never repeated, so we can assume that those signs were descriptive in nature.

The New Testament relates two other situations where the evidence of tongues is implied. We are told that Paul received the gift of Holy Spirit (Acts 9:17). Later, Paul told the Corinthians, “I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you” (1 Corinthians 14:18). This was not a gift restricted to apostles. Again, Paul wrote to the Corinthian believers, “I would like everyone of you to speak in tongues” (1 Corinthians 14:5).

What about the process for selecting deacons for church leadership? Can we use Acts 6:1–7 as a normative pattern? Yes, the idea of appointing deacons to assist in the ministry is confirmed in 1 Timothy 3:8–12 and Philippians 1:1. What is not confirmed is the method of selecting deacons. In Acts 6, the leaders set the standard for candidates and the congregation voted. In other instances, God gave a prophecy to call leaders (Acts 1–2), or a leader selected other leaders (Acts 6:5). Obviously, there is no clear testimony in Scripture for the process of selecting deacons.

Must Reflect the Intention of the Original Writer

The litmus test for determining if a practice is normative is to ascertain the original writer’s purpose. The modern student must always ask, “Do I have reason to believe that the author intended to present this practice as normative?”

Did Luke intend for the experiences of being filled with the Spirit and speaking in tongues to be normative for the church? Certainly there is strong evidence that Spirit anointing for prophetic ministry is a major theme of Luke in both his Gospel and in Acts. We also see a strong literary pattern in Acts that puts the baptism in the Holy Spirit in a central position in the Acts narrative.

1. The parallels between Luke and Acts indicate a pattern of Spirit empowerment for prophetic ministry: speaking through the anointing. Roger Stronstad (1984), in The Charismatic Theology of St. Luke , makes a strong argument for a continuity of themes between the Gospel of Luke and Acts. One of the consistent themes in both of Luke’s volumes is the anointing of the Spirit with special power to speak and serve. Nearly every time a person receives the Spirit or is filled with the Spirit, the result is some sort of prophetic ministry: speaking through the anointing (11).

The work of the Holy Spirit in Christ’s ministry shows Him as the promised prophet that was to be the new Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15,18; Acts 3:22; 7:37). Like Moses, Christ is empowered for service (Luke 4:14, 18). Just as Moses passed that anointing on to the seventy elders, so Christ, the new Moses, passes the Spirit anointing to His disciples (Numbers 11:10–30; Acts 1:5). This time, it is not limited to a few men. As Joel predicted, this gift would be available to all classes of believers (Joel 2:28–29; Acts 2:17–18).

Luke also consistently uses the phrases baptized with the Spirit (three times) and filled with the Spirit (nine times). He uses the first phrase to refer to an initial experience of commissioning for service. He uses the phrase filled with the Spirit to describe the continuous enablement for service. Luke never uses these phrases to refer to regeneration or salvation.

2. The pattern of Acts shows that Pentecostal power is emphasized in five of the six stages of church growth. Acts is carefully divided into the six waves of the expansion of the church. Each wave ends with a concluding comment that summarizes the spiritual and numerical growth of the church. The centrality of the charismatic anointing is seen in all but the final wave of growth. Clearly, the charismatic empowerment with the evidence of tongues is a major theme in Acts.

In Acts 2:1–4, the Jewish disciples in Palestine receive the gift of the Spirit. Peter preaches and explains that this is the promised outpouring of the Spirit that was for all believers. It was no longer limited to a select group of elect prophets. Now, all believers—regardless of their gender, race, or social standing—could be filled with the Spirit (2:17–18). That day, three thousand responded to Peter’s sermon.

We notice that the Spirit baptism of the Samaritans was delayed until the witnesses from Jerusalem could observe the event (Acts 8:14–17). How amazing that the early Jewish Christians could accept the Samaritans as brothers! Were they convinced because they witnessed a repeat of the speaking in tongues as on the Day of Pentecost?

The believers in Jerusalem criticized Peter’s experience in Cornelius’s home (Acts 10:34–48) until Peter explained how their experiences were parallel to what happened at Pentecost (Acts 11:16–18). In the same way, Paul’s first missionary trip was criticized until the testimony of the Holy Spirit was given coming on “them, just as he did to us” (Acts 15:6–9). During Paul’s third missionary trip, another Pentecostal experience occurs (Acts 19:1–6). I believe Luke used this event to authenticate the work of God among the Gentiles in Europe and Asia.

Wave of growth in geography, numbers, and unity

The role of the baptism in the Spirit

Concluding statement concerning growth in numbers and faith

1. Jerusalem. The church begins with explosive growth in Jerusalem and struggles to include the Greek-speaking Jews (Acts 1:1–6:7).

Event : Christ promises the baptism in the Spirit (1:5) and the gift is given on the Day of Pentecost (2:1–41). Sermon : In Peter’s sermon, he claims that this fulfills the promise that in the last days the Spirit would be poured out on “all flesh” (2:17–18, 28, 39).

“So the word of the Lord spread. The number of disciples in Jerusalem increased rapidly, and a large number of priests became obedient to the faith” (Acts 6:7).

2. Samaria. The church reaches out to the Samaritans, an African Eunuch, and an ex-persecutor of the church (Acts 6:8–9:31).

Event: Philip, a Greek-speaking deacon, evangelizes the Samaritans. Peter and John are present to witness the Samaritans receiving the Holy Spirit. This helps the Samaritans to be accepted as brothers (Acts 8:14–17).

“Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria enjoyed a time of peace. It was strengthened; and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it grew in numbers, living in the fear of the Lord” (Acts 9:31).

3. Caesarea. The church extends to the Gentile part of Palestine up to Antioch (Acts 9:32–12:24).

Event: The household of Cornelius receives the Holy Spirit and speaks in tongues (Acts 10:44–48). Sermon: Peter explains that the miracle continues to fulfill Christ’s promise of Spirit baptism and shows that God accepts the Gentiles (Acts 11:16–18).

“But the word of the Lord continued to increase and spread” (Acts 12:24).

4. Galatia. Paul goes on his first missionary trip. The church includes Gentiles on an equal standing as Jewish Christians—even without the keeping of Jewish customs (Acts 13:1–16:5).

Sermon: The church councils hear the report of Paul and Barnabas concerning the Gentiles. Because they had a similar Pentecostal experience, they are accepted without circumcision (Acts 15:8–19).

“So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers” (Acts 16:5).

(continued)

Wave of growth in geography, numbers, and unity

The role of the baptism in the Spirit

Concluding statement concerning growth in numbers and faith

5. Ephesus. Paul plants churches in Eastern Europe and Asia Minor (Acts 16:6–19:20).

Event: Another Pentecost takes place in Ephesus (Acts 19:1–20).

“In this way the word of the Lord spread widely and grew in power” (Acts 19:20).

6. Rome. Paul meets with kings and the Word of God reaches Rome (Acts 19:21–28).

Events: No Pentecost is reported in these chapters, but the result of previous fillings is noted, since Paul healed many.

“Boldly and without hindrance he preached the kingdom of God and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 28:31).

**Q:** Acts 20:7 says the church broke bread on the first day of the week. Does this mean we must have communion once a week?

**A:** No. As we have already noted, a single example in the Bible does not make a normative practice. In the same way, simply finding another reference to the same practice does not make it doctrine. The practice must be presented consistently and uniformly in Scripture to call it normative.

**Q:** The Ethiopian eunuch was baptized the same hour he was saved. Is this normative for modern churches?

**A:** No.

**Q:** Would it be right to use the example of the thief on the cross to prove that water baptism is not normative for believers today?

**A:** No.

**Q:** What is a major theme in Acts regarding church growth?

**A:** Pentecostal power

### Epistles: Occasional Documents

#### 12.4.1 — Define what it means when we say that the Epistles are occasional documents.

Some time ago, I was sitting in an airport, and a stranger sat down beside me. “So why did you want to talk to me?” “Excuse me?” I asked. He looked irritated and turned away. Just then I saw a telephone wire hanging from his ear. He continued his conversation with his back to me.

Reading the Epistles is a bit like overhearing phone conversations in public places. With some thought, you can guess the conversation on the other end of the line. If you hear a woman say, “I am so happy for you; I know you wanted a boy. How much does he weigh?” you can assume the friend on the other end of the line has had a baby boy. It is unlikely her friend would ask about the weight of a boyfriend. In the same way, if the writer of an epistle stresses a doctrine or repeats an exhortation, you can use this emphasis as a clue to the problems, issues, or spiritual conditions facing the original readers.

The Epistles are not addressed to us directly. We are eavesdropping on real and personal correspondence sent in the first century. God has chosen the epistolary method for twenty-two of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament. This method of communication is far more powerful and interesting than direct theological sermons or a list of commands. At the same time, the Epistles interweave the historical circumstances with the teachings, and this can challenge the interpreter.

Clues to the Historical Context of the Readers

In a quick reading of 1 Peter, we find repeated references to suffering and persecution. Knowing that the readers were probably facing Nero’s persecution gives the interpreter a historical peg on which to hang the truths in the Epistle.

Understanding that Paul is writing to the Philippians while he is under arrest and waiting for Nero’s sentence adds depth to the interpretation of his message. Paul is in chains, yet he takes time from his crisis to pray for the Philippians and thank them for their gift. At any moment, he could be called before Caesar, yet his mind is on the unity in the church in Philippi (Philippians 1:24; 2:1–4) and specifically on the tension between two women in the congregation—Euodia and Syntyche (Philippians 4:2). With his life in danger, he still is concerned that the church maintains its unity (Philippians 1:27; 2:1–4).

Bible dictionaries, commentaries, or study Bibles can help the reader understand the overall purpose and historical background of an epistle. Sometimes this information is essential to the interpreter. First Corinthians contains some short, proverb-style sentences that most scholars consider flawed teachings of the Corinthian church, not Paul’s instruction. Apparently, the Corinthians had written to Paul, asking his advice on these practices. Paul addresses their questions in a systematic checklist format (see 1 Corinthians 1:11; 7:10). Paul introduces each of these issues with a statement such as now concerning or a similar phrase (1 Corinthians 7:1; 8:1; 11:3; 12:1; 15:1; 16:1).

In response to their questions, Paul often restates one of their slogans and then explains why the teaching is not balanced, using a yes/but literary pattern. It is as if he is saying, “Yes, there is a bit of truth in what you say, but you cannot take it to that extreme.”

“Everything is permissible for me” [their slogan] “but not everything is beneficial” [Paul’s correction] (1 Corinthians 6:12; 6:13; 10:23). Certainly, Paul would not have taught such an extreme. Even in the immediate context, he strongly refutes the teaching of the slogan. It appears that one group in the Corinthian church exploited their spiritual freedom to such a point that they allowed for sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:13–17) and eating meat that had been offered to idols (Corinthians 10:23–33).

“It is good for a man not to marry” [their slogan]. But since there is so much immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” [Paul’s correction] (1 Corinthians 7:1). In this statement, Paul is responding to another group in the church who went to the other extreme and was overly zealous for celibacy. Paul basically tells the Corinthians that married couples should not deprive each other of sexual fulfillment (vv. 2–7); that widows and widowers should consider remaining unmarried only if they can do so without self-destructive lust (vv. 8–9); that divorce is not a legitimate way to avoid sex (v. 10–16); and that it is good for those who have never married to consider celibacy, though marriage is not a sinful option (vv. 25–38) (Klein, Bloomberg, Hubbard 1993, 363).

“We know that we possess all knowledge” [their slogan]. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. The man who thinks he knows some things does not yet know as he ought to know. But the man who loves God is known by God” [Paul’s correction] (1 Corinthians 8:1–3). In this case, the knowledge was related to eating meat offered to an idol. The more knowledgeable Christians understood that the meat had not changed just because it was offered to an idol. Eating it was not a sin for them. The weaker Christians, however, associated the meat with their former lifestyle. To eat the meat was to open themselves to temptation.

For All Christians or Only for the Original Readers

We have already seen the principle of normative/descriptive applied to the actions of Bible heroes and the laws written under the Mosaic covenant. The same principle applies to instruction given to readers of the first-century letters. In most cases, the instruction is normative for both the original readers and the modern readers. At other times, however, the instruction is limited to a specific cultural problem or historical issue. This type of instruction may have no parallel to the life of the modern believer. In this case, the instruction is called descriptive or culturally or historically specific.

Descriptive instruction illustrates how a truth was applied in one historic case. The application is limited to the first century, but the truth it illustrates is still eternal. Here are some examples of passages in Paul’s Epistles that have caused confusion. Several are hotly debated as to whether they are normative or descriptive. We can understand why Peter lamented that some times his “dear brother Paul” wrote things that were hard to understand. Even in Peter’s day, some teachers had already distorted Paul’s teaching (1 Peter 3:15–16).

• Greet one another with a holy kiss (Romans 16:16).

• Eat what is set before you without raising questions of conscience (1 Corinthians 10:27).

• Women should pray with their head covered (1 Corinthians 11:5).

• A woman ought to have a veil on her head when she prays (1 Corinthians 11:10, 15).

• Long hair on a man is a disgrace (1 Corinthians 11:4).

• Women should not ask their husbands questions during church (1 Corinthians 14:35).

• Slaves, obey your earthly masters (Ephesians 6:5).

• Work with your hands (1 Thessalonians 4:11).

• Have self-employed pastors (2 Thessalonians 3:7–8).

• If a man will not work, he shall not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

• Lift your hands when praying (1 Timothy 2:8).

• Dress modestly, not with braided hair or gold, or pearls or expensive clothes (1 Timothy 2:9).

• Do not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man (1 Timothy 2:12).

• Drink wine for the sake of your stomach (1 Timothy 5:23).

The same rules used to distinguish if an action is normative or descriptive in the book of Acts apply to the instructions in the Epistles. Here we will reword them as questions. When you suspect that an instruction in the Epistles is descriptive rather than normative, you should ask the following four questions.

1. Is the instruction mentioned more than once in the Bible? An interpreter should never form a doctrine or establish a practice based on one verse of instruction.

2. Is the instruction confirmed or clarified by other passages? To be normative, the instruction should be clearly taught in other passages and be the uniform testimony of Scripture.

3. How does this instruction fit into the entire message of the Epistle? The original intent of the author and the circumstances of the readers should guide the interpretation.

4. What truth does the passage teach to the modern believer? If the instruction is descriptive, the interpreter must look for the underlying truth it illustrates.

Let us consider two sample passages where we can apply these questions. First, read the instruction of John to his readers: “You do not need anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things . . . remain in him” (1 John 2:27). If that is true, why are you studying this course? I suspect that this reference to teachers must be dealing with a local issue that relates to the culture and history of the time. We can test it with the four questions.

Is this teaching given anywhere else in the Bible? The answer is a resounding no . Automatically, this indicates that the instruction is most likely descriptive.

Is this instruction confirmed or clarified by other passages? Paul instructs believers in an entire ministry of teaching given to the church (Ephesians 4:11), and Timothy is told to train men to be teachers (2 Timothy 2:1–2). Apparently, a teacher who teaches biblical truth is not the issue here.

How does this instruction fit into the entire message of the Epistle? As we examine the entire letter, we see repeated references to a unique heresy that plagued the second generation of the church. In many early churches, Christian teaching and gnosticism (an ancient spiritism) had blended together. The new cult claimed that a person could not be completely saved without special extra-biblical knowledge. Every believer had to pay a price for a special mystical teacher who would give them hidden knowledge ( gnosis ).

The gnostics also believed that the body was bad and the spirit was good. For this reason, they did not accept that the man Jesus could have a human body and still be the Christ. They taught that the spiritual Christ descended on Jesus at His baptism in water and left Him before His death on the cross. Jesus and the Christ were not the same. They claimed that one was flesh and the other was spirit and that Christ never came in the flesh, nor did the Christ shed blood on the cross. Now read the passages below against this historical background. The historical background aids our interpretation.

• Every spirit that acknowledges that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. (1 John 4:2)

• This is the one who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ. He is not come by water only, but water and blood. (1 John 5:6)

What truth does the passage teach to the modern believer? If we determine that the instruction is limited to a local situation, then we must ask ourselves what truth is taught by the illustration. The basic message of this passage is that we can have confidence that all we need to know to be saved is found in Scripture. Further, we should evaluate all teachers’ words, except for the Word of God.

Try this experiment. Spin your right hand in a clockwise manner and at the same time try to move your right foot counterclockwise. You cannot do it! Your body’s internal balance has linked the motion of your right hand to that of your right foot. If you could cause them to act separately, you would not be able to walk.

In the same way, the content of a passage cannot be separated from the form in which it was written. Understanding how to interpret a story, a stanza of poetry, or a paragraph in an epistle is inseparably linked to understanding the rules of interpretation within the specific literary type.

The variety of literary methods that God used to write the Bible should not be viewed as an obstacle to learning. It is God’s gift for providing a way to touch the head as well as the heart. We can thank God that the Bible is not simply a series of theological lessons and a list of what to do and what not to do. God wisely adds beauty and variety to His message. The goal is to touch our hearts, assist our memories, and transform our wills.

**Q:** What are the benefits of the epistolary method for teaching doctrine?

**A:** God has chosen the epistolary method for twenty-two of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament. This method of communication is far more powerful and interesting than direct theological sermons or a list of commands. At the same time, the Epistles interweave the historical circumstances with the teachings, and this can challenge the interpreter.

**Q:** What is the purpose of descriptive instruction?

**A:** The purpose of descriptive instruction is to describe how a truth was applied in a specific historical situation rather than how it should be applied normatively. UNIT 4

It appears that one group in the Corinthian church exploited their spiritual freedom to such a point that they allowed for sexual immorality (1 Corinthians 6:13–17) and eating meat that had been offered to idols (Corinthians 10:23–33).

“It is good for a man not to marry” [their slogan]. But since there is so much immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” [Paul’s correction] (1 Corinthians 7:1). In this statement, Paul is responding to another group in the church who went to the other extreme and was overly zealous for celibacy. Paul basically tells the Corinthians that married couples should not deprive each other of sexual fulfillment (vv. 2–7); that widows and widowers should consider remaining unmarried only if they can do so without self-destructive lust (vv. 8–9); that divorce is not a legitimate way to avoid sex (v. 10–16); and that it is good for those who have never married to consider celibacy, though marriage is not a sinful option (vv. 25–38) (Klein, Bloomberg, Hubbard 1993, 363).

“We know that we possess all knowledge” [their slogan]. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up. The man who thinks he knows some things does not yet know as he ought to know. But the man who loves God is known by God” [Paul’s correction] (1 Corinthians 8:1–3). In this case, the knowledge was related to eating meat offered to an idol. The more knowledgeable Christians understood that the meat had not changed just because it was offered to an idol. Eating it was not a sin for them. The weaker Christians, however, associated the meat with their former lifestyle. To eat the meat was to open themselves to temptation.

For All Christians or Only for the Original Readers

We have already seen the principle of normative/descriptive applied to the actions of Bible heroes and the laws written under the Mosaic covenant. The same principle applies to instruction given to readers of the first-century letters. In most cases, the instruction is normative for both the original readers and the modern readers. At other times, however, the instruction is limited to a specific cultural problem or historical issue. This type of instruction may have no parallel to the life of the modern believer. In this case, the instruction is called descriptive or culturally or historically specific.

Descriptive instruction illustrates how a truth was applied in one historic case. The application is limited to the first century, but the truth it illustrates is still eternal. Here are some examples of passages in Paul’s Epistles that have caused confusion. Several are hotly debated as to whether they are normative or descriptive. We can understand why Peter lamented that some times his “dear brother Paul” wrote things that were hard to understand. Even in Peter’s day, some teachers had already distorted Paul’s teaching (1 Peter 3:15–16).

• Greet one another with a holy kiss (Romans 16:16).

• Eat what is set before you without raising questions of conscience (1 Corinthians 10:27).

• Women should pray with their head covered (1 Corinthians 11:5).

• A woman ought to have a veil on her head when she prays (1 Corinthians 11:10, 15).

• Long hair on a man is a disgrace (1 Corinthians 11:4).

• Women should not ask their husbands questions during church (1 Corinthians 14:35).

• Slaves, obey your earthly masters (Ephesians 6:5).

• Work with your hands (1 Thessalonians 4:11).

• Have self-employed pastors (2 Thessalonians 3:7–8).

• If a man will not work, he shall not eat (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

• Lift your hands when praying (1 Timothy 2:8).

• Dress modestly, not with braided hair or gold, or pearls or expensive clothes (1 Timothy 2:9).

• Do not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man (1 Timothy 2:12).

• Drink wine for the sake of your stomach (1 Timothy 5:23).

The same rules used to distinguish if an action is normative or descriptive in the book of Acts apply to the instructions in the Epistles. Here we will reword them as questions. When you suspect that an instruction in the Epistles is descriptive rather than normative, you should ask the following four questions.

1. Is the instruction mentioned more than once in the Bible? An interpreter should never form a doctrine or establish a practice based on one verse of instruction.

2. Is the instruction confirmed or clarified by other passages? To be normative, the instruction should be clearly taught in other passages and be the uniform testimony of Scripture.

3. How does this instruction fit into the entire message of the Epistle? The original intent of the author and the circumstances of the readers should guide the interpretation.

4. What truth does the passage teach to the modern believer? If the instruction is descriptive, the interpreter must look for the underlying truth it illustrates.

Let us consider two sample passages where we can apply these questions. First, read the instruction of John to his readers: “You do not need anyone to teach you. But as his anointing teaches you about all things . . . remain in him” (1 John 2:27). If that is true, why are you studying this course? I suspect that this reference to teachers must be dealing with a local issue that relates to the culture and history of the time. We can test it with the four questions.

Is this teaching given anywhere else in the Bible? The answer is a resounding no . Automatically, this indicates that the instruction is most likely descriptive.

Is this instruction confirmed or clarified by other passages? Paul instructs believers in an entire ministry of teaching given to the church (Ephesians 4:11), and Timothy is told to train men to be teachers (2 Timothy 2:1–2). Apparently, a teacher who teaches biblical truth is not the issue here.

How does this instruction fit into the entire message of the Epistle? As we examine the entire letter, we see repeated references to a unique heresy that plagued the second generation of the church. In many early churches, Christian teaching and gnosticism (an ancient spiritism) had blended together. The new cult claimed that a person could not be completely saved without special extra-biblical knowledge. Every believer had to pay a price for a special mystical teacher who would give them hidden knowledge ( gnosis ).

The gnostics also believed that the body was bad and the spirit was good. For this reason, they did not accept that the man Jesus could have a human body and still be the Christ. They taught that the spiritual Christ descended on Jesus at His baptism in water and left Him before His death on the cross. Jesus and the Christ were not the same. They claimed that one was flesh and the other was spirit and that Christ never came in the flesh, nor did the Christ shed blood on the cross. Now read the passages below against this historical background. The historical background aids our interpretation.

• Every spirit that acknowledges that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. (1 John 4:2)

• This is the one who came by water and blood—Jesus Christ. He is not come by water only, but water and blood. (1 John 5:6)

What truth does the passage teach to the modern believer? If we determine that the instruction is limited to a local situation, then we must ask ourselves what truth is taught by the illustration. The basic message of this passage is that we can have confidence that all we need to know to be saved is found in Scripture. Further, we should evaluate all teachers’ words, except for the Word of God.

Try this experiment. Spin your right hand in a clockwise manner and at the same time try to move your right foot counterclockwise. You cannot do it! Your body’s internal balance has linked the motion of your right hand to that of your right foot. If you could cause them to act separately, you would not be able to walk.

In the same way, the content of a passage cannot be separated from the form in which it was written. Understanding how to interpret a story, a stanza of poetry, or a paragraph in an epistle is inseparably linked to understanding the rules of interpretation within the specific literary type.

The variety of literary methods that God used to write the Bible should not be viewed as an obstacle to learning. It is God’s gift for providing a way to touch the head as well as the heart. We can thank God that the Bible is not simply a series of theological lessons and a list of what to do and what not to do. God wisely adds beauty and variety to His message. The goal is to touch our hearts, assist our memories, and transform our wills.

**Q:** What are the benefits of the epistolary method for teaching doctrine?

**A:** God has chosen the epistolary method for twenty-two of the twenty-seven books of the New Testament. This method of communication is far more powerful and interesting than direct theological sermons or a list of commands. At the same time, the Epistles interweave the historical circumstances with the teachings, and this can challenge the interpreter.

**Q:** What is the purpose of descriptive instruction?

**A:** The purpose of descriptive instruction is to describe how a truth was applied in a specific historical situation rather than how it should be applied normatively. UNIT 4

## 13 - The Covenants and the Kingdom

### The Relationship between the Old and New Covenants

#### 13.1.1 — Summarize five reasons we value the old covenant.

God has revealed more of himself and His kingdom to us than to Old Testament believers. God reveals himself, His will, and His kingdom progressively— little by little. He has revealed himself more to us under the new covenant than He did to the Jews under the old covenant. They knew God from a distance. Today, He has revealed himself to us in a personal way through Jesus, the writings of the New Testament, and His Spirit.

Consider how God revealed himself to His people under the old covenant:

You have not come to a mountain that can be touched and that is burning with fire; to darkness, gloom, and storm; to a trumpet blast or to such a voice speaking words that those who heard it begged that no further word be spoken to them, because they could not bear what was commanded: “If even an animal touches the mountain, it must be stoned.” The sight was so terrifying that Moses said, “I am trembling with fear.” (Hebrews 12:18–21)

Consider how much more God has revealed himself to us under the new covenant:

But you have come to Mount Zion, to the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the living God. You have come to thousands upon thousands of angels in joyful assembly, to the church of the firstborn, whose names are written in heaven. You have come to God, the judge of all men, to the spirits of righteous men made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. (Hebrews 12:22–24)

Under the old covenant, people approached God as a stranger they feared. Under the new covenant, we approach God as children come to their father at home (Long 1997, 91). Even so, we need the old covenant.

Christians and the Old Covenant

The Law served as a teacher, judge, and guide. Likewise, the entire old covenant—not just the five books of the Law—is valuable to us. We will look at five reasons for valuing the thirty-nine books of the Old Covenant or Testament.

Genesis 1–12 is the introduction of the whole Bible.

It teaches us about the beginnings of creation, sin, languages, and God’s covenant with Abraham.

The old covenant teaches us much about God.

It shows us that He is holy, righteous, and faithful. It emphasizes that He cares about all nations. For example, He sent Jonah to call the Assyrians to repent.

The five Poetic Books teach us much about God’s mercy, love, care, and wisdom.

These books teach us timeless truths about life and God—truths that do not change when covenants change. For example—as Psalm 23 declares—the Lord is the Shepherd of all who trust in Him.

The old covenant shows us our need for the new one.

Law on stone, animal sacrifices, priests, and people who sinned—all of these point to the need for a new covenan t.

The old covenant helps us understand the new covenant that contains over 1,100 references to the old one.

Because of the old covenant, we understand hundreds of verses in the New Testament.

Promises Under the New Covenant: Different but Better Than the Old Promises

Unlike Israel, we do not fight and take wealth away from people. The Old Testament was an agreement between God and the Israelites. He promised them an earthly land flowing with milk and honey. It was a territory marked by specific borders. Even today, this land is known as Israel .

To possess the Promised Land required war. The Canaanites lived in Canaan, but the time had come for God to judge them for their sins. In contrast, the Lord wanted to bless Israel as a light to the nations. God gave Canaan to Israel as their inheritance. The Israelites killed many living in Canaan, or drove them out through war. God promised that if the Israelites served Him, their enemies would flee in seven different directions (Deuteronomy 28:7).

In Old Testament times, the nation of Israel was under the rule of God. He made a covenant with the whole nation. Their part was to keep the six hundred laws. His part was to give the nation protection and blessing. We have said that the Old Testament is not our covenant today. God does not require us to sacrifice animals or keep the six hundred laws of the Old Testament. Also, unlike Israel, we do not fight and take wealth away from people. These questions arise: If the Old Testament is not our covenant, are the promises of the old covenant for us? Can the church claim the promises God gave the nation of Israel?

Today, no nation is a church and no church is a nation (Stott 1977, 235). Still, God gives the church many promises that are better than the promises of the old covenant (Hebrews 8:6).

God communicated four things to Abraham regarding their covenant:

1. His children would be like the stars—so many that he could not count them (Genesis 15:5).

2. He would give him the land of Israel (Genesis 15:7).

3. His descendants would become slaves and be mistreated for four hundred years in a foreign country (Genesis 15:13).

4. All of the people on earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3).

Look closely at Galatians 3:14 . What is the blessing that came to Abraham and that also comes to Gentiles? “Those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith” (Galatians 3:9). Paul’s point is that our relationship with God is by faith in Christ, not by keeping the Law. The blessing that comes to us by faith is the Holy Spirit (Ridderbos 1953, 128). The Spirit causes us to be born of God (John 1:13; 3:6). This same Spirit assures us that we are God’s children and that the Father has counted us righteous (Romans 8:16). In Galatians 5, Paul will emphasize that walking in the Spirit is the key to overcoming the sinful nature and receiving our inheritance. So Galatians 3:14 is not a basis for claiming that those under the new covenant can claim all of the promises of the old covenant. Galatians is a letter about being saved by faith and keeping in step with the Spirit (Galatians 5:24–25).

“For no matter how many promises God has made, they are ‘Yes’ in Christ. And so through him the ‘Amen’ is spoken by us to the glory of God” (2 Corinthians 1:20). Does 2 Corinthians 1:20 mean that those under the new covenant can claim all the promises made to the nation of Israel under the old covenant? No. Paul wrote this verse, but he did not claim the promise that his enemies would flee in seven different directions (Deuteronomy 28:7). Paul’s enemies did not flee from him; they followed him. Jesus did not promise that enemies would flee from apostles. Rather, He told apostles to flee from their enemies (Matthew 10:23).

So what does 2 Corinthians 1:20 mean? Some of Paul’s enemies were accusing him, saying he was not trustworthy. He had been to Corinth and told the Corinthians that he would return soon. Then, he heard about the sin of incest among them. So Paul delayed his visit to them, to spare them pain and shame (2 Corinthians 1:23). He sent a letter telling them to deal with the sin in the church. Thus the apostle gave them a chance to avoid the shame they would feel if he came and found sin among them (1 Corinthians 5:1–13). When Paul changed the timing of his visit, his enemies said that people could not believe Paul’s word or his gospel. Paul responded by saying that his word and gospel could be trusted.

Notice that Paul places the emphasis on Christ, through whom God fulfills all of His promises to us (2 Corinthians 1:20). Through Jesus, God fulfills the promises the prophets made about the Messiah (Luke 1:69; 24:44). The promises God made to Abraham come to us through Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:16). In Him all the fullness of God dwells (Colossians 1:19). In Jesus Christ alone we have wisdom, righteousness, holiness, and redemption (1 Corinthians 1:30). He is the cornerstone of the Church, God’s holy temple (Ephesians 2:20–21). He is the First and Last, the Beginning and the End (Revelation 22:13). We receive all that God has planned for us through Jesus Christ (Hughes 1962, 31–38). Amen!

Paul tells us that our inheritance is different than that of the children of law (Galatians 4:30–31). The promises under the new covenant are the best! Promises under the old covenant were mostly temporary and for the Jews’ lives on earth. Our promises under the new covenant are for both time on earth and eternity. None of us under the new covenant wants to be under the old covenant. We rejoice to be children of God and know Him as our Heavenly Father.

**Q:** Summarize five reasons for valuing the Old Testament.

**A:** 1. Genesis 1–11 is the introduction of the whole Bible. 2. The old covenant teaches us much about God. 3. The five Poetic Books teach us much about God’s mercy, love, care, and wisdom. 4. The old covenant shows us our need for the new one. 5. The old covenant helps us understand the new covenant, which contains over 1,100 references to the old one.

**Q:** How are our promises of inheritance different from Israel’s?

**A:** The emphasis is not on the literal land of Canaan; it is on heaven and on being a joint heir with Christ.

**Q:** How are our promises about warfare different from Israel’s?

**A:** As believers are filled with the Spirit, pray, and have faith, we have spiritual authority over Satan and demons. Israel was fighting human enemies.

**Q:** Contrast Old Testament and New Testament promises on expansion.

**A:** The emphasis is not on making the church a great nation; it is on building a church universal that Satan cannot conquer.

**Q:** Read 2 Corinthians 11:24–27. Why did Paul not try to claim the promise of Deuteronomy 28:7?

**A:** Paul wrote this verse, but he did not claim the promise that his enemies would flee in seven different directions (Deuteronomy 28:7). Paul’s enemies did not flee from him—they followed him. Jesus did not promise that enemies would flee from apostles. Rather, he told apostles to flee from their enemies (Matthew 10:23).

**Q:** What does 2 Corinthians 1:20 mean?

**A:** We receive all that God has planned for us through Jesus Christ.
