There are several truths related to the issue of God’s reign. We will briefly consider them here.

God’s Eternal Rule

His decree created the earth; He spoke and it was so. His rule set boundaries for the oceans. He ordained the relationships between the sun, moon, and earth. He ordered humanity, birds, animals, and fish to be fruitful and multiply. From Genesis through Malachi, we see God ruling the earth. As Paul said, “The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth . . . From one man he made every nation of men, that they should inhabit the whole earth; and he determined the times set for them and the exact places where they should live” (Acts 17:24, 26).

God has not ruled like a dictator, who allows no choices.

He permits rebellion. One day He will rule with an iron scepter (Revelation 12:5). Then, He will judge all who have rebelled against Him. But until the final judgment, God chooses to give some freedom to humans, angels, and demons.

God’s kingdom and Satan’s kingdom are at war.

The Almighty allows Satan to be a lesser ruler over earth (John 14:30; 18:36; Ephesians 2:2; 6:12). For a discussion of Satan’s kingdom and spiritual warfare, see the Life in the Spirit Study Bible on Ephesians 6:11; also read the Bible’s article on “Power Over Demons and Satan,” Mark 3:27; and the article on “The Kingdom of God,” based on Matthew 12:28.

Sometimes, God acts as a king and brings justice.

When Adam and Eve fell into sin, God stepped in. As King of all, He punished them for their sins. Still, He showed mercy and promised a Redeemer (Genesis 3:15). At times, God reminds us that He is in control and reigning on earth. He sent a flood to destroy evil; He sent angels to destroy Sodom and Gomorrah. He delivered Israel from Egypt. He used Israel to punish the Canaanites. Later He used the Assyrians and Babylonians to punish Israel. There is much evidence to show that God’s kingdom has always included the earth.

Personal Relationships Lacking Under the Old Covenant

The kingdom of God—His ruling over people and places—was like a shadow, haze, or a dim sunlight in Old Testament times. The King could not have the personal relationship He desired when the Law was on stone. People could not come close to Him because of their sins and sinfulness. Even the high priest could not come near to God often. The curtain was always there to keep people away from God. So Jesus told Nicodemus that all must be born-again to see the kingdom of God (John 3:3). That is, to identify, comprehend, and experience the personal rule of God over our lives, we need a new heart.

The Kingdom of God in a Clear, Personal, and Powerful Way through Jesus

The kingdom of God is like a shining light, coming closer and closer to the earth. As time continues, the light gets closer, brighter, and people see more. The Old Testament prophets announced the kingdom, but were not in its fullest phase or revelation. Reflect on Jesus’ words about John: “I tell you the truth: Among those born of women there has not risen anyone greater than John the Baptist; yet he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has been forcefully advancing, and forceful men lay hold of it. For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to accept it, he is the Elijah who was to come. He who has ears, let him hear.” (Matthew 11:11–15)

John the Baptist looked at the fullness of the kingdom of God as a person presses his or her face to the window glass to look inside a house. John Wesley comments, “The least true Christian believer has a more perfect knowledge of Jesus Christ, of his redemption and kingdom, than John the Baptist had, who died before the full manifestation of the gospel” (Wesley 1755). John recognized Jesus, but we know Him personally.

John came preparing the way for Jesus and preaching, “‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near’” (Matthew 3:2). Early in His ministry, Jesus told the people, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 4:17). Those who bow to Jesus to rule their lives receive the King and His kingdom. Thus they inherit the righteousness, joy, and peace of the kingdom of God (Romans 14:17). The revelation of the kingdom is like phases of sunlight.

Of the Kingdom

Kingdom phase: Predawn > Sunrise > Noonday

Event: Creation > Incarnation > Second Coming

From the beginning of earth, God’s kingdom was present, like the light that comes before dawn. But at the coming of Jesus to earth, God’s kingdom came like a sunrise. The Kingdom came when the King came (Fee and Stuart 1993, 119, 138). In the person and mission of Jesus, the kingdom of God came into history. At some time in the future, Jesus will return. Then the kingdom of God will come like the sun shines at the full light of day.

Signs, wonders, healings, miracles, and deliverance show the kingdom (ruling) of God. As Jesus said,

“Every kingdom divided against itself will be ruined, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand. If Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then can his kingdom stand? And if I drive out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your people drive them out? So then, they will be your judges. But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” (Matthew 12:25–28)

In spite of signs of the kingdom of God, many Jews refused to accept Jesus as the King. He spoke tragic words about many Jews in relation to the kingdom of God. “‘I say to you that many will come from the east and the west, and will take their places at the feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the subjects of the kingdom [unbelieving Jews] will be thrown outside, into the darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth’” (Matthew 8:11–12).

Daniel’s Interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar’s Dream (Daniel 2)

Daniel told the king:

“While you were watching, a rock was cut out, but not by human hands. It struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay and smashed them. Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver and the gold were broken to pieces at the same time and became like chaff on a threshing floor in the summer. The wind swept them away without leaving a trace. But the rock that struck the statue became a huge mountain and filled the whole earth. This was the dream, and now we will interpret it to the king.” (Daniel 2:34–36)

“In the time of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people. It will crush all those kingdoms and bring them to an end, but it will itself endure forever. This is the meaning of the vision of the rock cut out of a mountain, but not by human hands—a rock that broke the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver and the gold to pieces. The great God has shown the king what will take place in the future. The dream is true and the interpretation is trustworthy.” (Daniel 2:44–45)

The rock that Nebuchadnezzar saw struck the earth when Jesus was born. Since that time His kingdom has been growing like a mustard seed. When Jesus returns, God’s kingdom will fill the whole earth.

Jesus died to redeem us through His blood. Now, He invites all to accept Him as King over our lives. His desire is to live in people, not in a tent. Under the new covenant God writes His Law on our hearts and puts His Spirit within us. We delight in pleasing Him. We enjoy His presence within as He rules over our lives in His kingdom.

**Q:** Did the rule or kingdom of God have a beginning? Explain.

**A:** From Genesis through Malachi, we see God ruling the earth.

**Q:** Under the old covenant, why could the King not have close relationships with people?

**A:** The King could not have the personal relationship He desired when the Law was on stone. People could not come close to Him because of their sins and sinfulness. Even the high priest could not come near to God often.

**Q:** How is a healing or deliverance a sign that God’s kingdom is present?

**A:** As Jesus said, “‘Every kingdom divided against itself will be ruined, and every city or household divided against itself will not stand. If Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then can his kingdom stand? And if I drive out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your people drive them out? So then, they will be your judges. But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you’” (Matthew 12:25–28).

**Q:** Are those who rebel against God day by day in His kingdom—that is, under His rule?

**A:** They can be said to be in His kingdom, but not of His kingdom.

**Q:** Matthew 13:40–41 (see John 17:14–16) shows that some are in the kingdom, but not of the kingdom. Explain.

**A:** Although it is God’s desire that all humans receive Christ as Savior, not everyone will. So until the Rapture occurs, we must live among those who are in the kingdom but not of it.

### The Already and Not Yet Aspects of the Kingdom of God

#### 13.3.1 — Explain: The kingdom of God has already come, but has not yet been fully revealed.

Overview of the Already but Not Yet Aspects of the Kingdom of God

We have said that the kingdom of God is the realm over which the King reigns. The kingdom of God came like a sunrise when Jesus came to earth. His kingdom has already begun, but it is not yet complete on the earth. The noonday phase of God’s kingdom will come when Jesus comes again. Likewise, you have already started studying hermeneutics, but you have not yet completed your study. This chart compares the already and not yet aspects of the kingdom of God on several topics. It will give you an overview of this section. Examine the chart, and then we will discuss each topic in detail.

Topic

Already

Not Yet

1. Salvation

Christians are forgiven and growing in grace.

Christians will be perfect, having attained “the whole measure of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13).

2. Knowledge

“We know in part and we prophesy in part . . . Now we see but a poor reflection as in a mirror” (1 Corinthians 13:9–12).

“Then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

3. Rewards

We have joy, peace, love, acceptance, assurance, and fatherly care.

“‘Behold, I am coming soon! My reward is with me, and I will give to everyone according to what he has done’” (Revelation 22:12).

(continued)

Topic

Already

Not Yet

4. Health

The prayer of faith heals the sick (James 5:14–15). Also, God has given us doctors, dentists, and medicine to help with health.

“There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away” (Revelations 21:4).

5. Wealth

God supplies our needs, but not our greeds, as we seek His kingdom first (Matthew 6:33; Philippians 4:19).

We will see, touch, and possess the unlimited treasure of our Father’s kingdom that is now reserved for us in heaven (Luke 12:32–34).

6. Suffering

Our sufferings are measured and tempered. God does not allow us to be tried beyond what we can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13; 2 Timothy 2:12; 1 Peter 2:19–23; 4:19).

“He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away” (Revelation 21:4).

7. Protection

Sometimes miraculous protection takes place, yet God does not always overrule the destructive forces of this world. Thieves still break in, moth and rust still corrupt, accidents still happen, persecution occurs (Matthew 6:19–20).

No weapon formed against us will prosper (Isaiah 54:17).

8. Believer’s judgment

Christians are partially disciplined, punished, and judged (John 15:2; 1 Corinthians 11:30; Hebrews 12:5–6).

“For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive what is due him for the things done while in the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

9. Sinner’s judgment

Sinners receive a portion of the wages of sin. They are separated from fellowship with God and suffer some results of their evil acts (Ephesians 2:1; 1 Timothy 5:24).

The dead will be raised and every sinner will be judged according to what he has done. Each one whose name is not written in the book of life will be cast into the lake of fire (Revelation 21:8).

10. Satan’s judgment

Satan has been thrown out of the highest heaven. Believers rejoice in partial victory over him (Luke 10:18–19).

The devil will be thrown into the lake of fire and tormented day and night forever and ever (Revelation 20:10).

11. Will of God

It is accepted by a few but rejected by most (Matthew 6:10; 18:14; 1 Timothy 2:3–4).

Every knee will bow and every tongue will confess that Jesus is Lord. God will dwell on earth with His people (Philippians 2:10–11; Revelation 21:1–4).

Topical Study of the Already but Not Yet Aspects of the Kingdom of God

Salvation

John Wesley once said, “I was saved, I am being saved, and I will be saved.” This threefold view of salvation is helpful.

I was saved declares that, at a time in the past, a person was born-again. A Christian has been forgiven of his or her past sins and moved from the kingdom of darkness to the kingdom of light.

I am being saved refers to the present process of Christian growth. We are growing in holiness, perfecting holiness in the fear of the Lord (2 Corinthians 7:1). Daily, as we grow in grace we are being changed into His likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).

I will be saved refers to the future when we will no longer press toward the mark. We will then be saved from this world, this body, and any possibility of sin. Thus, there was a time when we entered the kingdom of God. We are now growing as children of the King. One day we will receive our glorified bodies. Then we will be saved in the fullest sense in the kingdom of God.

Our Knowledge

“For we know in part and we prophesy in part…. Now we see but a poor reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:9, 12). We have the mind of Christ in part, but not completely. There are yet a billion mysteries we do not understand in this stage of the kingdom. When the kingdom comes in perfection, we will know, even as we are known by God (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Rewards

Even now we are rewarded. We receive joy, peace, love, acceptance, assurance, and fatherly care. Some of the rewards of the kingdom of God are already here. But all of our rewards are not yet here. Jesus promised the apostles a hundredfold in this life, and sitting on twelve thrones “at the renewal of all things” (Matthew 19:27–28). Each Christian will be rewarded personally, for his or her own work, when Christ comes (Revelation 22:12).

Health

The prayer of faith heals the sick (James 5:15). Nevertheless, we are on earth and not in heaven. We need medicine to prevent crippling and deadly diseases. Being born-again does not do away with the need for a balanced diet, purified water, and regular sleep. Certainly those who claim to be the most spiritual still visit the dentist or the eye doctor. The body we have weakens and decays with age. Consider the fact that a large percentage of Olympians are young. The oldest Olympic competitor was Oscar Swahn from Sweden. He won a silver medal in shooting in 1920 at the age of 72 and 280 days. Obviously, that kind of physical accomplishment among seniors is rare. Eventually, our health fails completely and we die.

However, when the kingdom of God fully comes, “There will be no more death, or mourning or crying or pain for the old order of things has passed away” (Revelation 21:4). We will not even need to let our bodies rest: “There will be no more night” (Revelation 22:5). So we thank God for the present health benefits of His kingdom, but we know the best is yet to come.

Wealth

Already, we have enough wealth. As we seek first the Kingdom and the right relationship with the King, He meets our needs (Matthew 6:33). But He does not promise to satisfy our greed! Christianity is not the gate to money! Believers at Smyrna were poor by the world’s standards, but rich spiritually (Revelation 2:9). A third of the world lives on less than two dollars per day, and this includes many Christians. Paul says that those who teach that godliness is a means to financial gain are corrupt men who have been robbed of the truth (1 Timothy 6:5).

But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. People who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge men into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs. (1 Timothy 6:6–10)

We do teach that God meets our financial needs as we sow generously. We do not teach that generous givers will become rich. It is right to want sufficient wealth to meet family needs and to share. Jesus often emphasized the need for a pilgrim’s attitude toward this earth. The deceitfulness of riches can choke out the Word in our lives and cause us to be unfruitful (Luke 8:14). He told His closest disciples, “‘Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom. Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide purses for yourselves that will not wear out, a treasure in heaven that will not be exhausted, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also’” (Luke 12:32–34).

In this stage of the Kingdom, a person as spiritual as the apostle Peter may have to say, “Silver or gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6). In this stage of the kingdom, a person as spiritual as the apostle Paul may confess, “To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are in rags, we are brutally treated, we are homeless” (1 Corinthians 4:11).

Sometimes the most spiritual are at the end of the line when it comes to material blessings. But in the kingdom age to come, gold will be so plentiful that we will use it for streets instead of blacktop.

Suffering

When an individual is born into the kingdom of God, some suffering stops. Jesus gives us freedom from the oppression of Satan. When Jesus saves us, He delivers us from the torment of sin. Jesus gives us rest and relief even now.

But the coming of the kingdom of God did not end suffering. In fact, the Kingdom often brings new suffering. Jesus did not come to bring peace, but a sword (Matthew 10:34). Often, because we follow Him, we are hated and persecuted. Millions have died for their faith. Tens of thousands have lost their possessions because of Him (Hebrews 10:34). Also, after God becomes our Father, we will suffer when He disciplines us (Hebrews 12:5–6).

Paul and Barnabas taught the believers in Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, “We must go through many hardships to enter the [future] kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). Nevertheless, there are many who will persevere through the sufferings of this life, endure to the end, and be saved (Matthew 24:13; Revelations 12:11). Then God will wipe away every tear from our eyes (Revelation 21:4). “‘Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven’” (Matthew 6:10).

Protection

Already, there are times—in this period of the Kingdom—when God protects us in a miraculous way. The Holy Spirit often warns of danger. Angels sometimes assist as they did in freeing Peter from prison (Acts 12:6–11). God may choose to intervene. Forty men could not kill the apostle Paul (Acts 23:12–22).

Nevertheless, God does not always overrule the evil forces of this present darkness. The apostle James was beheaded (Acts 12:1–2). Church traditions state that Peter and Paul were martyrs. Thieves break in and steal. Moth and rust corrupt. Persecution occurs. Accidents happen. Following Jesus does not make us immune to the problems of earth. Not yet! Each year, there are 160,000 martyrs—believers who are murdered for their faith and “considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (Romans 8:36). “When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and the testimony they had maintained. They called out in a loud voice, ‘How long, Sovereign Lord, holy and true, until you judge the inhabitants of the earth and avenge our blood?’ Then each of them was given a white robe, and they were told to wait a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers who were to be killed as they had been was completed” (Revelation 6:9–11).

The future will be better. God promises: “No weapon formed against you will prevail, and you will refute every tongue that accuses you. This is the heritage of the servants of the Lord, and this is their vindication from me” (Isaiah 54:17).

When that day comes,

Clubs will no longer bruise us; swords will never behead us;

We will need no locks on our homes; prison cells will not confine us.

When that day comes,

Rats will bypass our grain; moths will not eat our clothes;

Rust will not corrode our metal; fungus will not destroy our trees.

When that day comes,

Harsh words will not hurt our feelings; the sun’s rays will not burn our skin;

Mosquitoes will bite only sinners; a virus will not dare come near us.

Until then we have Kingdom Protection Limited!

Believer’s Judgment

Already in this age of the Kingdom, believers are being judged. Our Father prunes the vine, and cuts off fruitless branches (John 15:2). He disciplines all of His children (Hebrews 12:7–11). This is a mild form of judgment. The believers at Corinth were severely judged, some with sickness, others with death (1 Corinthians 11:30). As Paul said, God may judge the body now so that the spirit may be spared on the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5:5).

Peter encourages us: “However, if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but praise God that you bear that name. For it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who do not obey the gospel of God?” (1 Peter 4:16–17).

Judgment has indeed begun in the church, but it will not end during this age. There is still a future judgment for Christians. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive what is due him for the things done while in the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

We must build on the foundation of Jesus Christ with the proper doctrine and motives.

But each one should be careful how he builds. For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. If any man builds on this foundation using gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay or straw, his work will be shown for what it is, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will test the quality of each man’s work. If what he has built survives, he will receive his reward, if it is burned up, he will suffer loss; he himself will be saved, but only as one escaping through the flames. (1 Corinthians 3:10–15)

Sinner’s Judgment

The judgment of God upon sinners has also already begun. Even now sinners are separated from God. As a leper was not permitted to fellowship with society, a sinner is prevented from drawing close to our Creator. The curse of sin is a judgment that cancels fellowship with the Father.

Sinners are being judged. There are wages for sin now. Alcohol eats away at the liver. Immorality results in deadly sexual diseases. Misusing God’s money prevents His blessings. The stains of sin on the soul produce guilt. The absence of God in one’s life results in emptiness and loneliness. Sinners already suffer some results of their sin.

And yet a much worse judgment is coming in the next time period of the kingdom of God.

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Another book was opened, which is the book of life. The dead were judged according to what they had done as recorded in the books. The sea gave up the dead that were in it, and death and Hades gave up the dead that were in them, and each person was judged according to what he had done. (Revelation 20:12–13)

But the cowardly, the unbelieving, the vile, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practice magic arts, the idolaters, and all liars—their place will be in the fiery lake of burning sulfur. This is the second death. (Revelation 21:8)

Jesus gave us a parable in Luke 16 that illustrates the future judgment of sinners. The flames tormented the rich man in hell. He cried for one drop of water. He begged for someone to warn his five brothers about the future torment. The judgment of those outside the kingdom of God is already but not yet.

Satan’s Judgment

God has already judged Satan in these Kingdom days. When he rebelled against God, he was cast out of heaven. Jesus said, “‘I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. I have given you authority to trample on snakes and scorpions and to overcome all the power of the enemy; nothing will harm you’” (Luke 10:18–19).

Satan suffered another judgment at Calvary. Jesus said, “‘Now is the time for judgment on this world; now the prince of this world will be driven out’” (John 12:31). And yet he has not yet been fully judged. He is still “the ruler of the kingdom of the air, the spirit who is now at work in those who are disobedient” (Ephesians 2:2).

Some teachers have made bold jokes about the devil. They say he is a roaring lion but cannot bite because Jesus pulled his teeth at Calvary. This is a childish and foolish joke. The roaring lion still has enough power to keep entire nations under false religions. The serpent still has enough poison to martyr thousands of Christians. The dragon still has enough freedom to hinder the mightiest apostle (1 Thessalonians 2:18; Romans 15:22).

The seventy triumphed over demons for a few hours (Luke 10). But a short time later, nine apostles together could not cast one demon out of a boy (Matthew 17). Our faith is not as strong as we would like it to be. The apostle Jude teaches us not to slander the devil, even though Satan has already been partly judged. Jude rebukes bragging men who claim more power than they show and have no idea how much power Satan still has. Jude wrote this:

In the very same way, these dreamers pollute their own bodies, reject authority and slander celestial [heavenly] beings. But even the archangel Michael, when he was disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a slanderous accusation against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” Yet these men speak abusively against whatever they do not understand; and what things they do understand by instinct, like unreasoning animals—these are the very things that destroy them. Woe to them! They have taken the way of Cain; they have rushed for profit into Balaam’s error; they have been destroyed in Korah’s rebellion. These men are blemishes at your love feasts, eating with you without the slightest qualm—shepherds who feed only themselves. (vv. 8–12)

Satan has already been partly judged, but he will not be fully judged until the Kingdom fully comes. However, just as the King of Tyre was humbled (Ezekiel 28:11–19), Beelzebub will be totally judged. “And I saw an angel coming down out of heaven, having the key to the Abyss and holding in his hand a great chain. He seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil, or Satan, and bound him for a thousand years. He threw him into the Abyss, and locked and sealed it over him, to keep him from deceiving the nations anymore until the thousand years were ended. After that, he must be set free for a short time” (Revelation 20:1–3).

When the thousand years are over, Satan will be released from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth—Gog and Magog—to gather them for battle. In number they are like the sand on the seashore. They marched across the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of God’s people, the city he loves. But fire came down from heaven and devoured them. And the devil, who deceived them, was thrown into the lake of burning sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet had been thrown. They will be tormented day and night for ever and ever. (Revelation 20:7–10)

Satan is the commander-in-chief of the kingdom of darkness, the great enemy of the kingdom of God. He is judged already, but not yet.

The Will of God

Jesus taught us to pray: “‘Your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven’” (Matthew 6:10). We have seen that the Kingdom has already come; God’s will is being done. But can we declare that God’s will is being done on earth as it is in heaven? Since God has all power, it would be easy for us to think that His will is always done. The words “the will of God” are quite popular. When a child dies, some may say, “It was God’s will.” When a bus has an accident and people are killed, some who believe strongly in fate say, “It must have been God’s will.”

Some believe that God predestines everything, that He plans everything in advance and all we do is watch it happen. But it is not fair to God to say (as Calvin did) that murder, adultery, child abuse, disease, and masses going to hell are God’s will (Wesley n.d., 259–266). These things are the devil’s will, not the will of our loving heavenly Father. Perhaps some have been confused about the will of God because they have not discerned the already and not yet aspects of the Kingdom.

The Kingdom has begun, and God’s will has partly come to earth. But it has not yet completely come. That is why we keep praying, “Your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). At this time in the Kingdom, most people are rejecting God’s will.

For example, God loves children. Jesus told the story of the shepherd who left the ninety-nine to search for one lost sheep. “In the same way your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should be lost” (Matthew 18:14).

It is not God’s will that children be lost in sin, but millions are being lost. In fact, one-half of the children of the world never even hear the gospel before they grow up and die. Therefore, we keep praying, “‘Your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven’” (Matthew 6:10).

The apostle Paul tells us that God “wants all men to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:3–4). God wants all men, women, boys, and girls to be saved. This is His will for earth. But most reject His will and His kingdom on earth. Few take the narrow road to heaven; masses take the broad road to hell.

God’s will and His kingdom have already begun on earth. But the fullness of His kingdom has not yet come. When the Kingdom comes fully, we will stop praying Matthew 6:10. When the Kingdom comes perfectly, all suffering, sickness, and sin will cease. The lion will lie down with the lamb.

When and how will the kingdom of God fully come? Will it come, as some say, by Christians turning this present earth into a paradise? Do the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven teach us that our influence will spread throughout the earth until it becomes completely Christian? No! This dream is humanistic, mimics the philosophy of the New Age movement, and is definitely not biblical.

Jesus did not prophesy that the earth would get better. He warned that it would get worse and worse. Search the Scriptures. The Last Days are terrible days. False christs, earthquakes, famines, and wars are only the beginning of birth pains, not the end (Matthew 24:4–8). Christians can expect to be hated by all nations because of Him. Most believers will turn away from the faith and betray other Christians. “Because of the increase of wickedness, the love of most will grow cold” (v. 12). But those who endure to the end will be saved.

**Q:** Has the kingdom or rule of God come fully? Explain.

**A:** His kingdom has already begun, but it is not yet complete on the earth. The noonday phase of God’s kingdom will come when Jesus comes again.

**Q:** Relate salvation to your past, present, and future.

**A:** I was saved declares that, at a time in the past, a person was born-again.. I am being saved refers to the present process of Christian growth. I will be saved refers to the future when we will no longer press toward the mark. We will then be saved from this world, this body, and any possibility of sin.

**Q:** Contrast the rewards you already have with future rewards of the kingdom.

**A:** Even now we are rewarded. We receive joy, peace, love, acceptance, assurance, and fatherly care. Some of the rewards of the kingdom of God are already here. But all of our rewards are not yet here. Jesus promised the apostles a hundredfold in this life, and sitting on twelve thrones “at the renewal of all things” (Matthew 19:27–28). Each Christian will be rewarded personally, for his or her own work, when Christ comes (Revelation 22:12).

**Q:** In the kingdom of God, contrast our judgment already and not yet.

**A:** Already in this age of the Kingdom, believers are being judged. God disciplines all of His children (Hebrews 12:7–11). This is a mild form of judgment. Judgment has begun in the church, but it will not end during this age. There is still a future judgment for Christians. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive what is due him for the things done while in the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

**Q:** Has Satan been judged and lost his power? Explain.

**A:** God has already judged Satan in these Kingdom days. Satan suffered another judgment at Calvary. And yet he has not yet been fully judged. He is still “the ruler of the kingdom of the air, the spirit who is now at work in those who are disobedient” (Ephesians 2:2).

#### 13.3.2 — Compare the already and not yet aspects of five topics related to the kingdom of God.

Overview of the Already but Not Yet Aspects of the Kingdom of God

We have said that the kingdom of God is the realm over which the King reigns. The kingdom of God came like a sunrise when Jesus came to earth. His kingdom has already begun, but it is not yet complete on the earth. The noonday phase of God’s kingdom will come when Jesus comes again. Likewise, you have already started studying hermeneutics, but you have not yet completed your study. This chart compares the already and not yet aspects of the kingdom of God on several topics. It will give you an overview of this section. Examine the chart, and then we will discuss each topic in detail.

Topic

Already

Not Yet

1. Salvation

Christians are forgiven and growing in grace.

Christians will be perfect, having attained “the whole measure of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:13).

2. Knowledge

“We know in part and we prophesy in part . . . Now we see but a poor reflection as in a mirror” (1 Corinthians 13:9–12).

“Then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

3. Rewards

We have joy, peace, love, acceptance, assurance, and fatherly care.

“‘Behold, I am coming soon! My reward is with me, and I will give to everyone according to what he has done’” (Revelation 22:12).

(continued)

Topic

Already

Not Yet

4. Health

The prayer of faith heals the sick (James 5:14–15). Also, God has given us doctors, dentists, and medicine to help with health.

“There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away” (Revelations 21:4).

5. Wealth

God supplies our needs, but not our greeds, as we seek His kingdom first (Matthew 6:33; Philippians 4:19).

We will see, touch, and possess the unlimited treasure of our Father’s kingdom that is now reserved for us in heaven (Luke 12:32–34).

6. Suffering

Our sufferings are measured and tempered. God does not allow us to be tried beyond what we can bear (1 Corinthians 10:13; 2 Timothy 2:12; 1 Peter 2:19–23; 4:19).

“He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away” (Revelation 21:4).

7. Protection

Sometimes miraculous protection takes place, yet God does not always overrule the destructive forces of this world. Thieves still break in, moth and rust still corrupt, accidents still happen, persecution occurs (Matthew 6:19–20).

No weapon formed against us will prosper (Isaiah 54:17).

8. Believer’s judgment

Christians are partially disciplined, punished, and judged (John 15:2; 1 Corinthians 11:30; Hebrews 12:5–6).

“For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive what is due him for the things done while in the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

9. Sinner’s judgment

Sinners receive a portion of the wages of sin. They are separated from fellowship with God and suffer some results of their evil acts (Ephesians 2:1; 1 Timothy 5:24).

The dead will be raised and every sinner will be judged according to what he has done. Each one whose name is not written in the book of life will be cast into the lake of fire (Revelation 21:8).

10. Satan’s judgment

Satan has been thrown out of the highest heaven. Believers rejoice in partial victory over him (Luke 10:18–19).

The devil will be thrown into the lake of fire and tormented day and night forever and ever (Revelation 20:10).

11. Will of God

It is accepted by a few but rejected by most (Matthew 6:10; 18:14; 1 Timothy 2:3–4).

Every knee will bow and every tongue will confess that Jesus is Lord. God will dwell on earth with His people (Philippians 2:10–11; Revelation 21:1–4).

Topical Study of the Already but Not Yet Aspects of the Kingdom of God

Salvation

John Wesley once said, “I was saved, I am being saved, and I will be saved.” This threefold view of salvation is helpful.

I was saved declares that, at a time in the past, a person was born-again. A Christian has been forgiven of his or her past sins and moved from the kingdom of darkness to the kingdom of light.

I am being saved refers to the present process of Christian growth. We are growing in holiness, perfecting holiness in the fear of the Lord (2 Corinthians 7:1). Daily, as we grow in grace we are being changed into His likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).

I will be saved refers to the future when we will no longer press toward the mark. We will then be saved from this world, this body, and any possibility of sin. Thus, there was a time when we entered the kingdom of God. We are now growing as children of the King. One day we will receive our glorified bodies. Then we will be saved in the fullest sense in the kingdom of God.

Our Knowledge

“For we know in part and we prophesy in part…. Now we see but a poor reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:9, 12). We have the mind of Christ in part, but not completely. There are yet a billion mysteries we do not understand in this stage of the kingdom. When the kingdom comes in perfection, we will know, even as we are known by God (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Rewards

Even now we are rewarded. We receive joy, peace, love, acceptance, assurance, and fatherly care. Some of the rewards of the kingdom of God are already here. But all of our rewards are not yet here. Jesus promised the apostles a hundredfold in this life, and sitting on twelve thrones “at the renewal of all things” (Matthew 19:27–28). Each Christian will be rewarded personally, for his or her own work, when Christ comes (Revelation 22:12).

Health

The prayer of faith heals the sick (James 5:15). Nevertheless, we are on earth and not in heaven. We need medicine to prevent crippling and deadly diseases. Being born-again does not do away with the need for a balanced diet, purified water, and regular sleep. Certainly those who claim to be the most spiritual still visit the dentist or the eye doctor. The body we have weakens and decays with age. Consider the fact that a large percentage of Olympians are young. The oldest Olympic competitor was Oscar Swahn from Sweden. He won a silver medal in shooting in 1920 at the age of 72 and 280 days. Obviously, that kind of physical accomplishment among seniors is rare. Eventually, our health fails completely and we die.

However, when the kingdom of God fully comes, “There will be no more death, or mourning or crying or pain for the old order of things has passed away” (Revelation 21:4). We will not even need to let our bodies rest: “There will be no more night” (Revelation 22:5). So we thank God for the present health benefits of His kingdom, but we know the best is yet to come.

Wealth

Already, we have enough wealth. As we seek first the Kingdom and the right relationship with the King, He meets our needs (Matthew 6:33). But He does not promise to satisfy our greed! Christianity is not the gate to money! Believers at Smyrna were poor by the world’s standards, but rich spiritually (Revelation 2:9). A third of the world lives on less than two dollars per day, and this includes many Christians. Paul says that those who teach that godliness is a means to financial gain are corrupt men who have been robbed of the truth (1 Timothy 6:5).

But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. People who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap and into many foolish and harmful desires that plunge men into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs. (1 Timothy 6:6–10)

We do teach that God meets our financial needs as we sow generously. We do not teach that generous givers will become rich. It is right to want sufficient wealth to meet family needs and to share. Jesus often emphasized the need for a pilgrim’s attitude toward this earth. The deceitfulness of riches can choke out the Word in our lives and cause us to be unfruitful (Luke 8:14). He told His closest disciples, “‘Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom. Sell your possessions and give to the poor. Provide purses for yourselves that will not wear out, a treasure in heaven that will not be exhausted, where no thief comes near and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also’” (Luke 12:32–34).

In this stage of the Kingdom, a person as spiritual as the apostle Peter may have to say, “Silver or gold I do not have” (Acts 3:6). In this stage of the kingdom, a person as spiritual as the apostle Paul may confess, “To this very hour we go hungry and thirsty, we are in rags, we are brutally treated, we are homeless” (1 Corinthians 4:11).

Sometimes the most spiritual are at the end of the line when it comes to material blessings. But in the kingdom age to come, gold will be so plentiful that we will use it for streets instead of blacktop.

Suffering

When an individual is born into the kingdom of God, some suffering stops. Jesus gives us freedom from the oppression of Satan. When Jesus saves us, He delivers us from the torment of sin. Jesus gives us rest and relief even now.

But the coming of the kingdom of God did not end suffering. In fact, the Kingdom often brings new suffering. Jesus did not come to bring peace, but a sword (Matthew 10:34). Often, because we follow Him, we are hated and persecuted. Millions have died for their faith. Tens of thousands have lost their possessions because of Him (Hebrews 10:34). Also, after God becomes our Father, we will suffer when He disciplines us (Hebrews 12:5–6).

Paul and Barnabas taught the believers in Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, “We must go through many hardships to enter the [future] kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). Nevertheless, there are many who will persevere through the sufferings of this life, endure to the end, and be saved (Matthew 24:13; Revelations 12:11). Then God will wipe away every tear from our eyes (Revelation 21:4). “‘Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven’” (Matthew 6:10).

Protection

Already, there are times—in this period of the Kingdom—when God protects us in a miraculous way. The Holy Spirit often warns of danger. Angels sometimes assist as they did in freeing Peter from prison (Acts 12:6–11). God may choose to intervene. Forty men could not kill the apostle Paul (Acts 23:12–22).

Nevertheless, God does not always overrule the evil forces of this present darkness. The apostle James was beheaded (Acts 12:1–2). Church traditions state that Peter and Paul were martyrs. Thieves break in and steal. Moth and rust corrupt. Persecution occurs. Accidents happen. Following Jesus does not make us immune to the problems of earth. Not yet! Each year, there are 160,000 martyrs—believers who are murdered for their faith and “considered as sheep to be slaughtered” (Romans 8:36). “When he opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of those who had been slain because of the word of God and the testimony they had maintained. They called out in a loud voice, ‘How long, Sovereign Lord, holy and true, until you judge the inhabitants of the earth and avenge our blood?’ Then each of them was given a white robe, and they were told to wait a little longer, until the number of their fellow servants and brothers who were to be killed as they had been was completed” (Revelation 6:9–11).

The future will be better. God promises: “No weapon formed against you will prevail, and you will refute every tongue that accuses you. This is the heritage of the servants of the Lord, and this is their vindication from me” (Isaiah 54:17).

When that day comes,

Clubs will no longer bruise us; swords will never behead us;

We will need no locks on our homes; prison cells will not confine us.

When that day comes,

Rats will bypass our grain; moths will not eat our clothes;

Rust will not corrode our metal; fungus will not destroy our trees.

When that day comes,

Harsh words will not hurt our feelings; the sun’s rays will not burn our skin;

Mosquitoes will bite only sinners; a virus will not dare come near us.

Until then we have Kingdom Protection Limited!

Believer’s Judgment

Already in this age of the Kingdom, believers are being judged. Our Father prunes the vine, and cuts off fruitless branches (John 15:2). He disciplines all of His children (Hebrews 12:7–11). This is a mild form of judgment. The believers at Corinth were severely judged, some with sickness, others with death (1 Corinthians 11:30). As Paul said, God may judge the body now so that the spirit may be spared on the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5:5).

Peter encourages us: “However, if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but praise God that you bear that name. For it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God; and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who do not obey the gospel of God?” (1 Peter 4:16–17).

Judgment has indeed begun in the church, but it will not end during this age. There is still a future judgment for Christians. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive what is due him for the things done while in the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

We must build on the foundation of Jesus Christ with the proper doctrine and motives.

But each one should be careful how he builds. For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. If any man builds on this foundation using gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay or straw, his work will be shown for what it is, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will test the quality of each man’s work. If what he has built survives, he will receive his reward, if it is burned up, he will suffer loss; he himself will be saved, but only as one escaping through the flames. (1 Corinthians 3:10–15)

Sinner’s Judgment

The judgment of God upon sinners has also already begun. Even now sinners are separated from God. As a leper was not permitted to fellowship with society, a sinner is prevented from drawing close to our Creator. The curse of sin is a judgment that cancels fellowship with the Father.

Sinners are being judged. There are wages for sin now. Alcohol eats away at the liver. Immorality results in deadly sexual diseases. Misusing God’s money prevents His blessings. The stains of sin on the soul produce guilt. The absence of God in one’s life results in emptiness and loneliness. Sinners already suffer some results of their sin.

And yet a much worse judgment is coming in the next time period of the kingdom of God.

And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne, and books were opened. Another book was opened, which is the book of life. The dead were judged according to what they had done as recorded in the books. The sea gave up the dead that were in it, and death and Hades gave up the dead that were in them, and each person was judged according to what he had done. (Revelation 20:12–13)

But the cowardly, the unbelieving, the vile, the murderers, the sexually immoral, those who practice magic arts, the idolaters, and all liars—their place will be in the fiery lake of burning sulfur. This is the second death. (Revelation 21:8)

Jesus gave us a parable in Luke 16 that illustrates the future judgment of sinners. The flames tormented the rich man in hell. He cried for one drop of water. He begged for someone to warn his five brothers about the future torment. The judgment of those outside the kingdom of God is already but not yet.

Satan’s Judgment

God has already judged Satan in these Kingdom days. When he rebelled against God, he was cast out of heaven. Jesus said, “‘I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven. I have given you authority to trample on snakes and scorpions and to overcome all the power of the enemy; nothing will harm you’” (Luke 10:18–19).

Satan suffered another judgment at Calvary. Jesus said, “‘Now is the time for judgment on this world; now the prince of this world will be driven out’” (John 12:31). And yet he has not yet been fully judged. He is still “the ruler of the kingdom of the air, the spirit who is now at work in those who are disobedient” (Ephesians 2:2).

Some teachers have made bold jokes about the devil. They say he is a roaring lion but cannot bite because Jesus pulled his teeth at Calvary. This is a childish and foolish joke. The roaring lion still has enough power to keep entire nations under false religions. The serpent still has enough poison to martyr thousands of Christians. The dragon still has enough freedom to hinder the mightiest apostle (1 Thessalonians 2:18; Romans 15:22).

The seventy triumphed over demons for a few hours (Luke 10). But a short time later, nine apostles together could not cast one demon out of a boy (Matthew 17). Our faith is not as strong as we would like it to be. The apostle Jude teaches us not to slander the devil, even though Satan has already been partly judged. Jude rebukes bragging men who claim more power than they show and have no idea how much power Satan still has. Jude wrote this:

In the very same way, these dreamers pollute their own bodies, reject authority and slander celestial [heavenly] beings. But even the archangel Michael, when he was disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a slanderous accusation against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” Yet these men speak abusively against whatever they do not understand; and what things they do understand by instinct, like unreasoning animals—these are the very things that destroy them. Woe to them! They have taken the way of Cain; they have rushed for profit into Balaam’s error; they have been destroyed in Korah’s rebellion. These men are blemishes at your love feasts, eating with you without the slightest qualm—shepherds who feed only themselves. (vv. 8–12)

Satan has already been partly judged, but he will not be fully judged until the Kingdom fully comes. However, just as the King of Tyre was humbled (Ezekiel 28:11–19), Beelzebub will be totally judged. “And I saw an angel coming down out of heaven, having the key to the Abyss and holding in his hand a great chain. He seized the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil, or Satan, and bound him for a thousand years. He threw him into the Abyss, and locked and sealed it over him, to keep him from deceiving the nations anymore until the thousand years were ended. After that, he must be set free for a short time” (Revelation 20:1–3).

When the thousand years are over, Satan will be released from his prison, and will go out to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth—Gog and Magog—to gather them for battle. In number they are like the sand on the seashore. They marched across the breadth of the earth and surrounded the camp of God’s people, the city he loves. But fire came down from heaven and devoured them. And the devil, who deceived them, was thrown into the lake of burning sulfur, where the beast and the false prophet had been thrown. They will be tormented day and night for ever and ever. (Revelation 20:7–10)

Satan is the commander-in-chief of the kingdom of darkness, the great enemy of the kingdom of God. He is judged already, but not yet.

The Will of God

Jesus taught us to pray: “‘Your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven’” (Matthew 6:10). We have seen that the Kingdom has already come; God’s will is being done. But can we declare that God’s will is being done on earth as it is in heaven? Since God has all power, it would be easy for us to think that His will is always done. The words “the will of God” are quite popular. When a child dies, some may say, “It was God’s will.” When a bus has an accident and people are killed, some who believe strongly in fate say, “It must have been God’s will.”

Some believe that God predestines everything, that He plans everything in advance and all we do is watch it happen. But it is not fair to God to say (as Calvin did) that murder, adultery, child abuse, disease, and masses going to hell are God’s will (Wesley n.d., 259–266). These things are the devil’s will, not the will of our loving heavenly Father. Perhaps some have been confused about the will of God because they have not discerned the already and not yet aspects of the Kingdom.

The Kingdom has begun, and God’s will has partly come to earth. But it has not yet completely come. That is why we keep praying, “Your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). At this time in the Kingdom, most people are rejecting God’s will.

For example, God loves children. Jesus told the story of the shepherd who left the ninety-nine to search for one lost sheep. “In the same way your Father in heaven is not willing that any of these little ones should be lost” (Matthew 18:14).

It is not God’s will that children be lost in sin, but millions are being lost. In fact, one-half of the children of the world never even hear the gospel before they grow up and die. Therefore, we keep praying, “‘Your kingdom come, your will be done on earth as it is in heaven’” (Matthew 6:10).

The apostle Paul tells us that God “wants all men to be saved and to come to a knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:3–4). God wants all men, women, boys, and girls to be saved. This is His will for earth. But most reject His will and His kingdom on earth. Few take the narrow road to heaven; masses take the broad road to hell.

God’s will and His kingdom have already begun on earth. But the fullness of His kingdom has not yet come. When the Kingdom comes fully, we will stop praying Matthew 6:10. When the Kingdom comes perfectly, all suffering, sickness, and sin will cease. The lion will lie down with the lamb.

When and how will the kingdom of God fully come? Will it come, as some say, by Christians turning this present earth into a paradise? Do the parables of the mustard seed and the leaven teach us that our influence will spread throughout the earth until it becomes completely Christian? No! This dream is humanistic, mimics the philosophy of the New Age movement, and is definitely not biblical.

Jesus did not prophesy that the earth would get better. He warned that it would get worse and worse. Search the Scriptures. The Last Days are terrible days. False christs, earthquakes, famines, and wars are only the beginning of birth pains, not the end (Matthew 24:4–8). Christians can expect to be hated by all nations because of Him. Most believers will turn away from the faith and betray other Christians. “Because of the increase of wickedness, the love of most will grow cold” (v. 12). But those who endure to the end will be saved.

**Q:** Has the kingdom or rule of God come fully? Explain.

**A:** His kingdom has already begun, but it is not yet complete on the earth. The noonday phase of God’s kingdom will come when Jesus comes again.

**Q:** Relate salvation to your past, present, and future.

**A:** I was saved declares that, at a time in the past, a person was born-again.. I am being saved refers to the present process of Christian growth. I will be saved refers to the future when we will no longer press toward the mark. We will then be saved from this world, this body, and any possibility of sin.

**Q:** Contrast the rewards you already have with future rewards of the kingdom.

**A:** Even now we are rewarded. We receive joy, peace, love, acceptance, assurance, and fatherly care. Some of the rewards of the kingdom of God are already here. But all of our rewards are not yet here. Jesus promised the apostles a hundredfold in this life, and sitting on twelve thrones “at the renewal of all things” (Matthew 19:27–28). Each Christian will be rewarded personally, for his or her own work, when Christ comes (Revelation 22:12).

**Q:** In the kingdom of God, contrast our judgment already and not yet.

**A:** Already in this age of the Kingdom, believers are being judged. God disciplines all of His children (Hebrews 12:7–11). This is a mild form of judgment. Judgment has begun in the church, but it will not end during this age. There is still a future judgment for Christians. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive what is due him for the things done while in the body, whether good or bad” (2 Corinthians 5:10).

**Q:** Has Satan been judged and lost his power? Explain.

**A:** God has already judged Satan in these Kingdom days. Satan suffered another judgment at Calvary. And yet he has not yet been fully judged. He is still “the ruler of the kingdom of the air, the spirit who is now at work in those who are disobedient” (Ephesians 2:2).

## 14 - Timeless, Cross-Cultural, Biblical Principles

### Recognizing and Valuing Principles

#### 14.1.1 — Define a biblical principle, identify four types of principles, and illustrate each.

Remember that this last unit of hermeneutics is about applying Scripture. Interpreting Scripture is not our final goal; it is only a step toward ministry. A main goal of ministry is to interpret and apply Scripture to help people. In this chapter, we will study biblical principles. The purpose of finding and stating biblical principles is to live them and to teach and preach them.

Jesus taught His disciples to summarize the truth of a story or event by stating a principle. For example, in Mark 2:23–28, the Pharisees accused the disciples of violating the Law by picking grain on the Sabbath. However, the priests in the temple worked on the Sabbath and were not guilty. Then Jesus stated the principle based on these events: “The Sabbath is made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Likewise, the Spirit led the apostles to state principles based on Scripture. For example, Paul referred to Deuteronomy 25:4: “When an ox is working in the grain, do not cover its mouth to keep it from eating” (NCV). From this Scripture, Paul gives us the following principle: “Ministers who labor should reap benefits from their work” (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard, 31). In this chapter, we will guide in recognizing, valuing, and learning to state biblical principles.

Characteristics of Principles

Principles are like handles. They give people something to grab and hold on to. A suitcase with no handle would be hard to lift or carry. But a handle makes a suitcase easy to use. Likewise, when you teach and preach, state your main points as biblical principles. People will take hold of principles, remember them, and apply them to their personal lives.

A biblical principle is a broad, cross-cultural certainty in the form of a command, promise, warning, or timeless truth. It is a truth from God’s Word that will work anytime, anywhere in the world. A principle is like a roof—it is a broad general law, rule, or truth that covers many lesser, specific truths. For example, a principle from Matthew 6 is do not do righteous deeds to be seen by others (Matthew 6:1). This principle covers lesser specific truths like not giving, praying, or fasting to be validated by other people (Matthew 6:2–18). Praying in secret is an example of obeying the principle of Matthew 6:1.

In this course, we encourage you to state a principle in four different ways (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard, 422).

A command

• “You shall not commit adultery.” (Exodus 20:14)

• “Do to others what you would have them to do to you.” (Matthew 7:12) [Note that the Golden Rule is a Golden Principle.]

• “Go and make disciples of all nations.” (Matthew 28:19–20)

• Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. (James 4:7)

A warning (Note that a warning is a form of a command.)

• “Watch out! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” (Luke 12:15)

Notice that the second part of Luke 12:15 explains why we should guard against greed.

• “Watch out that no one deceives you. For many will come in my name, claiming, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will deceive many.” (Matthew 24:4–5)

• We must pay more careful attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. (Hebrew 2:1)

A promise

• Jesus is “with [us] always, to the very end of the age.” (Matthew 28:20)

Note some promises are words Jesus spoke and contain the words I , me , or my . For example, Jesus said, “‘I am with you always, to the very end of the age’” (Matthew 28:20). It is easy and often helpful to change such a promise to a timeless truth. So in our example above, we changed the first person pronoun I to Jesus. This made it easy to state the promise as a principle. Then it was both a promise and a principle.

If you cannot state a promise as though you spoke it, it is not a principle. For example, it is not true if I say, “I am with you always.” I can only be one place at once. But it is true if I say, “Jesus is with you always.” Some promises are only true when spoken by certain people. But a principle is true, no matter who says it.

• “If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me.” (John 14:3)

• Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved. (Acts 16:31) This promise is a true principle, no matter who says it.

• “Ask and it will be given to you, seek and you will find, knock and the door will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7). Note that this promise is a principle spoken by Jesus. It is in the literary context of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). The sermon teaches us to pray in secret and according to God’s will (Matthew 6:5–15). So the principle of Matthew 7:7, and all other principles, must be interpreted in context.

A timeless truth or proverb

• “It is not good for man to be alone.” (Genesis 2:18)

• “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me [Jesus].” (Matthew 28:18)

• To bear fruit, a believer must abide in Jesus, the True Vine. (John 15:1–5)

• Love is patient. (1 Corinthians 13:4)

• Faith without deeds is dead. (James 2:26)

• Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. (2 Corinthians 9:6)

• Temptation is linked to evil desires within us. (James 1:14)

• God is light; in him there is no darkness at all. (1 John 1:5)

A few principles may be considered as more than one type. For example, some promises are also timeless truths, and some commands are warnings. So there may be more than one correct answer on some questions.

Benefits of Principles

Main Points Stated as Topics

Main Points Stated as Principles

I. The Call of Joshua (Joshua 1:1–2)

II. The Command of Joshua (Joshua 1:3)

Principles attract attention and pique interest. There are many preachers today, like Rick Warren (Bisagno 2002, 3), George O. Wood, and John Lindell, who often state their main points as principles. In contrast, many preachers make a big mistake. They state their main points as topics instead of principles. A topic by itself rarely creates much interest. For example, the four topics about Joshua are biblical, but they are not interesting. But a principle grabs the attention of people. Notice how the principles in the chart above create interest. State your main ideas as principles, and you will hold the congregation’s attention throughout your sermons.

Consider the attention and interest these principles attract:

• “With God all things are possible.” (Matthew 19:26)

• I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me. (Philippians 4:13)

• Without faith it is impossible to please God. (Hebrews 11:6)

• The earnest prayers of a righteous person influence God. (James 5:16)

Relevance of Principles

They are up-to-date and ready to use if you state your points as principles and avoid using any names (within the principle) except God’s. This introduces your sermon as one that will help people with today’s problems (Kaiser 1981, 152). Sharing a principle with someone is like handing money to the poor, or a cane to a lame man.

Note that these principles are current, ready to help anyone:

• A person who walks with Jesus is never alone (Hebrews 13:5).

• A gentle answer turns away wrath. (Proverbs 15:1)

• Love is patient. (1 Corinthians 13:4)

Principles and Illustrations

If your main point is a topic like “The Call of Joshua,” how will you illustrate that point? It would be difficult. In Luke 15, Jesus stated a principle: Heaven rejoices when one sinner repents (Luke 15:7, 10, 32). He illustrated this principle with the stories of the lost sheep, the lost coin, and the lost son. In this course we will teach you to state your main points as principles. Then, it will be easy for you to illustrate them. One of the biggest reasons preachers do not use more illustrations is that they do not use more principles. It is either hard or impossible to illustrate a topic, but principles are easy to illustrate.

Principle

Illustration

The earnest prayers of a righteous person influence God (James 5:16).

“A gentle answer turns away wrath” (Proverbs 15:1).

“Love is patient” (1 Corinthians 13:4).

Applying Principles

All sermons should be purpose-driven, that is, preached for a purpose. We preach to help people with their problems. There is never more than one step from a principle to the place people live. Look again at the examples in the three types of principles above. All of them are easy to apply. Principles answer the question: Why does God want me to read this biblical passage?

Principles and Responses

After you apply the truth, you want your listeners to respond. How can someone respond to “Balaam fought”? Perhaps they can smile, frown, or go to sleep! But these are not the types of response a preacher wants. In contrast, stating main points as principles enables the preacher to ask the listeners to respond to the truth (Kaiser, 151). Preaching principles makes it easy for you to invite people to pray at the altar. Listeners can choose to accept or reject the biblical principles you preach. Some pastors do not invite people to respond after a sermon because their sermon had no purpose. Preach principles and invite people to embrace them.

**Q:** What is a biblical principle?

**A:** A biblical principle is a broad, cross-cultural certainty in the form of a command, promise, warning, or timeless truth. It is a truth from God’s Word that will work anytime, anywhere in the world.

**Q:** What broad principle covers Matthew 6:2–18?

**A:** This principle is like an umbrella. It covers lesser, specific truths like: Do not give so others will see you. Do not pray so others will see you. Do not fast so others will see you.

**Q:** Give an example of the Golden Rule or Principle.

**A:** “Do to others what you would have them to do to you” (Matthew 7:12).

#### 14.1.2 — Summarize five benefits of principles and illustrate each.

Remember that this last unit of hermeneutics is about applying Scripture. Interpreting Scripture is not our final goal; it is only a step toward ministry. A main goal of ministry is to interpret and apply Scripture to help people. In this chapter, we will study biblical principles. The purpose of finding and stating biblical principles is to live them and to teach and preach them.

Jesus taught His disciples to summarize the truth of a story or event by stating a principle. For example, in Mark 2:23–28, the Pharisees accused the disciples of violating the Law by picking grain on the Sabbath. However, the priests in the temple worked on the Sabbath and were not guilty. Then Jesus stated the principle based on these events: “The Sabbath is made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Likewise, the Spirit led the apostles to state principles based on Scripture. For example, Paul referred to Deuteronomy 25:4: “When an ox is working in the grain, do not cover its mouth to keep it from eating” (NCV). From this Scripture, Paul gives us the following principle: “Ministers who labor should reap benefits from their work” (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard, 31). In this chapter, we will guide in recognizing, valuing, and learning to state biblical principles.

Characteristics of Principles

Principles are like handles. They give people something to grab and hold on to. A suitcase with no handle would be hard to lift or carry. But a handle makes a suitcase easy to use. Likewise, when you teach and preach, state your main points as biblical principles. People will take hold of principles, remember them, and apply them to their personal lives.

A biblical principle is a broad, cross-cultural certainty in the form of a command, promise, warning, or timeless truth. It is a truth from God’s Word that will work anytime, anywhere in the world. A principle is like a roof—it is a broad general law, rule, or truth that covers many lesser, specific truths. For example, a principle from Matthew 6 is do not do righteous deeds to be seen by others (Matthew 6:1). This principle covers lesser specific truths like not giving, praying, or fasting to be validated by other people (Matthew 6:2–18). Praying in secret is an example of obeying the principle of Matthew 6:1.

In this course, we encourage you to state a principle in four different ways (Klein, Blomberg, and Hubbard, 422).

A command

• “You shall not commit adultery.” (Exodus 20:14)

• “Do to others what you would have them to do to you.” (Matthew 7:12) [Note that the Golden Rule is a Golden Principle.]

• “Go and make disciples of all nations.” (Matthew 28:19–20)

• Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. (James 4:7)

A warning (Note that a warning is a form of a command.)

• “Watch out! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.” (Luke 12:15)

Notice that the second part of Luke 12:15 explains why we should guard against greed.

• “Watch out that no one deceives you. For many will come in my name, claiming, ‘I am the Christ,’ and will deceive many.” (Matthew 24:4–5)

• We must pay more careful attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. (Hebrew 2:1)

A promise

• Jesus is “with [us] always, to the very end of the age.” (Matthew 28:20)

Note some promises are words Jesus spoke and contain the words I , me , or my . For example, Jesus said, “‘I am with you always, to the very end of the age’” (Matthew 28:20). It is easy and often helpful to change such a promise to a timeless truth. So in our example above, we changed the first person pronoun I to Jesus. This made it easy to state the promise as a principle. Then it was both a promise and a principle.

If you cannot state a promise as though you spoke it, it is not a principle. For example, it is not true if I say, “I am with you always.” I can only be one place at once. But it is true if I say, “Jesus is with you always.” Some promises are only true when spoken by certain people. But a principle is true, no matter who says it.

• “If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me.” (John 14:3)

• Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved. (Acts 16:31) This promise is a true principle, no matter who says it.

• “Ask and it will be given to you, seek and you will find, knock and the door will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7). Note that this promise is a principle spoken by Jesus. It is in the literary context of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). The sermon teaches us to pray in secret and according to God’s will (Matthew 6:5–15). So the principle of Matthew 7:7, and all other principles, must be interpreted in context.

A timeless truth or proverb

• “It is not good for man to be alone.” (Genesis 2:18)

• “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me [Jesus].” (Matthew 28:18)

• To bear fruit, a believer must abide in Jesus, the True Vine. (John 15:1–5)

• Love is patient. (1 Corinthians 13:4)

• Faith without deeds is dead. (James 2:26)

• Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. (2 Corinthians 9:6)

• Temptation is linked to evil desires within us. (James 1:14)

• God is light; in him there is no darkness at all. (1 John 1:5)
