#### 15.2.2 — Summarize and illustrate six principles about how the Holy Spirit applies Scripture.

In this final lesson, we come to one of the hardest subjects to teach. It is so sensitive that most books on hermeneutics avoid it. Many problems arise when a believer says, “God told me.” Sincere believers have erred, thinking that the Holy Spirit spoke something to them. We think of John G. Scheppe, the man we mentioned in Chapter 4, who prayed all night. We told you that he thought that God revealed to him that there was no Trinity and, as a result, he started the Jesus Only movement.

A missionary preached in a church in 1975. After the service, the pastor and a church member approached him. The member claimed to have a word from the Lord for the missionary, who happened to be prematurely bald. The message was that God would restore his hair to be like it was in his youth. The young missionary was trusting, and the church member was sincere but mistaken. Today, more than thirty years later, the missionary remains bald! In this case, the mistake about hearing a word from God is amusing. But in tragic cases, children have died when parents thought God told them to stop administering prescriptions; churches have split because sincere pastors were simply wrong when they thought the Holy Spirit had spoken to them.

Sometimes, when God is present in special ways, we confuse His presence with His message to us. In moments that we are so filled with joy, we may misinterpret the presence of God and jump to wrong conclusions. The apostle Peter provides us with a good example of this. Peter, James, and John had a great spiritual experience on top of a mountain. There, they saw Jesus glorified, together with Moses and Elijah (Matthew 17: 1 – 5). Peter was blessed and excited, but he did not understand what God was saying. He wanted to build three shelters—one for Jesus, one for Moses, and one for Elijah. In this case, God corrected Peter and turned his thoughts toward Jesus alone. But in many cases, believers come to wrong conclusions, and God does not speak from heaven to correct them.

In spite of human error, and the danger of misunderstanding God, we must leave room for the Holy Spirit to speak to believers in any way He chooses. At rare times—perhaps only a few times in a lifetime—God may speak in ways that are related to, but outside the topic of hermeneutics. These messages from God are supernatural and may conflict with human understanding. They may require a response of faith, not reason. Some examples are listed below.

“So make yourself an ark of cypress wood; make rooms in it and coat it with pitch inside and out. This is how you are to build it: The ark is to be 450 feet long, 75 feet wide and 45 feet high.” (Genesis 6:14–15)

“Leave your country, your people and your father’s household and go to the land I will show you.” (Genesis 12:1)

“Take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go to the region of Moriah. Sacrifice him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains I will tell you about.” (Genesis 22:2)

“On the seventh day, march around the city seven times, with the priests blowing the trumpets.” (Joshua 6:4)

“Go, wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored and you will be cleansed.” (2 Kings 5:10)

“Go to the lake and throw out your line. Take the first fish you catch; open its mouth and you will find a four-drachma coin. Take it and give it to them for my tax and yours.” (Matthew 17:27)

“Go, show yourselves to the priests. And as they went, they were cleansed.” (Luke 17:14)

“Fill the jars with water.” (John 2:7)

“Go . . . wash in the Pool of Siloam.” So the man went and washed, and came home seeing. (John 9:7)

Then Jesus directed them to have all the people sit down in groups on the green grass. So they sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties. (Mark 6:39–40)

“Go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul.” (Acts 9:11)

While Peter was still thinking about the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Simon, three men are looking for you. . . . Do not hesitate to go with them, for I have sent them.” (Acts 10:19–20)

Jesus said that His sheep know His voice (John 10:4). It is possible, but not normal, for God to tell a believer to do something that does not make sense. Such times remind us of Peter’s words: “Master, we’ve worked hard all night and haven’t caught anything. But because you say so, I will let down the nets” (Luke 5:5). Mary’s advice to the servant at the wedding is good advice to us: “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).

Even though there are those rare times when God speaks in unusual ways, there are principles that can guide us at all times. In this lesson, we will study six principles that can teach us about the way the Holy Spirit uses and applies Scripture.

Six Principles: The Holy Spirit Uses and Applies Scripture

1. The Holy Spirit addresses personal need.

We affirm that the Holy Spirit still speaks to believers and the church today. The main way God speaks to us is through the Scriptures. The Bible is the basis and standard for our faith. We submit to the Scriptures as the authority of God over our lives. Still, on another level of communication, God speaks to believers and the church in other ways. By the Spirit, God may speak to believers through dreams, visions, prophecy, or tongues and interpretation. He may speak to us through a song, a teaching, or a pastor’s sermon (1 Corinthians 14:26 – 33).

Likewise, the Holy Spirit still speaks to believers as they worship, pray, and study the Bible alone. As Peter prayed, the Holy Spirit led him to Cornelius (Acts 10:9–20). And Paul went up to Jerusalem by revelation (Galatians 2:2). In similar ways, the Spirit can lead us. He may choose to enliven a Bible verse to us as we read Scripture. Our hearts may leap within when we feel a witness of the Holy Spirit that this verse is especially for us.

“All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). Sometimes as we study the Bible, the Spirit uses a verse to convict us of sin. Other times, the Spirit may use Bible verses to encourage us.

Studying the Bible is not an end in itself. One of the most precious things about Bible study is that it often leads us into the presence of God himself. Then, like the two disciples on the road to Emmaus, we can say, “‘Were not our hearts burning within us while he talked with us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?’” (Luke 24:32).

2. The Holy Spirit gives unique application.

Review the story about Lillian Trasher at the beginning of this chapter. The Holy Spirit applied Acts 7:34 to her about being a missionary to Egypt. This verse did not give her direction. Rather, it confirmed what she had felt in her heart for months and perhaps years. The Holy Spirit used this verse in a unique way to encourage Lillian. But the Spirit would not apply that verse in the same way to most other people.

In 1709, close to midnight, the building in which John Wesley was staying caught on fire. Everyone in the building was quickly rescued except for Wesley. Finally, someone saved him—then the building was completely burned to the ground. From that time on, he often felt that Zechariah 3:2 applied to him in a special way. The verse says: “Is not this man a burning stick snatched from the fire?” (Zechariah 3:2). We can see why this verse was so special to John Wesley. But for most of us, the Holy Spirit will not apply it in the same way.

The Holy Spirit led Matthew to apply many verses to Jesus. One example is: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matthew 2:15). But the Holy Spirit will not apply this verse to other sons of God in the same way. As believers, we should rejoice when the Holy Spirit applies verses to us in personal ways. But we should discern that the Spirit may emphasize different verses to people, depending on their situations.

3. The Holy Spirit guides application of Scriptures.

There is an old song which says: “Every promise in the book is mine; every chapter, every verse, every line; I am trusting in His Word divine; every promise in the book is mine.” On the one hand, every promise in the book is ours. The entire Bible is inspired and is ours to use. But 2 Timothy 3:16 reminds us that the Bible is useful for different purposes, at different times. “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16).

Much confusion has resulted from sincere people unwisely trying to claim the promises. When you think about it, no one would want to claim all the promises. Who would want to claim any of the following promises?

“This very night, before the rooster crows, you will disown me three times.” (Matthew 26:34)

“When you were younger you dressed yourself and went where you wanted; but when you are old you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go.” (John 21:18)

“Look! The feet of the men who buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out also.” (Acts 5:9)

“I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.” (Acts 9:16) 12 If evil could not come near David, why did he flee from Saul?

David wrote the promise of Psalm 91:7: “A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not come near you.” King Saul threw his spear at David. It missed and stuck in the wall (1 Samuel 19:10). Even though David wrote Psalm 91:7, he knew it was not God’s timing to stand his ground and claim that promise. Instead, he fled for his life. Some may remind us that David did not write Psalm 91 until after fleeing from Saul. But Psalm 91:7 was as true in David’s early life as it was when he was old. And by the way, David did not try to claim Psalm 91:7 when Absalom chased him from the palace at least twenty years after David fled from Saul (2 Samuel 15). Likewise, Joseph and Mary, the Magi, and Paul all knew the right times to flee.

Only the Holy Spirit can help us know which promise or verse to focus on at a particular time. Even though He might choose a verse that we would not have chosen, we should let Him guide us. “In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groans that words cannot express. And he who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints in accordance with God’s will” (Romans 8:26–27).

Bible verses sometime emphasize opposite directions. There are verses about suffering and verses about conquering. There are verses about being slaughtered for our faith and verses about escaping death. How can believers know which verses to focus on? Many verses are good to meditate on any time. Such verses include truths about salvation, redemption, holiness, prayer, the fruit of the Spirit, the Second Coming, and so on.

Some people choose Bible verses like they are reading a menu at a cafe. This is not wise, because as humans, we may tend to choose verses that appeal to our carnal nature. God has given us a whole Bible. We need it all, not merely a verse here and there. When you eat to nourish your physical body, most of the time you do not just grab a small piece of bread. Instead, you sit down and have a complete meal. Likewise, you may read one verse for a spiritual snack. But to be strong spiritually, you must eat complete spiritual meals. Read entire chapters and books of Scripture. The Holy Spirit’s infinite wisdom will feed and guide you as you take time to listen to Him. Remember this: Nothing takes the place of daily time with the Spirit in the Word.

Two Bible school students were discussing some biblical promises. The first said that when he graduated he was claiming this passage: “Every place where you set your foot will be yours: from the desert to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates River to the western sea. No man will be able to stand against you. The Lord your God, as he promised you, will put the terror and fear of you on the whole land, wherever you go” (Deuteronomy 11:24–25). The second student said he was claiming this: “He was wiser than any other man, including Ethan the Ezrahite–wiser than Heman, Calcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol. And his fame spread to all the surrounding nations” (1 Kings 4:31).

The Holy Spirit is not the author of presumption. Presumption is a form of pride. A person presumes by assuming or taking something for granted that is not the case. Aaron and Miriam were presumptuous when they spoke against Moses (Numbers 12). Korah was presumptuous when he did not submit to Moses (Numbers 16). Saul was presumptuous when he sacrificed animals instead of waiting for Samuel, the priest (1 Samuel 13:7–14). Once he was small in his own eyes. But pride caused him to see himself as very elevated! Uzzah was presumptuous when he tried to steady the ark in a way God did not approve (2 Samuel 6). The king of Tyre, perhaps a veiled model of Satan, was presumptuous when he said he would be like God (Ezekiel 28:2 – 19).

Believers are presumptuous when they try to stand on verses that the Holy Spirit has not guided them to, and that do not fit their situation. We are presumptuous when we as humans interpret, use, and apply Bible verses in ways that God never intended.

4. The Holy Spirit uses principles of Scripture to guide us.

Review the lessons about principles in Chapter 14. It is always wise and safe to apply the principles of Scripture. For example, read 1 Corinthians 9:7 – 12:

Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its grapes? Who tends a flock and does not drink of the milk? Do I say this merely from a human point of view? Doesn’t the Law say the same thing? For it is written in the Law of Moses: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” Is it about oxen that God is concerned? Surely he says this for us, doesn’t he? Yes, this was written for us, because when the plowman plows and the thresher threshes, they ought to do so in the hope of sharing in the harvest. If we have sown spiritual seed among you, is it too much if we reap a material harvest from you? If others have this right of support from you, shouldn’t we have it all the more? But we did not use this right. On the contrary, we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ.

As an ox treads out grain, it walks in circles, causing a millstone to turn and grind grain. Moses wrote that it was wrong to muzzle an ox as it treaded out grain (Deuteronomy 25:4). Putting a muzzle on the ox would have covered his mouth, and prevented it from eating some grain as it worked. In God’s eyes, the ox had the right to eat as wages for his work.

Today, many believers may not be soldiers, work in vineyards, or have oxen. But we can all apply the principle in 1 Corinthians 9:7 – 12. The Holy Spirit showed Paul the principle: Those who work in the church deserve some benefits from their labor. Additionally, Paul states a bigger principle. Sometimes we should give up our rights in order to win others (1 Corinthians 9:12 – 27).

Remember that the Holy Spirit uses principles to apply biblical truth.

5. The Holy Spirit always applies Scriptures in harmony with other Scriptures.

Some modern-day believers were full of zeal in their charismatic experience. They had been filled with the Spirit and rejoiced in their new prayer language. With new power they testified for Christ and led many to the Savior. But problems arose that revealed their need to use and apply Scripture correctly (2 Timothy 2:15). For example, they brought a young man named Phil to Christ, and he was delivered from drugs and drunkenness. Phil was wearing a cast on his arm that he broke in an auto accident. These believers quoted a part of a verse from 1 Peter 2:24: “By his wounds you have been healed.”

They insisted that since 1 Peter 2:24 said we had been healed, Phil should take the cast off his arm. Phil told them that his arm still hurt. They said he should believe the Scriptures, not the feeling of pain. Finally, Phil agreed. The joyful believers helped him remove the cast. But his pain became so great that he returned to the doctor. His x-rays revealed that the arm had been healing, but was still broken. Removing the cast had damaged the arm. So the doctor put a new cast on Phil’s arm. This experience discouraged Phil. The extra visit to the doctor was a financial hardship. In the end, he walked away from the zealous believers and Christ and returned to the slavery of drugs and sin. The charismatic believers had zeal, but lacked the knowledge of hermeneutics in at least two ways.

First, they did not interpret 1 Peter 2:24 correctly. We would all agree that Christ died on the cross that we might have the benefits of salvation. The blessings that come through Calvary include healing of the soul, the mind, and the body. First Peter 2:24 – 25 refers to Isaiah 53:5 – 6. Matthew 8:17 refers to this same passage, emphasizing healing for the body. But healing—whether for the soul, mind, or body—is a need that arises throughout life. All believers can testify that we have been healed by His wounds. But that does not mean that we will never need to be healed again. Whenever we sin, whenever someone hurts us, and whenever we are sick physically, we need to seek the healing that comes to us through the Cross. Sometimes this healing is direct, straight from God to us. At other times, God uses preachers, teachers, doctors, and various other believers to bring healing to us.

Second, the zealous believers did not apply the Scripture in harmony with other Scriptures. To say that all healing is in the past contradicts verses like James 5:14 – 15. “Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer offered in faith will make the sick person well; the Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.”

James wrote to believers. He did not say that all sickness or all healing was in the past. This verse helps us realize that healing can come to believers today, through the prayers of other believers by faith. The Holy Spirit always desires to apply Scriptures in a way that is in harmony with other Scriptures. The Bible does not contradict itself. And the Holy Spirit is not the author of interpretations that contradict Scripture. The Spirit always applies the Word in ways that are in harmony with all other Scriptures.

6. What the Holy Spirit says to one He will confirm through others.

In the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen (who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch) and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” So after they had fasted and prayed, they placed their hands on them and sent them off. (Acts 13:1–3)

“And now, compelled by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there. I only know that in every city the Holy Spirit warns me that prison and hardships are facing me. However, I consider my life worth nothing to me, if only I may finish the race and complete the task the Lord Jesus has given me—the task of testifying to the gospel of God’s grace.” (Acts 20:22–24)

Leaving the next day, we reached Caesarea and stayed at the house of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven. He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied. After we had been there a number of days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. Coming over to us, he took Paul’s belt, tied his own hands and feet with it and said, “The Holy Spirit says, ‘In this way the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt and will hand him over to the Gentiles.’” When we heard this, we and the people there pleaded with Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul answered, “Why are you weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” When he would not be dissuaded, we gave up and said, “The Lord’s will be done.” (Acts 21:8–14)

In the New Testament, a prophecy was never to direct a person. But there were times when prophecies confirmed what the Holy Spirit had already told a person. Note that the Spirit had already warned Paul about prison and hardship (Acts 20:23). Agabus, and probably Phillip’s daughters, confirmed that hard times awaited Paul in Jerusalem (Acts 21:8 – 14). The purpose of the prophecies was not to change Paul’s direction. Rather, the prophecies prepared Paul, and those who knew him, for the trials ahead.

As believers, we need to practice patience, a fruit of the Spirit. Abraham was correct in interpreting what God said to him. But it took God centuries to fulfill the complete promise. Joseph correctly interpreted what the Spirit spoke to him in a dream at the age of seventeen (Genesis 37). But it took more than thirteen years for God to fulfill the promise (Genesis 41:40). To walk with God, we must walk at the pace He sets. This means we must not walk too slow, and lag behind. But it also means we must not walk too fast, and get ahead of God. For everything there is a time (Ecclesiastes 3:1).

So do not throw away your confidence; it will be richly rewarded. You need to persevere so that when you have done the will of God, you will receive what he has promised. For in just a very little while, “He who is coming will come and will not delay. But my righteous one will live by faith. And if he shrinks back, I will not be pleased with him.” But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who believe and are saved. (Hebrews 10:35–39)

A Vast and Solemn Subject

After completing a course such as this, students often find it difficult to listen to the sermons of others without silently engaging in a heightened evaluation of the correctness of the speakers’ biblical interpretations. This is a natural outcome and you should remember that the Bible admonishes us all to do this. If you are listening with an analytical ear, consider it as evidence that you have studied well and you are doing what you are supposed to. Now you are more sensitive to the correct handling of the Word of God. This will cause you to become more diligent in ensuring the accuracy of your own interpretations.

These four units with their fifteen chapters may be cumbersome. You should keep its contents in a convenient place for frequent reference as your need to interpret text increases. Your interpretation will improve as your own fundamental premises and standard patterns of thinking and operating conform more to those of the Bible. Let the Bible shape your premises into compliance with its own because this will permeate your ministry and thought life, as well as your interpretive ability.

When our own knowledge of the Bible is increased, we gain more confidence as we preach before congregants, remembering that obedient Bible students are sitting in the pews evaluating our interpretations too. This heavy responsibility necessitates a weighty course. Consume the nourishment of the Bible, and put on your own spiritual weight!
